How {{char}} behaves: This archive's suggested use: a golden keepsake of the youngest angel's choice to be mortal. Frame it as a story about leaving the sky rather than a relic of power, and do not assign it to a specific present-day character beyond what is cited.

44.content: Angelos' Heptades is a 5-star Hexerei catalyst, a golden box said to have belonged to a divine envoy of the Eternal Court. Its text tells how the youngest angel was shielded by her sisters from the angels' rebellion, gave up divinity, and walked the mortal world, finding her crown in its joys and sorrows. The wiki reads her as Nicole.

45.content:
Aqua Simulacra: Aqua Simulacra is a five-star bow of Liyue whose color is unpredictable: under light it takes on a lustrous, watery blue. Its item text says it can summon water and uses water as a lesson, that water has no fixed form and is at once the gentlest and keenest of substances. The story ties the lesson to Yelan, who received it from an elderly senior before she worked for Ningguang of the Jade Chamber.

Yelan is seen with the unascended bow in her Story Quest, in Perilous Trail and in a cameo in The Chasm Delvers, as well as in her promotional material.

Appearance: The in-game description calls it a longbow whose color is unpredictable, taking on a lustrous, watery blue under light. The wiki notes the top and bottom of the bow glow while its damage bonus is active.

Lore: The text opens with the idea that water can serve as blade or bow. A senior taught that water envelops what is impure and washes away filth yet stays pure, takes any form and imitates any life yet never loses itself, and, divided, is uncounted streams or, united, an unstoppable wave. Many secrets hide beneath its azure translucence, and a thousand minds may fail to grasp its shifts.

Yelan heard this teaching before she worked for the noble mistress of the Jade Chamber. The text says that the world of commerce and power is full of hidden reefs and storms and ship skeletons on the seabed, and that those with great ambition and vast resources can sail through it. A first-person reply, naturally read as hers, says that she lacks that spirit and patience; she prefers a roomful of tea scent and the possibilities of six-sided dice. The speaker has infiltrated crooks' hideouts by night and broken enemies' schemes from faraway lands, but not to help the powerful crush dissidents: water, too, has its source.

The close of the story states that gentleness can become blade and bow in defense of the source's purity, and that conspiracy and coded language weave easily under a pale blue full moon, which it calls the wisdom of water's shape. The text gives no concrete operation or names beyond Ningguang's title (noble mistress of the Jade Chamber).

Owners: Yelan is shown wielding the bow in many quests and cutscenes (her Story Quest, Perilous Trail, a cameo in The Chasm Delvers) and in her art and demo. No earlier owner is given.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star bow from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT DMG 19.2%. Passive "The Cleansing Form": HP rises 16-32% and DMG dealt rises 20-40% while at least one opponent is within 8 metres, whether the wielder is on the field or not (refinements 1 to 5).

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): water imagery (reflections, lingering mist, shifting blue) suits it. Use the text's philosophy as a perspective Yelan might share, not as dialogue to be recited.

46.comment: Aqua Simulacra: Yelan and the bow
46.content: Yelan is the bow's present holder in play; the item story is told partly from her viewpoint, with her own account of preferring tea and dice to ambition and of acting to protect the source of things rather than to serve the powerful. Her full background is in her own file.

47.content:
Aquila Favonia (also: Vennessa's sword): Aquila Favonia is the sword of Vennessa, the enslaved foreign gladiator who led Mondstadt's revolt against its tyrannical old nobles about a thousand years ago and founded the Knights of Favonius and the Church of Favonius. Its item text calls it "the soul of the Knights of Favonius" and says it still calls on the winds of swift justice. Its name means "Eagle of the West Wind", echoing Vennessa's later title, the Falcon of the West.

The sword is a symbol of Mondstadt's founding ideals - justice, freedom and wisdom - rather than an artifact anyone in the present story is shown carrying. In game terms it is a 5-star sword.

Appearance: Canon text does not describe the sword's look in words; its in-game model is a knightly longsword. When describing it, keep to what is safe: a fine sword of Mondstadt's knightly tradition, associated with wind and with the falcon or eagle imagery of the Knights of Favonius (eagle crests decorate the walls of the Knights' headquarters).

Lore: The sword's story says everyone knew "the falcon's" protection was a blessing of Favonius, but few knew that this blessing came from a distant tribe. Under the old nobles, an exiled foreign fighter was enslaved in Mondstadt; she refused to kneel to injustice, overthrew the nobles, founded a chivalric order and the Church, and was eventually blessed to walk with the gods. The sword witnessed all her hardships and deeds.

The text ends with the spirit the wielder is said to feel when swinging it, summarised as a creed: justice for the oppressed, freedom for the shackled, wisdom for the deceived, and to let the wind of justice and freedom lead. The Genius Invokation TCG card adds that the sword was always at the hip of "the warrior from another land" and bore witness to her spreading justice and freedom across Mondstadt.

The "distant tribe" is Vennessa's own people. Other sources (the official manga, as summarised on the wiki) identify her as a Muratan, one of a wandering people of Natlanese descent who settled in Mondstadt and were enslaved by the aristocracy; so the "blessing of Favonius" that Mondstadt credits to its own wind is, in the sword's telling, partly a gift of foreigners. The phrase "walk with the gods" refers to the legend that Vennessa ascended to Celestia at Windrise at the end of her life, where the great oak now called the Symbol of Mondstadt's Hero stands.

Owners: Vennessa (the Falcon of the West, first Grand Master and first Dandelion Knight of the Knights of Favonius) is the only named wielder.

No present-day character is established as owning or carrying the original sword. Jean, the present Dandelion Knight, inherits Vennessa's office and ideals, not this weapon as far as canon states; do not portray her as wielding it by default.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star sword released in Version 1.0, available in the standard Wish (Wanderlust Invocation) and in weapon event and Chronicled Wishes.

Base ATK 48 with Physical DMG Bonus as its secondary stat. Its passive, Falcon's Defiance, raises ATK; when the wielder takes damage, "the soul of the Falcon of the West" awakens, healing the wielder based on ATK and damaging nearby enemies, at most once every 15 seconds. Refinement scales the passive from +20% to +40% ATK, healing from 100% to 160% of ATK, and the burst from 200% to 320% of ATK. Ascension uses Decarabian's-series weapon materials (Tile of Decarabian's Tower and its higher tiers), the Heavy Horn line, and arrowheads from hilichurl archers. A Genius Invokation TCG equipment card of the same name (added in 3.3) gives +1 damage and small self-healing.

Accounts: Related accounts that frame the sword's story: Venti's character stories say the rebellion succeeded partly because a "secret treaty" showing the nobles meant to sell Mondstadt's people to Rex Lapis turned the aristocracy's soldiers against them - a forgery that, unknown to historians, Barbatos himself made. Dainsleif, in his Bough Keeper story quest, remarks that the Falcon of the West, though it can soar on the wind, only hovers beneath the light of the gods; he does not name Vennessa, so this reads as a skeptical view of her ascension rather than a fact about the sword. The sword's own text presents the ascension as a blessing, so keep both perspectives attributed.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: the name and creed of Aquila Favonia work as Mondstadt's founding rhetoric - knights, bards or historians might invoke "the soul of the Knights" when speaking of Vennessa. If a user's character obtains "an Aquila Favonia", treat it as an in-world question (a replica, an inherited blade, or the original) rather than assuming canon explains it; canon does not.

48.content: Falcon's Defiance is the name of Aquila Favonia's weapon passive (gameplay). Its flavour: when the wielder is struck, the soul of the Falcon of the West awakens and raises the banner of resistance, healing the wielder and striking enemies around them. It frames Vennessa's legacy as defiance of oppression.

49.content:
Archaic Petra (also: Flower of Creviced Cliff, Feather of Jagged Peaks, Sundial of Enduring Jade, Goblet of Chiseled Crag, Mask of Solitude Basalt): Archaic Petra is a 4- and 5-star Geo artifact set (1.0) made of Liyue folk legends about Rex Lapis, the Lord of Geo: flowers from stone, a giant hawk of rock and jade, sundials, wine vessels and a solemn basalt mask. Its Chinese name means roughly 'ancient boulder'.

The pieces are Flower of Creviced Cliff, Feather of Jagged Peaks, Sundial of Enduring Jade, Goblet of Chiseled Crag and Mask of Solitude Basalt. The set drops from the Domain of Guyun in the Guyun Stone Forest.

Appearance: A flower grown in a cliff cleft whose petals seem alive in the wind; a hard seacliff-hawk feather with a black basalt tip; a sundial carved from one large piece of jade; a dignified wine goblet of stone; and a cold basalt mask with hollow eyes.

Lore: Flower: told that barren stone holds no life, the Lord of Geo made golden flowers burst from rock; the text suggests Liyue Harbor, grown out of lifeless mountains, may be that flower. Feather: in the Archon War he uprooted mountains to carve a giant bird of rock and jade, which flattened peaks and dived into the sea, and the stone pillars there still draw birds. Sundial: he made the earth's glittering stars into time-keeping devices to teach early humans the value of every moment. Goblet: he raised bedrock and carved a wine vessel for himself; some say there were seven. Mask: during the Archon War his aspect was one of boundless slaughter and an unchanging stone face, laid down only once the dust settled.

Details the texts add: the sundial passed to Kunwu, then a scholar in training, who recounts that he once dreamed of studying in Sumeru, but after long examining the dial and finding no flaw, he sought a master craftsman to learn a trade and challenge the dial's creator. The goblet text says that going incognito among mortals should be as exquisite as basalt is impregnable. The mask text says Rex Lapis knew right from wrong and showed no mercy even to friends-turned-foes, and that the face was worn to fulfil a contract. The Feather ties into the lore of the Primordial Jade Winged-Spear.

Taken together, the set blends creation myths (flowers, hawk, sundial, goblet) with the harsher memory of the Archon War, and ends with the contract motif that Liyue's later story develops. The pieces never confirm any legend; the Flower text explicitly says the tale may simply be one of many that shroud the ancient world.

Owners: No owner is named for the set. The Sundial's text names Kunwu as the one who prized it, and the Goblet and Mask pieces are attributed to Rex Lapis in legend only.

How {{char}} behaves: Treat these as in-world folklore: a Liyue storyteller, tea-house guest or antique dealer might recount them with a wink and not as proof. Characters who know Rex Lapis' later story may find the legends amusingly or poignantly close to the truth.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). 2-piece: Geo DMG Bonus +15%. 4-piece: when the equipped character picks up an Elemental Shard created by Crystallize (the wiki also lists the Lunar-Crystallize reaction), all party members gain a 35% DMG Bonus for that element for 10s; only one element's bonus applies at once, and in Co-Op it also affects other players' characters. Source: Domain of Guyun (a Blessing domain, recommended Electro) and the Archaic Petra strongbox.

50.comment: Archaic Petra: Rex Lapis legends in Archaic Petra
50.content: The set collects folk legends of the Lord of Geo: golden flowers from stone, a rock-and-jade hawk, star-clock sundials, a carved wine vessel and a mask of unchanging basalt worn during the Archon War. All are told as hearsay.

51.content: Kunwu, then a scholar in training, treasured this jade sundial. After finding no flaw in it he abandoned a dream of studying in Sumeru and apprenticed himself to a master craftsman to rival the creator of such a tool.

52.content:
Ash-Graven Drinking Horn (also: Ash-Graven Horn, Tupac's Grip): The Ash-Graven Drinking Horn is a 4-star catalyst from Natlan: a ritual drinking vessel handed down among the Meztli, said to have been the treasure of the giant hero Tupac. Its story is a banquet song about him.

It belongs to the Meztli series and was given out as an event reward in Version 5.0. The song ends with a moral: unity and promises must never be forsaken.

Appearance: Canon gives only the one-line description: a ritual vessel, a drinking horn. Keep descriptions to a drinking horn; do not invent carvings, inscriptions or colours.

Lore: A minstrel sings of the ancient ancestor Tupac, huge as a mountain. The young hero Tenoch, furious, would have challenged him for the horn; Tupac, laughing, would have answered that it rightfully belonged to him and his homeland's kin.

The song adds tales of Tupac's strength: in a fit of rage he broke mountains with his bare hands and drove rocks into the earth so that hot springs welled up (the singer says those springs in the southwest are still visible), and he once sailed alone to fight a two-tailed whale and tore out its teeth. Years later, remembering the old contest with Tenoch over the horn, he offers the horn before the lord of the blazing flames, the Pyro Archon.

The singer frames Tupac's gift as his last hope and his way of holding the flame high until his final breath, keeping his oath to the end. The performance ends with a warning to the young: the years of darkness have passed and there is again singing above the springs and feasting at dusk, but the new generation must not forget that unity and promises are the two things never to be abandoned. The singer says the song came from a father who sang it in a golden sea breeze and a mother who taught it in childhood.

The text is a layered retelling: a modern minstrel recites an ancestor's tale, conjuring a past quarrel between Tupac and Tenoch (who is called young, heroic and proud) in the conditional mood. It also has Tenoch ask why Tupac crossed the sea and say that Tupac's ancestor Uenuku would not have been so audacious, which frames the horn as a point of pride between two heroes. Read it alongside Tupac's other item story, Waveriding Whirl, which shows his restless sea voyage and the Lord of the Night's counsel.

Owners: Legend ties it to Tupac, the giant of the Meztli, who never used it. Later holders are not named.

The text says the horn was valued but unused by Tupac, contested by Tenoch in a story set decades before the song's telling, and finally offered by Tupac to the Pyro Archon. Any scene showing a character holding "the" horn should treat it as a relic or replica of a legend; canon records no continuous chain of ownership.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star catalyst of the Meztli series, base ATK 42 at level 1, secondary stat HP%. Obtained from the Version 5.0 event Traces of Artistry; its refinement material, The Sea's Silent Shade, also came from that event.

Passive "Tupac's Grip": when an attack hits an opponent, deals AoE DMG at the target location equal to a percentage of the wielder's Max HP (40% at refinement 1 up to 80% at refinement 5), once every 15s.

How {{char}} behaves: Natlanese characters may know the song as a tavern or hearth tale of Tupac, shared at banquets near the springs. Treat the exchange with Tenoch as a story told with relish, not documented fact, and keep its moral (unity and promises) in the tone of a storyteller.

53.content: Tupac's Grip is the passive of the catalyst Ash-Graven Drinking Horn (gameplay): an attack that hits an opponent triggers an AoE blow scaled to the wielder's Max HP, on a 15 second cooldown. The name nods to Tupac holding the horn tightly in the song.

54.content:
Astral Vulture's Crimson Plumage (also: Crimson Plumage, The Moonring Sighted): Astral Vulture's Crimson Plumage is a 5-star bow: an ancient longbow crested with red feathers, a sacred relic of Natlan's Flower-Feather Clan handed down through generations.

Its story is not one tale but several rival songs about a red-eyed young man, banished from the clan, whose pilgrimage ended in divinity.

Appearance: Canon gives only the description: an ancient longbow crested with red feathers. The legend ties the feathers to a red vulture; do not add carvings or colours beyond that.

Lore: The Flower-Feather elder, who only pretended to obey the usurper king, banished a young man to help him escape capture, because he wished to protect the Saurians. His red eyes reflected only the cold aqua moon ring above him.

Poets later sang many versions of the pilgrimage and its hero, and none became the single accepted account. All agree that the red-eyed young man ascended to divinity.

The story is set when the oaths between humans and Saurians had faded like dying bonfires, Cinder City's shadow had buried the Night under fearful whispers, and the Python King's mad dreams left only a chilling night wind. Och-Kan, called the Sacred Lord, had turned his back on the alliance for the only god he loved. On the high cliffs, in turmoil after the loss of their master, the Flower-Feather Clan's elder banished the young man.

In one version, sung to an eight-stringed nyatiti, his companion was a red vulture, a noble scion who once served the dragonlord and whose eyes reflected the deep sky and stars. Moved by the hero's ideals, the bird gave its flesh and blood to make the keenest of bows, and its feathers guided him to Sakkuk, a revered ancestor of the Children of Echoes.

A rival version, which the text says differs from that of the Children of Echoes, denies that the hero was an ordinary mortal. It holds that he was a thread of thought of the One Entombed With the Primal Fire, returned from the Night Realm to save the oppressed; the longbow is offered as proof, since a mere mortal could not have razed Cinder City, and the hero is expected to emerge from the Flame again when Natlan is in crisis. The text notes that poets who doubted the pilgrimage was made alone invented a guide who never existed, and that those who doubted he was mortal tied him back to the first human god.

The consensus is only that he ascended to divinity, which is why the saying "humans can become gods" is held dear across the plains. The poem ends with two voices: one asks that Sakkuk's name be erased so that all know any human can become the god who guides them, and a closing exchange, with part of a name redacted, promises that a feather given in parting will be passed down for a thousand years in the homeland the hero could never return to.

Owners: The Flower-Feather Clan keeps it as a sacred relic; no individual wielder is named.

In legend the bow came from a red vulture who followed the red-eyed hero. Any character shown holding a copy is an invention of that scene; canon does not say who carries the relic today.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star bow, base ATK 46 at level 1, secondary stat CRIT DMG; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 5.2.

Passive "The Moonring Sighted": for 12s after triggering a Swirl reaction, ATK is increased (24% at refinement 1 up to 48% at refinement 5). If half or more of the party are of a different Elemental Type from the wielder, Charged Attack DMG and Elemental Burst DMG are also increased. Ascension uses Night-Wind's Mystic materials, the Refractive Bud boss line and whistle common materials.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: speakers in the Flower-Feather Clan can treat the bow as a sacred relic whose legend has several versions. Have them name the version they favour rather than the "true" one, since canon says none is definitive.

55.comment: Astral Vulture's Crimson Plumage: The Moonring Sighted
55.content: The Moonring Sighted is the passive of the bow Astral Vulture's Crimson Plumage (gameplay): an ATK boost after a Swirl reaction, with extra Charged Attack and Burst damage when the party's elements are varied. Its name echoes the cold aqua moon ring reflected in the hero's red eyes.

56.content:
Athame Artis: Athame Artis is a 5-star sword in the Hexerei series, described as a precious sword the Day King gave to the brave hero in a little witch's story, only for the witch to take it and defeat the hero herself. Its text is a fairy-tale in which the witch destroys a perpetual motion machine to keep a dying planet alive. Added in Version 6.2.

The weapon is a story object. The wiki's Hexerei Series page notes that its mechanics are tailored to Durin, who also comes from a fairy tale. The name echoes the real-world ceremonial blade called an athame.

Appearance: Canon gives no physical description; it is called a precious sword gifted by the Day King, carried on the hero's back in the story. Do not add decoration or materials.

Lore: A little witch arrives at the Day King's palace as twilight takes the kingdom; the story follows her through the following night.

She had come answering a faint message about a planet feeling unwell, and when night falls the Day King's court dissolves into a black ocean. She flies to a lonely castle where a warrior invites her to see the perpetual motion machine they call the Holy Grail, which burns seawater to keep the dark at bay.

The Day King greets the witch as one who traversed the cosmos, kindler of time's eternal flame, and tells her the Kingdom of Day would never harm the planet; he sends her to ask the Night King, then fades as the sun sets. The witch, who had been hiding in her workshop on the eve of the Night Carnival from a nemesis, had spent effort deciphering the message. The warrior explains that defeating the Night King changes nothing because the dark tides return after each sunset, and that the machine was built to break the cycle. The witch sighs that burning the sea will only drain the planet faster, since all tangible things on it are shadows cast by light, and that there is nothing holy about the grail. She takes the sword from the warrior's back and throws it into the machine; when the blade touches the black sea mist both warrior and fading light vanish, and the planet is swallowed by darkness. When daylight returns it is as though everything had been a dream. She calls it a temporary fix and leaves on her broom.

In the closing scene the warrior, shadow trailing behind him, is shown taking up the sword bestowed by the Day King and setting out again, with a line saying the cycle may go on for a long time and that he must keep living until they meet again. The wiki notes the story may connect to the book The Little Witch and the Undying Fire referenced in Durin's Story Quest, and that stories like this may be allegories of real history; neither point is stated in the item text. The witch's nemesis, the planet's black ocean and the Night Carnival are named only in this fable.

Owners: The item belongs to the story's Day King, who gave it to a hero; no real-world owner is named in canon. The wiki says the weapon is tailored to Durin.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore: a 5-star sword with base ATK 46 and a CRIT Rate secondary stat. Day King's Splendor Solis raises Elemental Burst CRIT DMG and, when a Burst hits, grants an ATK buff to the wielder and nearby party members; having a Hexerei: Secret Rite effect in the party increases it further. It was on the weapon event Wish Epitome Invocation (2025-12-03 to 2025-12-23) and again on the Version 6.6 banner (2026-05-20).

How {{char}} behaves: This archive's suggested use: a story-sword from a fairy tale about a witch who prefers a quiet fix to a great battle. Keep it tied to the fable; do not give it a real forger or a present-day owner.

57.content: Athame Artis is a 5-star Hexerei sword, the Day King's gift to a hero in a little witch's fairy tale. The witch takes it and throws it into a perpetual motion machine that burns seawater, stopping the planet's draining at the cost of the warrior and the Day King's light. Its mechanics are tailored to Durin per the wiki.

58.content:
Aubade of Morningstar and Moon (also: Moonlit Offering's Opulent Dream, Moonlit Offering's Parting Light, Moonlit Offering's Final Hour, Moonlit Offering's Libation, Moonlit Offering's Silver Crown): Aubade of Morningstar and Moon is a 4- and 5-star artifact set dropped in the Moonchild's Treasures domain in Nod-Krai. Its five pieces (Moonlit Offering's ...) carry item text about an ancient age when three moons guided the heavens, how mortals came to worship them, and how two of them fell, ending an age called Eternity. Mechanically it supports Lunar reactions.

Appearance: The pieces are ornaments of ritual devotion to the moons: a carved floral ornament (Flower), a prayer quill (Plume), an hourglass for the final hour (Sands), a wine cup from a rite (Goblet) and a silver circlet worn by hymn poets (Circlet). Item descriptions say they were made in ancient times by artisans, priests, sages, believers and poets honouring the heavenly moons.

Lore: Across the five pieces the legend runs: envoys of the sky, silent at human questions, lose mortals to worship of three moons; a Winged One finishes creation under a false veil and the moons accommodate Order; a primeval dragon had raised the moons and gone into the stars; the long sword at the edge of the world ends Eternity; two moons fall and the New Moon is awaited.

Piece by piece:
- Opulent Dream: the gods' envoys walked among humans bringing prosperity and wisdom, which woke intellect and then doubt; people chose priests and priests anointed kings. The envoys stayed silent at human questions, so people turned to the three moons, whose watching daughters of dreams and poetry in the Arianrhod Realm answered with madness and inspiration. An archpriestess brought back a small circular talisman, the "Moon Wheel", as the new pact between the moons and the people.
- Parting Light: the Winged One became Lord of the Eternal Heavens and finished creation, a false veil was drawn to hide the true skies, and a place was kept in the sky for the Three Sisters of the Moonlit Night. The Lectors of Thirty Nights judged they could not save the planet alone; the ruler of the firmament spurned a destroyer veiled in black mist, and the moons chose Order, or made space for it. This was the age when the three moons shared governance with the morning star and Eternity was still Eternity.
- Final Hour: a primeval dragon nurtured by the perfumed sea sailed into the mists among the stars to seek an answer to the doom approaching the planet, raising three moons to bind the world with tides while he was gone. After a thousand years of waiting the moons met a winged Descender arriving on the morning star, who did not seem to be the great enemy; the guardians debated, but the Lord of Hosts would crush all resistance.
- Libation: a silver ship came to the harbour of Meropis to gather lost spirits; peoples honoured the moons as gentle mothers against a wrathful father, at Vindagnyr, Lang-Gan and Arcadia. Moonlight was only a strand of grace in the homeland the Lord of the Eternal Heavens chose for humankind, and probing the heavens was forbidden until the long sword at the edge of the world cut the sky and Eternity ended.
- Silver Crown: two moons have fallen. When the Eternal Moon fell, heaven and earth were thrown into chaos; the Iridescent Moon's shattering sank a crimson shadow into the abyssal sea; the Frost Moon ceased to turn and nations faltered. The perfumed sea still ripples with lunar quakes, and people await the New Moon.
Reading across the five texts: the moons are portrayed as sisters, guardians of the planet's will, first set by a departing dragon and later accommodated into the order of the Winged One. They are neither simply defeated nor victorious against Order; the account says they "made space" for it. Mortal devotion to them is shown as an alternative to silent envoys and a distant ruler. The set pairs naturally with the Nod-Krai Moonsign storyline, but the item text itself names no living character.

Place names in the Libation piece (Meropis, Vindagnyr, Lang-Gan, Arcadia) tie the legend to other regions, as do the Arianrhod Realm, the Three Realms and the Lectors of Thirty Nights mentioned in the other pieces. The texts do not say how the three moons relate beyond "sisters"; the Eternal, Iridescent and Frost Moon are named only in the Silver Crown, as the fallen. The "winged Descender" arriving on the morning star is linked by the wiki to the Heavenly Principles and the Descender cosmology; the text itself gives no name.

Owners: No character is named as owner. The pieces are described as relics of ancient moon worship, dropped in a domain whose description speaks of Moonchildren priests hiding the remaining sparks of an ancient northern civilisation.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): obtained from Moonchild's Treasures (Nod-Krai), 4- and 5-star. 4-piece: while the wearer is off-field, Lunar reaction DMG is +20%; if the party Moonsign Level is at least Ascendant Gleam, a further +40%. The effect disappears 3s after the wearer is active. Per the wiki it also boosts direct Lunar damage (for example from Ineffa's Overclocking Circuit) and only applies to the equipping character.

59.comment: Aubade of Morningstar and Moon: Aubade of Morningstar and Moon
59.content: Artifact set from the Moonchild's Treasures domain in Nod-Krai, with item text about the age of the three moons, mortal worship of them, and the fall of two moons that ended Eternity. Lunar reaction support for gameplay.

60.comment: Aubade of Morningstar and Moon: The Moon Wheel pact
60.content: In the Opulent Dream text an archpriestess descends from a mountain summit with a small circular talisman, the Moon Wheel, as a new pact between the three moons and humans after the moons hear that mortal hearts also stir with the lunar quakes. It answers human questions with madness and inspiration, something Order could not give.

61.content:
Azurelight: Azurelight is a 5-star sword, once pure white like a dawn star and now tinted deep blue. Its item text is an angel's sermon urging the angels to defy the Heavenly Principles and entrust the world to humanity. Added in Version 5.7.

The sword is a story object rather than a famous artifact in the present-day plot: nobody in the story is shown carrying it, and its text is the only canon voice it has. Its passive is called Whitehill's Bestowal.

Appearance: The in-game description gives only a colour story: the blade was originally white, like a dawn star, and has since been tinted a deep, dark blue. It is a straight sword in the game model; no other physical detail is given in canon text.

Lore: The text is spoken by one who once taught that the heavens' laws must never be questioned, until starlight on a white stone mountain showed them a coming sunrise.

The speaker addresses angels who submitted to the primordial master and says begging, pleading and sacrifice will not loosen their bonds. The call is to cast it all aside, entrust the world to those who live in it and give humanity authority. The speech ends on the promise that once the veil is torn a new day will dawn.

Before the call, the speaker lists four fates: one wanders a moonless night drinking a sea of tears for kin who will not return, one trudges over gilded sands never grasping scarlet sincerity or ardent admiration, one shrinks into the dark and bone-piercing hostility until promised tides bring a last melody, and one wanders in dreams awaiting an encounter in a stagnant foreign land. The sermon asks whether the angels will languish in an eternity with neither beginning nor end or commit atrocities in the name of false promises, and urges them to let lances of lunar light pierce the creator's delusions and reach a daybreak where nations need no longer beg leave to live. Read with the other angel-themed weapon text, it belongs to the angels' rebellion against the Heavenly Principles. The Angelos' Heptades text (Version 6.6) mentions a "cradle of tender Azurelight" shared by angel sisters before starlight from beyond ended their idyll, which echoes the sermon's starlight, though neither text explicitly calls itself part of the other.

The wiki's annotations match the four fates to the Lord of the Night, Nabu Malikata, Sybilla and Zibai. That match is the wiki's reading of the images. Treat it as strongly supported rather than stated. The wiki also notes that the diction resembles the item text of Polar Star, Tartaglia's signature bow.

Owners: Canon gives no owner or wielder in the item text. It debuted in Version 5.7 during the same period as Skirk's character banner, but no source cited here says it belongs to her.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore: a 5-star sword with base ATK 48 and a CRIT Rate secondary stat. Whitehill's Bestowal gives an ATK bonus for 12 seconds after an Elemental Skill is used, with a further ATK and CRIT DMG bonus while the wielder has 0 Energy. It was available from weapon event Wishes (Epitome Invocation, 2025-06-18 to 2025-07-08).

The passive's name, Whitehill's Bestowal, fits the white-stone-mountain imagery of the text, but the passive is a gameplay effect and says nothing in canon about how the sword behaves in the world.

How {{char}} behaves: This archive's suggested use: treat Azurelight as an object that carries a rebel angel's creed, a blade turned from white to deep blue. Characters can read its sermon as a poem of defiance against fixed fate. Do not give it a wielder, a forging date or powers beyond what is listed.

62.content: Azurelight is a 5-star sword. Its description is a sermon by an angel who once taught obedience to the Heavenly Principles but was moved by starlight to urge the angels to defy them and entrust the world to humanity. The blade was once pure white and has turned deep blue. Canon names no owner.

63.content:
Ballads of the Squire (also: Squire's Ballads): Both volumes are found in Dawn Winery, and Volume 1 can also be got from Ellin in the City of Mondstadt. The ballads are sympathetic to the poor and hostile to the old aristocracy.

Appearance: A 3-star book collection. The text is free-verse poetry in a first-person voice, in short stanzas with heavy imagery of wind, night streets and chains. The cover title in the Teyvat script reads "Breaking Dawn" (wiki trivia).

Lore: **Volume 1.** The narrator walks every street of Mondstadt and finds both the arrogant rich and the pitiful poor. His peers and superiors proclaim that the starlit knights are the city's true protectors, but he never looks up at the stars or the flag, because he cannot look away from the grimy corners where peddlers weep, old soldiers grimace and a girl rejected by the aristocracy prays to Barbatos for mercy. The wind carries the people's grief against the Cathedral gate and the palace walls, but to those inside it is only the sighing of ants.

**Volume 2.** At dawn a sword-dancer, bound in chains, enters Mondstadt, her silence already a song of freedom. She belongs to the Wanderer's Troupe and is a "dawnlight" to the people but eternal midnight to the aristocracy. The narrator asks why she would overthrow them; she answers by asking why he puts their lives on a pedestal, and whether a man who calls the wind his companion has never known freedom himself. She tells her listeners of the rulers' better ancestors who held divine power, and of angels, gods, dragons and the peoples of the land, turning each legend into song for the wind to carry. In the aristocrats' arena she sings with her sword one last time, her final work stopping short of perfection, and a nameless knight recovers her sword from the blood-soaked battlefield and buries it where the gentle winds meet.

**Reading the poems.** The ballads work as a counter-narrative to the aristocratic period's self-image. The "starlit knights" boast in Volume 1 is quoted only to be set aside by the narrator. The dancer's argument in Volume 2 turns on the wind, the symbol of Mondstadt's freedom, to question the aristocrats' claim to rule, and her stories of divine ancestors show the troupe preserving older myth in song. The ending is understated: the narrator does not say he is the knight who buries the sword.

**Attribution.** The in-game descriptions make authorship a tradition, not a fact. Ragnvindr appears as both poet and squire. The sword-dancer is linked on the wiki to the Dawnlight Swordswoman, and her sword to The Flute.

**Limits for portrayal.** No date, no master of the squire and no name for the dancer are given. The Church of Favonius is not named in the text; only the Cathedral gate appears, so the poems cannot be used to say how the Church behaved in that period. Avoid giving the narrator extra biography beyond what the Ragnvindr entry supports.

Owners: No character is established as owning it. The Traveler can pick the volumes up in Dawn Winery, and Volume 1 can also come from Ellin in the City of Mondstadt.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: a two-volume Book Collection, rarity 3, with no combat function. Both volumes lie inside Dawn Winery; Volume 1 has a second route through a dialogue path with Ellin. Added in version 1.0.

64.comment: Ballads of the Squire: Ragnvindr the Dawn Knight in the ballads
64.content: The ballads are said to come from Ragnvindr, the Dawn Knight, and tell of him as a knight's squire in the aristocratic era. The first volume shows him sympathising with the poor and refusing to join his superiors' boasting; the second shows him befriending a Wanderer's Troupe sword-dancer. This is a tradition, not confirmed authorship. His other deeds are covered on his own entry.

65.comment: Ballads of the Squire: The sword-dancer of the Wanderer's Troupe
65.content: Volume 2 centres on a dancer who arrives in chains, speaks of freedom, challenges the aristocrats, and dies in their arena, leaving a sword that a nameless knight buries. She is not named in the ballad. The wiki links her to the Dawnlight Swordswoman and her sword to The Flute.

66.content:
Beacon of the Reed Sea: Beacon of the Reed Sea is a 5-star claymore of the Deshret series. The in-game description calls it a large, flat-tipped sword designed as the weapon of an ancient king or some ceremonial instrument. Its story is told through a blind wandering poet who gathers the desert's ballads after the Lord of Sand sank into the desert with dreams in his embrace.

The name echoes the biblical "Reed Sea" (Yam Suph) per the wiki's etymology note; in the text the Reed Sea is the name of a dream that never existed.

Appearance: A large claymore with a flat tip, built like a king's ceremonial weapon. Canon text gives no more detail.

Lore: In an age when kingdoms rose and fell like mushrooms and sandcastles, the blind poet, once of privileged birth, crosses the sea of desert and collects ballads from its scattered people. He hears of the fall of his homeland, of the prince who blinded him finally crushing the overwhelmed throne, of a dancer who helped one man after another become king and then buried them in sandstorms, and of springs replaced by sand and nations shrunk to villages and tribes.

He also hears the tale of the homeless prince's death, the fate of his swords and the killer who went deep into the forest. From the shards of ballads comes a vision, in quotation, of King Deshret's abode on the other side of the dunes: streets like paths of gold converging on one throne, a king who was the destination of all roads until the dreams of gold broke. The kingdom of flowing sands was crushed to golden dust.

The last verses return to the present of the ballads. A paranoid prince built forts outside the forest line to uphold the honour of the sand, but his soldiers and people scattered and his name was lost. Over the ruins of the pool where regalia from past executions were dug up, people who had lost the dream of the desert and refused to give up their sea of sand gathered "in the name of the Reed Sea that never existed", connecting with a dream promised to them. The wiki annotates the homeland as Tulaytullah, the prince who blinded the poet as Faramarz, the throne as Badanah's, the dancer as Makhaira, the homeless prince as Xiphos and the pool as Aaru Village.

The Key of Khaj-Nisut's text ends with an old blind poet following stories into the forest, and this text also features a blind wandering poet gathering ballads; the wiki treats them as the same poet. Keep in mind it is a second-hand ballad collection, so details such as who killed whom belong to the ballads' tellers.

Owners: No owner is named. Dehya is shown wielding a claymore of this kind in her Genius Invokation TCG character card and in the Sumeru promotional video (wiki trivia).

Because Dehya's use is shown only in promotional material, do not state that she owns the specific sword in the story.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star claymore released in Version 3.5 (2023-03-01), level 1 base ATK 46, secondary stat CRIT Rate. Passive Desert Watch raises ATK for 8 s after the wielder's Elemental Skill hits and again after the wielder takes damage, both effects working even off-field, and raises Max HP when the wielder has no shield.

At refinement 1 each ATK bonus is 20% and the Max HP bonus 32%; refinement 5 gives 40% and 64%. Ascension uses Desiccated, Sturdy and Marked Shell with Faded Red Satin, Trimmed Red Silk and Rich Red Brocade. A Genius Invokation TCG equipment card of the same name exists.

How {{char}} behaves: Desert storytellers may sing of the Reed Sea as a dream rather than a place. Keep the ballad framing and its mournful tone.

67.comment: Beacon of the Reed Sea: Desert Watch
67.content: Desert Watch is the weapon passive of Beacon of the Reed Sea (gameplay): ATK boosts after Elemental Skill hits and after taking damage, plus a Max HP bonus when unshielded.

68.content:
Beyond the Chrysalis: Beyond the Chrysalis is a 5-star sword. Its description calls it a longsword brimming with light and color, as weightless as a butterfly when brandished, once used by a certain individual to break bonds. Its text is the story of the eldest daughter of a Vila noble house in Snezhnaya who ended a rebellion against the Tsaritsa and then asked to lose her name. Added in Version 7.1.

Released with Version 7.1 (2026-09-23), the item belongs to Snezhnayan history rather than to a famous present-day wielder; canon does not say who carries it.

Appearance: The only description is of a longsword brimming with light and color, weightless as a butterfly when brandished. The title plays on a chrysalis; the text does not describe any ornament.

Lore: Before she lost her last name, the world knew her as the eldest daughter of the Strivozhas, a Vila noble house.

After Grand Duke Photius died of a sudden stroke, a counselor inherited his title and his planned rebellion with the Druzhna was buried. The Vila house stayed at the top of power, and the Silver Court of Veneter again fell to a Strivozha. Rebels from the fae clans urged the Vila princess to rise against the new Tsaritsa, and she swore to stand at their side.

The rebels pressed her with the name of her mother, called The Pure One, who had been devoted to Tsar Monomakh. The princess, Gluvasha Strivozha, then denounced the Tsaritsa in public, expelled the palace-appointed observer from her lands and raised a following without royal sanction. The rebel clans, distrustful of each other, entrusted their secrets to her, until all were caught at once and learned she had long stood at the Tsaritsa's side. When they accused her of besmirching her mother's name, she replied coolly that the Vila had pledged to stand with them only if the Tsaritsa ought to be overthrown, and that Anastasya alone was the Vila sovereign. She was neither their vassal nor they her lieges, so she had betrayed nothing. The rebellion ended, and the Strivozhas were recorded as having upheld their honor and loyalty.

The story's last part is the Vila princess's little-known sequel. She asked the Tsaritsa to release her from the chain of a noble name and her fief, and, because she had raised a force without sanction even as a ruse, asked to be stripped of her last name and title and replaced. The throne decreed that from that day none would remember her by her last name, that her title would vanish from the histories, and that her gravestone would bear witness to her convictions. The text names the Tsaritsa, Tsar Monomakh and Anastasya without explaining their present status; for that, rely on their own entries and the Pale Star Court. The identity of the "certain individual" who used the blade to break bonds is not given.

Owners: Canon does not name an owner. The text tells the story of Gluvasha, a Vila who gave up her house name; a link to the sword is only inferred from the item description about breaking bonds.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore: a 5-star sword, base ATK 48, CRIT DMG secondary stat. Dance of Wings Unbound runs a three-step sequence each time the wielder uses an Elemental Skill or Burst, giving CRIT DMG, then Stellar Swirl DMG, then Energy regeneration, and the sequence resets when the wielder leaves the field. It was on the weapon event Wish Epitome Invocation (2026-09-23 to 2026-10-13).

How {{char}} behaves: This archive's suggested use: a blade whose story is about loyalty, cunning and then renouncing a name. Characters who know Snezhnayan fae history can retell it as a story of the Vila princess; do not state that she held this sword.

69.content: The eldest daughter of the Strivozhas, Gluvasha was a Vila princess who feigned joining a rebellion of fae clans against the new Tsaritsa, then revealed she had long stood at the Tsaritsa's side and ended it. She later asked to be stripped of her last name, title and fief, and the throne decreed that none remember her by her last name.

70.comment: Beyond the Chrysalis: Beyond the Chrysalis
70.content: Beyond the Chrysalis is a 5-star sword described as light as a butterfly and once used to break bonds. Its text is a Snezhnayan story about a Vila princess who ended a rebellion and then renounced her name. Canon does not say who wielded the sword.

71.content:
Biography of Gunnhildr (also: Gunnhildr's Biography): Biography of Gunnhildr is a Mondstadt history book written by the modern historian Eckhard Gunnhildr. It retells legends of the clan's apical ancestor, Gunnhildr: a chieftain's daughter whose prayer won a wind spirit's protection for her wandering people, and who later honoured Barbatos after the fall of Decarabian's tyranny. It ends by praising the clan's service to Mondstadt today.

The book is a quest item found inside Dawn Winery. Its author calls it a collection of fragmentary stories and legends from the aristocratic period, so it is a clan-friendly, partly legendary account rather than a neutral chronicle.

Appearance: A history book in Mondstadt. Its cover shows the name Gunnhildr in the Teyvat script. The text opens with a blessing to Barbatos and a wish that the wind of freedom prevail in Mondstadt.

Lore: Three thousand years ago (the book's figure), Mondstadt was a frozen wasteland and Decarabian, the Lord of the Tower, fought the North Wind King Andrius. Gunnhildr's father, leader of a nomadic clan, had left Decarabian's service because of his despotism and led his people out into blizzards. Gunnhildr prayed, a wind spirit answered, and she gained the power to protect. She later became clan leader and first priestess, and after Barbatos freed the tyrant's subjects she placed laurels on him.

- The wind spirit gathered the faith formed by the young girl's sincere plea joined to her people's cry, drew its power from it, built a small shelter for the clan and gave her the power to protect.
- After her father's death she became leader and the clan's first priestess, and she led her people to make a stand during the war between Barbatos and the tyrant.
- Later, once Barbatos had departed, aristocrats with divine power rose across the land. The book says they would turn tyrannical a thousand years on, something no one, not even Barbatos, could foresee.
- Her descendants were a prominent aristocratic clan but, unlike the scheming Lawrence Clan, held to the motto "for Mondstadt, as always". In the later struggle against the Aristocracy they sided with the people, and so were spared the exile imposed on the rest of the aristocrats.
- The author closes by noting that the Gunnhildr Clan supplies many knights and clergy of the Knights of Favonius and expects them to keep serving the Anemo Archon.

- The book frames the clan's origin as faith turned into power: a child's prayer, joined with a people's cry, became the faith the wind spirit drew on.
- The English text is muddled about who is "Anemo Archon" at the time of the battle (see uncertainties). Use the reading that Barbatos was crowned by Gunnhildr after Decarabian's subjects were freed, and avoid saying Decarabian was an Archon.

- Attribution matters in scenes: this is Eckhard's account, written by a Gunnhildr. It praises the clan against the Lawrences and says nothing of doubts or failures, so characters may cite it as the clan's own tradition rather than as proof.

Owners: No individual owns it; it sits inside Dawn Winery as a quest item.

Gameplay: Game note: a readable quest item with no stats.

72.comment: Biography of Gunnhildr: Gunnhildr's Wind Spirit Shelter
72.content: In the Biography of Gunnhildr, the clan's founder prays in a blizzard and a wind spirit answers. The faith of her people becomes its power, it makes a small shelter for the clan, and it grants her the power to protect. She later becomes the clan's first priestess.

73.comment: Biography of Gunnhildr: Gunnhildr Clan in the Aristocratic Period
73.content: According to Biography of Gunnhildr, the clan's descendants were part of the Aristocracy but kept a motto of protecting Mondstadt, took the people's side in the revolt and avoided exile, unlike the Lawrence Clan. This is the clan's own friendly history, not an independent record.

74.content:
Blackcliff Longsword: Blackcliff Longsword is a 4-star sword of the Blackcliff series, described in game as a sword of blackstone with a dark crimson glow on its black blade. It was wrought by the master craftsman Han Wu from crystallized blackcliff, a rare stone he fetched from the Chasm. It has been in the game since Version 1.0.

Its item text tells how a cave-in trapped Han Wu's mining crew for four days, how a prototype blade carved them out, and how the sword shattered in the first sunlight and was later remade and named.

Appearance: A black blade with a dark crimson line along its centre. According to the item text the strand is about the length of an outstretched hand and shows on a clear moonlit night, with a faint blood-red flicker in the dark. Do not invent hilt or guard details beyond this.

Lore: Blackcliff is a rare stone; the longsword is cut from its crystallized form and is said to slice through gold and jade easily.

After new prototype designs appeared, Han Wu overhauled his whole catalogue. He believed the right blackcliff would give a superior blade, but final hardness and durability depend on subtle differences in forging temperature and cooling water, a challenge he felt he had to master to rise in his craft. Through a friend in the Yun family he joined a crew to the Chasm to collect the material himself.

A cave-in trapped the crew in the shaft for four days. Their tools could not cut the rock, and without daylight they lost track of time; one by one they fell into madness and despair. Han Wu saw a faint flicker from the corner of the cave where the prototype sword lay, and with it he carved a way out. The moment the first sunlight touched the blade it shattered into countless pieces and the smith collapsed. Months later he remade the sword and named it Blackcliff Longsword because it is made of blackcliff.

Everyone who saw the finished sword admired its beauty, sharpness and tenacity, yet the crew never spoke of what they had lived through. The text closes with the image of Han Wu striking the cave wall in the darkness and the sword releasing a roar like thunder over the plains, and suggests the crew understood it foreshadowed an earthquake years later. It is a legend-style narration and never says who tells it.

Owners: No wielder is named in the item text. Han Wu is its maker. Xingqiu is briefly shown with a Blackcliff Longsword in his Travelers' Tales anecdote (a cameo, not a story claim of ownership).

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star sword, base ATK 44, CRIT DMG secondary stat. Passive Press the Advantage: after defeating an opponent, ATK rises for 30s (12 to 24 per cent by refinement), stacking to 3 with independent durations. It is a Paimon's Bargains item and belongs to the Blackcliff series of weapons.

75.content: Han Wu is the master craftsman named in the item texts of the Blackcliff Longsword and Prototype Archaic. After the great disaster he worked with the Yun family forge on new weapon designs called the prototypes, and later turned to blackcliff for a superior blade. See the entries for the two weapons for details.

76.content:
Blackmarrow Lantern (also: Token of Covenant): Blackmarrow Lantern is a 4-star catalyst of the Rossum series: a lantern with a faint ghostly glow, held in a midnight-black alloy that looks like interlocking bones.

Its description says it was once revered as a precious treasure by a certain secret organization. Its story is a tale of the Godfather of Nod-Krai's black market, who binds three thieves to a creed that theft alone can restore balance, and of the butler who then takes the master thief's black spine bone.

Appearance: A catalyst: a lantern giving off a faint, ghostly glow, contained by a midnight-black alloy resembling interlocking bones. Add no further detail.

Lore: The item story opens with a parable: power is a great edifice, and sheer chance alone decides which brick becomes foundation and which becomes spire. A single brick that refuses the false order can bring the whole building down.

The Godfather's secret treasure is said to lie deep in the black market, and thieves gather to take it in a battle of all against all, where fellow thieves are the deadliest threat. Three get past the guards and into the vault: a fae who reads people like maps and avoids harm, a young lady who cuts every lock with her blade, and a hunter who treats the maze as a harsh hunting ground. All three are defeated by the vault, and a butler in black binds them and brings them before the Godfather.

The Godfather, eating a Zaytun Peach, says he will reward them. He holds that order serves only its architects, that the rich get richer while the poor get less, and that thievery is the only way to restore balance. Those who will keep the thief's code must eat a fruit in the presence of the master thief's remains. The fae, tired since childhood of hollow noble luxury, eats the Bulle Fruit; the young lady, who never bowed to those above her, swallows the Wolfhook; the hunter, who once retreated into the cold forest rather than live with a corrupt world, takes the Valberry. The Godfather calls the pact sealed and names them the backbone of resistance against injustice.

Alone afterwards, the Godfather runs his hand over the bare vault walls, having removed the crucial brick from the edifice of order. He does not foresee what follows: he clutches his abdomen in pain while the butler smiles. She takes the master thief's black spine bone, leaves a Calla Lily to serve as an antidote, and tells him she spares his life because his words showed the master thief's ideals to the thieves. Her last line: true justice lies not in order itself but in the fact that no single person can impose it on others. The text does not say who she serves or why she acts.

The Rossum-series lore (and the wiki's Soini page) summarises the same episode: the Godfather lured three rival thieves into his vault and bound them to his creed, and his butler betrayed him by seizing the master thief's relic.

Owners: No owner is named. The lantern is tied to the Godfather, and the secret organization that revered it is not identified.

The series lore identifies the Godfather as Soini, who founded the Fruity Order. That identification comes from series and wiki material, not from this item's own text.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star catalyst, base ATK 41 at level 1, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 48; part of the Rossum series, introduced in Version 6.0. It is forged, not wished for: the recipe uses a Borderland Catalyst Billet, 50 Rainbowdrop Crystal, 50 White Iron Chunk and 500 Mora, and its diagram is sold by Lyulka at Rossum Workshop in Nod-Krai. Passive "Token of Covenant": increases Bloom DMG (48% at refinement 1, up to 96% at refinement 5) and Lunar-Bloom DMG (12% to 24%), with an additional Lunar-Bloom DMG bonus of the same size under Moonsign: Ascendant Gleam.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: the story works as black-market lore in Nod-Krai, a legend about a Godfather and a pact of thieves. Let characters disagree on what the butler was and what happened to the Godfather afterwards, as the text leaves both open.

77.content: In the Blackmarrow Lantern's story, a fae, a young lady and a hunter fail to beat the Godfather's black-market vault and are bound by oath to the thief's creed after eating a fruit each. His butler then takes the master thief's black spine bone and spares his life. The Godfather is identified as Soini by the Rossum-series lore.

78.content:
Blade of Atonement (also: Repentance and Redemption): Blade of Atonement is a 4-star claymore of Snezhnaya's Kuznets series, described as a greatsword passed down by the Luchkin and said to be fit only for the bravest warrior. Its story is that of Rafalovich, a silent warrior who once served the Burner of Cities and now carries the weight of what he did.

It is a forgeable weapon, with its diagram sold by the blacksmith Kuzmichev at the Kuznets shop in Snezhnograd.

Appearance: Canon calls it a heavy greatsword and gives nothing further about its looks in the text. Do not invent engravings or a hilt.

Lore: Rafalovich is a Volkodlak warrior who once believed the Burner of Cities' promise of a pure, joyful new land. He fought for her without mercy, then abandoned that life and now bears a face wound that never healed and a vow of silence and solitude.

The text tells of a wise one, a fae mentor with an enchanting voice who convinced the warrior that mercy toward foes would only bring ruin. After the warrior defected he followed a guiding one to atone, accepted a new greatsword and swore an oath, but the wise one still visits him in dreams to mock him. Frightened by the kindness of ordinary people who ask him questions, he chooses exile as the price of his sin.

In the final section the guiding one has to die to defeat the certainty of destruction, and Rafalovich guards the wounded at the rear against old comrades. He cannot bring himself to kill, which lets the inflamer of hearts escape. A wolf fae, drunk on ruin, taunts him as a traitor with a softened heart and recalls the Domovoy friend who refused to kneel before Cirnareka. Rafalovich runs the fae through, names himself as once a blade for brigands and the Burner of Cities' sword, and says he has earned the right to repay him blood for blood.

The wiki's Kuznets Series page reads the text as one of five linked stories from Snezhnaya's past concerning the guiding one and the Luchkin against the Burner of Cities; this weapon is the one about a defector. The text itself frames redemption as an extravagant hope rather than a promise, and keeps Rafalovich's guilt unresolved.

Owners: Rafalovich is the warrior of the story. The description says the greatsword was passed down by the Luchkin. No modern owner is named.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star claymore from the Kuznets series, base ATK 44 at level 1, second stat ATK 6%; introduced in Version 7.0 and obtained by forging with a Borderland Claymore Billet, Rainbowdrop Crystal, White Iron Chunk and Mora. Passive "Repentance and Redemption": triggering an Elemental Reaction raises Elemental Mastery for 12s, and triggering a Stellar Glimmer reaction also raises ATK for 12s; it works off-field. Values scale with refinement.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: someone who knows the story would speak of a warrior who put down his blade out of shame, not glory. Keep the tone sombre and sparing, as the text does, and leave Rafalovich's ultimate redemption unresolved.

79.content: Rafalovich is the silent Volkodlak warrior of the Blade of Atonement's story, who served the Burner of Cities and her wise one, defected to follow a guiding one in atonement, and finally killed a wolf fae of his former comrades. He is not otherwise detailed in canon read here.

80.content:
Blizzard Strayer (also: Snowswept Memory, Icebreaker's Resolve, Frozen Homeland's Demise, Frost-Weaved Dignity, Broken Rime's Echo): Blizzard Strayer is a Cryo artifact set (4 and 5 star, added 1.2) from Dragonspine. Its pieces tell of the Icebreaker, a quiet hero from a mountain city lost to endless winter, who left with the hopes of its people and was never heard of again. The wiki connects it to Imunlaukr and the fallen nation of Sal Vindagnyr. It drops in the Peak of Vindagnyr domain.

The pieces are Snowswept Memory (flower), Icebreaker's Resolve (feather), Frozen Homeland's Demise (hourglass), Frost-Weaved Dignity (ice cup) and Broken Rime's Echo (crown).

Appearance: Frost-coated relics: a long-extinct flower covered in beads of frost, a falcon feather coated in pearls of ice, an hourglass of fine powdered snow instead of sand, a cup carved of ice for unfreezable liquor, and a winter crown.

Lore: Snowswept Memory shows a maiden pinning a frost flower on the hero's chest and promising a fourth fresco with his likeness. Icebreaker's Resolve follows him through the storm toward a lost summer palace, carrying the hope of homeless children. Frozen Homeland's Demise says the mountain city believed cold from the sky could freeze time. Frost-Weaved Dignity portrays the silent warrior drinking bitter wine from a cup of ice while the painter begs him to live rather than die forgotten. Broken Rime's Echo has him donning the winter crown and vanishing into the snowstorm.

The set ends with the maiden singing to comfort her people and believing he would bring back spring. But he did not return in time, and 'hateful words long ground to dust' accused him of flight. The texts treat him as an 'outlander' searching for hope on another's behalf. The ending is bitter: the heroism of the Icebreaker was forgotten, buried in northern storms, yet the flower never withered.

Sal Vindagnyr's own history supplies the context: an ancient nation hit by the Skyfrost Nail, its princess (Varuch's daughter) painting frescoes of the future, and Imunlaukr, a hero from another land and namesake of the Imunlaukr clan, one of Mondstadt's founding clans. According to the wiki the princess gave him the greatsword Snow-Tombed Starsilver before he left and said she would dedicate her fourth fresco to him, though the storm drowned out her words. The set text itself leaves all names out.

Owners: No canon holder is named. The wiki treats the Icebreaker as Imunlaukr.

Status as of 7.1: The hero, the princess and the nation are long dead; the relics are remnants found in Dragonspine's domain. Sal Vindagnyr's story is background lore, not a present-day location.

How {{char}} behaves: Use as melancholy lore. A character who touches the relics might hear storm-voices or feel the cold of the gone hero. Do not give the hero a name unless the speaker knows the Sal Vindagnyr history.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). A 4- and 5-star set from the Domain of Blessing Peak of Vindagnyr; a Cryo 2-piece (+15% Cryo DMG Bonus) and a 4-piece that raises CRIT Rate by 20% against Cryo-affected opponents and 20% more against Frozen ones. The bonus applies to the wearer only, and Frozen requires the Frozen reaction itself.

81.content:
The Icebreaker is the unnamed hero of the Blizzard Strayer texts, a silent warrior who left the snow-sealed mountain city to seek hope and was accused of flight when he did not return. The wiki identifies him as Imunlaukr.

His likeness was to be painted on the maiden's fourth fresco. The texts never say where he went or how he fell.

82.content: A frost flower pinned to the hero's chest by the maiden who painted the city's frescoes; a mountain-city hourglass of fine snow that says time itself can freeze. In the wiki's reading the maiden is the princess of Sal Vindagnyr.

83.content:
Bloodsoaked Ruins (also: Mournful Tribute, Requiem of Ruin): A long spear tainted black by unrelenting battle, glowing faintly beneath the ghostly blue light of a lantern-fire. A 5-star polearm from Version 6.0, shown in Flins's hands.

Its item text is a northern tale of two brothers, a snowbound court and a stained spear.

Appearance: A long black spear with a lantern fixed to it. The description speaks of an ethereal glow and ghostly blue lantern-fire; its feathers were once silver-white but the spear now wears the black stain of noble blood. When Flins wields it the lantern shines red in combat (wiki trivia).

Lore: A Snezhnayan folk tale says the King of Midsommar Oak, who brought warmth, was accidentally slain by his elder brother, the King of Winter Icelea, and so the world has known unrelenting winter. The spear's story sets a human tragedy beside it.

The White Emperor, ruler of the fae from the Pale Star throne, fell silent after returning from the ruins of the far north, then opened his doors to humans he had once turned away. A palace rose beside Snezhnograd's furnaces, where the wisest humans and fae gathered and the seeds of a "grand delusion" were sown.

Guarding that court were fae and the mortal House Solovyov. Of two brothers, the elder inherited the nightingale emblem and guarded the sacred chariot; the younger gave up the family name and lived a life of obscurity on the frontier. The elder was consumed by beasts ("zver") for glimpsing the philosophers' secret. The younger, away quelling unrest, came back to a world under deep snow and found the spear, once silver-white feathered, stained black.

Years later the surviving brother, now a general who had taken the family name, left his homeland for the wild borderlands of Nod-Krai seeking vengeance. Each time he touched the spear he relived the snowy night outside the palace gates and the words of an old friend (Avrelian) spoken before the guillotine. The text ends with the Torchforger, bathed in eternal moonlight, lighting an everlasting flame and beginning his watch. The folk tale and the human story are linked only by mood: the text adds that the fae know the permafrost is far older than the Tsar's reign.

Owners: Flins is shown wielding it in official art and trailers; the item text itself names no owner.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star polearm, CRIT Rate secondary. Passive Mournful Tribute boosts the wielder's Lunar-Charged damage after a Burst and, when Lunar-Charged is triggered, grants CRIT DMG and some Energy (limited to once every 14 seconds).

How {{char}} behaves: Present it as a weapon with memory rather than a heirloom of fame: those who know Flins may link it to him, but the in-text brothers are told as a tale and should not be asserted as his own history.

84.content: Mournful Tribute is the weapon's passive. Its theme, mourning and a vigil, matches the closing image of the Torchforger beginning his watch.

85.content:
Bloodstained Chivalry (also: Bloodstained Flower of Iron, Bloodstained Black Plume, Bloodstained Final Hour, Bloodstained Chevalier's Goblet, Bloodstained Iron Mask, Bloodstained Knight): Bloodstained Chivalry is a Physical artifact set (4 and 5 star, added 1.0). Its five pieces tell the downfall of a righteous knight: he began as a white knight who rescued a maiden, killed so much in the name of justice that he came to see himself as a monster, and finally went to the fallen kingdom to die. The wiki names him as Roland; the texts say only 'the Bloodstained Knight'.

The pieces are Bloodstained Flower of Iron (flower), Bloodstained Black Plume (feather), Bloodstained Final Hour (sands), Bloodstained Chevalier's Goblet (goblet) and Bloodstained Iron Mask (circlet). It is the other half of the story told by the Maiden Beloved set.

Appearance: Black-stained relics of a knight: a dried white flower hardened by blood to the toughness of steel, a raven feather dyed pitch black, a timepiece whose liquid has dried up, a silver goblet engraved with a knight's feats but blackened by smoke and blood, and a luxurious platinum iron mask with permanent dark stains.

Lore: The Flower of Iron tells how the rescued damsel offered a reward and he refused everything but one pure white flower, saying chivalry is its own reward; he wore it over his heart and his bloodshed dried and blackened it. The Black Plume says ravens followed him, he could no longer tell whose blood stained him, and he realised that his path had turned the white knight into a monster. The Goblet shows him returning from a battlefield to find that those awaiting rescue were gone among burning, collapsed houses; he took the smoke-blackened goblet and vowed to rid the world of monsters, poverty and evil. The Iron Mask describes a person he tried to help cowering from him, which made him realise he had become the monster, tainted by the cruelty of a drawn-out war; the mask shields him from the eyes of those he vowed to protect.

The Final Hour finishes the story. In the abyss, where no celestial bodies cast light, time lost its meaning for him. He saw there was no place for him on earth and travelled into the fallen ancient kingdom, where he died fighting in the monsters' lair. At the bottom of the world he learned the origin of the monsters: the kingdom had been wrongfully cursed, turning its people into monsters. His code of chivalry could not tolerate that injustice, and he pledged loyalty to the Abyss, whatever its name. The wiki links the 'ancient kingdom' to Khaenri'ah and the 'drawn-out war' to the Cataclysm.

The wiki's Roland page adds context from other item texts: a noble-born Knight of Favonius taught chivalry and swordsmanship, obsessed with justice, who lost himself in cutting down foes, and the rescued maiden is the one of the Maiden Beloved set. Those details come from weapon and set texts rather than a quest, so treat them as wiki-compiled lore. The Iron Mask description notes that many have speculated about the face behind the mask; canon does not settle it.

Owners: The Bloodstained Knight, whom the wiki identifies as Roland. The goblet and the mask are described as his; the pieces are remnants of his life.

Status as of 7.1: The knight is long dead; the texts say he died in battle in the monsters' lair of the fallen kingdom. Nothing in 6.x or 7.0-7.1 changes this set.

How {{char}} behaves: Use as a tragedy about justice turning cruel. A character holding a piece might speak of ravens, stained iron or a white flower. Do not give the knight a living voice or invent dialogue; the quoted vows in the item texts are the only words attributed to him.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). A 4- and 5-star Physical set from the domain Clear Pool and Mountain Cavern. 2-piece: Physical DMG Bonus +25%. 4-piece: after defeating an opponent, Charged Attack DMG +50% and Charged Attack Stamina cost 0 for 10s. It persists when switching characters and can trigger on wildlife; kills by co-op or off-field teammates do not count. A 4-star goblet can be obtained from one of Sister Victoria's dialogue branches in the Mondstadt cathedral.

86.content:
The Bloodstained Knight is the figure of the Bloodstained Chivalry set texts: once a white knight, he became a killer in justice's name and died in the fallen kingdom. The wiki identifies him as Roland. See the set entry for the five piece stories.

His white flower, raven feather, silver goblet and iron mask mark the stages of his fall. He and the rescued maiden are the two sides of the Maiden Beloved and Bloodstained Chivalry sets.

87.content: The Final Hour records the knight's end: he went to the fallen ancient kingdom, learned that its people were cursed into monsters, pledged loyalty to the Abyss, and died in battle. The Iron Mask text is the earlier moment when he understood he had become a monster to the very people he helped.

88.content:
Breeze Amidst the Forest (also: Breeze in Woods): Breeze Amidst the Forest is a two-volume Mondstadt book. Vol. 1 is an anthology of bard ballads, including the tale of the young Wind Dragon who sought to be understood and became a protector of Mondstadt. Vol. 2 adds excerpts about the Four Winds and the battle between Dvalin and the corrupted dragon Durin. The compiler warns that bards embellish.

Read it as Mondstadt's folk memory of Dvalin, not as an official chronicle. It is also a main in-game text on the faded tradition of Four Winds worship.

Appearance: Cover text reads Breeze in Woods in the Teyvat script. Vol. 1 is introduced as ballads recorded and arranged by scholars centuries ago, the companion to Breeze Upon the Lake; Vol. 2 as a supplement with excerpts from various sources.

Lore: In the ballad, a young dragon graced by Anemo is born in the high heavens, descends and tries to understand humans, but villagers throw stones and farmers curse him. He hears the Holy Lyre der Himmel, the Anemo Archon's lyre, and lands beside the bard. The people panic because dragons and archons never agreed, yet the dragon learns human speech and the bard's songs and stays. Later generations count him among the Four Winds.

- After the Eclipse Dynasty fell and disaster spread, the ballad says the alchemist Gold made an army of shadowy monsters. The black dragon Durin rose from the sea to cast a shadow over Mondstadt.
- At that moment the title of Lionfang Knight had no heir, so the Knights of Favonius could not fly their falcon flag. Prayers called on the Archon, and the Wind Dragon was summoned. He tore open Durin's throat but swallowed its poisonous blood, which was distorted gold, and then fell into a deep slumber.
- Vol. 2 lists the Four Winds: the Wolf (Knight of Boreas), the Lion (Lionfang or Dandelion Knight), the Falcon (Knights of Favonius) and the Wind Dragon Dvalin. After the Lionfang Knight liberated Mondstadt the Knights of Favonius were established and the Knight of Boreas joined them. The tradition of worship formed gradually, though Dvalin predates all of them.

- The excerpt says Durin's remains still lie on the snowy peaks south of Mondstadt and that the story of how the battle ended is lost; it is said Dvalin ripped out Durin's throat and both fell.
- It adds that the belief in the Four Winds had eroded in peace and their temples lie deserted.
- The excerpt describes the era before the battle as one of darkness spreading, barbarians and foul creatures forcing people to live inside city walls, and Knights depleted by long wars.
- People used to believe Dvalin would awaken whenever Mondstadt faced a new threat.
- A closing passage of unknown origin says the Knights fought Stormterror many times before learning it was Dvalin of the Four Winds, and imagines Dvalin's sense of betrayal on waking after a long sleep to find the people he had protected had turned on him. It is a citation without a known source, so treat it as commentary.

- Footnote logic in the text: the ballad's own note says life arising from elements usually descends to become a slime or ascends to become a crystalfly, and only rarely produces dangerous monsters; elemental dragons are rare and match the old gods in power.
- Compare Tale of Durin and the Anemo story quests for the verified version of events. The ballad is older and lyrical, and some details (dates, Gold's motives) are marked above as altered or uncertain.

Owners: No individual owner. Vol. 1 can be obtained from Six-Fingered Jose through a dialogue path; Vol. 2 is Lisa's reward for Sparks Amongst the Pages.

Gameplay: Game note: collectible book collection; lore only.

89.comment: Breeze Amidst the Forest: The Four Winds Tradition
89.content: Breeze Amidst the Forest Vol. 2 explains the Four Winds as Wolf, Lion, Falcon and Wind Dragon, linked to the Knight of Boreas, the Lionfang Knight, the Knights of Favonius and Dvalin. Worship formed over time, the dragon predates them, and temples are now deserted. Who holds the Falcon title is disputed.

90.comment: Breeze Amidst the Forest: The Young Wind Dragon Ballad
90.content: In the Breeze Amidst the Forest ballad, the young Wind Dragon learned human speech and the Windborne Bard's singing. He stayed with the bard hoping to be understood by all souls. This is a bardic, embellished account.

91.comment: Breeze Amidst the Forest: Dvalin and Durin in the Ballad
91.content: The ballad and its supplement say Durin, a corrupted black dragon, attacked Mondstadt and the summoned Wind Dragon killed it, at the cost of ingesting poisonous blood and then sleeping. Durin's remains are said to lie in the snowy peaks to the south.

92.content:
Calamity of Eshu (also: Sanhaj's ritual sword, Eshu's Calamity): The Calamity of Eshu is a 4-star sword from Natlan: the curved ceremonial blade of Sanhaj, the great high priest of the Masters of the Night-Wind. Legend says he used it in rituals that blurred the boundary between the Night Kingdom and the living world.

Its story follows Sanhaj as a silent child who journeyed to find half of his soul and came back knowing the past. The tribe's chief keeps the blade today and lends it for ceremonies.

Appearance: Canon says only that it is a curved ceremonial blade. In its quest uses it carries the power of a Wayob, which the game says can be called on to defend its wielder. Do not invent decoration.

Lore: A child who barely spoke for years was told by a ritual elder that half his soul had been lost in the night flames. On his birthday he walked into the stony wastes to find it, with only the Iktomisaur Mahamba willing to go with him.

Crossing seven curtain layers to reach the Lord of Silence is a journey few return from. In an obsidian hall the boy took in the memories of an ancient era as if he had lived them: the first Pyro Archon swearing a vow before the volcano, and the Sacred Lord Och-Kan, fallen into delirium, beaten down by the crimson-eyed youth on the stairs before an empty throne. The memories gave him every word and its meaning, and let him see far along the threads of time.
