Gurabad fell to a "great plague" of a mob under a brass-masked leader, and her soul was split. The survivors formed seven desert states, with the "city of sapphires", Tulaytullah, among the greatest. Two other pieces step outside Gurabad: Jinn fragments trapped in machines cry out against a "mother who never bore" them, and the Jinni Ferigees seals herself into a crystalline cup to restrain the desert's wrath and protect mortal cities.

The poet tells the story to Xiphos, who is setting out for Tulaytullah. The Plume lists later tales without names: a general led by a slave, a king killed over a hunting falcon, a dancer sworn to a prince, a lost prince remembering his burning palace. The wiki ties the poet to Xiphos's blind teacher; the set never says so. The poem presents Gurabad as a human state under divine patronage and records its end in the language of epidemic and mob rule, not conquest. Other lore (Liloupar's own account and The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin) fills in the scheme the poem only hints at. The Goblet's Ferigees chooses her dead mistress and the mortals over King Deshret's order and accepts that bonds are temporary.

The "city of sapphires" and the lost prince place the end of the golden age shortly before Tulaytullah's era. The Plume's list of nobles enslaved, princes cast down by slave-soldiers and dancers seizing power summarises a long period of instability, not one event, and is best read as the poet's moral rather than a ledger. The closing lines have the poet tell Xiphos that hatred burns like wildfire and leaves ash, but uncontrolled love is wilder still: the poem's thesis.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a 4- and 5-star set from the City of Gold domain and the Desert Pavilion Chronicle strongbox. 2-piece: Anemo DMG Bonus +15%. 4-piece: when Charged Attacks hit, Normal Attack SPD rises 10% and Normal, Charged and Plunging Attack DMG rise 40% for 15s. Released in 3.3; the wiki lists no later change.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the set as a moral tale told by an elder. A character may quote its warnings but should not claim to know who the unnamed figures were. The Gurabad stories are specialist knowledge, not common in modern Sumeru.

key: The First Days of the City of Kings
143.comment: Desert Pavilion Chronicle: The First Days of the City of Kings
143.content:
The flower piece of Desert Pavilion Chronicle: an artificial bloom that shimmers and seems to laugh when held to the ear. Its poem tells of the Lord of the Sands' pact with mortals through the Jinn, of Ormazd and the lily-born Liloupar, and of Gurabad blooming "like a man-made flower in a cliff wall". It ends with Xiphos setting out for the city of sapphires.

Liloupar warns of a "hundred generations of blessings" paid for with sharp retribution and spilled red wine, because the Jinn's mad love is chained to greed and want. Ormazd, under the moon, did not take heed. With her guidance he led his nomadic clan, beat his divided rivals and was crowned vassal king, proxy of the Lord of the Sands.

144.comment: Desert Pavilion Chronicle: End of the Golden Realm
144.content:
The plume piece: a clear artificial feather from an ancient human realm, with eagle cries sealed inside. Its poem records Gurabad's fall to a "great plague" and a brass-masked leader, Liloupar's split soul, the seven desert states with Tulaytullah among the greatest, then unnamed tales of a general, a falcon-killed king, a dancer and a lost prince.

A feather-shaped body of mortal craft held a broken Jinni and flew from Gurabad's cliffs past the desert states until it reached "gilded descendants", its lost memories flaking off like sand. The poet closes by saying one figure lost sight and another lost a throne.

145.comment: Desert Pavilion Chronicle: Timepiece of the Lost Path
145.content:
The sands piece: an old mechanical clock with Jinni fragments glowing and trembling at its core. Its voices curse a "mother who never bore us" and swear to return to their birth mother, Shirin. The text does not explain who the speakers are.

The voices describe themselves as born old, with power resting on shattered consciousness, voices replaced by copper tubes, and hatred as fuel. They name no individual speaker.

146.comment: Desert Pavilion Chronicle: Defender of the Enchanting Dream
146.content:
The goblet piece: an ancient gold cup that murmurs from its empty inside. Its poem covers the Lord of Flowers' death, her Jinn passing to King Deshret, the Eternal Oasis, and Ferigees binding herself in frost-like chains as a crystalline cup to hold back the desert's wrath and guard the mortal cities.

Ferigees was given governance of the oasis by King Deshret, spread greenery over the desert to shelter people who had lost their homes, and later disobeyed his charge to make her sacrifice. In her speech she says she is waiting for the King of Sand to fulfil an ancient promise. The wiki places her spirit in a machine on Deshret's Glass Goblet.

147.comment: Desert Pavilion Chronicle: Legacy of the Desert High-Born
147.content:
The circlet piece: amber-gold earrings. Its poem shows Ormazd turning a young state into a slave-fed tyranny and his Jinni consort laying aside the earrings he gave her as the sign of her intent to curse his line with three generations of ruin. The wiki notes the earrings are implied to be the ones Ormazd gave Liloupar.

Ormazd took the Lord of the Desert as patron, built palaces and temples, took slaves from tribes, demanded service from states and sacrifices from cities. The Jinni, once an attendant of the Goddess of Flowers, advised him gently in private and was dismissed as a lover's whispering.

148.content:
Dialogues of the Desert Sages: Dialogues of the Desert Sages is a 4-star polearm: a caduceus symbolising the glory of alchemy, made from special alloys. Its story names the seven sages of King Deshret and tells how the Crocodile King and the Ibis King wagered on a transmutation, with the sage Hermanubis ruling that the two powers must balance.

It was a reward of the Version 4.5 event Alchemical Ascension. The description jokes that it is so rigid and heavy that it would hurt as a cudgel.

Appearance: A caduceus of special alloys, exceedingly rigid and heavy. The description says it symbolises the glory of alchemy.

Lore: King Deshret's seven sages vanished long ago; their deeds are blown away and only their names, carved in stone, remain, now eroded to golden grains of sand. The text lists four: the Goat King (Heryshaf), right hand of the King and head of the sages; the sun-bound bird that was the King's soul, Bennu; the human-headed lioness that was the King's will, Shesepankh; and the dragon Al-Apep, who obtained the King's flesh and blood and never counted himself among the Seven. These four have nothing to do with the story that follows.

The Crocodile King and the Ibis King (Sobek and Thoth) were arguing, as ever, about the changing of things. The Crocodile King produced a man blessed by an Oceanid, through whose hands any liquid became perfect wine. The Ibis King produced a man cursed after touching the tomb of an ancient god, whose touch slowly turned things to pure silver. The text adds that turning things to gold and Mora is the province of Deus Auri alone. They bet on which effect would win and asked Hermanubis, the last of the seven sages, to predict.

Hermanubis was a desert sage, a warrior and leader of the priestly class, and learned in alchemy, so he was a fitting judge. He said the two powers clash like sharp spears against sturdy shields and each must yield a step: the principle of equilibrium. The result was a cup turned to pure silver and a fine liquor with suspended grains of silver. The two kings failed to take his admonition to heart and kept fighting.

In the end the kings devised a strange summoning magic, and the text says they now carry their battle across millennia onto the field of the Genius Invokation TCG, as part of this version of the tale "King of Invokations".

Owners: No owner is named, and no character is recorded wielding it.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star polearm, level 1 base ATK 42, secondary stat HP 9%. Passive Principle of Equilibrium: when the wielder heals, restore Energy, once every 10 s, even when off-field. Refinement uses the material Exalted Earth from Alchemical Ascension instead of duplicate weapons.

Energy restored is 8 at refinement 1 and 16 at refinement 5.

How {{char}} behaves: Present the Crocodile King and Ibis King as a bickering pair of old rivals, and Hermanubis as measured and learned. Do not treat the wager tale as established history of Sobek and Thoth; the item frames it as a story.

149.comment: Dialogues of the Desert Sages: Principle of Equilibrium
149.content: Principle of Equilibrium is the weapon passive (gameplay: Energy on healing) and the in-story ruling of Hermanubis that two clashing powers each yield and balance.

150.content:
Diary of Roald the Adventurer (also: Roald's Diary, Roald's diaries, Adventurer Roald's diary): Diary of Roald the Adventurer is an 11-volume book collection of travel diaries by Roald, a seasoned adventurer. He walks through Liyue (Sal Terrae, Qingce Village, Jueyun Karst, Yaoguang Shoal, Guyun Stone Forest), climbs Dragonspine, waits out the Sakoku Decree in Ritou and ends on Tsurumi Island in Inazuma. Each entry pairs a travel log with local legends and a note to himself not to lose the diary again, which he keeps doing.

The diaries are a good in-world source for folk legends and how an outsider reads them. Roald is curious, a little accident-prone and wry, wanting above all to find an adeptus and to find out what ancient peoples left behind. The legends are what locals told him, not verified history.

Appearance: A worn travelling notebook with a leather case, left behind at camps. The in-game descriptions mention small salt crystals (Vol. 1), the smell of Mt. Qingce herbs, a fox-paw watermark, sea breeze, moss, ice crystals, sakura and tobacco, and fog and fungus on the pages, matching each place he wrote in.

Lore: Roald records places and the legends told about them, from the God of Salt's fall at Sal Terrae (Vol. 1) and the sea monster Chi at Qingce to Dragonspine, Ritou and Tsurumi Island.

- Recurring thread: Roald keeps misplacing diaries, tries safeguards such as a moss marker on the case, and in Vol. 9 swaps his soggy diary for a new one. In Vol. 3 he jokes about wasting paper and hoping the Dendro Archon will not mind.
- Roald's own inferences: Vol. 9 argues from matching architecture that a "mountain civilization" may lie beneath Dragonspine, though he found no solid inscriptions; Vol. 8 calls his theory about Lisha's ruins simple and still in need of evidence.
- Placement of his route: volume numbers follow the in-game collection, not strictly his chronology. Vol. 2 says he left Dragonspine, while Vol. 9 describes the climb and ends with the plan to explore Liyue next.

- Voice and tone for scenes: Roald writes in first person, practical and lightly self-mocking, noting aches, wet shoes and food. He is respectful of local legends but weighs them against what he sees, and flags when a story is only a tale.
- Roald crosses paths with the Traveler and Paimon only in Vol. 11; do not place him with them elsewhere unless a scene needs it.

Owners: No individual owns the diaries; they are left at campsites and other spots in the world for the Traveler to find. Their author is Roald, whose fate is not stated in the text beyond Vol. 11.

Gameplay: Game note: a book collection with no stats. Volumes sit at camps in Liyue and Dragonspine and in Ritou; Vol. 11 is on Tsurumi Island and needs the quest The Saga of Mr. Forgetful to be complete.

151.comment: Diary of Roald the Adventurer: Roald
151.content: Roald is the adventurer who wrote the Diary of Roald the Adventurer. He is a seasoned traveller who tracks legends, searches for an adeptus and keeps losing his diaries. In Vol. 11 he thanks a blonde traveler and Paimon for helping him gather Fluorescent Fungus and bring back pictures of ancient murals on Tsurumi Island.

152.comment: Diary of Roald the Adventurer: Salt God's Fall in Roald's Diary
152.content: In Roald's Vol. 1 account, the God of Salt sheltered civilians during the Archon War and built a settlement at Sal Terrae. Her city fell when its first and last king killed her, hoping to turn it into a military power. The king's fate is uncertain in the text. This is folklore Roald collected, and other sources should be used for the canonical history.

153.comment: Diary of Roald the Adventurer: Chi and Qingce Village in Roald's Diary
153.content: Roald reports the elders' story that Morax slew the sea serpent Chi, whose body became Mt. Qingce and the terraced fields. He doubts it, since the rock looks impact-shattered and shows no sign of a Hydro monster. The diary also remarks that Chi was once pronounced Qingce.

154.comment: Diary of Roald the Adventurer: Roald on Tsurumi Island
154.content: In Vol. 11 Roald reaches Tsurumi Island through the fog with the help of a youth named Kama, then meets a small child he suspects may be a hallucination. When he returns without telling Kama he cannot get through the fog; a blonde traveler and Paimon help him collect Fluorescent Fungus. He gives them credit for the discovery of the ancient murals.

155.comment: Diary of Roald the Adventurer: Roald's Diary Volume Summaries
155.content:
- Vol. 1, Sal Terrae: from the ruin's scale Roald suspects it is the refuge temple built by the God of Salt. Folklore calls her the gentlest of the gods. Her followers settled the area, and the city stood several centuries until the king, wanting military strength and thinking gentleness unfit for the times, killed her. Theories on the king's end differ: he ruled alone from the ruins until he turned to dust, or he took his own life from guilt. Survivors scattered across Liyue and, in Liyue Harbor under the Geo Archon, their stories survived. Rumour says her body, turned to salt, remains in the ruins in the pose of her death.
- Vol. 2, Qingce Village: elders say Morax defeated the sea serpent Chi; its body became stone, blood water, scales the terraced fields and its nest Mt. Qingce. Roald thinks the rocks look shattered by impacts and sees no sign of a Hydro monster, so wonders if it is just a tale. He also notes that young people moved to Liyue Harbor for work, which brings prosperity but will eventually empty the village.
- Vol. 3, Aocang Lake: he loses another diary and swims in the mountain lake. A farmer's tale says adepti can turn to mist and roam the sea of clouds. He meets Eduardo, a treasure-hunting Adventurers' Guild member who insists she has no tie to the Treasure Hoarders.
- Vol. 4, Luhua Pool: a herb gatherer says the pond was once a garden where two lovers met; the man went to fight for the Geo Archon and never returned, and the girl's tears gathered into the pond. Roald falls asleep bathing, and a baby fox steals a shoe and his food.
- Vol. 5, Yaoguang Shoal: fisherman's legend says Greenconch Lodge belonged to an adeptus who was the conch itself and sheltered the lost; older fishermen say it housed a family living in a giant shell. The lodge seems empty.
- Vol. 6, Guyun Stone Forest: legend says the Geo Archon carved a huge stone polearm and drove it through a sea monster; wind has worn it into the pillars. Roald dreams he is the impaled monster and decides not to camp there. He sees the Crux setting sail and wonders what Captain Beidou has been assigned.
- Vol. 7, Qingyun Peak: a cold, sleepless night above the clouds before his climb to the adeptus's dwelling.
- Vol. 8, Qingxu Pool: a Sumeru scholar named Soraya told him the Lisha ruins belong to an evil god whose name was erased and its people, flooded during the Archon War and exposed when the tide fell. He meets Eduardo again. Monsters now occupy the ruins since the Chasm mining stopped.
- Vol. 9, Dragonspine: he sets up camp on the southern slope, notes ruins whose style matches other ancient sites, finds old clothing and broken weapons from the aristocratic era that suggest a chase or murder, and discovers unfrozen water in a ruin. He nearly breaks a leg, gets frostbitten toes and decides the trip was a disaster. He hears a gentle yet disturbing song in a dream. Mondstadt tales call the mountain a place abandoned by the Wind of Time.
- Vol. 10, Ritou: delayed by the Kanjou Commission, he is helped by Mr. Kurisu, a reserved commerce chairman from Fontaine. He describes how the Sakoku Decree emptied the port, recalls that Hiroshi of the Hiiragi Clan founded it, notes rumours of a Shogunate attack on a Sangonomiya outpost, and hopes the Crux Fleet can smuggle him out.
- Vol. 11, Tsurumi Island: a youth named Kama helps him reach the fog-shrouded island. He glimpses ancient ruins and dream-like scenes and meets a small child he cannot explain. He is later guided out by a blonde traveler and Paimon, who help him gather Fluorescent Fungus, said to have formed from the memories of the island's dead. He finds it calming and plans to send some to a friend in Sumeru.

156.content:
Disaster and Remorse (also: Dolorous Stroke): Disaster and Remorse is a 5-star Hexerei-series polearm, described as forged from Whitestone and Starsilver, its point always wrapped in a bone-piercing chill. Its text tells how the outlander warrior Imunlaukr hurled this astral-silver lance to protect a maiden of Sal Vindagnyr, and the blow that legend names dolorous destroyed three kingdoms and killed her. Released in Version 6.6.

The Hexerei Series page reads the lance as Imunlaukr's weapon. The item is a record of the Mondstadt-region legend of his throw and its aftermath, and of how it ended his life as a warrior.

Appearance: Canon says it is forged from Whitestone and Starsilver, with a keen point constantly enveloped in a bone-piercing chill; the text calls it an astral silver lance. Do not describe its hilt or length.

Lore: In the moonless city of snow, an outlander warrior mourned a shattered realm and left his old greatsword to the frost.

He wandered the frozen plains believing he could forget his weakness in endless battle, but abandoned that pretense at the first moonfall after leaving the Mural Room. When he saw the maiden of Sal Vindagnyr attacked, instinct made him hurl the lance into a black tide of beasts, to save her.

The text says he had buried a hope that would no longer bear fruit and left his unspoken longings beside the last mural. He thought he had long broken a warrior's oath and wanted only a diversion, and he never wished to see silver hair or a moonlike face buried in ice and snow again. The throw is called dolorous; the songs say he came for the joy of conflict and shattered the snow-covered mountains, leveling three thriving kingdoms and leaving multitudes to wander wastelands. The text then says the song is only a song: he stood dazed in the ruins, his spear had pierced the stone that held up the earth, and the maiden had died in the billowing darkness. Survivors named him Imunlaukr and hunted him without end. He had claimed to entertain the gods with strife, then sought redemption and brought only more grief, and so ceased to long for salvation and left the life of a warrior forever.

The wiki ties the setting to Sal Vindagnyr during the Funerary Year, where the city was destroyed, and reads the tide of beasts as abyssal monsters. The Sacrificial Series wiki page, discussing Dragonspine and the Imunlaukr Clan, treats the warrior as an ancestor figure; the item text itself does not. The lance in this text, the old greatsword he abandoned (Snow-Tombed Starsilver) and the mural room are items and places with their own entries.

Owners: Imunlaukr is the warrior of the text; the wiki's Hexerei Series page states that the polearm once belonged to him.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore: a 5-star polearm, base ATK 48, CRIT Rate secondary stat. After an Elemental Skill, the wielder gains Path of Conflict; its Unforgivable effect raises Normal and Charged Attack DMG, Irreparable raises Skill and Burst DMG, and hits of the matching kind extend each other. Hexerei: Secret Rite raises the boosts by 75%. It was on the weapon event Wish Epitome Invocation (2026-06-09 to 2026-06-30).

How {{char}} behaves: This archive's suggested use: a weapon of a tragic legend, where the story the songs tell and the grieving truth behind it differ. Keep both versions: the tale of ruin and the account of a man trying to save one person.

157.content: Disaster and Remorse is a 5-star Hexerei polearm of Whitestone and Starsilver. Its text tells how the outlander warrior Imunlaukr threw his astral-silver lance into a tide of beasts to save the maiden of Sal Vindagnyr; legend says the blow leveled three kingdoms, while the text adds that she died and he abandoned warriorhood.

158.content:
Disenchantment in Deep Shadow (also: Iridescence That Ceased Amidst Glory, Sharpness That Ceased Upon Wondrous Creation, Moment That Ceased Upon Waking From Grand Dreams, Ovations That Ceased Upon Festivity, Pendulum That Ceased Amidst a Great Fall): Disenchantment in Deep Shadow is a 4- and 5-star artifact set for Superconduct and Stellar-Conduct teams, released in version 6.6. Its five pieces are all about Aksinya, the silver-haired human scholar of the old Snezhnayan court: her friendship with a frost-wielding fae princess, her work among the ruins of the Shadow Realm, a long-haired alchemist who joined her research, and the Tsar who found her as an infant.

Every title begins "...That Ceased...", pointing at the dream of the Belyi Tsar's project that stopped when he fell. The items are keepsakes of Aksinya's life, given to her by friends, colleagues and her master.

Appearance: Keepsakes: a silk flower, a feathered quill, a fleeting moment given as a reminder, a wine goblet, and a delicate piercing trinket.

Lore: All five stories centre on Aksinya, who is not named in some pieces but is addressed by name in the Flower and the Goblet. The Flower is her friendship with the Snegurochka princess in a fae manor; the Quill her teaching of a young Domovoy; the Sands her first meeting with a long-haired alchemist; the Goblet a toast from the old Domovoy lord Alvis; the Pendulum the Tsar's trinket, given in celebration of her birth.

- Iridescence That Ceased Amidst Glory: Aksinya, then a court attendant following the Emperor of the North, slipped away from a banquet at the manor of the foremost Snegovik (the House of Hesperides per wiki) and got lost. The mistress of frost, a Snegurochka princess, found her, shared paintings, sculptures and puzzles and showed her a courtyard of ice that never melts. She warned that even that ice was magic and fleeting, engraved in the blood of former servants. She pinned a silk flower on Aksinya as proof of friendship, saying it is never the craft that is artful but the heart.
- Sharpness That Ceased Upon Wondrous Creation: in the Shadow Realm Aksinya and her apprentice, a young Domovoy, walked among the ruins of a golden civilisation struck down by the heavens' master. She sketched a grand design while he begged her to turn back. Aksinya answered that they sought to see by the fire's light, not to inherit it, and that their bones could be the next step for others to climb. She handed him her pen.
- Moment That Ceased Upon Waking From Grand Dreams: before the Tsaritsa took the throne, a young black-haired alchemist who had defied taboos, even on the fae, was sent by the Snow-King to labour where taboos are touched. At their first meeting he secretly made an ear grow in her palm out of spite. She treated it as an interesting trick, asked him to request permission next time and gave him his schedule. The encounter made him sense something above the material, and wounded and drew him at once.
- Ovations That Ceased Upon Festivity: a company gathered by the guilt-ridden Snow-King sought the stairway to a vacant seat in the court of the stars. After years of descending into ancient ruins, the Domovoy lord Alvis, who held Kitezhgrad's mines, toasted her, a human, for outpacing everything earlier generations left. Aksinya saw that he now cared for her like an elder.

- Pendulum That Ceased Amidst a Great Fall: the towering man on the throne had given her a trinket in celebration of her birth; in the scene she is grown and has a fresh ear piercing. He remembered walking the shadows, finding the broken golden homeland, "the mother he had never met", and the Hyperboreans' secrets about himself, which gave him pain, not freedom. In one ruined structure of life-sustaining devices he had found an unconscious silver-haired infant. When Aksinya asked what she could give in return, he told her of the vision he had held, perhaps for far too long.
Read together with Heart of the Furnace (Aksinya's apprentice) the picture is of a human woman who earned a Domovoy lord's respect, the Snegovik's friendship, and the Tsar's trust, and whose project fell with him.

Owners: Aksinya is the recipient of each keepsake. No other owner is named.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): 4- and 5-star set from the Thorny Crown of the Mountain Wind domain (Windrest Peak, Mondstadt). 4-piece: Superconduct reaction DMG +80% and Stellar-Conduct reaction DMG +40%; when the wearer attacks opponents affected by Superconduct or Stellar-Conduct, that attack's CRIT Rate +16%.

159.comment: Disenchantment in Deep Shadow: Disenchantment in Deep Shadow
159.content: Artifact set whose item text recounts episodes from the life of Aksinya in the old Snezhnayan court, through gifts from friends, colleagues and her master.

160.comment: Disenchantment in Deep Shadow: The Snegurochka's silk flower
160.content: In the Iridescence That Ceased Amidst Glory text the Snegurochka princess hosts Aksinya in the thousand-year-old mountain manor of the foremost Snegovik. She shows her ice that never melts, warns that magic is fleeting, and gives her a silk flower as a token of friendship. The wiki links the friend to Pavlina.

161.content:
Divine Bridle: The Divine Bridle is a bridle-shaped quest item from Enkanomiya (Byakuyakoku). It was the badge of the Sunchild's office, the sign that a child was the nation's puppet ruler. It has no power of its own. The spirit Aberaku hid it and gave it to the Traveler; the Traveler then used it to help the official Clymene release the souls of the seven Sunchildren.

Its journey spans two linked world quests of Enkanomiya: Hyperion's Dirge, where Aberaku hands it over, and The Phaethons' Syrtos, where it becomes the medium that lets Clymene reach the dead children's souls. It is a quiet, sorrowful object, not a weapon or relic of power.

Appearance: Shaped like a bridle; the in-game text gives no further description of materials or markings.

Lore: Byakuyakoku was ruled by a Sunchild, an infant chosen to be the nation's figurehead and said to be a child of the sun. Per the quest accounts, the real power lay with people behind the scenes. The bridle marked the office. Aberaku, who built the Dainichi Mikoshi, calls it proof that a child is a child of the sun, and says he hid it intending to alert the people. Clymene, the official who raised the Sunchildren, believed it lost.

Aberaku's account (Hyperion's Dirge): the Sunchildren were puppets of schemers, and none ever grew up, because a grown ruler would see through the manipulation. He quotes a verse about the Sunchild riding Pegasus to the feast of the sun, which he ties to the children being led into the inner sanctum of the Dainichi Mikoshi on their birthdays. He gives the bridle to the Traveler as a testament to the nation's "laughable" history and tells them to keep it or do what they like.

Clymene's account (The Phaethons' Syrtos): she had the Traveler pay respects at the seven royal tombs, then at the Soul Guide's Locus explained the Rite of Solar Return, after which only shreds of each child's soul returned to the Locus. Her own memories could not call them back, but she believed the Divine Bridle, the badge of the Sunchild's office, could serve as a medium. Seeing the real one she was overcome. The Traveler placed it in the waters of the Locus. She said it had passed through the hands of every Sunchild, so its memories could fill the gaps in their souls, memories of the children themselves and of how the nation saw them as children of sin. She then spoke to Piramumon and Orupeusu, whom she had raised, and let them go.

The seven Sunchildren named on their tombs are Orupeusu, Surepio, Risutaiosu, Isumenasu, Rikoru, Ion and Piramumon (each with "no Mikoto"). The tomb inscriptions describe them as young people with interests in music, medicine, sculpture, boating, building, fortune-telling and books; the wiki says Rikoru was the first Sunchild. Per the wiki summary, Orobashi later took control of Enkanomiya after a child asked him to become their god, ending the Sunchild's rule.

The people of Byakuyakoku, in Clymene's telling, hated the Sunchildren and held their ignorance to be sin; she nonetheless could not hate children she had watched grow up, but was forbidden to speak to them while under surveillance. She says the official who serves the Sunchildren is meant to stay pure and never marry. These details color the bridle as an object the nation remembered with bitterness and she with grief.

Owners: Made as the Sunchild's badge, so carried by each Sunchild in turn, per Clymene. Aberaku hid it before the events of Hyperion's Dirge and gave it to the Traveler. The Traveler offered it to Clymene, who had it placed in the waters of the Soul Guide's Locus. Its fate after that is not stated.

Gameplay: Quest item received as a reward for Hyperion's Dirge (2.4) and needed for The Phaethons' Syrtos; the hidden exploration objective Sunchildren Hide and Seek opens after that quest. It has no use outside these quests.

162.comment: Divine Bridle: The Rite of Solar Return
162.content: Per Clymene, a Sunchild of a certain age was taken in a ceremony into the Dainichi Mikoshi on their birth date, to return to the "seat of the sun" before the mortal world could taint them. Only shreds of their souls came back to the Soul Guide's Locus. Aberaku ties it to a verse about riding Pegasus to the feast of the sun. The wiki's summary adds that the nobles used it so that no Sunchild would live long enough to see through their manipulation; the quests themselves are less explicit.

163.comment: Divine Bridle: Clymene and the Seven Sunchildren
163.content: Clymene was a female official who tended the Sunchildren's daily lives within the Dainichi Mikoshi. Her request, in The Phaethons' Syrtos, was for the Traveler to lay a Sango Pearl at each of the seven royal tombs, and later to find the Divine Bridle. Her own character has its own entry; this file covers only the bridle's role in her release of the children's souls.

164.content:
Dodoco Tales: Dodoco Tales is a 4-star catalyst, a small children's book of cheerful adventure stories about the Dodoco, furry creatures from the Golden Apple Archipelago. Its text is told in a child's voice and says the book was given by the freest mother in the world to the luckiest daughter in the world. It was an event reward from Midsummer Island Adventure (Version 1.6), a limited-time event.

The wiki notes that Klee is shown holding this catalyst in her Genius Invokation TCG card. The book itself is not tied to a named owner.

Appearance: A small, precious picture book. Its description says it is filled with childish short stories that make readers laugh and that even long-grown adults get absorbed in the innocent, naive little adventures.

Lore: The tale says there is a group of islands in a foggy sea called the Golden Apple Archipelago, where the cute, peace-loving Dodo Clan live without troubles. They call each other "Dodoco", which means "the best of friends".

Like dandelion seeds, every Dodoco must one day ride the wind and waves into the wider world to find a red, blazing four-leaf clover. Having lived together so long, the Dodocos have all become alike and cannot tell each other apart, with no "you" or "me". Only the clover, the story says, lets a Dodoco learn what "Dodoco" truly means and tell friends apart. The narrator adds that this is "what my mom says".

A Dodoco tumbling into the sea or leaping into the wind and drifting away means a lucky child is about to meet their bestest friend. The closing paragraph says the book chronicles the Dodoco's adventures before meeting the daughter and the bigger, sparkly adventures since, with sparks, splashes, treasures and many friends. The wiki's trivia ties the catalyst to Klee through her TCG card; the text does not.

Tone: wholly warm and childlike, written as a child retelling a mother's story. When using it in a scene, keep the Dodoco legend as stories the book tells rather than as verified facts about the Golden Apple Archipelago.

Owners: No owner is named in the text. The book is described as given by a mother to a daughter.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star catalyst obtained from the Midsummer Island Adventure event (Version 1.6, 2021-06-17 per the wiki infobox), base ATK 41, secondary stat ATK 12%. Passive Dodoventure!: Normal Attack hits raise Charged Attack DMG for 6 s, and Charged Attack hits raise ATK for 6 s. It is refined with the event material Fragments of Innocence rather than duplicate weapons.

The Charged Attack DMG bonus from Normal Attack hits is 16% at refinement 1 and 32% at refinement 5.

165.content: Dodoventure! is the weapon passive of Dodoco Tales (gameplay). Normal Attack hits buff Charged Attacks, and Charged Attack hits buff ATK.

166.content:
Dragon's Bane: Dragon's Bane is a 4-star polearm of the Kunwu series, described as a polearm with an entwining golden dragon, light and sharp, that may well kill dragons with ease. It is rumoured to be a legendary polearm of Liyue. It has been in the game since Version 1.0.

The item text says the master craftsman Kunwu forged it with a dragon's spine as the haft and a dragon's claw as the tip.

Appearance: A dragon motif runs from handle to tip. It once had a dragon-shaped wooden sheath, but according to the text it no longer needs to contain its might. Do not invent colours beyond the golden dragon the in-game description mentions.

Lore: It is called a legendary Liyue polearm that pierces anything in its way.

Because of its materials, the body is said to be unbreakable and the tip sharp beyond compare, gleaming with a dragon's malice.

The text tells of a dragon slayer of immense strength and courage who defied the ocean's wrath and fought the monstrosities in it. Many years after the slayer vanished without a trace, a dragon's hopeless cry was still heard across the ocean.

The slayer became an urban legend, and in the end both the legend and the polearm were lost. Freed from the shackles of its past, the weapon is said to have shown its full ferocity once and for all, as if marking the dragon's return to the ocean where it belonged. The text is a tale told as rumour and never confirms it.

Owners: Only the unnamed dragon slayer of the item text is tied to it in story. Yun Jin, Yaoyao and Xiangling are shown with it in promotional art, demos and trailers, which is a cameo and not an ownership claim.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star polearm, base ATK 41, Elemental Mastery secondary stat (48). Passive Bane of Flame and Water: increases DMG against opponents affected by Hydro or Pyro by 20 to 36 per cent by refinement. A Kunwu series weapon, shared with the 4-Star Bane series (see Lion's Roar).

167.content: Kunwu is the legendary master craftsman named in the item texts of Dragon's Bane, Lion's Roar and Solar Pearl. He is not described as a character who appears in the game; only these items' stories mention him.

168.content:
Dragonspine Spear: Dragonspine Spear is a 4-star polearm of the Dragonspine series, in-game description "a spear created from the fang of a dragon" that is oddly warm to the touch. It is made from teeth of the shadow dragon Durin and is the reward of the world quest The Festering Fang. Added in Version 1.2.

Its archive entry is Durin's own dying dream. The weapon shares its source dragon with Festering Desire.

Appearance: Canon says only that it is a spear made from a dragon's fang, oddly warm to the touch. Do not invent a colour or length.

Lore: The text narrates a very long dream. He dreamed that he and everyone had journeyed to a land of green grass and soulful songs, where he sang with the gentle people and danced in the skies with a dragon as beautiful as a jewel.

He woke in the sky above a mountain swept by roaring snowstorms. The green land was already painted crimson with fire and blood, the song of a sky-blue bard's lyre almost drowned out, and the jewel-like dragon had pierced his neck with sharp fangs.

His last thoughts: "Farewell, Mother! My journey is ended." He will sleep beneath the white, shining silver and thinks that perhaps this too is good; he bids farewell to the bard and the dragon, wishes they had met at another time and place to sing and dance together, and gives them the blessing in his veins and the sight of the dark universe that bore him.

Canon context: the wiki identifies the dreamer as Durin, the mother as Rhinedottir, the bard as Venti and the dragon as Dvalin; the same battle is told from Dvalin's side in Skyward Spine, where Durin is a poisonous attacker. Take the dream as Durin's perception, not neutral history, and as a reason Dvalin's victory carries sorrow.

Owners: No owner is named. In The Festering Fang the Traveler collects the materials and the craftsman Orban forges the spear; the weapon passes to the Traveler as the quest reward.

Quests: In The Festering Fang (a Version 1.2 Dragonspine world quest), the Traveler picks up a Strange Tooth, asks around the adventurers' camp and learns from Orban that it may be dragon tooth. He asks for three more teeth, 50 Starsilver and a Northlander polearm prototype, then finds that ordinary tools cannot cut the tooth. A tooth must absorb dragon "vitality" first: either from the heart in Wyrmrest Valley (where Fatui skirmishers interrupt) or, if the Traveler has already progressed through The Gardener, via a Runestone that Albedo sent through Sucrose. Orban then forges the spear.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 4-star polearm with base ATK 41 and a Physical DMG Bonus secondary stat. The Dragonspine series passive Frost Burial gives Normal and Charged Attack hits a chance (60 to 100 per cent by refinement, once per 10s) to drop an Everfrost Icicle that deals area ATK damage, much more against Cryo-affected enemies. It is a forgeable polearm obtained as a World Quest reward, with a diagram also given by the quest.

169.content: The Festering Fang is a Version 1.2 world quest in Dragonspine. Orban, an artisan, works with the Traveler to turn a strange dragon tooth into the Dragonspine Spear, after the tooth is first infused with dragon vitality. Festering Desire, a sword, is a related weapon from the same dragon.

170.content:
Dream-Mirror Remnant (also: Skirk's Abyss Crystal): The Dream-Mirror Remnant is an Abyss Crystal that Skirk gave the Traveler, received at the end of the quest Unbounded in Version 5.7. When worn, it can be used during sleep to "dream-mirror" with her; using it again lets the holder revisit certain scenes from what happened during that case.

It is a quest item (listed as 4-star), not equipment. It belongs to the closing stretch of Skirk's Crystallina Chapter, Act I (Whispers Betwixt Stars and Night), after the Traveler and Skirk beat the Khaenri'ahn man Skofnungr in the Abyssal space near the Chasm.

The description frames it as a keepsake of a two-way exchange: to find the culprit, Skirk entered the Traveler's dreams, while the Traveler saw memories deep within her heart. The item preserves that experience as something that can be revisited.

Appearance: Described only as an Abyss Crystal that is worn. No shape, colour or setting is given in canon text read. The item page shows five illustrated scenes, each with a short, poetic caption.

The captions evoke a view of the universe far above the sky, a nest burning with hatchlings unable to fly, a broken frame under dim stars, a fledgling bound by cobwebs setting out on a new journey, and lost people far from home who may share a common solitude. These are the item's own words; whether each maps to a specific memory is not stated.

Lore: Skirk, Surtalogi's disciple, is an outsider who visits Teyvat to grow stronger. In Whispers Betwixt Stars and Night she offers to dream-mirror with the Traveler and Paimon so she can experience the Traveler's stolen-soul dream herself. Later, while the Traveler sleeps, they wander through Skirk's inner world and see her memories.

In the quests, those memories include fragments of her childhood on her home planet, training under Surtalogi, and arriving in Teyvat. In Heart and Mind the Traveler reaches Skirk's inner world, a shattered river that stands for her emotions, and helps her accept the emotions she had suppressed. In Unbounded Skirk is restored to full strength and the Traveler and she defeat the culprit, Skofnungr, who stole part of her power.

Skirk gave the Traveler the crystal as a gift after this. The description casts the memory-viewing as mutual: she infiltrated the Traveler's dreams to find the culprit, and the Traveler saw her heart in return. Skirk had earlier asked the Traveler to keep what they saw secret from Paimon, which gives the keepsake some weight as a shared secret, though the item text itself says nothing of that.

Context for the "case" the item commemorates: the culprit, Skofnungr, was a Khaenri'ahn friend of Surtalogi who had grafted flesh of the All-Devouring Narwhal into his heart and stole part of Skirk's power (and, per Skirk, a fragment of the Traveler's soul) by exploiting their ability to purify Abyssal energy. At the end Skirk offered to shatter his consciousness and the power inside it so that his mind and body could regenerate under the curse of immortality, and he accepted. The Traveler's dream-mirror view of Skirk's memories happened earlier in that same quest chain; the crystal is a remembrance of the whole episode rather than of the final fight alone.

Owners: The Traveler holds it; Skirk is the giver.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (labelled as mechanics): quest reward in Unbounded alongside Primogems, Mora and other materials. It is a non-equippable quest item.

171.content:
The Dream-Mirror Remnant is the Abyss Crystal Skirk gave the Traveler after the events of Unbounded. Worn in sleep, it opens a "dream-mirror" with her and can replay certain scenes from the case in which she and the Traveler tracked down Skofnungr.

Dream-mirroring first appears in Whispers Betwixt Stars and Night, when Skirk offers to experience the Traveler's dream herself. The Traveler then sees fragments of Skirk's inner world, which is why the crystal is described as the Traveler witnessing the memories deep within her heart.

172.content:
Dull Golden Bridle (also: Dull Golden Bridle of Byakuyakoku): The Dull Golden Bridle is a quest item found in Enkanomiya's library ruin during the world quest The Subterranean Trials of Drake and Serpent. Its description calls it the hereditary national treasure of Byakuyakoku, drained of all power.

The power was removed deliberately, so that thieves who entered by irregular means would not see its value. It is the disguised form of the Golden Bridle that the quest needs.

Appearance: No in-world description of its look is given. Enjou, the guide, says the Golden Bridle is a device smaller than an armful and not a rope; the name comes from a Byakuyakoku legend in which the sun and moon were moved by the chariots of the gods.

Lore: The item text says it is Byakuyakoku's hereditary national treasure and has lost all its own power, a measure meant to stop intruders from recognising its worth. The full Golden Bridle, per its own item text, represents the highest authority in Byakuyakoku and lets its wielder control Evernight and Whitenight.

In the quest Enjou, a self-described researcher, explains that the people of Byakuyakoku, saved by the Great Serpent, left the depths for the surface, and that the library was one of the facilities the people of Watatsumi archived afterwards. To ease later trials the Bridle was moved to the back of the library. Finding it is the first part of the trial and is needed to bring down the barrier around the Dainichi Mikoshi.

Enjou also notes that ordinary intruders could not get far: the trial does not activate without the Key of the Moon-Bathed Deep, and they could not read Byakuyakoku's script. Later the Bridle serves as the core of the Reins, to which three other fragments must be fitted. Completing the quest gives the ability to switch freely between Whitenight and Evernight.

The quest belongs to the series From Dusk to Dawn in Byakuyakoku and was commissioned by Tsuyuko of Sangonomiya Shrine, who wanted the Bloodbranch Coral for Watatsumi Island. After the Bridle is handed over in part one, three side quests (The Trail of Drake and Serpent, The Heart of Ouroboros, Dreams in the Gaps) gather three fragments, which Aru says must be pieced with the Bridle as the core of the Reins. No later content through 7.1 was found to give the object new significance.

Owners: No named owner. It is held by the Traveler during the quest and handed to Enjou to disable the barrier. Its nominal owner is the nation of Byakuyakoku.

Gameplay: Game mechanics only: a quest item with no combat use. The quest skips a step if the Dull Golden Bridle was picked up before the Traveler met Enjou.

173.comment: Dull Golden Bridle: Dull Golden Bridle
173.content: Byakuyakoku's hereditary treasure, found in a drained, unremarkable form in the library of Byakuyakoku so thieves would not value it. It is used in The Subterranean Trials of Drake and Serpent to open the way to the Dainichi Mikoshi, and is tied to control of Evernight and Whitenight.

174.content:
Echoes of an Offering (also: Soulscent Bloom, Jade Leaf, Symbol of Felicitation, Chalice of the Font, Flowing Rings): Echoes of an Offering is a 4- and 5-star artifact set that rewards Normal Attacks. Its five pieces (Soulscent Bloom, Jade Leaf, Symbol of Felicitation, Chalice of the Font, Flowing Rings) carry item text made of Chenyu Vale legends: tea served when the spiritscent flowers bloom at Qiaoying Village, the first tea tree, a jade split into hidden pieces, and the friendship of the vale's adepti.

Added in version 2.6. The pieces are told as tales and rumours, and mostly name no one; the wiki ties the unnamed figures to the Herblord and the carp adeptus Fujin (see uncertainties).

Appearance: Jade ornaments with a water-and-tea theme: a jade carved as a flower, a leaf-shaped jade pendant, a circular jade loop that sounds like running water, a small teacup that holds a spring and the reflected sun and moon, and a pair of jade earrings.

Lore: The pieces recount Qiaoying Village's tea ceremony, the first tea tree planted in Chenyu Vale, a rain-bringing jade split into hidden pieces, and a pair of adepti friends, one bound to water and one to the mountain.

Soulscent Bloom: Qiaoying Village holds a tea-serving ceremony each year when the Spiritscent Flowers bloom, and remembers a vanished adeptus nicknamed the Herblord, of whom there are many foggy legends. Jade Leaf: long ago, before the ford existed, someone planted the first tea tree on the Herblord's mountain, promising friends tea once it grew; the tree's branches were later grafted across the river by mountain people, and tea spread from Chenyu Vale to Liyue Harbor. Symbol of Felicitation: a jade ornament said to come from the long-sealed Mt. Laixin; rumours say the mountain's master split a rain-bringing jade into pieces and hid them from demons, and the ornament sounds like flowing water. Chalice of the Font: a gift cup with a tiny spring-fed realm inside, which a water-bound adeptus took on a journey to Liyue Harbor, and whose shape later became the common teacup. Flowing Rings: variants of the legend of a precious gem lost to the waters, ending with koi leaving the water to fly on the wind.
The pieces share a frame: a pair of adepti who were close friends, one tied to the water, one tied to the mountain. Soulscent Bloom ends with a moment in which a young lady scrambles ashore, jokes angrily with the one who made her swim, and the glittering figure sinks never to return. Jade Leaf has the mountain's master returning later in a changed form and no longer able to untie the pendant, and says the vale's tea trees thrive only in Chenyu Vale because they remember a promise made beside the sapling. Symbol of Felicitation has a priest showing the jade to a friend every year before a departure, while the friend, busy grinding herbs, does not listen; artisans of Yilong Wharf still make such loops, and merchants hold them to their ears to hear rain on stone. Chalice of the Font describes a water adeptus who compared herself to the yaksha and judged herself luckier, whose inherited rites kept her from living long on land, and who imagined Liyue Harbor as a distant dream.

In the item text the figures are anonymous, and the wiki marks them as Fujin (the carp planter and cup-owner) and the Herblord (the mountain's master). The set's own treatment is selective: Flowing Rings explicitly offers several 'tributaries' of one legend and lets the reader choose. Jade Leaf's promise to invite Cloud Retainer and Mountain Shaper to the tea, and Chalice of the Font's reference to the Guili Assembly and the harbour city, place the story in the age before Liyue Harbor, which fits the text's own phrase that the sweet waters did not flow across Liyue in such abundance then. The Chalice names no cause for the fate of the yaksha it mentions; it only contrasts that with the speaker's own lot.

Owners: No owner is named. The pieces speak of a young lady master of a mountain, a priest, and a friend who carries a teacup; the wiki ties these to the Herblord and Fujin.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): obtained from The Lost Valley domain and the Artifact Strongbox. 2-piece: ATK +18%. 4-piece: Normal Attack hits have a 36% chance to trigger Valley Rite, increasing Normal Attack DMG by 70% of ATK until the next Normal Attack deals damage; each failure raises the next chance by 20%; triggers at most once per 0.2s.

175.comment: Echoes of an Offering: Echoes of an Offering
175.content: Artifact set whose item text collects Chenyu Vale legends: Qiaoying Village's tea ceremony, the vale's first tea tree, a sacred jade split and hidden, and the friendship of the adepti.

176.comment: Echoes of an Offering: The first tea tree of Chenyu Vale
176.content: In Jade Leaf, the first tea tree was planted on the Herblord's hillside by someone who promised to brew tea for friends, including Cloud Retainer and Mountain Shaper, once it grew. A jade pendant was tied to its branches. Mortals later grafted its branches across the river, and tea spread from Chenyu Vale to Liyue Harbor. The text says the trees thrive only in Chenyu Vale because they remember an old promise.

177.comment: Echoes of an Offering: The hidden jade of Mt. Laixin
177.content: Symbol of Felicitation and Flowing Rings preserve rumours that Mt. Laixin held a jade able to bring sweet rain; the mountain's master split it into pieces and hid them underwater, in hills and in shrines so that demons could not use its power. Variants say it was carved by Rex Lapis, or was merely a lesser jade or a cup, or that the 'jade' is a figure of speech for a beautiful person. Treat all as legend.

178.content:
Electro Gnosis (also: Inazuma's Gnosis, Ei's Gnosis, Gnosis of the Electro Archon, Electro Archon's Gnosis): The Electro Gnosis is the Gnosis of Inazuma's Electro Archon: a small object shaped like a chess piece that connects an Archon to Celestia. Ei, the Raiden Shogun, gave it up and entrusted it to Yae Miko. Yae traded it to the Fatui Harbinger the Balladeer (Scaramouche) to save the Traveler. In Sumeru, Nahida took it from him, then gave it to the Harbinger Dottore. As of 7.1 it is one of the six Gnoses held by the Tsaritsa.

Ei had no further use for it once she withdrew into the Plane of Euthymia and left Inazuma to her puppet, the Shogun. She told Yae she had cut her ties with Celestia. Paimon learned only after Signora's death that the Fatui had in fact got Inazuma's Gnosis.

Appearance: Like the other Gnoses it looks like a small, gleaming chess piece; Yae Miko calls it "the little thing that looks something like a chess piece." A Gnosis normally rests inside an Archon's chest and can be drawn out or made to appear. The source texts read for this entry do not describe how the Electro Gnosis differs in look from the others.

Lore: A Gnosis grants and strengthens elemental power and links its holder to Celestia; Nahida calls the Gnoses symbols of the Heavenly Principles' control over Teyvat and its "laws." Archons keep their thrones and their power without one: Ei is still the Electro Archon after giving hers away.

Ei had first tried to turn the Gnosis into an energy supply device, but none of her techniques had any effect on it. She then gave it to Yae Miko, her old friend, knowing Yae might "sell" it but would only do so for something of equal value. Yae kept it at the Grand Narukami Shrine. When the Traveler fell into the Balladeer's trap at the Fatui's Delusion factory and collapsed, Yae gave him the Gnosis in exchange for the Traveler's safety, judging it useless to Ei and a likely source of conflict.

The Balladeer was Ei's prototype puppet. Yae says Ei built him before her final puppet, then sealed his power instead of destroying him. The artifact Song of Life says he was made as a vessel for a "heart", that Ei later dropped designs able to hold such a heart, and that the "proof" which then had no home went to the great shrine. In the Fatui, the Balladeer took the Gnosis and then broke off contact. At Signora's funeral, Capitano asked Dottore about Scaramouche and the Gnosis; Dottore said only that he was waiting for Scaramouche to move first.

Yae's line to Paimon after the deal: she was not the sort to risk her life for "any old reason," and judging by the results she had struck a good bargain. Paimon agreed the Traveler was worth more than a Gnosis. The Song of Life text says the heart the puppet finally got held no blessings, only selfishness, hypocrisy, cunning and curses, yet tearing it out would leave him unable to feel anything at all.

Owners: Ei (Raiden Shogun) -> Yae Miko -> the Balladeer (Scaramouche, later the Wanderer) -> Nahida -> Dottore -> the Tsaritsa (Anastasya).

- Ei: original holder as Electro Archon. Canon does not say whether her twin Makoto, the earlier Raiden Shogun, ever held it.
- Yae Miko: kept it for Ei, then traded it away during the Inazuma Archon Quest (2.1).
- The Balladeer: used it as the core of the Sumeru god-creation plan (3.2).
- Nahida: took it from him after his defeat (3.2).
- Dottore: received it from Nahida in a bargain, and also got her Dendro Gnosis (3.2).
- The Tsaritsa: Dottore presented both Gnoses to her at Zapolyarny Palace.

Sumeru: In Sumeru, Dottore and four sages of the Akademiya altered the Balladeer so the Gnosis could power him as a new God of Wisdom. Joined to it, he could call down lightning and change the weather: he struck Fatui soldiers with a living-seeming lightning storm at Pardis Dhyai. Encased in a giant machine with the Gnosis as its power source, he became Shouki no Kami, the Everlasting Lord of Arcane Wisdom. He claimed that strife is "engraved upon every god and every Gnosis"; Nahida took this as a reference to the Archon War.

After the Traveler and Nahida defeated him, Nahida pulled the Gnosis from the machine's core. The Balladeer, whose obsessions it now held, begged her not to and fell from the shell in despair. With the power of another Gnosis, Nahida could reach the last memory of Greater Lord Rukkhadevata. Dottore's Omega segment then arrived. He pointed out that she could not use the Electro Gnosis in battle. Nahida threatened to destroy it and asked whether that would wake the Heavenly Principles. She judged that a foreign Gnosis would only bring disaster to Sumeru, and gave it to him on condition that he erase all his other segments. He agreed, then also traded knowledge of the "false sky" for her Dendro Gnosis.

Nahida's character story says she barely knew more about the Gnoses than about the truth of the world: to her a Gnosis was a core that gathers elemental power at will. That left her wondering why a god would want them all.

Status as of 7.1: Dottore later recalled, in memories recovered from Irminsul's burnt trunk (6.6), presenting the two Gnoses to the Tsaritsa as battle trophies. As of 7.1 the Tsaritsa holds six Gnoses, Electro among them; only the Pyro Gnosis is missing.

In "Light and Shadow, Intertwined" (7.1) the Tsaritsa told the Traveler that the Gnoses, formed from the Third Descender's remains, amplify their bearers' power, and that only a Gnosis responds to the seal he left in her palace; she hopes it may open once his remains are no longer scattered. In the 7.1 Archon Quest "A Rekviem for the Underworld", she arranged the six Gnoses as energy nodes around a hall of Zapolyarny Palace. Her Cryo power, greatly enhanced by them, slowed time there while she stalled Rhinedottir over tea. The resurrection window Rhinedottir had agreed with Ronova, meant to bypass the Heavenly Principles' monitoring, passed unnoticed, and Celestia reclaimed Ronova's Authority of Death. The Tsaritsa said the Gnoses were only one part of it; her own insights from the past thousand years mattered too.

Gameplay: Gameplay note: the Electro Gnosis is a story object. It cannot be obtained, equipped or used by the player.

179.comment: Electro Gnosis: Ei entrusts the Gnosis to Yae Miko
179.content: Ei set the Gnosis aside before withdrawing into the Plane of Euthymia, after failing to turn it into an energy supply. She gave it to Yae Miko on the understanding that Yae might trade it, but never at a loss. Yae kept it at the Grand Narukami Shrine. Then the Traveler fell into the Balladeer's trap at the Fatui's Delusion factory, and Yae gave him the Gnosis in exchange for the Traveler's safety. She told the Traveler and Paimon only afterwards, in the Archon Quest "Wishes" (2.1).

180.comment: Electro Gnosis: Shouki no Kami and the Gnosis
180.content: Shouki no Kami was the false god the Balladeer became in Sumeru, built around his puppet body and a giant machine powered by the Electro Gnosis. Nahida defeated him with the Traveler's help and extracted the Gnosis. Losing it left the Balladeer in despair, since it had come to hold his obsessions.

181.comment: Electro Gnosis: Nahida's bargain with Dottore
181.content: Nahida could not use the Electro Gnosis in battle and would not keep a foreign Gnosis in Sumeru. She used it as leverage, threatening to destroy it, and Dottore's Omega segment agreed to erase all his other segments to get it. He then traded knowledge of the false sky for her own Dendro Gnosis and took both Gnoses to the Tsaritsa.

182.comment: Electro Gnosis: The six Gnoses in Zapolyarny Palace
182.content: In "A Rekviem for the Underworld" (7.1), the Tsaritsa placed her six Gnoses, the Electro Gnosis among them, as nodes of a field in her palace. Her Cryo power, enhanced by them, slowed time in that hall. This kept Rhinedottir from completing the resurrection she had agreed on with Ronova before the Heavenly Principles' monitoring cycle came around.

183.content:
Elegy for the End (also: The Parting Refrain, Millennial Movement: Farewell Song): Elegy for the End is a five-star bow released in version 1.4, one of the Millennial Movement weapons, each of which carries a song of Mondstadt's history. Its story tells of the Cataclysm, when a venomous dragon crushed the land, and of a dour knight who could be made to forget his duty only by a girl's song. He fell in the battle; she came home to find the song changed.

Appearance: The item text describes no particular look for the bow beyond comparing it to a bard's lyre: "a bow as lovely as any bard's lyre", whose arrows pierce the heart like a lamenting sigh. Its in-game passive effect is shown as a lyre string lighting up.

Lore: The story opens with a verse about the wind carrying wine's fragrance, news from the mountains and longing. Long ago there was a knight (Rostam) who was always grave, and only one song and one girl who sang it in the square could make him forget his burden. Then the Cataclysm came, and a venomous dragon, Durin, drowned the songs and ripped apart the cries and flames. The Anemo Archon, though he had refused to rule, heard the agony; to protect his old friends' dream he woke and flew into battle beside the sky dragon, Dvalin. The knight and his knights fought as well.

When the venomous dragon fell on the ice-sealed peak (Dragonspine), the blue sky dragon fell asleep in the ancient tower (Stormterror's Lair). The knight lay spent in the valley, and as he fell he thought that she was studying abroad and so must be safe, and that he wished to hear her sing again; he also took comfort that Arundolyn and Roland were all right, believing the calamity would blow over before she returned.

Many songs praised the Archon and recorded the battle of the two dragons, but they were slowly lost. The girl's own song changed on her return: where it once spoke of summer wind, grain and the wind that fetched her love's gaze, it now ends with "no wind in any season" bringing him back. After her voice and tears ran dry she swore to use her life's flame to cleanse the world's crookedness. The Millennial Movement series page summarises this as the girl devoting her life to burning away the world's evil. Which historical girl this is rests on the wiki's link to Signora rather than a printed name.

Owners: No canon owner is named. The story concerns Rostam and the girl but does not say the bow was theirs. The bow is a song-weapon in the series sense, not an inherited relic.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star bow from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 46, secondary stat Energy Recharge 12%. Passive "The Parting Refrain": raises Elemental Mastery; Elemental Skill or Burst hits give a Sigil of Remembrance, and at four Sigils all are consumed and nearby party members get "Millennial Movement: Farewell Song" for 12 seconds (more Elemental Mastery and ATK), then a 20-second lockout. Buffs of the same Millennial Movement type do not stack.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): suited to scenes about parting, songs that outlive their singers and the cost of the Cataclysm. Do not state the girl is Signora to a character who has no way to know it.

184.content: The knight in the Elegy for the End story is Rostam according to the wiki's link. The text calls him a knight who was ever dour and fought with his knights against the venomous dragon, dying in the valley. No further detail is printed in the item.

185.comment: Elegy for the End: Millennial Movement series
185.content: The Millennial Movement series is the wiki's (unofficial) name for five-star Mondstadt weapons built around songs of the country's history: Freedom-Sworn (the rebellion against Decarabian), Song of Broken Pines (the fight against the corrupt nobility) and Elegy for the End (the Cataclysm). Each grants party-wide effects after collecting Sigils, and same-type effects do not stack.

key: Emblem of Severed Fate artifact set
186.content:
Emblem of Severed Fate (also: Emblem of Severed Fate artifact set, Magnificent Tsuba, Sundered Feather, Storm Cage, Scarlet Vessel, Ornate Kabuto): Emblem of Severed Fate is a 4 and 5 star Inazuma artifact set. Its five item texts tell, in fragments, of the half-oni swordsman Iwakura Michihiro, also called Douin, and of the black-winged tengu Teruyo of Yougou who gave him his new name and fought him in thirteen yearly duels. Mechanically it rewards Energy Recharge with Elemental Burst damage.

The set is dropped by the Momiji-Dyed Court domain on Yashiori Island. The texts read as memory and farewell: a mother lost to a failed bid for glory under the Shogun's banner, a son starting over under a new name, a tengu who cannot keep a promise, and a friend's broken seal cage. Several of the narrated people also appear in the Amethyst Series weapons Amenoma Kageuchi, Katsuragikiri Nagamasa and Hakushin Ring.

Reading the five pieces together gives a compact tragedy in two strands. One is Michihiro's: disgrace of his house, exile in a village, renaming, duels, and the final strike that ends the duels and makes his career. The other is the Storm Cage's, a separate and more melancholy memory of a gambler, a seal cage and a promise that could not be kept, told by an unnamed narrator who is not Michihiro.

Appearance: Five pieces: Magnificent Tsuba (flower, an ornate sword hand guard said to belong to a blade given to an oni who betrayed the Shogun), Sundered Feather (plume, the black feather of a tengu warrior kept as a swordsman's souvenir), Storm Cage (sands, an inro-style seal cage with pansies on a black ground, inlaid shell and gold work), Scarlet Vessel (goblet, a finely made wine vessel once drunk from by a famous martial artist), and Ornate Kabuto (circlet, a sturdy noble samurai's helmet).

Lore: The texts follow Michihiro, the son of an oni mother who lost her standing with the Shogun. After his family's fall he lived in seclusion; a black-winged tengu, Teruyo of Yougou, renamed him "Iwakura" (a seat of rock) to free him from the burden of oni blood and challenged him to yearly duels.

The pieces dwell on a fallen oni house, a renaming and a long rivalry: the mother of the Mikoshi line turned on the Shogun and was ruined; her son withdrew from the clan; the tengu renamed him Iwakura, and after thirteen years of duels he finally touched her, breaking his sword and her shrine. He then became the Kujou Clan's sword instructor, "Douin".

Magnificent Tsuba: the mother, of the war-oni line, had been shown kindness by the Shogun and given a prized sword. She turned on the Shogun and ended in ruin, and only the sword's guard came back to the Mikoshi Clan. Her eldest son, who should have inherited, withdrew to a village outside the city. A tengu with black wings gave him the name Iwakura, told him that names given by the Yougou Tengu carry divine blessing, and set a duel for the next cherry-blossom season, promising that if he could touch her he could name his secret blade for a victory over a tengu.

Sundered Feather and Scarlet Vessel: after thirteen years of duels in the courtyard of a small branch shrine, Michihiro finally cut her black feathers and caught her. His sword broke from his own strength, and the shrine was wrecked. She said the tengu had duties to her clan, told him to forget her, and urged him to use his sword for the Iwakura line and make a path of his own. He became the Kujou Clan's sword instructor, earned the title "Douin" and founded a successful school, and later walked into the ruined branch shrine remembering her and the thirteen years that passed like a dream.

Ornate Kabuto is a brief exchange with a young head of the Kanjou Commission, Hiroshi, who built up Ritou, asking Douin whether his sword could cut lightning. Douin says at most it could strike a tengu from the air, though no tengu has ever been brought down. Hiroshi says he would have recruited him had the old Kujou not moved first, and that with such a sword even Ako Domeki of Seirai would be no match. The passage closes on Douin's memory of the tengu who gave him a new name and a new life, throwing him a rusty blade and telling him to strike her down, and the words she spoke to him after the blade broke.

Storm Cage is separate in tone. It describes a time before Seirai Island was wrapped in storm clouds, and a seal cage that holds thunderstorms and tremors and could not be delivered to the one it was promised to. A rough but affectionate exchange follows between the narrator and a gambling, wandering samurai who is also a Hatamoto and a married man; the narrator mended his broken seal cage, he offered to teach tengu archery, spoke of Teruyo of the shrine and of nightmares in which he cut off his own head, and took the narrator to watch ships in the harbour. Long afterward the narrator stood on the heights again, holding the cage she had made, gathering thunder in hope of retrieving those memories and praying for the gambler's safety. The text mentions "Lady Saiguu", linking it to the Kitsune Saiguu's circle.

Trivia and cross-references: the Amethyst weapon Amenoma Kageuchi (Michihiro's blade line, with his Tengu Sweeper technique said to need a heart without confusion), Katsuragikiri Nagamasa (belonging to Mikoshi Nagamasa, adoptive brother of Michihiro, though he is not named in this set), and Hakushin Ring (narrated by the Kitsune Saiguu) all intersect with these texts. The weapon text for Amenoma Kageuchi says the Tengu Sweeper was first performed in the courtyard of a small shrine where incense no longer burned, broke Douin's sword in two, and that the Iwakura Art grew from it.

Owners: No named owner holds the set. The pieces are described as belonging to or associated with Michihiro (hand guard, feather, vessel), the Kitsune Saiguu's circle (seal cage), and an unnamed noble samurai (helmet).

Gameplay: Gameplay, not lore: the 2-piece bonus is Energy Recharge +20%. The 4-piece bonus increases Elemental Burst damage by 25% of the wearer's Energy Recharge, up to 75%. The set drops from the Momiji-Dyed Court domain on Yashiori Island, and a strongbox variant exists. It first appeared in Version 2.0.

187.comment: Emblem of Severed Fate: Iwakura Michihiro (Douin) in the artifact texts
187.content: In the Emblem of Severed Fate texts, Michihiro was born into the Mikoshi line of war-oni, withdrew to a village after his mother's disgrace, and was renamed "Iwakura" by the tengu Teruyo to free him from his oni heritage. After thirteen years of duels he perfected the Tengu Sweeper, became the Kujou Clan's sword instructor with the title Douin, and founded a successful school. The weapon Amenoma Kageuchi, a copy of the sword Hakuen Michimitsu Amenoma, descends from his school; the weapon text says he gave a copy to the Saimon Clan for sheltering him in Konda Village.

188.comment: Emblem of Severed Fate: Teruyo of Yougou
188.content: A black-winged tengu who, in the set's texts, gave Michihiro the name Iwakura, fought him in yearly duels at a small branch shrine, and was finally touched by him after thirteen years. She told him tengu names carry blessings and that she had duties to her clan; she said goodbye and asked him to forget her. A line in the Storm Cage mentions "Teruyo of the shrine" inheriting her master's beauty and skill, but the set says no more of her.

189.content:
Engulfing Lightning (also: Kusanagi no Inabikari, Ei's naginata, the Shogun's naginata): Engulfing Lightning is the polearm (a naginata) of Ei, the Electro Archon who rules Inazuma through her puppet, the Raiden Shogun. Its item text calls it a lethal weapon for cutting away "scattered dross" and speaks of Ei's vow to prune mortal obsession and unchecked desire in order to keep an unchanging, eternal world. Its Japanese name means roughly "grass-cutting lightning".

It is a 5-star polearm of the Inazuma weapon series. The Raiden Shogun uses a polearm in ordinary combat and switches to the sword Musou Isshin for her Elemental Burst.

Appearance: A long-hafted naginata, a polearm with a curved blade, charged with Electro. Its in-game model gains a more ornate form at the second ascension phase. Canon text gives no materials or measurements beyond calling it a naginata; the writers have said only that the weapon Ei used to slay Orobashi weighed thousands of tons (see uncertainties).

Lore: The weapon's story is told as Ei's reflection. From high above the storm clouds she looked on the mortal world she loved and saw petty disputes and fleeting obsessions that, to her, were enemies of eternity. Like weeds among crops, they had to be swept away by lightning, so that nothing needed to wither or be lost.

The text recalls a remembered scene under the sakura tree: Yae Miko, drinking wine with Ei, asked what kind of eternity Makoto's eyes would reflect. Ei dismisses it as a pointless question, though the answer she gave was lost to the alcohol. She had already settled the matter countless times in memory: just as fruit trees are thinned for quality, so not one speck of dross could be allowed in an eternal paradise.

The passage then turns to what drives her. She imagines using a great blade of light to uproot all obsession and to remove the chance of any dream taking root and withering, producing a tranquil world with no dispute, gain or loss, but an "amnesiac world, lost to itself". Her old friends still appear clearly in the heart of eternity and the scent of the sakura is still fresh. Having watched the Cataclysm's pitch-dark annihilation consume those precious to her, she regards the impermanence of life and death, and destiny itself, as her mortal foe. Since no one can overturn impermanence, the text ends by saying the eternal euthymia in her heart should be carried forward into the nation she loves, Inazuma.

Read with the rest of the Inazuma story, this is the philosophy behind her pursuit of eternity and the Plane of Euthymia: eternity as protection against loss. The item text itself stops at her resolve and never shows the change of heart she later reaches in the Archon Quest; do not attach that resolution to the weapon's own text.

Owners: Ei is the wielder the text names. The Raiden Shogun, her puppet, fights with the same style of polearm.

Ei's other signature blade, Musou Isshin, belonged first to her sister Makoto and is a separate object (see the Musou Isshin entry). No present-day character other than Ei is established as owning Engulfing Lightning.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star polearm in the Inazuma series, released in Version 2.1 and obtainable from the weapon event Wish. Base ATK 46 with Energy Recharge as its secondary stat.

Its passive, Timeless Dream: Eternal Stove, raises ATK by a percentage of the wielder's Energy Recharge above the base 100% (capped), and grants extra Energy Recharge for 12 seconds after using an Elemental Burst. Refinement scales these values: at refinement 1 the conversion is 28% of surplus Energy Recharge, capped at 80% ATK, and at refinement 5 it is 56%, capped at 120%.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: treat the weapon as Ei's personal symbol, not as something handed out. A scene may invoke it as the instrument of her old pursuit of eternity; do not give it to other characters as an heirloom, and do not claim canon says where the physical weapon is kept.

190.comment: Engulfing Lightning: Timeless Dream: Eternal Stove
190.content: Timeless Dream: Eternal Stove is the weapon passive of Engulfing Lightning (gameplay). Mechanically it converts surplus Energy Recharge into ATK and adds Energy Recharge after an Elemental Burst; its title echoes the weapon's theme of an unchanging, timeless dream of eternity.

191.content:
Envoy's Medal (also: Envoy's Medal of the Tsaritsa, Tsaritsa's special envoy medal): The Envoy's Medal is a medal the Tsaritsa gave the Traveler at Zapolyarny Palace in Version 7.1. It is proof that the Traveler is her special envoy, officially titled "Consultant to the Tsaritsa", and it gives unrestricted access to Zapolyarny Palace.

The Traveler did not swear fealty to the court, so the Tsaritsa chose the looser title of Consultant rather than a formal court position. The medal is the token of that arrangement.

Lore: The in-game description calls it a medal specially bestowed by the Tsaritsa, bearing the weight of her authority, proof of the holder's status as her envoy, with unrestricted access to Zapolyarny Palace.

It was awarded in the quest A Letter From Zapolyarny Palace. Vesna sent the Traveler and Paimon a cheerful letter promising a "prize" after some formalities. At the palace they found the Tsaritsa (Anastasya), Vesna, Danica and her secretary Chayka. Vesna proposed the Traveler as the Tsaritsa's new adviser: someone of great skill who belongs to no faction, to carry out decrees that ministers handle poorly and the military would overshadow. Danica doubted anyone who comes and goes freely would carry out orders without hesitation.

The Tsaritsa explained that she wanted to understand her nation from a viewpoint outside military and political affairs. She said she cannot walk among her people as a god and ruler, and that her Harbingers, as court ministers, are shaped by their ties to her and by the interests at stake. The Traveler first asked what the decrees were for, then declined to become a servant of the court but offered to help as a friend. In return the Tsaritsa asked what the Traveler does while traveling other nations; the Traveler answered with stories of great events and also small amusing details. She accepted on the condition that the Traveler travel through Snezhnaya in the same way.

She then told Chayka to record the title "Consultant to the Tsaritsa" and to issue proof of the role, granting authority to carry out its duties. Chayka was assigned to receive the Traveler at audiences and arrange needed resources. Obtaining the Envoy's Medal is the result.

The quest is the first part of Secret Tsarist Assignment, a reputation system tied to the Tsaritsa at Zapolyarny Palace, with Chayka as the contact; the next quest in the chain is The Tsaritsa's New Portrait. The quest is a world quest and is permanent, not a limited event. Danica's reservation is the main in-story resistance: she accepts the Traveler's skill but not the idea of an unbound outsider handling the Tsaritsa's orders.

Owners: Held by the Traveler. Bestowed by the Tsaritsa; Vesna championed the Traveler for the role and Danica voiced reservations.

Gameplay: Gameplay note: a quest item received on completing A Letter From Zapolyarny Palace. It does not itself appear as a usable item in play, and the invitation letter that leads to it is read through quest navigation rather than the inventory.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (project guidance, not canon): the medal works as a pass in scenes at Zapolyarny Palace, and as a reminder that the Traveler holds a consultant's title on friendly terms rather than service. Avoid treating it as a rank within the Fatui or as a vow of loyalty; the Traveler explicitly refused to be a servant of the court.

Status as of 7.1: The Traveler holds the medal as of Version 7.1.

Nothing in the canon read suggests it has been revoked.

192.comment: Envoy's Medal: Consultant to the Tsaritsa
192.content: The title the Tsaritsa gave the Traveler in A Letter From Zapolyarny Palace instead of a court post, because the Traveler would not swear fealty. It comes with the Envoy's Medal as proof, and the authority to carry out the position's duties. Chayka, the Tsaritsa's secretary, is the contact for questions and arrangements.

193.content:
Etherlight Spindlelute (also: Last Singer): Etherlight Spindlelute is a 4-star catalyst: a lute whose golden strings shine like sunlight, which appears to be a relic from the Seelie of old.
