Owners: Only an unnamed exalted Harmost of the distant past, according to legend.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not story. Passive Day and Night in Counterpoint rotates a 10-second Harmonic Movement (ATK, Elemental Mastery, Stellar Glimmer reaction DMG) that works even when the wielder is off-field, and a Stellar Glimmer reaction adds a 12-second Contrapuntal instance. Base ATK 42, CRIT Rate 6% secondary stat.

246.content:
Fractured Halo (also: Purifying Crown, Electrifying Edict): A spinning mechanical blade produced by the Clink-Clank Krumkake Craftshop, seeming to hide secrets from a bygone era. A 5-star polearm from Version 5.8, wielded by Ineffa.

Its item text is Ineffa's fragmentary memory of the age of the three moons.

Appearance: A spinning, halo-like mechanical blade with a cyclonic mechanism whose centre holds a hidden remnant of the Moon. In her portrait art and demo Ineffa carries the unascended version.

Lore: After her revival, Ineffa remembers an age even bards forget, but her memories feel hollow, like thoughts flaring and fading in a trance.

She recalls following the Master of Light and Flame to visit the moon-dwelling wills on their three jade thrones, at a time when the king who set the moons aloft had vanished into the fog between the stars. The Master received only three silences in three palace halls.

The king had sought the world beyond, and the moons governed the cycles in his place. A reaver from beyond the skies replaced the primordial creator and took the vows that kept the world turning. When the king returned corrupted by darkness his fury was boundless; the Master of Light and Flame, waking from feigned death, stopped the lords and the regent from exploring the stars and replicating moon-forging. Whether the jade-crowned goddesses truly betrayed the dragonborn kingdom is left open, and none who knew the answer survived the war.

Ineffa tells the girl who rebuilt her body and forged her weapon (Aino) that these snapshots are all she can recall. Aino, clever, suppresses her own inquiring gaze, and it becomes Ineffa's private secret that when the heavenly ring shattered, a jade plate fell from the sky. The dragons cheered the death of the moons that had betrayed them, but she remembered the silent shadows in their palaces quietly hiding the fallen Moon's remnant. That remnant now sits at the centre of the cyclonic mechanism, hidden where no one else will know. The text describes the snowfields turning to blackened earth and volcanoes clogging with ice as an after-effect of the silences.

Owners: Ineffa wields it; the text says Aino forged it for her.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star polearm, CRIT DMG secondary. Passive Purifying Crown raises ATK for 20 seconds after a Skill or Burst, and if the wielder creates a shield the party deals more Lunar-Charged damage.

How {{char}} behaves: Ineffa treats it as hers and as a keeper of a secret; she does not volunteer the hidden remnant to others. Keep the ancient-war memories as uncertain recollection.

247.content: Purifying Crown is the weapon's passive; Electrifying Edict is the party buff it grants. Mechanics are in the gameplay section.

key: The Grand Jape of the Turning of Fate
248.content:
Fragment of Harmonic Whimsy (also: Harmonious Symphony Prelude, Ancient Sea's Nocturnal Musing, The Grand Jape of the Turning of Fate, Ichor Shower Rhapsody, Whimsical Dance of the Withered): Fragment of Harmonic Whimsy is a 4- and 5-star artifact set from Fontaine, added in Version 4.6. Its five pieces are written as one story: Remus, a god who lost his homeland, becomes the God King of Remuria, is told that his glorious empire will drown, and chooses to fight fate with a "Grand Symphony." The set is a Remurian legend, not a family heirloom.

The bonuses reward the Bond of Life mechanic (see gameplay). The five pieces are Harmonious Symphony Prelude (flower), Ancient Sea's Nocturnal Musing (plume), The Grand Jape of the Turning of Fate (sands), Ichor Shower Rhapsody (goblet) and Whimsical Dance of the Withered (circlet).

Appearance: The flower is described as an honorary medal in the shape of a blooming flower, adorned with blue stone and gold, once bestowed upon immortals. The other pieces are known only by their names and lore text.

Lore: The five pieces run in order: a homeless desert god meets the prophet Sybilla and is told he will rule the High Sea; he builds a glorious kingdom yet grieves at its foretold fall; he confronts a vishap prince and the imprisoned Mistress of Many Waters and finds no salvation; as Sebastos he resolves to compose his own symphony against fate; and after the realm sinks, a new nation of Many Waters rises.

Piece by piece, the text runs as follows.
- Harmonious Symphony Prelude: in an age when the High Sea's people were still unenlightened, a god who had lost his homeland between the scarlet sands and the murky mountains was once an oasis singer. His home fell to the Lord of the Blazing Sun, and he refused to serve the Sand King's throne, so he wandered. At the sea he stumbled into a ruined city older than the land, found a silver tree guarded by golden bees, and was told by the prophet Sybilla, once an envoy protecting the tree, that he would rule the whole High Sea, bring it civilization and justice, and be undone by that same justice. He asked whether fate left room for choice. This was the first meeting of the future king and Sybilla.
- Ancient Sea's Nocturnal Musing: the king, now glorious, built a great tower in Meropis, united scattered peoples and brought peace, but grew mournful as the prophesied century of glory wore on. His singer-advisor answered that empires rise and fall by the law of Fortuna. The king could not accept this and was told that the Mistress of Many Waters lay imprisoned in the lightless depths and might have answers.
- The Grand Jape of the Turning of Fate: before the Grand Symphony was played, the king went to find the sourcewater, fought a vishap prince who guarded the Mistress's prison for thirty days and nights, and was taken to see her. He learned terrible secrets but no salvation, since her sin and the resulting curse could not be undone. He took a cup of the purest water, vowing to seal his subjects' souls in an Ichor insoluble in water and to forge bodies of bronze and stone against time.
- Ichor Shower Rhapsody: the king, now the Sebastos, ruled from a golden capital with the Legion Athanatoi. Told his empire would fall, he searched the Musica Mundana of Fortuna for a flaw and resolved to compose his own symphony, asking Sybilla to help. His wildest hope was to put fate's baton into humanity's hands. Sybilla, in whose eyes there was already no future, agreed without hesitation.
- Whimsical Dance of the Withered: after the Domus Aurea was rubble and the judgment day came, waves sank the realm and a gray steed carried away surviving life. A new nation of Many Waters rose, and the golden authority became legend. The piece closes on the idea that dreams born of the ruins will one day merge into one.
Cross-check with wider canon (not stated in this set): Remus was a god from Sumeru whose land was conquered by King Deshret. He founded Remuria above Fontaine's waters, sharing rule with four human Harmosts. Remuria ultimately fell because of the Grand Symphony, and its end led to Egeria's return, which is why the set's dream-like tone is at odds with the empire's real fate.

Reading the pieces together, the king is never shown as a simple tyrant. Each piece frames his drive as grief at a foretold end, as the pieces describe. The set also shows how the empire's ideas of "justice and salvation", Ichor and bronze bodies were present before the catastrophe; for the Harmosts' side of the story see the Golden Troupe set.

Owners: No named owner. The set is narrative item text. Remus and Sybilla are the characters it speaks of.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): 2-piece bonus is ATK +18%. The 4-piece bonus triggers whenever the wearer's Bond of Life value increases or decreases, giving 18% increased DMG for 6s, stacking up to 3 times. It is obtained from the Faded Theater domain (located in Fontaine's Nostoi Region at Petrichor) and from the matching artifact strongbox.

Faded Theater's Ley Line Disorder also rewards Bond of Life changes with an All Elemental and Physical DMG Bonus. The domain's text describes an ancient troupe performing the elegies of an ancient civilization under an immortal musician, and monsters of unknown provenance now holding the stage.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the set as a theatrical, mournful retelling that characters in Fontaine may know as an old opera or legend. Do not present its words as proven history; Remuria's fall is better documented in books and quests than in these verses.

249.content: In the Fragment of Harmonic Whimsy, Remus is the God King of Remuria, once a singer of the oases whose homeland fell to the Lord of the Blazing Sun. He is told by the golden-bee prophet Sybilla that he will rule the High Sea and bring a justice that ruins it, and he spends his reign trying to escape that fate.

250.content: In this set Sybilla is the golden-bee prophet who once guarded the silver tree in a forgotten city below the lightless depths. She foretells Remus's rise and fall, and later agrees to help him with the Grand Symphony even though, in the text's words, her eyes already saw no future.

251.content:
Freedom-Sworn (also: Revolutionary Chorale, Millennial Movement: Song of Resistance): Freedom-Sworn is a five-star sword released in version 1.6, a Millennial Movement weapon whose story is a Mondstadt resistance song. The song says that if someone takes your tongue you can still sing with your eyes, and that stealing your song and your freedom "shall never do". It was sung through Decarabian's reign and the aristocracy's, and when five rebels climbed Decarabian's tower.

Appearance: The in-game description calls it a straight sword, "azure as antediluvian song, and as keen as the oaths of freedom taken in the Land of Wind". The text gives no further visual detail.

Lore: The item's story begins with the drinking song itself: even if your tongue is plucked out you can sing with your eyes; even if you are blinded you can see with your ears; and if someone plots to destroy tomorrow, raise them a glass, for the song will live on. It then reflects on whether the Anemo Archon's love of freedom and wine shaped the people or the people shaped him; the text says this can no longer be answered.

The song was sung in dark times: when Decarabian ruled from his gale-crowned tower, and again when the corrupt nobility (the Lawrence clan) overturned the Archon's statue. It was heard in cellars, alleys and taverns, seeped through the wind and the iron fist, and became an anthem for resisting heroes.

In the distant past a group stood before the tower, a youth, a spirit, an archer, a knight and a wandering flame-haired warrior, and swore to be free and to shatter the lone tyrant's rule. Those too weak to climb sang the song that had only been whispered where the wind did not reach, a lyre's sound finally piercing the prison of raging winds, and the chorus shook the city walls. The final verse changes the last line to: anyone who steals your song, the freedom you yearn for, will never be allowed. The wiki's series page ties the group to the Nameless Bard, Barbatos the wind spirit, Amos, Gunnhildr and the Red-Haired Warrior.

Owners: No owner is named in the text. The sword stands for the song rather than a single wielder.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star sword from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 46, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 43. Passive "Revolutionary Chorale": raises DMG (10-20%); triggering Elemental Reactions gives a Sigil of Rebellion, and at two Sigils nearby party members get "Millennial Movement: Song of Resistance" for 12 seconds (more Normal, Charged and Plunging Attack DMG and ATK), followed by a 20-second lockout. Buffs of the same type do not stack.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the song works as a toast or defiance chant at taverns. Ordinary Mondstadters can know the song; the identity of the five rebels is more specialist history.

252.content: The resistance drinking song of Mondstadt, quoted in Freedom-Sworn, is said to have been sung whenever the people were oppressed, under Decarabian and under the aristocracy. Its line "even if tomorrow dies, this song shall live on" frames music as the thing tyrants cannot remove.

253.comment: Freedom-Sworn: The climb up the tower
253.content: Freedom-Sworn lists five rebels at the tower: a youth, a spirit, an archer, a knight and a flame-haired warrior. Amos' Bow tells the same climb from the huntress's side and names only four; the wiki records that the later Freedom-Sworn text established the Red-Haired Warrior as a fifth member. In this archive the group is the Nameless Bard, Barbatos, Amos, Gunnhildr and the Red-Haired Warrior.

254.content:
Frostbearer: Frostbearer is a 4-star catalyst of the Dragonspine series. Its in-game description is "a fruit that possesses a strange, frosty will," with a faint sense of agony. It is the one weapon of the series obtained only by forging, using a diagram from the Frostbearing Tree. Added in Version 1.2.

Its text recounts the Frostbearing Tree of Sal Vindagnyr from the princess's birth to the tree's revival by dragon blood, and ends with the tree's own voice offering a bitter fruit to whoever can deliver justice on a poisoned world.

Appearance: Canon text calls it a crimson, icy fruit borne by a silver-white tree. No further physical description is given.

Lore: When the daughter of the priest of Vindagnyr was born beneath the white tree, the verdant mountain kingdom rejoiced at her blessing. Those who wrote the kingdom's annals believed that Sal Vindagnyr's blessing, like the undying silver-white tree, would last forever.

Then the nail that froze the world fell from the sky and shattered the tree. The princess took the most complete branch and tried to graft it to give the tree new life, but the grafted life did not flourish, and the snowstorm covered the moonlight like a curtain of blades.

Long afterward, when the deathmatch between the dragons of darkness and wind (Durin and Dvalin) ended and corrosive blood stained the ashen valley red, the tree remembered it had not died with the entombed city. It reached for the warm ichor in the soil. When a certain someone poured crimson essence on it, it bore one fruit with all its remaining strength.

The tree speaks last: it gives this icy fruit to those who dwelt in its shadow, the priests who eulogized it and the maiden who painted upon it, containing all the happiness they never had, and asks that it go to someone who can render recompense upon the poisonous world and carry its innocent, bitter fruit as they enact justice. Compare Snow-Tombed Starsilver, which tells the princess's and a hero's story in the same ruined kingdom.

Owners: No owner is named in canon. It is a crafted weapon, made at the forge from the diagram for Frostbearer.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 4-star catalyst with base ATK 42 and an ATK% secondary stat. The Dragonspine series passive Frost Burial gives Normal and Charged Attack hits a chance (60 to 100 per cent by refinement, once per 10s) of dropping an Everfrost Icicle that deals area damage, more against Cryo-affected enemies. The wiki notes it is the only Dragonspine weapon that can be obtained only by forging; its diagram comes from raising the Frostbearing Tree to level 10.

255.content: The Frostbearing Tree is the silver-white tree of Sal Vindagnyr whose roots pierced the earth. After the Skyfrost Nail shattered it, the princess tried to graft a branch to revive it; in much later times, dragon blood and crimson essence gave it one fruit, the source of Frostbearer. In game it is a Dragonspine tree the player can level up.

256.content:
Frostbreath (also: Frostbreath polearm, A Cast Real Far): Frostbreath is a four-star polearm in the Gnostic Hymn 3 series, added in version 7.0 as a Battle Pass weapon. Its in-game description calls it a spear of solid ice imbued with a chill, said to have belonged to the Belyi Tsar who ruled Snezhnaya long ago. Its story follows the young Monomakh, trained by his master, who asked whether stronger spears exist.

Appearance: The description gives only "a spear of solid ice imbued with an icy chill". The item has a base and a second-ascension look in the game, but the text describes no further detail such as shaft, tip or decoration.

Lore: The story opens with the young Monomakh asking his master whether stronger spears exist, during training so harsh that even a fae could hardly imagine it. He is described as lean as a white-barked birch and gasping on the ice. Looking at him, the crimson princess of the snow, whose eyes had survived the ruin of the golden city, answers that a spear once existed that could shoot down the Lord of the Sky. She tells him he cannot do it, since he cannot yet even defeat her, and that he asked only whether stronger spears exist. He says he would like to learn it so as to protect more people, and she tells him to firm up his stance.

The years pass and war sets the far north ablaze. Monomakh, who swore to become king, keeps honing the spear and throws it like a silver star at the Water Imp in a frozen lake, the bull Skoldyryt in the forest and the mountain-sized beast Miscislav. The text calls this his supreme spear art, taught by the Knyazhna of Blood who had slaughtered countless fae in an earlier age, and notes that it differs somewhat from her personal teaching. He becomes emperor and unifies the northern realms; fae and mortals alike sing his praises. A deliberately fawning passage lists his titles (conqueror of countless winters, most merciful father).

Yet he cannot reproduce what his master described, a spear that crossed countless snowfields at once; hurling his polearm like an arrow carries it only about half of Snezhnaya, and he blames his own lack of strength, trusting that his master would never lie. Thousands of winters later he visits a workshop where artisans mass-produce muskets from steel and Prime Ice, and falls silent. The story ends on his realisation that his master never said the golden city's spears were thrown. The reader is left to infer that she meant something other than a thrown spear (the text links the idea to the Arrow of Terpikeraunas; the item itself never names the weapon).

Owners: Per the short description, the Belyi Tsar who ruled Snezhnaya in the distant past once owned it. The story's protagonist, Monomakh, is the only wielder shown, and the item text links him to the same ruler; his teacher is the Knyazhna of Blood (Yalyane Morevna).

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star polearm, obtained from the Battle Pass (Gnostic Hymn). Base ATK 42, secondary stat Energy Recharge 10.0%. Passive "A Cast Real Far": triggering a Cryo- or Hydro-related reaction raises the wielder's ATK for 15 seconds and restores Elemental Energy to the other party members, once per 16 seconds.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a northern soldier or scholar might know the polearm as a relic of the old Tsar. The tale's irony, a king who never doubted his teacher and learned too late what she had actually said, makes it a good prop for stories about misunderstood advice or loyalty.

257.content:
In Frostbreath's story, Monomakh is a lean, determined youth trained on the ice by the crimson princess of the snow, Yalyane Morevna, called the Knyazhna of Blood. Asked whether stronger spears exist, she tells him of a spear she saw in the lost golden city that could shoot down the Lord of the Sky. He cannot reproduce it, though he later becomes a conquering emperor who unites the northern realms.

His thrown spear defeats the Water Imp, the bull Skoldyryt and the giant beast Miscislav. His spear art differs somewhat from his master's own teaching, which the text calls unimportant.

258.comment: Frostbreath: The muskets and the golden city's spear
258.content: Thousands of winters after his training, the aged emperor watches artisans mass-produce muskets from steel and Prime Ice. His silence marks the moment he realises that his master never said the golden city's spears were thrown, so the weapon she had seen may have been a bow-like arrow, as the text hints but does not state.

259.content:
Fruitful Hook (also: The Weight of Falling Branches): Fruitful Hook is a 4-star claymore from Natlan: a hooked blade made by the courier-hero Burkina of the Scions of the Canopy, with the hero Tenoch's help, to harvest the finest Flamegranates from the great mother tree.

Its story explains why the best Flamegranates are called "Mountain Kings" and how Burkina became companions with the Saurian Kongamato.

Appearance: A hooked blade or sword with a hook, used to cut fruit loose and to block attacks. Do not add decoration.

Lore: A young courier, Burkina, was royally annoyed at a Saurian living on the mountain's other side who mocked his movements, so he swore to climb to the peak and harvest the Flamegranates of the mother tree to show off to the most agile Yumkasaurus of all.

Skill alone did not help: winged Saurians harassed him at the summit and wild beasts waited under the tree. Burkina trained in patience: looking after the Saurians of the Flower-Feather Clan to learn their movements, hardening his body on boulders with the people of the mountain below the volcano, and seeking guidance from the Night-Wind high priests. Tenoch, travelling there, offered to join him; Burkina refused, since the training was the price of the result and he sensed that Tenoch's kindness might one day need to be repaid. Tenoch only said he could still do a small favour.

On the day the fruit ripened Burkina climbed faster than a sprint over flat ground, waving the hooked sword to dodge or block the beasts. He had read the winged Saurians' tactics, and they lost their composure. As he reached the fruit a gust staggered him, and he nearly fell with the fruit in his arms; a green figure shot out its long tongue and pulled him back from death. It was the Yumkasaurus that had always tussled with him and had been following in the shadows. Burkina gave it the Flamegranates and earned its acknowledgement; this is how the Turnfire hero and The Mountain King Kongamato became companions.

Later the heroes of the Scions of the Canopy transplanted the mother tree to the foot of the mountain, and in memory the best Flamegranates were also named "Mountain Kings". The tree grows beneath Coatepec Mountain today. The text mixes pride and its cost: Burkina's complacency nearly kills him, and the rescue comes from the rival he scorned.

Owners: Made by Burkina with Tenoch's help. No later wielder is named.

Treat the story as the Scions of the Canopy's tale of how a rivalry became a friendship, not as a documented history of the blade.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star claymore of the Heroes of Natlan series, base ATK 44 at level 1, secondary stat ATK%. Weapon Event Wishes from Version 5.1.

Passive "The Weight of Falling Branches": raises Plunging Attack CRIT Rate (16% at refinement 1 up to 32% at refinement 5); after a Plunging Attack hits, Normal, Charged and Plunging Attack DMG rise by the same percentage for 10s.

How {{char}} behaves: Scions of the Canopy characters may tell it as a fond cautionary story: skill needs patience, and rivals may save you.

260.comment: Fruitful Hook: The Weight of Falling Branches
260.content: The Weight of Falling Branches is the passive of the claymore Fruitful Hook (gameplay): it boosts Plunging Attack CRIT Rate and then Normal, Charged and Plunging Attack damage after a Plunging Attack lands, echoing Burkina's near-fall from the tree.

261.content:
Funerary Mask (also: Signora's mask, mask of La Signora): The Funerary Mask is a quest item the Traveler receives after defeating La Signora, Eighth of the Fatui Harbingers, in a duel before the Raiden Shogun's throne in Tenshukaku, Inazuma (Version 2.1). Its text calls it a trophy and uses it to reflect on why Fatui wear masks.

It is a memento: a keepsake of the duel with no use in play, tied to the end of Signora's story.

Appearance: Canon gives no physical description of the mask. Its name suggests mourning, and its item text speaks of the faceless masks the Fatui present to the world.

Lore: The Archive text first says it is a trophy for defeating Signora. It then says the Fatui often face the world from behind masks, and that this is said to be because everything they were counts for nothing once they become Fatui: they must give up their true names and share one face.

The text adds that giving up everything that makes up an "I", past and bonds included, is hard. It suggests those willing to join a group that rebels against the Heavenly Principles may have an obsession close to or beyond that of a Delusion holder, binding the rest of their days to the Delusion and burning like stars. It also notes that many Fatui are simply drunk on power or sadistic, and that the states are not mutually exclusive.

The last paragraph turns to Signora herself, naming her as Rosalyne-Kruzchka Lohefalter, who may once have lived a more innocent, naive life. It says her eyes were filled with raging fire and her innocent days burned away, until an icy Delusion put out the flames that gnawed at her. The frozen power protecting her was then shattered by the Traveler, an "eternal outlander", whose determination matched hers, and the flames burst forth again. The text is written as a reflective narrator's voice rather than as a character's speech.

The item therefore ties together the Fatui practice of surrendering one's name, Signora's concealed past, and the cost of her Cryo Delusion. Her own biography is not told in the item and belongs in her entry.

Owners: Held by the Traveler. It came as a quest reward alongside experience, Primogems, Mora and materials.

Origin: Obtained on completing Duel Before the Throne (Archon Quest, Chapter II, Act III), set in Tenshukaku in Inazuma City. After Kujou Sara stormed toward the throne, the Traveler found Signora already there before the Raiden Shogun and accused her of distributing Delusions and of the harm done in Liyue and to Venti's Gnosis. Signora answered as a mere Snezhnayan diplomat, mocking the Traveler's status as a wanted criminal. The Traveler then challenged her to a duel before the throne, which the Shogun allowed.

Signora warned that the loser must die and accepted. During the fight she shed her Delusion's shield and emerged as the Crimson Witch of Embers. After the Traveler won, the rules of the duel left the loser to the Shogun: Signora threatened diplomatic consequences and then shouted orders for the Shogun and others to stop, but the Raiden Shogun executed her with the Musou no Hitotachi. The Shogun called her an enemy of eternity but, as the victor, let the Traveler leave Tenshukaku alive.

Gameplay: Gameplay note: a quest item with no function in play. The wiki lists it as a memento, so it can be viewed in the inventory but not used.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (project guidance, not canon): a good prop for scenes about Signora's fall, the Fatui's loss of self, or the Traveler reflecting on the duel. Do not give the mask powers, a known owner history, or a claim that it was physically worn by Signora; canon does not state these.

Status as of 7.1: The Traveler holds it as of Version 7.1; nothing read says otherwise.

Signora died at the end of the duel; the mask is her only keepsake in the Traveler's possession.

262.comment: Funerary Mask: Duel Before the Throne
262.content: The Chapter II Archon Quest in which the Traveler challenged La Signora in Tenshukaku and won. The Raiden Shogun executed her afterward, and the Traveler received the Funerary Mask as the reward.

263.content:
General History of Snezhnaya (also: General History of Snezhnaya (I), General History of Snezhnaya (II)): General History of Snezhnaya is a two-volume book sold by Moes at Torchlight Books in Snezhnograd (added in 7.0). Written by Y. S. Klyucheva and dedicated in fawning terms to Tsaritsa Anastasya, it is Snezhnaya's flattering "official" history: legends of golden Hyperborea, then the youth and campaigns of Tsar Monomakh (the Belyi Tsar) and his fae companions.

Lore: Volume 1 sets out rival legends of Hyperborea, a warm golden realm where Snezhnaya now lies. Volume 2 tells how young Monomakh learned the spear from Yalyane Morevna, beat the shapeshifter Filipov and made him his "Synaimos" (sworn comrade), and spared the human warrior Nepla Korolevitsna's clan.

The in-world work has many volumes: Polar Night legends first, Monomakh's campaigns in the middle, and the Tsaritsa's deeds at the end. The game shows only the preface and excerpts of Volumes I, III and VII. The preface states the thesis: Monomakh conquered by force, but virtue renews the world, and the Tsaritsa's virtue is greater still.

Volume VII deals with the war against King Miscislav's Volkodlak coalition. It records the ambiguous role of Vaselisa Strivozha of the Vila. It also tells how Vaselisa Vodyanovna, the "Zmey Maiden" and daughter of Vodyanoy the Lackland, defected to Monomakh, after which Miscislav massacred his own Water Imp allies. The book says Filipov later fell for the "mad monk" Rotwang's tricks out of grief for Nepla, and vanished after the Tsar's death in the Cataclysm.

Reliability: This is the court-approved version of history. It passes on a genealogy that makes Monomakh Hyperborea's rightful heir, which other canon contradicts (he was an incomplete Primordial Human born of the Cryo Dragon's remains). Still, the author names competing sources and marks legends as legends.

The sources named in the book are all in-world: *The Volkhov Chronicles* (the oldest, still thousands of years after the golden age it describes), Grand Duke P. N. Kostomarov, the *Songbook of Saint Strivozha*, *The Davograd Chronicles* (hostile to Yalyane), *The Belovodye Annals* and *A History of the Snezhnyi Expedition*.

Nothing is known of Klyucheva beyond the preface, where the author, calling themself a mortal, thanks the Tsaritsa for release from "the afflictions of my former days"; this is never explained. In the text shown in game, the author deals with fae and human matters even-handedly. The author records that fae of Monomakh's age saw humans as fragile and unimportant, yet praises human valour (Nepla) and Monomakh's mercy toward human clans. For a scene, a Snezhnayan scholar or a reader at Torchlight Books might quote the book as the respectable mainstream account. A fae noble of another house, or anyone who knows the truth of the Tsar's origin, could reasonably dispute its genealogy and its tidy moral framing.

Appearance: A 3-star Book Collection item in two volumes, (I) and (II). Gaps in the excerpted text are marked by ellipses.

Gameplay: Gameplay: Archive Book Collection (Snezhnaya). Each volume is bought once from Moes at Torchlight Books; the stock does not refresh.

264.comment: General History of Snezhnaya: Klyucheva's preface to the Tsaritsa
264.content: In the preface of General History of Snezhnaya, Y. S. Klyucheva addresses Tsaritsa Anastasya Feodorovna Snezhnaya by a long chain of titles. They include Eternal Sovereign Under the Pale Star, Protectress of the Fae Kindreds and of the Lineages of the Peoples of the North, Holy One of All Winters, and Grand Suzerain of the Princes of Snezhnograd, Glupov, Kitezh and Belovodye. The author thanks her for release from "former afflictions" and for being allowed to stand among the immortals, then signs as her loyal subject and child. The preface contrasts Monomakh's conquests, fierce as a winter gale, with the Tsaritsa's greater virtue.

265.comment: General History of Snezhnaya: Legends of Hyperborea (General History)
265.content: Volume I of General History of Snezhnaya says many sources agree Snezhnaya was once a warm, fertile plain. Fae poems name the realm there Hyperborea. The author warns that even *The Volkhov Chronicles* was written thousands of years after the age it describes. Grand Duke P. N. Kostomarov pictures virtuous people in golden cities in eternal spring, living on heavenly honey and dew. When their descendants grew idle and lost their nobility, spring left and the long winter came. The author then turns to "true history": before founding Kitezhgrad, Monomakh wandered the blizzard lands for centuries as a young hero, gathering companions and imagining a realm of virtue and mercy.

266.comment: General History of Snezhnaya: Songbook of Saint Strivozha
266.content: In-world source quoted in General History of Snezhnaya and attributed to Vaselisa Strivozha. It says the King of Light imprisoned his daughter in darkness. The King of Hyperborea freed her, and from then on night existed; she became the Mother of Night. They had seven Preexistent Gods and twelve Preexistent Men, whose descendants founded Hyperborea of gold and white stone. The King of Light then destroyed it and killed the seven divine bloodlines, except Tsar Monomakh, the last monarch's young son. The book calls this a "strange fable". Its claim about Monomakh's descent conflicts with other canon about his origin.

267.comment: General History of Snezhnaya: Yalyane Morevna in the General History
267.content: General History of Snezhnaya (Volume III) says the Snegurochka of Hesperides were closest to Monomakh. He openly called Yalyane Morevna his teacher; she was the grandmother of Hesperides' first Grand Duchess. Real history barely mentions her, and she vanished before Kitezhgrad was founded. Folk accounts make her a Hyperborean survivor called the "Knyazhna of Blood" for savagely raiding other fae kindreds. Yet she never preyed on the destitute human clans of the snowfields; *The Davograd Chronicles* even says she sheltered humans from monsters. She took in young Monomakh and taught him the spear. The author reflects that before courage became a virtue it was a crime, cradled by plunder and nursed by greed.

268.content: "Synaimos" is a word from the fae tongue that General History of Snezhnaya glosses as comrade-in-arms, brother or kinsman. Monomakh offered Filipov Vseslavyevich crystals of the purest kind to become his Synaimos. Filipov first refused and challenged him to a contest.

269.comment: General History of Snezhnaya: Filipov's contest with Monomakh
269.content: In General History of Snezhnaya, the young Filipov Vseslavyevich, progenitor of the shapeshifters, scorns Monomakh and demands his submission. He becomes a weasel and destroys Monomakh's weapons, then becomes a falcon, a white wolf, a great bear, a hill-sized bull, a giant the size of a mountain range, and finally Monomakh's own likeness. Each time Monomakh seizes him by the scruff and throws him like a spear over one more mountain, from one up to seven. Moved by Monomakh's purity of heart, Filipov becomes his Synaimos and dearest friend, and later the first Commander of the Druzhna. Legends of the pair sailing into a whale's belly and facing a dragon for seven days are noted as unverifiable. Chronicles always link Filipov with cunning and victory. He lost only three times: to Monomakh, to his wife, and to the pitch-black calamity from beneath the earth.

270.comment: General History of Snezhnaya: Nepla Korolevitsna in the General History
270.content:
In General History of Snezhnaya, Nepla Korolevitsna is a human warrior guarding her clan with a huge war hammer and a fire-breathing horse; her shout alone drives Filipov's horse to its knees. Filipov unhorses her at the cost of one eye. Under the law of the age the victors could kill or enslave her clan, but Monomakh spares it, citing the mercy his teacher Yalyane taught him, and settles it at the future Port Belovodye. Filipov marries Nepla, saying her arrow took one eye and her valour and beauty the other. She soon dies of sickness, and only friendship and oaths keep him alive.

The book says this grief is why, thousands of years later, Filipov trusted the "mad monk" (Rotwang, "The Professor") who summoned her phantom, and stopped warning the Tsar. During the Cataclysm the Abyss took her shape to lure him away. He claimed she had a mole behind her ear, and when the impostor showed him one, he laughed that she never had one and that all the world longs to be deceived. He fought on, deserted only when news came of the Tsar's death, and has not been seen since.

271.comment: General History of Snezhnaya: Strivozha and Filipov's sword
271.content: Volume VII of General History of Snezhnaya admits nobody knows what Vaselisa Strivozha told King Miscislav's envoy. Without wishing to defame her, the author notes that the Volkodlak coalition never attacked the Vila, even after the Vila denounced it and paid tribute to the Pale Star court. By contrast, Miscislav slaughtered his loyal Water Imp allies after Vaselisa Vodyanovna defected. Citing *A History of the Snezhnyi Expedition*, the book says Filipov laid a long sword before Strivozha at the war's end, warning that winter freezes even the wind. She answered that colder winters only make people wrap themselves tighter. Laughing, he revealed the sword was a trophy from Monomakh, sent to keep her an ally. She agreed and held a banquet lasting seven days and nights.

272.content:
Geo Gnosis (also: Morax's Gnosis, Gnosis of Morax, Geo Archon's Gnosis, Rex Lapis's Gnosis): The Geo Gnosis was the Gnosis of Morax, the Geo Archon, who now lives in Liyue as Zhongli. A Gnosis is a gleaming, chess-piece-like focus that an Archon carries in their chest. Zhongli gave his to the Fatui Harbinger Signora in Liyue Harbor (1.1), fulfilling a secret contract with the Tsaritsa that he called his "contract to end all contracts".

It was the second Gnosis the Fatui obtained, after the Anemo Gnosis, and the first one given up willingly. Canon has not revealed what the Tsaritsa gave in return.

Lore: Zhongli staged his own death at the Rite of Descension to test whether Liyue could thrive without its god. Meanwhile Childe (Tartaglia), kept in the dark, tried to seize the Gnosis and finally freed the ancient god Osial. The Qixing, the adepti and the Traveler stopped Osial together. At the Northland Bank, Signora asked Morax to honour the agreement. Zhongli materialised the Gnosis and gave it to her, saying his promise was "solid as stone" and that the matter lay "solely between the Tsaritsa and I".

Zhongli said he had kept the Gnosis as a fallback: had the chaos gone too far, he could have returned and used his divine power to restore order. Once Liyue proved itself, the Gnosis he had kept for so many years "suddenly seemed to have lost its meaning". At his request Signora had kept the plan secret, even from Childe, who complained that the two had deceived him. She left for Zapolyarny Palace with the Gnosis. His character story asks what the Cryo Archon could have wagered to balance a loss so great. His ascension voice line later recalls "letting go" of it.

Consequences: The Golden House, Teyvat's only Mora mint, stopped working because minting needs the Geo Archon's power; existing Mora did not vanish.

Zhongli later told the ancient dragon Azhdaha, "I am no longer the Geo Archon", and Azhdaha said he could sense it. Elsewhere canon shows an Archon's divine throne does not depend on holding a Gnosis, so the link stays unclear.

Owners: Morax (Zhongli), then Signora, then the Tsaritsa (Anastasya), who holds it as of 7.1.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the Tsaritsa holds six Gnoses, the Geo Gnosis among them; only the Pyro Gnosis is missing. She collects them to amplify her power against the Heavenly Principles and to open a seal the Third Descender left beneath Zapolyarny Palace. In 7.1 she used all six to slow time around Rhinedottir.

Origin: Like every Gnosis it is made from the remains of the Third Descender, Saarelainen (hinted in 4.2, told in full in 7.1). Whether Morax knew this is not stated.

Gameplay: Gameplay note: a story object only, never an obtainable item. Zhongli's playable Geo powers are not tied to it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay guidance (project recommendation, not canon): keep the Geo Gnosis with the Tsaritsa after 7.1. Zhongli remains powerful without it, declines to discuss the contract's terms and does not voice regret. Ordinary Liyue citizens believe Rex Lapis died and know nothing of the trade. Never invent the Tsaritsa's side of the bargain.

273.comment: Geo Gnosis: Contract to End All Contracts
273.content: Zhongli's final contract as Geo Archon was made with the Cryo Archon, the Tsaritsa. He would surrender the Geo Gnosis, and Signora would collect it as her emissary. Asked what could be worth a Gnosis, Zhongli said that realistically nothing was. Even so, as God of Contracts he would never agree to a deal that brought him no benefit. One clause forbids him to reveal the contract's terms. He told the Traveler to discover the Tsaritsa's "bargaining chip" on their own journey. As of 7.1 it remains unknown.

274.comment: Geo Gnosis: Childe's search of the Exuvia
274.content: In Heart of Glaze (1.1), Childe used the Traveler's work on the Rite of Parting to learn where the Qixing had hidden the Exuvia, the god's shed body. At the Golden House, where the Millelith guards had been knocked unconscious, he reached into the Exuvia for Morax's Gnosis, but came out empty-handed. He fought the Traveler, believing they had taken it, then realised they had not. He guessed that the Exuvia was a diversion and freed Osial with a swarm of Sigils of Permission to force the god to reveal himself. The handover itself later took place at the Northland Bank, not the Golden House.

275.comment: Geo Gnosis: Signora and the Geo Gnosis
275.content: Signora was the Tsaritsa's liaison to Zhongli in Liyue. She knew of the contract and kept it secret at his request. When she claimed the Gnosis, she taunted Childe that the pressure he created was what turned Liyue into "a dazzling diamond of a city". Childe refused to share a boat home with her, and she left alone for Zapolyarny Palace with the Gnosis. The Fatui's Ninth Company had been working in the Chasm under a separate deal with the Qixing, unaware of the Gnosis mission. The Qixing cancelled that deal after Osial's release. Signora died in Inazuma in 2.1, after the Gnosis was already in Snezhnaya.

276.comment: Geo Gnosis: The six Gnoses in Zapolyarny Palace
276.content: In Black Feathers Scattered at Parting (7.1), the Tsaritsa placed her six Gnoses, the Geo Gnosis among them, as energy nodes around a hall of her palace. Her Cryo power, amplified by them, slowed time inside the hall. This stalled Rhinedottir until the resurrection window she had agreed with Ronova, meant to bypass the Heavenly Principles' monitoring, had passed, and Celestia then reclaimed Ronova's authority. Rhinedottir called this power beyond what a god should have; the Tsaritsa credited her own insight too. She had earlier told the Traveler that the Gnoses come from outside Teyvat's system and can let a bearer go beyond the limits of their authority, and that only a Gnosis responds to the Third Descender's seal.

277.comment: Geo Gnosis: Gnoses as chess pieces
277.content: In the official teaser A Winter Night's Lazzo (2022), the Harbingers gather to mourn Signora. Before the ceremony the Tsaritsa plays chess with Pierro, and the Anemo and Geo Gnoses, the only two collected so far, sit on the board as pieces. The 2026 trailer Sudden Snow shows the Tsaritsa playing chess with Rhinedottir, with Gnoses among the pieces. Fans read the Geo Gnosis as a rook, but canon assigns no roles.

278.content: The limited 2026 web event Snezhnaya Awaits, a recap before the Snezhnaya chapter, showed each collected Gnosis with a line from its handover. The Geo Gnosis appeared with Zhongli's words about the contract being fulfilled, from A New Star Approaches.

279.content:
Gest of the Mighty Wolf (also: Indomitable Chivalry, Four Winds' Hymn): Gest of the Mighty Wolf is a five-star claymore of the Hexerei series, released in version 6.4. Its description says it was forged by Ravenwood, who inherited the name of Boreas, before he became a knight. The item story is a Mondstadt tale of a nameless northern knight and his wolf companion Andrius, and of the blacksmith's son who admired him.

Appearance: No visual description is given in the item text beyond calling it a greatsword. The story speaks of a heavy, fearsome sword, but it is describing the weapon Ravenwood carried at the end, not necessarily this one.

Lore: Mondstadt's tales praise knights' martial feats, and the "wolf" stories are the best loved, as a free-roaming wolf suits a poet more than a stately lion. They often begin with a wandering knight arriving from the north with his companion Andrius, visiting a city freshly freed. Together they killed beasts plaguing the countryside and drove back a great serpent threatening the coast. The homesick wolf eventually left his spirit in the emerald wilds, and the knight quietly followed his companion's steps. No one learned his name.

Poets claimed the knight fought after drinking the snowlands' strong spirits, but he did not come from that snowy land. In Mondstadt he lived unassumingly; the Grand Master (Vennessa) never stopped trying to recruit him, while tavern guests thought him an ordinary drinker. Only a boy named Ravenwood, the city blacksmith's son, took notice. The knight had commissioned a sword from the boy's father, paying with unfamiliar coins, and the blacksmith, who had once forged only for nobles, simply gave him a heavy slab of iron (the Wolf's Gravestone), saying everyone should now take up arms in the new Mondstadt. Ravenwood followed him around, often watching him practise.

At sunset the tired knight sometimes spoke of a forgotten foreign land where flowers never withered and rivers ran with mead, and where a warrior kingdom once stood. Its warriors, who had sung of devotion and honour, bent to power and gold and offered their blades to a greedy tyrant; the law was abolished and virtue ruined until the enslavers were enslaved. The story ends on the knight's fate of wandering as a man with no homeland, nothing left to defend. Years later the tale of Andrius had become legend; the chain-breaking hero was gone, the knights' code was echoed but comrades had again sought the old aristocracy's embrace. Ravenwood took up a new longsword, quoted the knight's warning about freedom and courage, and set out into the wilds. Days later a knight in a tattered cloak appeared at a fortress, fighting as if guided by a god; an old man recognised the technique of "Andrius", the crowd cheered, and Ravenwood closed his eyes.

Owners: Ravenwood, said by the description to have forged it before his ascension to knighthood. The wiki identifies him as the second Knight of Boreas. The wandering knight, the first Knight of Boreas, is an earlier figure from the same story.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star claymore from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 46, secondary stat CRIT Rate 7.2%. Passive "Indomitable Chivalry": raises ATK SPD by 10% and builds Four Winds' Hymn stacks (up to four) that raise DMG dealt; with the team bonus "Hexerei: Secret Rite" each stack also raises CRIT DMG.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the story suits scenes about borrowed names and legend outliving the person. Treat the connection between Ravenwood, Andrius and Boreas as something characters know only if they have read the item or Varka's quests.

280.comment: Gest of the Mighty Wolf: Ravenwood
280.content: Ravenwood was the son of Mondstadt's blacksmith, later the second Knight of Boreas (wiki title). He wielded a greatsword in battle, a design later copied and used as a model for Ferrous Shadow. He is dead; he appears in canon only through Varka's quest and item text.

281.comment: Gest of the Mighty Wolf: Andrius, the wandering knight
281.content: The legend of Andrius mixes a wolf and a knight: the wolf Andrius ran with the nameless knight and, per the story, left his spirit in the wilds. Wolf's Gravestone, the heavy slab of iron given to the knight, is the companion weapon. The knight's arrival is dated by the wiki to about a thousand years before the game, after the fall of the aristocracy.

282.comment: Gest of the Mighty Wolf: Hexerei
282.content: The Hexerei series is a group of five-star weapons whose passives are enhanced by the team bonus "Hexerei: Secret Rite". The wiki lists Gest of the Mighty Wolf as one of three that recount Mondstadt history, the others being Disaster and Remorse and The Daybreak Chronicles.

283.content:
Gilded Dreams (also: Dreaming Steelbloom, Feather of Judgment, The Sunken Years, Honeyed Final Feast, Shadow of the Sand King): Gilded Dreams is a Sumeru desert artifact set (Version 3.0, Spire of Solitary Enlightenment domain). Its five pieces remember a lost golden age: a desert paradise ruled by a "God King" who judged every heart, three inseparable friends, and a law that hardened into chains. The set never names the God King; other lore points to King Deshret.

Its images are gilded: dark gold flowers that never open, molten metal weighing hearts, sundials, wine cups and sand-king crowns. The tone is mournful rather than triumphant.

Lore: Ancient legends tell of three inseparable friends: one withered like a rose in the mud, one made a great hidden oasis, one used all their intellect to build an eternal illusion in the sand. They meant for no one to suffer partings or bitter water, and promised a "golden slumber".

Long ago the heavens fell silent and the land lost its master. A God King then judged all life by law: a feather weighed hearts and molten metal measured wisdom. Tribes who lived by blood-law and the memory of famine imitated his thrones and walls. The priests ruled the oasis cities justly in his name, but later decrees were issued from "illusory madness", and the citizens' fates were chained to their God King's choice. A banquet of the three God Kings, with the moon, sun and green fields as their symbols, ended when time broke the oath between day and night.

The poem moves between ideals and failure. The Dreaming Steelbloom says obsessive remembrance rises "like a smokeless flame" and that those who look back with one eye and forward into dreams with the other get lost. Feather of Judgment says the law, once twisted by sorrow, made nobles abettors and let palace foundations sink into quicksand. The Sunken Years says that when time swept across the land the God King rose casting a long shadow, and the tribes imitated him and recalled days when kings spoke with the heavens. Honeyed Final Feast says the three God Kings were oathbound friends, one holding the banquet, one authority, one life, but dreams are "prey for reason", thrown into dead machinery from which "a new intelligence shall molt". Shadow of the Sand King records the pillar from the heavens that buried trees and meadows under sand.

A reading, not stated outright: three images recur: the dream (golden slumber), the law (the scales of feather and metal) and the machine (calculation unified into one mind). Each is presented as a good idea that reversed itself: the dream paralysed, the law entrapped, the machine promised humanity godhood at the price of its individual minds ("meld all thoughts into one"). Treat the set as the desert's own memory of Deshret's age, not a neutral history. Several lines are presented as quotations or prophecy: the circlet's "ruler shall come with light that blazes like the sun" to take the thorn crown, and the sands piece's vow to "stop the sands of time with divine power".

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a set from the Spire of Solitary Enlightenment domain (4 and 5 star) and its strongbox. 2-piece: Elemental Mastery +80. 4-piece: within 8s of triggering an Elemental Reaction, ATK rises 14% for each party member of the wearer's element and Elemental Mastery rises 50 for each of a different element (3 members counted each), once per 8s, even off-field; the triggering reaction itself is not buffed. Released in 3.0; no later change is listed.

284.content:
The flower piece of Gilded Dreams: a bud of hammered dark gold with a crimson core and petals that will never open. Its verses tell of three inseparable friends, one who withers in mud, one who builds a hidden oasis, one who builds an eternal illusion, and a promise that in the golden slumber no one need drink bitter water.

It says the "kingdom of flowers" would be ground by sandstorms into a tale in a song. The closing lines turn to a listener who has turned his gaze to "the wisdom of the depths" and inclined his ear to "honeyed whispers".

285.content:
The plume piece: a feather once used to weigh the hearts of the guilty, its original function lost. The verses describe the past of "civilization and ease" abandoned, then the new law: a feather to weigh hearts, molten metal to measure divine wisdom, the God King's blood-rooted law carved into the desert paradise, and sorrow twisting governance into shackles.

Dignitaries became abettors while palace foundations sank into quicksand, and "all betrayals must be mercilessly judged" with utter devastation. Citizens' fates were chained to the God King's choice.

286.content:
The sands piece: a dark-golden sundial that tells the desert's story. In the beginning tribes lived with the sands, bound by blood-law and the fear of famine, until a God King rose; they copied his walls and thrones into feudal kingdoms, and wise kings received oracles from the heavens.

Its closing prophecy says the king will, in wisdom, revive the golden past and stop the sands of time with undiminished divine power, so the age of the "king of the ocean of sand" will return and the "golden slumber" will summon wandering sand.

287.content:
The goblet piece: a wine cup from a grand ancient feast that has lost its luster. It recalls the three God Kings as oathbound friends, one for the banquet, one for authority, one for life, whose happiness ended when time broke the contract between day and night. The final lines hint at dreams ground in lifeless machinery.

The moonlight sank into quicksand and the sun covered everything in its fearsome gaze. The final dirge is for "the most lonesome king of kings", for whom the gilded sands long divined failure. The text quotes a plan to meld all thoughts into one and let humanity become the lord of lords and god of gods.

288.comment: Gilded Dreams: Shadow of the Sand King
288.content:
The circlet piece: a gold-inlaid headband once worn by desert priests, modelled on one worn by a legendary desert ruler. Its verses describe a divine pillar from the sky burying forest and meadow, sacred cities on fertile oases, priests ruling justly under the God King, and later absurd decisions that led the people toward a bitter end.

The text says kings and clergy once received divine oracles themselves and were masters of the land, while those who rule as proxies today are the shadows of the gods. It also promises that a ruler will come with blazing light and take from the people the "crown woven from rose thorns".

289.content:
Gladiator's Finale (also: Gladiator's Nostalgia, Gladiator's Destiny, Gladiator's Longing, Gladiator's Intoxication, Gladiator's Triumphus): Gladiator's Finale is an ATK artifact set (4 and 5 star, 1.0) about the champion gladiator of aristocracy-era Mondstadt, a slave who nearly won his freedom, was undone by pride and a master's flattery, and fell to a young girl in the arena. The girl is Vennessa, the later founder of the Knights of Favonius. Its weapon companion is the polearm Deathmatch.

The pieces are Gladiator's Nostalgia (flower), Gladiator's Destiny (feather), Gladiator's Longing (hourglass), Gladiator's Intoxication (goblet) and Gladiator's Triumphus (helmet).

Appearance: A brooch-flower, a feather of a free bird, a hand-made hourglass, a gold goblet and a feathered gladiator's helmet.

Lore: Nostalgia shows the master giving a flower to his silent slave and making it a brooch; years later the master called such gifts whims. Destiny says he was one battle from freedom when a young girl defeated him but refused to execute him, and a bird left a feather on his chest. Longing is the hourglass he flipped before each fight; in his last fight the sand stopped. Intoxication is a gold cup from his master; Triumphus a helmet that made him a symbol of invincibility to the crowd.

The pieces give conflicting endings. Destiny has the girl spare him so that he walks free as a bird. Longing says the girl's sword pierced his heart and the hourglass sand stopped. Intoxication and Triumphus argue that vanity and the master's care bound him; by lingering on victory he missed his chance to leave. Triumphus says he glimpsed the world outside his cell on the day of victory, but he was always only a worthless slave in his master's eyes.

The wiki reads the master as Eberhart, a noble of the aristocracy period, and the girl as Vennessa, a flame-touched slave gladiator of the Lawrence clan who later led the rebellion. It reads Destiny as a possible imagined ending. The Deathmatch weapon and Luther's expedition journal (which fears the gladiator's fate) are the other canon touches. The wiki also says that, as he died, he looked for Eberhart's seat and found it empty.

Owners: The unnamed gladiator owned the relics in the story; his master Eberhart gave the flower and cup.

Status as of 7.1: Both the gladiator and Eberhart's aristocracy-era world are long gone. Eberhart is recorded as the later mastermind behind the deaths of a Dragonspine expedition of young aristocrats; his ultimate fate is unknown.

How {{char}} behaves: Tone: tragic and moral, not glorifying. A character who knows the tale uses it as a warning about vanity and being used by one's master.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). 2-piece: ATK +18%. 4-piece: +35% Normal Attack DMG for Sword, Claymore and Polearm users. Dropped by Normal and Weekly Bosses and Domain Reliquary.

290.content:
A slave of Eberhart and champion of the aristocracy-era arena, who fought with the polearm Deathmatch and was slain by Vennessa. He is never named.

Luther's expedition journal fears he would suffer 'the gladiator's fate'.

291.content: Half-brother of Parsifal and Ingbert, resentful of his illegitimacy; he owned the gladiator and pushed him to keep fighting. The wiki notes he later orchestrated the deaths of the Dragonspine expedition and his fate is unknown.

292.content:
Glaze Lily (also: Glaze Lilies, Liuli Baihe): The Glaze Lily is a very old flower of Liyue, once common across the land and now rare in the wild. Its item text says it turns the land's memories into scent as it blooms. Legend says it opens to pure, beautiful music, and that someone once loved it above all other flowers.

It is a Liyue local specialty grown on the terraces of Qingce Village and in Liyue Harbor's Yujing Terrace, and blooms at night.

Appearance: A lily whose blossoms open at night, between 18:00 and 06:00 in-game. Wild plants smell stronger than the planted ones, per Solitary Fragrance as cited by the wiki.

Lore: The archive text calls it an extremely ancient flower, said to have been a common sight in Liyue, that converts the memories of the land into fragrance during florescence. A legend says it opens at the sound of pure, beautiful music, and that one person loved it more than any other; the wiki identifies that person as Guizhong, though the text does not name her. A full bloom in the wild is now rare.

Madame Ping explained in Farewell, Archaic Lord that the plant listens to people singing. She also said the lilies in Liyue Harbor are planted ones; the flower once grew throughout Liyue, especially around Dihua Marsh, until overpicking left few in the wild. According to her, where wild lilies grew thick, shimmersoil could be found by digging beneath them and following the roots; this soil is used in building the Serenitea Pot.

Kaedehara Kazuha, during the quest Tuned to the World's Sounds, used lily juice on the body of the Ancient Zither to repair it. Besides Qingce Village and the Harbor, scattered lilies grow near the Chihu Rock waypoint, on Mt. Tianheng, in Yaodie Valley, and near Mt. Xuanlian, per the wiki.

Gameplay: Gameplay note, not in-world lore: a Liyue local specialty used in crafting and character ascension. Madame Ping gives five on a first dialogue branch. It can be grown in the Serenitea Pot.

Scene use: Use it for quiet scenes at night near Liyue Harbor or Qingce Village: a bloom opening to someone humming, or a Liyue local mentioning how scarce wild ones have become. Do not assert Guizhong's feelings beyond the archive text.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 canon still describes the wild flower as rare, with planted lilies in the Harbor and Qingce Village.

293.content:
Golden Frostbound Oath (also: Dawn's Salutation Returned): Golden Frostbound Oath is a five-star bow released in version 6.5 (Luna VI). Its in-game description calls it a longbow carved from ancient whitewood, once wielded by the Jack Frost King of the northern lands. Its story follows the Knight of the Golden Bough, who walks into the frozen north seeking the Golden Bough to save fallen Arcadia and finds the sacred tree already ruined.

Appearance: The description says only "a longbow carved from ancient whitewood". The wiki shows a base and second-ascension look, but the text gives no further detail.

Lore: The story begins in an age when an idyllic land of oakwoods and plenty stood against even the fiercest storms. The Arcadians, exalted by the thousand winds, believed their holy city would last forever, but calamity struck and its spring was laid to rest in a deathly chill. The Knight of the Golden Bough, addressed in a prophecy as Gunnhildr, last light of the people, then walked alone into the endless frost. The prophecy says that only when the pure Golden Bough is severed can the withered wood live again and the sealed paradise endure.

In the frozen wastes the knight reached another sacred grove spared from ruin, tended by no priests. In their place a Jack Frost named itself king and watched from the high boughs left by a vanished envoy. It was not a rightful lord but a warden bound to an old, fading command, which delighted in riddles and mockery and in leading the lost astray. It set capricious trials and gave answers that were not answers. Wordless, the two fought until the knight's blade struck the crown from the fae king's brow.

After the storm the truth came out: the frenzied aurora had taken the Golden Bough long before, and with each tide of the Light Realm the last vestiges of mortal reason and the quiet breath of plant life were stripped away, leaving a pale, withered remnant on the branch. The oath-bound fae did not understand that the holy tree was gone and still guarded what it thought was hallowed ground. The knight hurled the longsword down beneath the withered tree and laughed without sound, accepting that a paradise sealed against change cannot last, then went south. The text says that in later years the hero led willing Arcadian survivors to the tower where the wicked dragon had been cast down, to seek shelter from its lord, Decarabian. The Jack Frost King never knew this: it took its defeat calmly, placed the emptied Golden Bough into the traveller's hands, blessed the mortal desire for a new dawn, and hoped that whoever had set the Jack Frost there might find a way home.

Owners: The short description names the Jack Frost King of the northern lands as the bow's wielder in ages past. The long story features the Knight of the Golden Bough as the traveller who confronts the king but does not give her or him the bow.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star bow from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT DMG 19.2%. Passive "Dawn's Salutation Returned": raises DEF; after the wielder's Elemental Skill or Lunar-Crystallize attack hits, Geo DMG and Lunar-Crystallize Reaction DMG rise for 6 seconds. If Moondrifts are near the wielder, other nearby party members gain a smaller Geo DMG and Lunar-Crystallize bonus, even when the wielder is off-field.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the weapon fits scenes about duty to a lost homeland, hope that has outlived its object, and a guardian loyal to an order whose meaning is gone. Treat the Arcadian tale as ancient history, not common knowledge.

294.comment: Golden Frostbound Oath: The Jack Frost King
294.content:
In Golden Frostbound Oath's story, a Jack Frost calls itself king of a sacred northern grove and guards it from the high boughs left by a vanished envoy. It delights in riddles and mockery and gives the knight answers that are not answers, but it is called a warden bound to an old command rather than a rightful lord.

Defeated by the knight, it gives the traveller the emptied Golden Bough and its blessing, and hopes that whoever stationed it there might find a path home.

295.comment: Golden Frostbound Oath: The Knight and the Golden Bough
295.content: A prophecy calls the knight Gunnhildr, the last light of the Arcadians, and says the Golden Bough must be severed to revive the withered wood and make the sealed paradise endure. The knight finds the bough already claimed by the frenzied aurora. Laughing, the knight gives up the effort to restore Arcadia, and later leads willing survivors south to seek shelter from Decarabian at the tower where the dragon had been cast down.

296.content:
Golden Troupe (also: Golden Song's Variation, Golden Bird's Shedding, Golden Era's Prelude, Golden Night's Bustle, Golden Troupe's Reward, Golden Troupe artifact set): Golden Troupe is a 4- and 5-star artifact set from Fontaine, added in Version 4.0. Its five pieces tell the story of Boethius: a boy from a conquered island tribe who became a musician and Harmost of Remuria, and, after the empire's fall, the troupe that clung to the dream of its golden age. Its bonuses boost Elemental Skill damage.

The pieces are Golden Song's Variation (flower), Golden Bird's Shedding (plume), Golden Era's Prelude (sands), Golden Night's Bustle (goblet) and Golden Troupe's Reward (circlet). The set and the Golden Troupe faction share a name: this entry is the artifact set, the faction is a separate entry.

Appearance: Only names and lore text describe the pieces. The theatrical, musical and golden imagery (songs, birds, preludes, a golden dome, a theater) is the set's recurring motif.

Lore: The pieces follow Boethius: a conquered child who becomes a musician and Harmost, a rift between two Harmosts over mercy toward the tribes, the God King's failed last orders, the people turned into golems, and the faded-castle troupe waiting for the symphony to return.

- Golden Song's Variation: the "song of fate" spread civilization along Remuria's waterways. A young musician from a short-lived tribe befriended a conquered warrior-servant (later famous as Cassiodor); both rose in golden Capitolium to become proud masters under the God King. The musician urges his friend to abandon the humble past and trust the glorious kingdom, which only has eyes for a perfect future.
- Golden Bird's Shedding: the harmonious symphony closed as empires do, when progress turned to arrogance and exploitation. After the unconquered banded together, one Harmost pleads for compassion toward the "people of bygone times" while the other answers with scorn, calls for purging the tribes (blaming the Bane Dragon Scylla for destroying towers and killing musicians), and the golden era breaks into war. The God King wakes startled.
- Golden Era's Prelude: the musician says he came from a lone isle, was taken as a child to the capital after Remuria's warriors announced conquest, and escaped bondage through his fingers and voice. He gave up his name and tribe to be known only as Boethius.
- Golden Night's Bustle: terrified and remorseful, the God King gave his last orders to his guards and musicians to restore peace, but arrogance and prejudice could not be undone in a night. The Harmosts and rulers fell, the Fell Dragon Prince's armies and the king's own were swept away with the palace, and the people, without the guiding song, became disfigured golems. Boethius lay in the rubble muttering about a betrayal.
- Golden Troupe's Reward: beneath the sea a faded golden castle stands. Its musicians, who have lost their score, mourn the perfect order and wait with silent golems for the symphony to play again, when the loyal will win the future as their prize.
Wider canon (not in these pieces) fills in names: Boethius became one of Remus's four Harmosts, his friend Cassiodor another, and after Remuria's fall Boethius mustered survivors into the Golden Troupe, who gathered in the Faded Castle. Cassiodor later founded the Marechaussee Hunters to fight the troupe and its golems (see the Marechaussee Hunter set, whose Hunter's Brooch makes this link).

Note how the same event looks different by piece. Golden Bird's Shedding shows two Harmosts divided, Golden Night's Bustle blames "arrogance and prejudice" for the collapse, and Golden Troupe's Reward shows the survivors justifying themselves with hope. None of the pieces says exactly who betrayed whom; Boethius's own words in the goblet text point to a single act of treachery, which wider canon treats as his betrayal of the empire.

Owners: No named owner; the set is narrative item text about Boethius, Cassiodor, Remus and their circle.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): the 2-piece bonus is Elemental Skill DMG +20%. The 4-piece bonus is Elemental Skill DMG +25%, with a further +25% while the wearer is off the field (cleared 2s after taking the field). Obtained from the Denouement of Sin domain in Fontaine's Belleau Region, near Romaritime Harbor, and the artifact strongbox. That domain's Ley Line Disorder gives a CRIT DMG bonus whenever a character's HP rises or falls; its enemies are out-of-control clockwork meka left after an accident at the Fontaine Research Institute of Kinetic Energy Engineering.

The domain text mentions legends of the first Lochknights hiding in the wilderness with Lochfolk to atone for a sin beyond redemption.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present the set as poetic, in-universe artifacts of Remurian memory, with a sadder, more faithful tone than the set's bonuses suggest. Characters should not casually know the Golden Troupe's real methods unless they have read the relevant Faded Castle materials.

297.content: In this set Boethius is the Remurian musician who left his island tribe, gave up his name and became a Harmost. Golden Night's Bustle shows him among the rubble, speaking of treachery, and Golden Troupe's Reward ends in the troupe he is later said to have led.

298.content: The set's last piece pictures the troupe in the faded golden castle beneath the sea, mourning a perfect order and waiting with silent, famished golems to hunt innocents. Wider canon's Golden Troupe faction is covered in its own entry.

299.content:
Great Song of Khvarena (also: Great Songs of Khvarena, Great Khvarena): The Great Songs of Khvarena are five large concentrations of Khvarena, the purifying power left by the divine bird Simurgh. The Pari elder Zurvan says she fused them long ago to cleanse the land of impurity. They hold immense power, but only a Pari who has earned the Khvarena's approval can unleash it, through a special ritual. In Vourukasha Oasis's quest series, Sorush the Pari and the Traveler gather all five, and Nasejuna, leader of the Order of Skeptics, is revealed to have been using them for his own plot.

They are needed to perform the Rite of Chinvat and open a path to the Harvisptokhm, so the Sign of Apaosha in the sky can be extinguished. Whoever holds them can seal or open lands: Zurvan once used them to seal Vourukasha Oasis and the nearby ruins against the Abyss Order.

Appearance: Paimon describes them as much bigger than ordinary Khvarena motes, and "kinda cute" when one rises out of Sunyata Lake; she jokingly calls it "Great Khvarena". The Khvarena's power forms a barrier around each one.

Lore: Zurvan says that after she scattered the monsters that invaded the sea of flowers, she fused the strongest Khvarena gathered into five Great Songs to purify the land. She hid one in Sunyata Lake for a time of need, and the rest were scattered. A Pari needs the Twin-Horned Chaplet, the symbol of the Khvarena's recognition, to touch them. Sorush earns it by being acknowledged as a Bloomguard.

Collection (As the Khvarena's Light Shows). The first Song is raised from Sunyata Lake by Sorush. Nasejuna claims to know the other four sites. Three are found through the sub-quests As the Khvarena's Light Shows: Samudaya, Dukkha and Nirodha; in Samudaya a Song is found after lowering water levels with control devices, and in Dukkha the Song's effect on a petrified Setekh Wenut is weak, which Nasejuna says shows it affects only things tied to the Abyss. The final one lies deep in an underground factory of the Dahri (the name Nasejuna uses for Khaenri'ahn) once owned by the Schwanenritter, reached by unsealing relays with Farrwicks and riding an elevator.

Nasejuna's betrayal. At the bottom he demands the Songs, then drops his pose of reverence for Sorush, reveals that his plan is to use them to reverse the Rite of Chinvat and release the seal on the Abyss, and summons the Abyss Herald Klingsor. The Traveler defeats them, but Nasejuna slips away. Pyrrho, another Skeptic, only believes the news when shown Nasejuna's handwritten notes.

Use (The Hymn of Tir Yazad, Part 1). Zurvan explains that the Songs, placed at trees around the Tunigi Hollow that were originally cultivated with Khvarena, would restore their power and let the Pari Mihir and Rashnu lift the seal. Sorush then purifies the trees, and the cleansed Hollow opens the way to the Harvisptokhm for the Rite of Ab-Zohr.

Zurvan tells the Traveler that Klingsor was once of the Order of Skeptics: several hundred years ago he accompanied an investigation team into Dahrian ruins and returned changed, having taken the defilement's blessing, while the team was gone. Followers of the dark hollow then summoned demons to attack Vourukasha Oasis in pursuit of the Songs. They were beaten back with the help of many Pari and human warriors but not wiped out, and Zurvan sealed the Oasis and many ruins with the Songs' power. The Order lost its ancient archives to fire and declined afterwards.

Rene's Investigation Notes (the fragments Nasejuna gives Sorush) record a researcher's view that Khvarena resembles the Abyss in assimilating whatever it touches while being opposed to it. They also describe a Dahri site producing a block of energy called Azosite. The notes mention children named Jakob and Karl and a return journey to Fontaine; the archive does not interpret them beyond what the text shows. They are not about the Songs themselves but guided Nasejuna's search for Farrwicks.

Owners: Fused by Zurvan (or by the first Pari, per the tutorial text), who hid one in Sunyata Lake. In the quests only Sorush, who has the Twin-Horned Chaplet, can pick them up. Nasejuna, with Klingsor and the Abyss Order, tried to take them; the Traveler and Sorush kept them and placed them at the Tunigi Hollow.

Gameplay: Quest items. The tutorial text says the Khvarena's power forms a barrier around each, that only a Pari with the Twin-Horned Chaplet can touch them, and that Sorush, with the Chaplet, may use her power to collect them. The Songs from Samudaya and Dukkha appear in inventory only once those sub-quests are started.

300.comment: Great Song of Khvarena: The Rite of Chinvat
300.content: Nasejuna says the Rite of Chinvat requires collecting the Great Songs so the Sign of Apaosha can be extinguished; Zurvan confirms the rite is real and that she once performed it alongside human heroes to cross the darkness and cleanse the mother-tree. Nasejuna's actual plan is to reverse it with the Songs and release the Abyss. Zurvan says it opens the path into the Harvisptokhm, where the separate Rite of Ab-Zohr then cleanses the tree.

301.comment: Great Song of Khvarena: Nasejuna's Betrayal
301.content: Nasejuna, whom the Skeptics call Vijnanapati, flattered Sorush as the destined Envoy while quietly guiding the party to the Songs. Paimon grew suspicious of his familiarity with the factory's machines. He claims to have read lost documents and to have entered the ruins in secret with a lector. When the last Song was found he revealed that he had never intended to help, insulted Sorush, and summoned Klingsor. The Traveler defeated them, and Nasejuna slipped away. His own account of the Sign of Apaosha is that Dahri records call it the Sign of Truth, reflecting the reality beyond the sky; the quests do not confirm this.

302.content:
Hakushin Ring (also: Hakushin no Wa, Ring of Kitsune Saiguu): The Hakushin Ring is a catalyst that carries the memory of the Kitsune Saiguu, a kitsune of the ancient Hakushin clan who lived in Narukami's mountains and walked among humans. Its short description admits that the device is "but an impoverished vessel" for the full breadth of her thought. Its text is her fond recollection of the friends she made and a final plea.

It is a 4-star catalyst of the Amethyst series that players forge, and it belongs to the Sacred Sakura Cleansing Ritual quest series.

Appearance: A ring-like catalyst; canon text does not describe it further than as a device that stores Saiguu's memory. Its Japanese name, Hakushin no Wa, means "ring of the Hakushin".

Lore: The speaker is the Hakushin Kitsune. She calls her life "simple and ordinary" and says she has lived it to the full, running with her agile and loveable comrades across the mountains and plains of Narukami. She hopes they will be able to run happily again once everything is over.

She remembers an oni maiden with a face as lovely as the moon, with whom she played divine music before the throne, and whose sword dance she applauded. She remembers racing the chieftain of the Yougou Tengu through the spirit mountains and, as a Hakushin, winning the contest, though she suspects the tengu let her off easy. She also remembers outwitting a bake-danuki who challenged her, making him surrender to the Shogun, and then tricking the Shogun into taking that great bake-danuki under her command. A moonlit night in the imperial garden still glows in her memory, and she hopes the Shogun will remember the motto she offered when they parted: do not be blinded, do not waver, keep walking the path you believe in. She hopes the tanuki will not hate her for her final deception.

She lists friends from all walks of life, those she did not expect to make: a shrine maiden who came to train in Narukami for her hometown shrine, a child separated from the adults by the divine palanquin's procession during a summer festival, an easygoing young man who finally went to Liyue to practise the adepti arts, the Kanjou who worked to make the city prosperous, a craftsman obsessed with making extremely sharp swords, and a clan who used ingenious techniques to make man-made meteors bloom in the sky. She hopes the barrier that guards them will not be eroded by darkness.
