The text closes with a plea addressed to a "dark will that gnaws at me". With her strength lost, she offers her Hakushin blood to it and asks, on behalf of those she treasures, that it return her ever-bright memory to the land she loves, so that she can still hope beautiful things endure after its rampage. The wiki links the place she speaks from to the Abyss and the "ever-bright memory" to Hanachirusato; neither is named by the item's own words.

Owners: The Kitsune Saiguu, the Hakushin of the text, is the originating figure; the physical ring is a memory-bearing device rather than a known heirloom.

In the text of Kagura's Verity, Yae Miko calls Saiguu her master and friend and says she departed never to return; this item does not state that Yae holds the ring.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star catalyst in the Amethyst series, released in Version 2.0. Base ATK 44, Energy Recharge as secondary stat. Forged from a Northlander Catalyst Billet, 50 Amethyst Lump, 50 White Iron Chunk and 500 Mora; the diagram Mask of Memories comes from completing Yougou Cleansing.

Its passive, Sakura Saiguu, gives nearby party members of an element involved in an Electro reaction triggered by the wielder an Elemental DMG Bonus for that element (10% at refinement 1, 20% at refinement 5) for 6 seconds, non-stacking. Wiki notes say it applies to Dendro and Electro allies on Aggravate, and to Dendro and Electro (not Hydro) allies on Hyperbloom, that Spread does not trigger it, and that it only triggers while the wielder is on the field.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: a narrative echo of the Saiguu. Characters who knew Yae Miko may react to it as a keepsake of a lost friend. Treat the ring's words as a record of her memories, not as a living voice, unless the scenario decides otherwise.

303.content: The Hakushin Ring's text is Saiguu's memory: running with her fellow kitsune, racing the tengu chieftain, outwitting a bake-danuki and the Shogun, and befriending people of many kinds, ending with a plea to a dark will to return her memory to Inazuma.

304.content:
Hamayumi (also: the shrine maiden's warbow, evil-banishing bow): Hamayumi is a four-star bow of the Amethyst series. Its text is told from a Seirai shrine maiden's point of view: she watches the bandit Ako Domeki (called Zaemon) refuse to bring her aboard the Seiraimaru, thinks of her late archery teacher, and secretly decides to use "true magic" learned on Mt. Yougou against the Electro Archon's ships. The name nods to the real hama yumi, a sacred evil-banishing bow carried by shrine maidens.

Appearance: Item text calls it a warbow and gives no description of its look.

Lore: Ako Domeki, the thief the shrine maiden knows as Zaemon, tells her to get off the Seiraimaru because women are a hindrance. His tone and the way he turns his back recall the person who taught her archery before going on campaign with the Shogun in the Cataclysm, and she reflects that had he not gone, their son would be Zaemon's age. She resolves not to let this person die. She had once secretly learned real magic on Mt. Yougou, from her Master, the tengu Reizenbou. She plans to undo the great barrier that had held for a thousand years and free the resentment of the dying violet thunderbird against the ships flying the Electro banner.

The sea shanties of the departing crew, with spears and swords sharpened and a call to show the Shogunate Seirai's strength, are the sound she hears as she sets down her bow. She is sorry to turn her tengu master's teaching to this use, and hopes only that "that old cat" will not charge into the storm. The text thus places the story on the eve of Seirai's resistance to the Raiden Shogun's forces, a theme that continues in The Catch.

Compared with The Catch, the two texts present the same people from opposite ends: Hamayumi gives the shrine maiden's quiet private resolve, The Catch gives Ako Domeki's later farewell, in which he lists himself as the former master of the Seiraimaru, calls an "old shrine maiden" gone, and sets out to see the edge of the world. The identification of the maiden with Asase Hibiki is the wiki's link, not a statement in the item.

Owners: The text's speaker is a Seirai shrine maiden, read by the wiki as Asase Hibiki. Promotional material shows Yoimiya and Kujou Sara with this bow; that is presentation, not canon ownership.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star bow. Base ATK 41, secondary stat ATK 12%. Passive "Full Draw" raises Normal and Charged Attack DMG, and the bonus is doubled once the wielder's Energy is at 100%. Forged from a diagram found as a reward from Takashi's Mysterious Conch chests, on the seventh opening.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a keepsake of quiet loyalty and of choosing to protect a stubborn friend despite being told to stay behind.

305.content: In the Hamayumi text, a great barrier over Seirai has held for a thousand years (the Chinese original can be read figuratively as "a very long time"). The shrine maiden plans to dissolve it and loose the resentment of the thunderbird against the Shogunate's ships.

306.content:
Haran Geppaku Futsu (also: Haran, Rippling Upheaval, Geppaku Futsu blade): Haran Geppaku Futsu is a celebrated sword of the Futsu school of smiths in Inazuma. It is the only surviving blade forged by the great smith Masagomaru (Futsu Masayoshi). Its name pairs "Haran", meaning turmoil or roiling waves, with the Geppaku Futsu series, of which it is the "Rippling Upheaval" blade.

Its item text is drawn from the "Anthology of Inazuman Blades" by Inspector Mikoshi Nagamasa of Tatarasuna. Two Geppaku Futsu swords were made by order of the school: Hasui, the Wavespike, and Haran, the Rippling Upheaval.

Appearance: Canon text describes the school's blades rather than this sword's fittings: the Hasui blade was pale blue with a hamon like rippling water, while Haran is said to be formidable as a driving hurricane. The two blades look very similar but differ greatly in quality, in the text's account.

Lore: Two Geppaku Futsu swords were made. Hasui was forged by Futsu Minori, third-generation head of the school; its pale blue blade and water-like hamon were often seen at the waist of the Shogun's valet. It was later broken in a mortal duel to decide the fate of the oni people and sent back for reforging.

By then Minori was worn down by drink, old wounds and the lingering memory of Tatarigami, and her son Futsu Hiroyoshi, fourth-generation head, could not match her skill. The task fell to Hiroyoshi's sworn brother Futsu Masayoshi, called Masagomaru, an orphan taken in by Minori, illiterate and mute from birth. Ordered to revive Hasui's beauty, he inscribed its name as it had been before, and the reforging let the school's masterpiece re-enter the world. He named only one work of his own: Haran.

Minori helped Masagomaru pass her techniques on to Hiroyoshi, and wished Masagomaru himself to inherit the school, but he declined repeatedly; the fame of Haran nearly affected Hiroyoshi's succession. Secure that his sworn brother was independent, he left for other lands and learned from other famed smiths. In his late years he had three pupils he was proudest of, Kaedehara Kagemitsu, Niwa Nagamitsu and Akame Mitsunaga, who created the Isshin Sansaku, the three great works of the Isshin Art.

The text includes Masagomaru's own recollections: a mute, abandoned child drawn like a moth to the warmth of the forge-fire, fed rice by the surly Minori, who named him after the metallic sand covering him. She told him of the old wound on one side of her body, her mother's and brother's wishes, the crimson hakama she could never wear and the giant wave that would devour everything. He once saw her weeping while hammering iron; she told him to forget it, then declared him a good keeper of secrets. He regrets not accepting her offer to drink together. Hasui was made as gently beautiful as the sea at night, while the mute Masayoshi's Haran was as fierce as a driving hurricane.

Owners: Futsu Masayoshi (Masagomaru) is the smith, not an owner. No wielder is named in the item text.

The Hasui blade was seen at the waist of the Shogun's valet; the wiki calls Hasui a currently unplayable sword. Nothing states that Haran passed to any specific clan, so avoid assigning it to the Kamisato.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star sword released in Version 2.6 on the weapon event Wish. Base ATK 46 with CRIT Rate as secondary stat.

Its passive, Honed Flow, grants an All Elemental DMG Bonus (12% at refinement 1, 24% at refinement 5). When other nearby party members use Elemental Skills, the wielder gains a Wavespike stack (maximum 2, once per 0.3 seconds). When the wielder uses an Elemental Skill, the stacks are consumed to grant Rippling Upheaval, increasing Normal Attack DMG for 8 seconds by 20% per stack consumed at refinement 1 (40% at refinement 5).

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: a smith-craft legend. Inazuman smiths and swordsmen may know the Anthology's account; most would not recognise the blade. Keep Masagomaru's muteness and the Futsu school's family bonds in mind, and do not invent a wielder.

307.content: The Futsu school of smiths made the Geppaku Futsu pair. Third-generation head Futsu Minori forged Hasui; her foster-son Futsu Masayoshi (Masagomaru), mute from birth, forged Haran and later taught three pupils who made the Isshin Sansaku. Her son Futsu Hiroyoshi became fourth-generation head.

308.content:
Heart of Depth (also: Ocean Conqueror, Gilded Corsage, Gust of Nostalgia, Copper Compass, Goblet of Thundering Deep, Wine-Stained Tricorne): Heart of Depth is a Hydro artifact set (4 and 5 star, added 1.2), also called Ocean Conqueror in the Adventurer Handbook. Its pieces show the last voyage of the Skipper's Chief Mate: a sardonic, hard-drinking exile from a gray aristocratic land, who joined a Liyue sea captain's hunt for the monster that haunted them both. The wiki names him as Parsifal.

The pieces are Gilded Corsage (flower), Gust of Nostalgia (feather), Copper Compass (sands), Goblet of Thundering Deep (goblet) and Wine-Stained Tricorne (circlet). The set text ties in with the Tales From the Waves books and the Serpent Spine weapon text.

Appearance: Sea-worn keepsakes: a corsage faded by sea-salt wind, a red feather stained by blood and brine, a bronze seaman's compass, a faded finely crafted wine cup ground down by sands in the sea's depths, and a tricorne hat thick with the smell of alcohol.

Lore: The Gilded Corsage shows the warship leaving harbour with the Skipper and the Chief Mate, who hums a shanty of his own that mocks his story: the scoundrel who gave up his family name and the witch who hunted him never reached the sea, and the step-brother who could not be an heir became head at last, 'or did he?'. The Gust of Nostalgia describes his arrival with only a slim sword and a sapphire-blue feather pinned to his mantle, the feather later stained red; at his last moment he remembers his drowned days. The Copper Compass is the Skipper's, guiding the ship over whirlpools and guiding the man whose hatred hid behind laughter; when he tries to leave, the Skipper reminds him he signed a contract aboard.

The Goblet falls from the Chief Mate's hand into the ocean and recalls a woman with sapphire eyes and a scar who promised to repay him for the mark. The Tricorne shows the hard-drinking officer given important duties by the Skipper, who does not reprimand him; storm and sea hat lead to the creature that gnaws at his dreams, and the call to set sail. Key beats from the texts: both men are 'people without a thing to our names'; the Chief Mate's shanty names a half-brother and a witch, and his memories contain the witch's scar. In the Goblet he questions how many times he has forgotten the past and concludes that all deaths are in vain and that what has sunk cannot be saved. The wiki, using the Parsifal, Eberhart and Blue-Eyed Spear Witch pages, reads these as the Mondstadt story of the Phantom Thief Parsifal, his half-brother Eberhart and the spear witch, which the set only hints at.

The wiki's Skipper page, drawing on the Tales From the Waves books and Serpent Spine, says the Skipper was a Liyue monster hunter from about a thousand years ago who lost his crew and navigator to a huge sea monster, swore revenge, took in the exiled Parsifal and later died killing it. Those details come from books and a weapon text, not from the set, so treat them as wiki-compiled lore.

Owners: The Chief Mate, whom the wiki identifies as Parsifal, and the Skipper (the compass is his). The wiki lists Parsifal as the set's subject.

Status as of 7.1: Both men are dead; the set is background lore about events around a thousand years ago. Nothing in 6.x or 7.0-7.1 changes this set.

How {{char}} behaves: Use as salty, bittersweet shanty-tavern lore: bravado over grief, humming, wine. Do not name the Chief Mate in a speaker's mouth unless they know the Parsifal story, and do not invent songs beyond the lines in the texts.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). A 4- and 5-star Hydro set from the domain Peak of Vindagnyr on Dragonspine. 2-piece: Hydro DMG Bonus +15%. 4-piece: after using an Elemental Skill, Normal and Charged Attack DMG +30% for 15s.

309.comment: Heart of Depth: The Chief Mate
309.content:
The Chief Mate of Heart of Depth is a cynical, hard-drinking exile from a gray land ruled by an aristocracy (the item text's link points to Mondstadt) who sailed under the Skipper. The wiki names him Parsifal. The texts show his drinking, his forgotten past and his blue feather, not his full story.

He carries a slim sword and a faded blue feather, keeps the memory of a sapphire-eyed woman's scar, and is promised the chance for revenge against a sea creature.

310.content: The Skipper is the rough, jovial captain of the great warship in the Heart of Depth texts; his real name is unknown. His compass guided the ship through whirlpools and his crew contract bound the Chief Mate. The wiki connects him to Serpent Spine and Tales From the Waves.

311.content:
Heart of the Furnace (also: Foundryman's Conjecture, Foundryman's Observation, Foundryman's Calculus, Foundryman's Magnanimity, Foundryman's Legacy): Heart of the Furnace is a 4- and 5-star artifact set for Stellar Glimmer teams, released in version 7.0. Its five pieces, all titled "Foundryman's...", tell the story of a young Domovoy from Kitezhgrad: his rise at the furnace core, his secret assignment, his apprenticeship under the human scholar Aksinya and his later power as president of the Royal Energy Commission.

Each piece starts with the same comparison: something true about the furnace's heart that does not hold for people, such as warmth, the outcome of events, friendship or resolve.

Appearance: No physical appearance is described; the pieces are the personal articles of a furnace worker and later official.

Lore: The Domovoy leaves Kitezhgrad young, with a letter of recommendation, and enters the furnace core where his keen hearing and speed set him apart. Grand Duke Alvis later orders him to join a secret project and watch the others. There, in the research institute Hvergelmir, he becomes the apprentice of the silver-haired human scholar Aksinya, who places a pen in his hand and changes his life. After the old sovereign falls, he takes control of the Energy Commission. In the end he returns the pen to his teacher.

- Foundryman's Conjecture: born in Kitezhgrad, he left on a beast-drawn sled and never saw the city again. He passed through the gates of the ever-burning furnace core and was recognised for hearing keen enough to diagnose the furnace by sound, speed in the narrow iron conduits and skill with Kresnik Kristall and the city's energy supply. He hoped to become a supervisor or president of the torches. At a private banquet, the elderly Grand Duke of mining and energy ordered him, "Izmaylov", to join a project of utmost secrecy and observe everyone.
- Foundryman's Observation: he first thought the silver-haired woman behind the palace curtains was a Tsar's orphan, a symbol of mercy. Inside Hvergelmir he found how wrong he was: she answered ideas before he finished them and understood the duty that made him report to the Grand Duke. He went with her into the Shadow Realm, where she gave him a pen; he added strokes to the blueprint for "the world within the egg". The Tsar fell in a tide that swept away all things, the new monarch's gaze left the forbidden researchers unprotected, and news came that she had died in the shadows.
- Foundryman's Calculus: he grasped that great power must be divided in three before it can gather, and that he had no right to claim it. The lady who shaped wind and snow left with "the heart", and the somber alchemist turned to eternal life. When the Grand Duke announced Aksinya's death, the Domovoy recognised the lie, declined his invitation and swore to return to the Shadow Realm until he found her. When the dark tide destroyed Kitezhgrad, grief gave way to elation: he won an audience with the new sovereign through a fellow Domovoy and, at a price only those present know, became master of the Energy Commission while Alvis was building Novokitezhgrad.

- Foundryman's Magnanimity: as president, he and Alvis opposed each other at every council, possibly as an act, with malice "sweeter than honeyed wine". The Tsaritsa wanted a human to run the new rail transport body; Alvis suddenly yielded his right to nominate, because he believed Izmaylov could not quell a rebellion by descendants of the purged old nobility. Vila raiders called the Burner of Cities roamed the plains by rail. Izmaylov forged weapons for the heroes of Luchkins and crushed the plot; the rebel and the heroes' leader burned in the same flame. The renown went to Izmaylov, and in the narrow alleys he swore an oath with the surviving heroes, thereby founding the High Table.
- Foundryman's Legacy: years later, white-haired and frail, he met Aksinya again. She had been spared by the Shadow Realm. He answered all she had missed, bowed, removed his hat as he did as an apprentice and gave back her pen. He said he had spent five hundred years believing she would never abandon her dream or life, and that the debt between them was cleared. He ends by saying her name.
The set's tone is of a loyal, ordinary-seeming engineer who rises through patience and calculation. Whether every political step was truly selfless is left open.

Owners: The set belongs to the Domovoy Izmaylov, who is addressed by that name in the text. No other owner is named.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): 4- and 5-star set from the Inverted Glacier domain (Everfrozen Earth, Snezhnaya). 4-piece: when the wearer triggers a Stellar Glimmer reaction or deals Stellar Glimmer reaction DMG, ATK +12% for 12s; Stellar Glimmer reaction DMG dealt by all nearby party members +50%. It works off-field, and the DMG bonus from several sets with this name does not stack.

312.comment: Heart of the Furnace: Heart of the Furnace
312.content: Artifact set whose item text narrates the life of the Domovoy Izmaylov, from Kitezhgrad's furnace core to the Royal Energy Commission and his devotion to his teacher Aksinya.

313.comment: Heart of the Furnace: Izmaylov and Alvis
313.content: In the Heart of the Furnace text, the Domovoy Alvis, Grand Duke of mining and energy in Kitezhgrad, orders the talented young Izmaylov to join a secret project. After the old court falls, Izmaylov takes the Royal Energy Commission while Alvis oversees the building of Novokitezhgrad, and the two oppose each other in council. The Magnanimity text says some believed it was an act and that only those involved knew the truth.

314.content:
Heretic's Molten Blade (also: Lone Light's Blessing, Och-Kan's blade): Heretic's Molten Blade is a 4-star sword from the Battle Pass, belonging to Och-Kan, the Sacred Lord of Ochkanatlan. A gift from the red-haired Pyro Archon, it was later turned against him.

The item text is a short tragedy: a half-dragon tyrant who was never a swordsman, a gift given at a bonfire, and a death at the hands of the crimson-eyed youth.

Appearance: Canon says only that the blade was made from smelted works of the ancient dragons and kept in a leather scabbard, with an edge that dulled from long disuse yet kept clean of dust. Keep descriptions to a well-kept, unused sword.

Lore: Och-Kan stood alone in his empty royal hall and drew a sword that had gone unused for so long its edge had dulled. He kept it spotless for decades, though he was no swordsman.

The sword had been a gift. At a bonfire after a battle, the heroes asked the red-haired Pyro Archon to judge the best weapon, and he asked Och-Kan what he wanted; the blade was made from smelted dragon works and tuned to his proportions.

Och-Kan's dragon blood gave him strength far beyond ordinary people, so he did not need a sword: he was known for commanding the golden language and its rainbow light, but none knew he could fight a dragon bare-handed. After the heroes swept a stronghold of draconic descendants, they lit a bonfire among the bones and broken mechanisms and bragged about their weapons. One argued for a great two-handed sword; Lianca replied that her venom-tipped arrows made such blows possible; Ixquieh was credited for luring the dragons into the trap with Phlogiston; her brother Ahpub, called elder brother, was praised for dodging claws and crashing a dragon's head into a cliff; Maghan's flute-playing and Uenuku's teasing round out the scene.

When asked to name a weapon, Och-Kan realized he saw himself as the other man's most perfect weapon. His answer is not given, but it pleased only Ahpub and the red-haired man, who then kept his word and had fire smelt the works of the dragons into a blade. The weapon was standard practice, made from materials gathered on the hunt. Och-Kan swore to use it to hunt every inhuman heretic and build a realm for humans alone for the giver.

The text ends in his fall. It had been too long since he last wielded the sword in battle, and he was never good at it. The crimson-eyed young man, immature but wrathful, appeared before him with a might like a god's, wrenched the sword from his hand, and drove it into his chest as he staggered toward the mud. As he sank into the black mire, Och-Kan murmured that it could only have been so, and in the youth's flames took a last glimpse of the shadow of a cunning crimson fox, face filled with sorrow, flashing across the corner of the collapsing palace. Read alongside the wiki's profile of Och-Kan, the weapon records the hinge between his time as a hero's comrade and his tyranny and fall; the text itself does not narrate the years in between.

Owners: Och-Kan, the Sacred Lord, is the owner. He received the blade from the red-haired Pyro Archon and died by it.

The blade passed from the red-haired man's gift into Och-Kan's keeping and, in the end, into the hand of the crimson-eyed youth who killed him with it. No source shows who holds it after that.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star sword, base ATK 42 at level 1, secondary stat CRIT Rate; Battle Pass (Gnostic Hymn, BP Bounty), Version 7.0; part of the Gnostic Hymn 3 series.

Passive "Lone Light's Blessing": after using an Elemental Skill, the wielder gains "Gleam of First Light" for 14s, usable once every 14s and removed when the wielder leaves the field. Each second it grants an ATK bonus based on the distance travelled in the previous second, from 18% to 36% at refinement 1 up to 36% to 72% at refinement 5.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: speakers can refer to the blade as the Sacred Lord's sword, a relic of the age when he fought beside the heroes. Keep the story's moral weight: it was a gift of trust that he later betrayed.

315.comment: Heretic's Molten Blade: Lone Light's Blessing
315.content: Lone Light's Blessing is the passive of the sword Heretic's Molten Blade (gameplay): an ATK bonus after an Elemental Skill that grows with the distance the wielder travels each second.

316.content:
Hilichurl Cultural Customs (also: Hilifolk Study): Hilichurl Cultural Customs is a four-volume study by Jacob Musk, a Mondstadt ecologist whom the books call the 'Poet Laureate of Hilichurlian'. It records how hilichurl tribes organise themselves, what they revere and how three tribes of Dadaupa Gorge differ. It is a field scholar's account, often condescending and incomplete.

The cover and spine carry the title 'Hilifolk Study' in the Teyvat script. The books are useful for what hilichurls are seen to do, less for why, because Musk could not speak to them.

Appearance: Four short volumes in an academic, observational tone, each headed by a topic. Vols. 1, 2 and 4 are kept in Mondstadt's library, and Vol. 3 in the Grand Master's office of the Knights of Favonius Headquarters.

Lore: Vol. 1 (social structure): hilichurl tribes are small and treated like a large family. The oldest member, the shaman, usually leads, wears a horned smiling mask and chants; but in some tribes a larger, stronger hilichurl with a horned mask takes over, which makes the tribe more aggressive. Resources seem to be shared according to need. Vol. 2 (spirituality): they worship elemental power itself rather than an Archon, and masks and body paint show a member's element. Vol. 3: the huge solitary Lawa are called 'king' but do not lead. Vol. 4: the Meaty, Sleeper and Eclipse tribes of Dadaupa Gorge show cultural diversity.

- Vol. 1: all members are gatherers and soldiers; those who prize combat become the heavyweights. Musk puzzles over how hilichurls, even shamans, use the elements without Visions, and calls the question one for further analysis.
- Vol. 2: shamans dye their hair and skin with the colour of their element and lead hymns and dances. Leftover meat is left raw on the altar, even though the tribe collects Mora and valuables. Musk says hilichurls seem to have no sense of past or future, do not store food or honour the dead, and that their 'writing' is poor copying of ruin inscriptions. He also notes their odd attachment to ruins as camp sites.
- Vol. 3: Lawa have great strength and elemental control and use the elements to strengthen their bodies. Adventurers meet them rarely and prudently avoid the areas they roam.
- Vol. 4: the Meaty tribe keeps a boar pen with a swineherd, cooks a stew in a pot warmed by a Pyro Slime, and has an arena where challengers who lose are mocked. The Sleeper tribe lives in wooden huts with hide beds and is the cleverest and most cunning. The Eclipse tribe is the most occult, worships a crude eclipsed-sun symbol, has stronger shamans and a grand throne at the centre of its settlement.

- Musk is an observer, not a participant: he cites Knights of Favonius patrol reports for resource sharing, and says language barriers and hostility make precise research on distribution impossible.
- Take the claims on hilichurl intelligence and memory as Musk's opinion. The book is one scholar's early field view; the Traveler's voice-over comment on the Eclipse tribe and the Khaenri'ah curse are separate lore.
- Comparison: Vol. 2 says hilichurls revere elements as abstractions, not as the Seven; this matters when a hilichurl is shown near an Archon statue or Mondstadt's religion.
- Vol. 4 is the only volume to name specific tribes; the Eclipse tribe is the one the wiki connects, through a Traveler voice-over, with the Eclipse Dynasty. The book itself makes no such link.

Owners: No individual owner. Copies are in Mondstadt's library and the Grand Master's office of the Knights of Favonius Headquarters. Author: Jacob Musk.

Gameplay: Game note: a four-volume collectible book collection added in version 1.0; reading is purely lore.

317.comment: Hilichurl Cultural Customs: Hilichurl Shamans and Chiefs
317.content: Per Musk, the shaman is normally the oldest member of the tribe and the tribe's parent-figure, but a stronger, larger hilichurl can replace him, after which the tribe grows more aggressive. Shamans wear horned smiling masks, carry a staff, chant to themselves and dye themselves in the colour of their element.

318.content: Lawa are very large and strong hilichurls who use elemental power to defend and strike harder. The tribe addresses them with a respectful word translating to king or chief, yet they do not lead, preferring to avoid the reverent stares of smaller hilichurls.

319.comment: Hilichurl Cultural Customs: The Dadaupa Gorge Tribes
319.content: The Meaty tribe feasts, keeps boars and has a combat arena. The Sleeper tribe sleeps in hide-bedded huts and is the most cunning. The Eclipse tribe is the most occult, worshipping a crude eclipsed-sun symbol and enthroning its strongest shaman. Described in Vol. 4.

key: The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria
History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria
320.comment: The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria
320.content:
The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria (also: History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria, Decline and Fall of Remuria, Pulteney's history of Remuria): The author is a Fontainian historian under the first Hydro Archon, Egeria. He claims to reconstruct Remuria's true shape with "the universal rationality of history" and distrusts the folklore around it, including the claims of the Golden Troupe, who say they are Remuria's descendants. The tone is pro-Egeria and moralising: Remuria fell because its people abandoned their duties for hedonism and because Remus tried to hand divine authority to humans.

It is the most direct in-world overview of Remuria that a Fontainian can read, and it contrasts with the satirical Anecdota Septentrionalis and the knightly La Chanson d'Erinnyes, which show Remuria from its own people and from its enemies.

Appearance: A 4-star book collection of three volumes. The cover title reads FALL OF REMURIA in the Fontaine script. In the game, Vol. 1 and Vol. 3 are sold by the NPC Hubel in the Quartier Narbonnais of the Court of Fontaine, and Vol. 2 is found in the Palais Mermonia.

Lore: Vol. 1 opens with the legend that the ocean gave birth to everything and also devoured it. Heaven drowned the early peoples for turning from their fate, and the survivors lived like animals until the great king Remus descended on Meropis in his golden ship Fortuna, taught farming, built cities and temples, and spread music and art.

Heaven's first-era envoys had guided people to peace until people tired of it; Heaven then sent huge waves and a hundred days of rain. With an immortal fleet Remus conquered all the islands on the high waters, and even the great dragon beneath the abyssal depths submitted. Seers prophesied that the greatest empire would meet utter destruction, and that this is Fortuna. In answer Remus composed a symphony of prosperity from the seven-day rotation and the flowing winds, believing that if every city echoed it, they would escape fate's judgment.

Vol. 2 describes the Eternal City as it was. Ships passed the Ocean Pillars along the royal fairway to a giant port, where the imperial ship Fortuna lay and a lofty tower guided ships by bell. The fairway led to Machimos, home of Remuria's warriors, and on to Capitolium, the centre of the empire, a paradise for artists where only top intellectuals and musicians were admitted and a golden palace with copper pillars stood. Remus listened to every note of the empire and corrected any discord with a pluck of his strings. He shared power with four capable humans, the Harmosts, to eliminate discord, and built fairways to carry his melody outward. The author counts Remus's worst sin as passing power reserved for the divine to humans, which brought corruption, decadence, violence and revolt.

Vol. 3 describes the end: the earth collapsed at once, the tower was uprooted and drowned in titanic waves, and the city with its people and its golden palace fell into a chasm of eternal darkness. When the royal city collapsed and the tribes were on the edge of barbarism, Egeria, the Noble Navigator, settled the conflicts among the tribes, and new cities were founded around the flowing springs under law.
In Vol. 3 the author says that the catastrophe was so swift that the researchers and records able to pass the knowledge on sank with the city, and that the Golden Troupe's "mysterious researchers" deliberately distorted what remained. He accepts that Remurians really made terrifying golems, which are still found ruined in the wild, but blames this on their moral decline. He objects to folklore that paints the greatest scholars of the age as soul-stealers who bound mortal spirits into golems.

Two readings matter for roleplay. The author states that the tragedy of Remuria occurred "merely a century ago", which is not consistent with other Fontaine material. And he calls the fall just punishment, a view that reflects Fontaine's official, Egeria-centred historiography.

Details worth keeping straight: the book names Gurabad in the far south and a noble kindred of the east (linked by the wiki to Chenyu Vale) as other powers that rose while Fontaine's ancestors were in ignorance. The golden ship Fortuna is linked by the wiki to the Domus Aurea. The Harmosts are four humans, and the book never names them individually. Its refrain about oceans rising and empires falling closes every volume.

Owners: No named owner. In the world it is sold in the Court of Fontaine and kept in the Palais Mermonia, so it reads as a common reference work.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a 4-star Book Collection added in 4.0; its three volumes are collected in the Court of Fontaine (Vol. 1 and Vol. 3 from the NPC Hubel, Vol. 2 in the Palais Mermonia).

321.comment: The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria: Pulteney
321.content: Pulteney is the great scholar credited in-game as the author of The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria, written in the early years of Fontaine's founding. Nothing else about him is established. He frames his work as an effort to extract Remuria's true shape with the universal rationality of history, in contrast to the legends and the Golden Troupe's distortions.

322.comment: The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria: Remus in Pulteney's history
322.content:
In Pulteney's account, Remus is the great king who descended on Meropis in his golden Fortuna, taught farming, building, music and art, conquered the islands of the high waters, and built a symphony of prosperity to escape the prophesied doom. He is called universal Harmost, immortal ruler and God King. The author judges his gravest sin to be the delegating of divine power to humans.

The Anecdota Septentrionalis calls him Sebastos, and La Chanson d'Erinnyes shows his emissary demanding water and earth from Erinnyes.

323.comment: The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria: The Harmosts of Remuria
323.content: Remus promoted four humans of great capability to be Harmosts, partners in governing every city and removing discordant sounds. Pulteney blames this delegation for the corruption and revolts that ended Remuria. The book does not name them; other sources identify Boethius and Cassiodor among them.

324.comment: The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria: The Eternal City's layout
324.content: Vol. 2 describes the approach to the capital: the Ocean Pillars, the royal fairway, the tower with its bell that guided ships between islands, the port where Fortuna lay, the warrior city of Machimos with temples and arenas of carved rock, and finally Capitolium with its theaters and the golden palace of copper pillars. Only the best intellectuals and musicians could live in Capitolium.

325.comment: The History of the Decline and Fall of Remuria: The Remurian golems in Pulteney's history
325.content: Pulteney admits that the Remurians did build terrifying golems, whose ruins can still be found in the wild. He rejects the folk story that the greatest ancient scholars trapped mortal spirits in them as magisters, and attributes the golems to the moral decay of Remuria's last days.

326.content:
Holy Lyre der Himmel (also: Holy Lyre, Barbatos's lyre, Lyre of the Heavens): The Holy Lyre der Himmel is Mondstadt's sacred lyre, said to be the instrument Barbatos, the Anemo Archon, once played. The Church of Favonius keeps it. In the Prologue the Fatui hide it, the Traveler retrieves it, and Dvalin's purified tears restore enough of its power for Venti to use it against the Stormterror's madness.

Its frame is rosewood carved with a pattern of flowing wind. By the time of the Prologue its Anemo power had run dry; restoring it takes Dvalin's own crystal tears, and it is damaged again in the final confrontation.

Only the Prologue (1.0) features it. Its in-game description calls it a treasure of Barbatos whose Anemo power has dried up, and Jean later calls it a blessing from Lord Barbatos with the power to purify evil.

Appearance: A lyre with a rosewood frame carved with flowing wind patterns. Venti notes the strings still feel cool to the touch. Its repaired and damaged states are separate quest items; the damaged lyre's description says its once-clear sound has become dull, ear-piercing noise.

Lore: Mondstadt treats the Holy Lyre as Barbatos's relic. It is used in the Ludi Harpastum ceremony, and otherwise borrowing it requires signed documents from the Grand Master, the Seneschal and a Community Representative. In the Prologue the Fatui hide it in a ruin; the Traveler fights through to retrieve it. Back at Angel's Share, Venti greets it with obvious nostalgia and says that although it is genuine, a thousand years have drained its Anemo power. The Traveler uses a purified teardrop crystal of Dvalin on it, partly restoring it.

Details of the repair. In State of the Holy Lyre der Himmel, Venti explains that the lyre itself is fine and the weakness is in the strings, whose Anemo intensity has faded. One purified tear stops it losing more power but does not refill it, so Jean mobilises the Knights to find more tears. Crystal Tears completes the repair after three teardrop crystals are purified. Venti then plays it to bring Dvalin back to himself; the lyre is broken during the final confrontation.

Ending Note (end of the Prologue). Venti, Jean and the Traveler take the wrecked lyre to the Cathedral to hand it back. Barbara, the deaconess, is horrified at its state. Venti casts an Anemo illusion so it appears repaired, then hints that it will not last and they should leave quickly. Barbara storms off with it, saying the Traveler and Venti will never touch it again. Outside, Signora ambushes Venti (see item.anemo-gnosis). Earlier, Venti told Diluc and the Traveler that the Fatui might be using Dvalin to draw out Barbatos, which prompted Diluc's wary question about why he thought so.

Owners: Originally Barbatos's own instrument; held by the Church of Favonius in modern times. The Fatui held it briefly in the Prologue. It ends the Prologue in Barbara's custody.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the lyre has no further role in the main story. The last canon image of it is the illusion-repaired but actually broken lyre taken back by the Church. Treat its present condition and location as unspecified.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): the lyre is a symbol of Mondstadt's faith in an absent god. Most townsfolk revere it without knowing Venti is Barbatos. If Venti is in the scene he is fond of it and reluctant to explain why. Do not have it play or summon anything now, since its power is gone, and do not hand it out as ordinary loot.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): it appears only as a quest item in the Prologue Archon Quest chain, in four states (Holy Lyre, Partially Repaired, Completely Repaired, Damaged), and cannot be kept or used afterwards.

327.comment: Holy Lyre der Himmel: Holy Lyre der Himmel in the Prologue
327.content: In the Prologue the Fatui take the Holy Lyre to use against Stormterror. The Traveler recovers it, restores its power with Dvalin's purified teardrop crystals, and Venti plays it to reach Dvalin. It is badly damaged in the fight and returned to the Church of Favonius, where Venti covers the damage with an illusion.

328.comment: Holy Lyre der Himmel: Venti and the lyre
328.content: Venti recognises the lyre by its carved rosewood and cool strings. Paimon scolds him for having once borrowed it to play for tavern drinkers; he answers with a laugh. He treats it as a friend's keepsake rather than a weapon, and says Dvalin used to listen to the wind's songs with him.

329.content:
Hunter's Path: Hunter's Path is a 5-star bow of the Sumeru series, a golden hunting bow made of precious white branches. Its description says it has felled countless wicked beasts trying to infiltrate the woods. The story is about a huntress who pursued a dark herd so long that she forgot the human tongue and became a beast herself.

The bow also appears, as a moon-white bow in the hands of a huntress, in the Light of Foliar Incision's text, tying the two weapons into one tale of the forest.

Appearance: A gilded bow of white branches containing "the blessing of the forest". The text adds that trees with such white branches are now rare and that the bow's blessings were once covered by darkened blood that water has since washed away.

Lore: A hunter pursues a dark herd in a hunt that never seems to end, waiting nights under rotten leaves and sleeping inside carcasses, always moving to the next target after the fatal arrow. She stops caring about the wind revealing her location or about camouflaging her scent with wildflowers, as her smell becomes like that of wild beasts. She forgot the human tongue before she became a hunter, and even the blind youth who first found her and gave her the white-branch bow was forgotten.

She is told that the bloodstained will never find the hunting grounds of endless viridescence, and replies that the world where barbarous beasts roam shall be her hunting grounds. Looking into clear water by moonlight, she sees that she too has turned into a wild beast. A black knight, whose form and sword are reflected in the water, follows the tracks of the beast and finds her at a loss. He says he took her for another beast to destroy, tempted by the illusory moon in the water, though for a moment he thought he saw a maiden lost in the forest, and states that he must continue west to settle the crime of twisting man into a beast's form.

The black knight is Roland by the wiki's annotation, and the "beast's form" he speaks of refers to the hilichurls. The text does not say what becomes of the huntress. The same white bow is described in Light of Foliar Incision as held by a huntress who drove an exiled prince through the forest's maze and spared him, which the wiki reads as the same huntress.

Tone: the item moves from praise of the bow to a lament. The change is the central point of the story, a hunter slowly becoming what she hunts. When using it in a scene, avoid giving the huntress a name; canon does not.

Owners: No owner is named. The huntress is the only wielder in the text.

The wiki reads the Light of Foliar Incision text as showing her later, still wielding the moon-white bow in Dharma Forest. No present-day character is established as owning it.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star bow released in Version 3.0 (2022-08-24), level 1 base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT Rate. Passive At the End of the Beast-Paths grants All Elemental DMG Bonus and, after the wielder hits with a Charged Attack, the Tireless Hunt effect, which raises Charged Attack DMG by a percentage of Elemental Mastery for 12 Charged Attacks or 10 s; it can be gained once every 12 s.

At refinement 1 the Elemental DMG Bonus is 12% and Tireless Hunt adds 160% of Elemental Mastery; refinement 5 gives 24% and 320%. Ascension uses Inactivated, Dormant and Robust Fungal Nucleus with Faded Red Satin, Trimmed Red Silk and Rich Red Brocade.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: speak of the bow as a relic of the rainforest and of a forgotten huntress. Do not turn the huntress into a named, speaking character unless the user supplies one.

key: At the End of the Beast-Paths
330.comment: Hunter's Path: At the End of the Beast-Paths
330.content: At the End of the Beast-Paths is the weapon passive of Hunter's Path (gameplay). It grants a permanent Elemental DMG Bonus and the Tireless Hunt buff after a Charged Attack.

key: Husk of Opulent Dreams artifact set
331.content:
Husk of Opulent Dreams (also: Husk of Opulent Dreams artifact set, Bloom Times, Plume of Luxury, Song of Life, Calabash of Awakening, Skeletal Hat): Husk of Opulent Dreams is a 4 and 5 star Inazuma artifact set that tells, in dream-like fragments, the life of a puppet made to hold a "heart": the figure once known as Scaramouche, Sixth of the Eleven Fatui Harbingers (the Balladeer), who now goes by the Wanderer. It is a defence and Geo-damage set.

It is dropped by the Slumbering Court domain on Seirai Island, and came with Version 2.3. The texts follow the puppet from creation and abandonment, through the faces and names he tried on, to the stage name he chose for himself, with the theme that he is still living out a story whose ending is not written.

Appearance: Five pieces: Bloom Times (flower, a golden six-petalled ornament that never wilts, symbol of the transience of mortal glories), Plume of Luxury (plume, a feather-shaped token from a secluded hall), Song of Life (sands, a mechanism with the heart removed and its hands no longer moving, a small overseas object to Inazuma eyes), Calabash of Awakening (goblet, a gourd gilded with powdered gold and black paint, original colour lost) and Skeletal Hat (circlet, a hat that shielded a wanderer from sun and rain and became a tool for hiding faces).

Lore: The pieces read as snapshots of a wanderer: a vessel made for a heart and left to sleep, a gold ornament of the Shogun's, a young traveller turned away by a rain, and a name taken from the villains of Inazuma's theatre.

Song of Life: the puppet was made to hold a "heart" but wept in his dreams; his maker judged him too fragile as a person or a tool, did not destroy him, and let him sleep, and in her later works left aside designs that could store such a heart. Later he awoke and wandered, watching hearts that were good, upright, strong and gentle, and he wanted one too. He eventually obtained one, the very purpose of his existence, but not what he wanted: it carried no blessing and was a sacrifice full of selfishness, hypocrisy, cunning and curses in an amiable husk. If he tore it out he would feel nothing at all.

Plume of Luxury: the wanderer no longer thinks about moonlit nights at Tatarasuna or the furnace fires. Four unnamed voices show the same gold ornament, a proof of identity from the Shogun, in different lights: a kind young deputy told him to keep his identity hidden on his travels; an upright Inspector explained that because he was neither man nor mechanism he had to be dealt with in a certain way; hopeful eyes saw it as something that could save people; and a shrine maiden said she would not abandon him and would send for help. In the end the golden arrow-feather lay in dust and all the tales burned in karmic flames.

Skeletal Hat: a child of a Tatarasuna craftsperson, a boatman, an underling who calls him "Lord Harbinger", and an old woman on Yashiori Island each ask where he is going. He tells the sick child he is bound for Inazuma City, gets onto a boat with a stranger's help, slaps the chatty underling, and tells him he is going east to Mondstadt; on returning, he says he is headed for an appointed meeting, and a lady in foreign garb throws him a small crystal sphere from the shore, which he lifts toward the dying sun.

Calabash of Awakening: the Raiden Gokaden had five branches (Amenoma, Futsu, Isshin, Hyakume, Senju), but only Amenoma still keeps its line, and Isshin barely has descendants. People think time did this, but the text says the wanderer did it as a revenge against the bladesmith, then dropped his plan halfway because it became dull, and would call it only a little experiment into human nature in a tone he learned from a researcher. Inazuman theatre has a stock role "Kunikuzushi" for schemers who topple nations; at the end of his wandering he chose that name himself, and no longer remembers the earlier one. Plays are named by joining the titles of their three acts, and the text ends with his third act still running.

Bloom Times: in a dream the wanderer sees a phantom dancing in moonlight, like a blank young man from long ago, and is told that the "heart" he once acquired was a prop for lies, that this false body can aspire to rule the world, and that it is only a passing dream of glory; he awakes, and what fades is the imagined future, not him.

Owners: The pieces are associated with the Wanderer; the Shogun's gold ornament in the Plume of Luxury is described as a token given by the Almighty Shogun, and the Skeletal Hat and the gourd are his travelling things.

Gameplay: Gameplay, not lore: the 2-piece bonus is DEF +30%. The 4-piece bonus grants "Curiosity" stacks: on the field, a stack per Geo attack (once per 0.3s); off the field, a stack every 3s; each of up to 4 stacks gives 6% DEF and 6% Geo DMG Bonus, and a stack drops after 6 seconds without gaining one. It drops from the Slumbering Court domain.

332.comment: Husk of Opulent Dreams: The puppet and the Shogun's gold ornament
332.content: In the Husk of Opulent Dreams texts, the wanderer is never named, but he is a puppet made to hold a "heart", has been a Lord Harbinger, lived at Tatarasuna, and carries a gold ornament that the Shogun gave as proof of identity. The texts describe his name "Kunikuzushi" as one he chose from Inazuman theatre, in which the name belongs to schemers who bring down states. The Raiden Shogun's voice-over line "About Kunikuzushi" and the Wishes quest are the wiki's cited corroboration.

333.comment: Husk of Opulent Dreams: Tatarasuna and the Kabukimono years
333.content: The Plume of Luxury recalls moonlit nights over Tatarasuna and its furnace fires. Wiki summary pages on Mikoshi Nagamasa say a puppet found in the Shakkei Pavilion was introduced to the workers at Tatarasuna and welcomed as one of them under the name "Kabukimono", though the artifact texts do not use that name. Treat the link as wiki-derived rather than stated in the item text.

334.content:
Hydro Gnosis (also: Fontaine's Gnosis, Gnosis of the Hydro Archon, Hydro Archon's Gnosis): Fontaine's Gnosis, the chess-piece-like divine focus of the Hydro Archon. Focalors, the real Archon, hid inside the Oratrice Mecanique d'Analyse Cardinale with it while Furina played the god in public for some 500 years. After Focalors's execution (4.2) it passed to Neuvillette, who gave it to the Harbinger Arlecchino as a "diplomatic gift".

He let it go because it had "lost all meaning" for Fontaine and because Skirk warned him it was the remains of the Third Descender, an object of "misfortune".

Appearance: A gleaming chess-piece shape like the other Gnoses; its crown resembles an inverted fleur-de-lis.

Lore: In 4.0 Lyney revealed that the Tsaritsa had let Arlecchino use its power first, to try to break the prophecy. In 4.1 Arlecchino recalled ambushing Furina in disguise, sensing no Gnosis on her and only real terror, and concluded the Archon was not what she seemed. In 4.2 Focalors told Neuvillette she had "become one" with the Oratrice, taking Fontaine's Gnosis with her.

When the Oratrice's blade fell on Focalors, the Hydro Archon's divine throne was destroyed but the Gnosis survived, and as her divinity faded she handed it to Neuvillette. A throne and a Gnosis are therefore separate things. A Gnosis embodies the Heavenly Principles' control over Teyvat, links its Archon to Celestia and amplifies elemental power; Furina, the public "Hydro Archon", never held it.

In Finale (4.2) Lyney says the gift could be read as an apology for the trouble Childe had in Fontaine, thanks for his part in holding off the All-Devouring Narwhal, or thanks for Arlecchino's relief work at Poisson, but that Neuvillette's attitude to giving it away had clearly changed. Neuvillette gives two reasons. The Fatui's only remaining goal in Fontaine was the Gnosis, so handing it over avoided needless conflict. And Skirk, repeating her master, had sensed it on him and urged him to get rid of objects of "misfortune", so keeping it would put Fontaine at risk.

Third descender: What the Gnoses are made of was revealed in two steps. In Finale (4.2) Skirk called the Hydro Gnosis the remains of the Third Descender. In the same scene Neuvillette concluded that the Gnoses in general come from the Third Descender. In the 7.1 Archon Quest the Tsaritsa confirmed that they do not originate from Teyvat's own system, and Rhinedottir explained that the Third Descender consented to have his remains split into seven pieces to consolidate the Heavenly Principles' rule. (The wiki identifies him as Saarelainen; the quest dialogue checked here calls him only the Third Descender.) The Tsaritsa collects them to amplify her power against the Heavenly Principles and because only a Gnosis seems to respond to the seal he left beneath her palace.

Owners: Focalors, then briefly Neuvillette (who says he does not need its power), then Arlecchino, then the Tsaritsa.

Arlecchino received it in negotiations with Neuvillette after Furina left. At the docks she told the Traveler that taking it to Snezhnaya was her duty as a Harbinger.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 it is in Snezhnaya, one of the six Gnoses the Tsaritsa holds.

In 7.1 she used all six as nodes of a field that, amplifying her Cryo power, slowed time around Rhinedottir. The Third Descender's seal in Zapolyarny Palace is still unopened.

Gameplay: Gameplay: a story object only; it cannot be obtained or used.

Gameplay event: During the limited web event "Snezhnaya Awaits" before Version 7.0, the Hydro Gnosis appeared on a recap card for the Fontaine Archon Quest (Masquerade of the Guilty), captioned with Neuvillette's line that it had lost all meaning for Fontaine.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay guidance (project recommendation): after 4.2 nobody in Fontaine has the Gnosis, and its absence does not weaken Neuvillette or Fontaine's power supply. Ordinary Fontainians do not know where it was hidden or that it was given away; the handover was a private negotiation. Never place it with Furina, and do not have Neuvillette or Arlecchino use it. Few people know of the Third Descender link: Neuvillette, the Traveler and Paimon (from Skirk in 4.2), and those present in Snezhnaya in 7.1.

335.content: After the prophecy was averted (Finale, 4.2), Neuvillette gave Fontaine's Gnosis to the Harbinger Arlecchino as a "diplomatic gift". Publicly it could pass as gratitude: the Fatui had helped at Poisson and Childe had helped hold back the All-Devouring Narwhal. Privately, Neuvillette judged that the Gnosis was meaningless to Fontaine now that the throne was gone, that the Fatui would otherwise keep pursuing it, and that it was dangerous to keep after Skirk called it the remains of the Third Descender.

336.comment: Hydro Gnosis: Arlecchino's hunt for the Hydro Gnosis
336.content:
In Calamitous Tread (4.1), Arlecchino pressed Furina at a tea party about the Oratrice and the Indemnitium it had stored. The quest also shows, in Arlecchino's recollection, how she had earlier approached Furina in disguise while Furina was chasing a stray cat, and struck at her to see whether she carried the Gnosis. She did not, and her terror was genuine, so Arlecchino left.

Arlecchino sensed a curse on Furina and began to suspect Neuvillette might be the true Archon, in which case he probably held the Gnosis; otherwise it might be hidden somewhere ordinary people could not reach. She then summoned Lyney and her other children. Her informants reported that Furina told no one, cried alone in her quarters and could not sleep that night.

337.content:
Hymn of the Maelstrom: Hymn of the Maelstrom is a 5-star catalyst, an exquisite lamp of blue chalcedony that looks like a treasure from a fairy tale. It is said that a song of praise, forgotten by all, slumbers sealed inside. Its text is a fairy tale a storyteller tells a young Water Imp about a child born of the waves. Added in Version 7.1.

The tale ends as a warning to the Water Imps to sing only for those who truly understand their song. The lamp's design and name are not tied to a character in canon.

Appearance: Canon describes only an exquisite lamp crafted out of blue chalcedony. The tale mentions silk, golden robes and agate in the prince's gifts and a sacred artifact brought by the sisters, but the text does not say that artifact is this lamp.

Lore: A young Water Imp who sings alone keeps close a fairy tale from her youth: a child born of the breaking waves, nobler than the daughters of the sea, whose voice made mariners sink into whirlpools and thawed frozen seas.

She followed a prince of the land despite her sisters' warnings and her father's call to stay in the sea, sang only for him, and was cherished like a jewel in a jewel-box palace. Her voice grew harsh, she could no longer sing the ancient hymns, and the prince grieved only that she had lost her worth.

Her sisters rose to shore and urged her to find her voice or turn to foam. Her kin made a blood bargain with the fae of the wind and brought her a sacred artifact, saying the prince's indifference had imprisoned her song and that if his heart spilled blood the artifact would return her to them. She raised the blade above the sleeping prince, her hands trembling, but the strike faded into a sigh, and the ancient hymns were lost in the twilight of the story. The young Water Imp, who had expected a happy ending, asks what the story means, and the storyteller says the Water Imps should sing only for those who truly understand their song.

The wiki links the "fae of the wind" in the tale to the Vila. The storyteller says the tale has been told by the Water Imp people for a hundred years, so it is folklore rather than recorded history. The lamp's description about a forgotten hymn is separate from the tale, and the text does not connect the two.

Owners: Canon names no owner. The text is about a Water Imp and her tale, not about a possessor.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore: a 5-star catalyst with base ATK 44 and an HP secondary stat. Rondo of Slumber raises Healing Bonus and, after the wielder heals, grants Max HP and a party ATK buff that scales with Max HP above 40,000; Frozen or Stellar Swirl reactions by a nearby party member raise the bonuses further, and the effect works off-field. It was on the weapon event Wish Epitome Invocation (2026-09-23 to 2026-10-13).

How {{char}} behaves: This archive's suggested use: a lamp that keeps a story about a voice lost to indifference. Use it for scenes about whom one sings for. Do not give the lamp a wielder or say its sealed hymn is known.

338.comment: Hymn of the Maelstrom: Hymn of the Maelstrom
338.content: Hymn of the Maelstrom is a 5-star chalcedony-lamp catalyst said to seal a forgotten song of praise. Its text is a Water Imp fairy tale about a child of the waves who gave her voice to a prince, lost it, and could not bring herself to harm him. Canon names no owner.

key: Prayer Songs of the Frostmoon Scions
339.content:
Hymns of the Far North (also: Hymns of the Far North (I), Prayer Songs of the Frostmoon Scions): The collection preserves the Scions' pre-Aila religion, which prayed to the gods of the far north with offerings and divination, and shows how Aila, five centuries ago, abolished or simplified those rites around the Frost Moon. Its tone is reverent and sorrowful: the singers are exiled heirs of Hyperborea who cannot go home while the moon is imprisoned.

Appearance: A 4-star book collection of three volumes with a verse opening, then numbered Prayer Songs. Each song gives the god's name, a parenthetical description of the rite (date, offerings, how many times the Runo is chanted), the hymn, and a note from Priestess Ehrnrooth. Some lines are blacked out.

Lore: The singer of the opening hymn is an exile who cannot return home while the moon is imprisoned. The numbered Prayer Songs address northern gods at solstices, births and funerals, beginning with Pitkamoonen, Lord of the Seven Calamities, then Maadteraahka, Tuonetar and Laimelea; Vol. 2 and 3 include Ianikuinen, Koitar, Saarelainen, Huurrekuutar and the Moon Maiden Kuutar. Ehrnrooth's notes explain how Aila replaced them with short prayers to the Frost Moon.

**Opening hymn.** A traveler's lament: the singer has left home and cannot return while "moonlight hangs in its prison on high". It praises rivers, peaks, the bronze-bound ship of Seutervoinen and the golden arrows of Ianikuinen, curses the poisonous plot of Pakkaisukko and the calamity of Pohjola, and calls the heirs of Hyperborea to remember that so long as hymn and Runo ring, the far North will endure.

**Vol. 1.** Prayer Song I appeases Pitkamoonen, Lord of the Seven Calamities, at the summer solstice, with a burnt sheaf, a hen, an ox and blood, the Archpriestess chanting the Runo seven times and reading entrails. Song II honors Maadteraahka, Mother of Life, at births. Song III is to Tuonetar, Mother of the Underworld, at autumn funerals. Song IV is to Laimelea, Mother of Time, on the winter solstice. Song V is missing. Ehrnrooth notes that Aila abolished the rites for the first three five centuries ago, replacing them with short blessings of the new moon.

**Vol. 2.** Song VI is to Takoja Ianikuinen, the Primeval Blacksmith, whose forged bow, chariot and shuttle were each stolen or lost. Song XI is to Koitar, the dawnstar, wife of Seutervoinen. Song XVI is to Saarelainen, the Stranger of Winter's Day, who rode to Pohjola to court the daughter of Pakkaisukko and was carved into seven pieces by the Lord of the Seven Calamities.

**Vol. 3.** Song XXI is to Huurrekuutar, goddess of the Frost Moon; Song XXII is to Kuutar, the Moon Maiden, asking for mercy and for the cleansing of those barred from Elysium.
**Aila's revisions.** For Songs VI, XI, XVI and XXI Ehrnrooth prints both the older form and "the standard for all recitations", a short prayer that begins "O pale white Frost Moon, in the name of the descendants of the far north" and asks the moon to soothe wrath, protect the descendants, heal the lost, or cast down its gaze from the celestial dome. For Song VI Ehrnrooth adds that a lost variant, whose last four lines called disasters rather than quelled them, vanished long before the Moon Maiden's birth. For Song XXI she says the old prayer was brief because only the protecting chief god and the moons' origin, past and future were too sacred to say at length.

**Rites in detail.** Song I includes a note that a god of unknowable gender is addressed and no one dares speak the name. Song II sprinkles sea salt on the sacred stone and bathes the newborn in water with Winter Icelea. Song III has animals sacrificed in boat-shaped vessels according to the dead's rank, with their eyes presented to the underworld's mistress and the Archpriestess veiled. Song IV burns a cloth of the year's events and anoints the Verdant Crest with the ashes in silver water.

**The Song of Saarelainen.** The hymn identifies Pakkaisukko (wiki: the Belyi Tsar) as the servant of the singers' forebears who offered his daughter in marriage if Saarelainen would open the gates of Pohjola, knowing he would be sacrificed. The Lord of the Seven Calamities then cut him into seven pieces and his bride was never wed. The wiki links the daughter to Anastasya and the gates to the Shadow Realm; the hymn itself names neither.

**Reading it as history.** The collection layers three periods: the exiles' old religion in Hyperborea, the long wait before the Moon Maiden, and Aila's reform after Kuutar's birth. The notes consistently credit Aila with turning a fearful, sacrificial religion into one directed to the Frost Moon alone, and the Scions' present prayers are those "standard" forms. Ehrnrooth also flags what she cannot explain (Song IV's reference to the four imprisoned moons and the Verdant Crest) and keeps it as written. Prayer Song XXII's simplified form matches a prayer the wiki says Lauma recites in the Song of the Welkin Moon teaser; Pitkamoonen's Chinese transliteration is a pun on Paimon's name per the wiki trivia, a translator's joke rather than lore.

**Link to the Heavenly Principles.** The wiki identifies the supreme sky god Pitkamoonen, "merciless" and "capricious winged", as the Heavenly Principles; Song IV's Mother of Time as Istaroth; Maadteraahka as Naberius (with a "heart for the primordial ocean" line linked to Egeria); and Tuonetar as Ronova. These are wiki identifications; the hymns themselves only supply the northern names.

Owners: No owner. Compiled by Priestess Ehrnrooth of the Frostmoon Scions; the volumes lie near the Meeting Point in the Frostmoon Enclave, where she is found.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: a 3-volume Book Collection in Nod-Krai, near the Meeting Point at the Frostmoon Enclave; Vol. 1 appears after the Enclave is upgraded to level 5.

340.comment: Hymns of the Far North: Aila's reform of the Frostmoon rites
340.content:
In Ehrnrooth's notes, Aila, the first Moonchanter, abolished the old rites to the Seven Calamities, the Mother of Life and the Mother of the Underworld five centuries ago, replacing them with brief blessings such as "May the new moon illuminate your path". She revised and simplified the prayers to Ianikuinen, Koitar, Saarelainen and Huurrekuutar into short forms addressed to the pale white Frost Moon, which are now the standard recitation.

For funerals the replacement is "May the new moon lead you to the shore of peace," followed by a simple and solemn funeral regardless of social status.

341.comment: Hymns of the Far North: Prayer Song of the Lord of the Seven Calamities
341.content: The first prayer song, performed at the summer solstice, begs a merciless sky god to turn from the mortal realm. Its offerings include grain, a hen and an ox. Portions of its text are blacked out because the Archpriestess chanted indistinctly so as not to provoke the god. The wiki identifies the god as the Heavenly Principles.

342.comment: Hymns of the Far North: Saarelainen's prayer and the daughter of Pakkaisukko
342.content: Prayer Song XVI honors Saarelainen, a gentle noble who rode across Hiisi Island and Pohjola to court Pakkaisukko's daughter. Pakkaisukko demanded he open the gates of Pohjola. Saarelainen went knowingly, to spare the girl, and the Lord of the Seven Calamities cut him into seven pieces. The wiki links Pakkaisukko to the Belyi Tsar and his daughter to Anastasya; the hymn does not name them.

343.comment: Hymns of the Far North: Frostmoon Scions' prayer to the Frost Moon
343.content: Prayer Song XXI honors Huurrekuutar, goddess of the Frost Moon, "mother of the silver shuttle" who leads lost souls through the cold night, and Song XXII addresses Kuutar, the Moon Maiden, asking her to cleanse sins and the tears of those barred from Elysium. The standard form beseeches the pale white Frost Moon to cast down its gaze from the celestial dome.

344.content:
Jadefall's Splendor (also: Jadefalls Splendor, Bìluò zhī Lóng): Jadefall's Splendor is a five-star catalyst and a ritual vessel carved from jade, reflecting the luster of the skies and clear waters. Its item story says jadeite fell from the sky, was washed clean and was shaped by mortal hands into a splendid instrument awaiting its sacred purpose. The rest of the text is a tea-table debate between a scholar from Sumeru and a consultant in dark robes about whether history bends toward decay or rebirth, framed by the story of Chenyu Vale's ancestors.

It belongs to the Primordial Jade series, though it is the later entry with a different focus. The text ends with the Bishui River flowing eternal and the jade's luster as constant as its former master.

Appearance: The in-game description calls it a ritual vessel carved from jade that reflects the luster of the skies and clear waters. The story adds a "splendid jade instrument" of primordial stone; nothing of its shape is given.

Lore: The story opens with jadeite that fell from the sky, was cleansed by water, freed of dark earth and rotten wood, and shaped by a mortal youth into a ritual instrument. A researcher from the rainforest realm of Sumeru then argues over tea that history bends toward decay: the fall of humanity can only be stopped by the wisdom and mercy of gods, and he points to deserted ruins and hilichurls without speech or spirit as proof that earlier peoples vanished without a ripple.

The text digresses to Chenyu Vale's people, who once lived among the crystal-veined mountains of the Chasm in mining settlements stretching from peak to peak. A buried ancient sin beneath their shafts brought catastrophe described as divine punishment, and the forebears had to move north. Qiaoying Village's elders say the ancestors came from the chasm to the south, brought a great jade altar and left enigmatic ruins. When the war of the gods brought tragedy they became wandering refugees; their descendants once believed in a now-forgotten god and are now lost to history.

The consultant answers that the history of mortals is one of rebirth: glory and ruin come from mortals themselves, and without agency there is no rise or fall. The ruins lie forsaken, but their former inhabitants live on, absorbed into the people of a new god; the fading of the ancestors gave rise to today's prosperity. He adds that the wisdom and laws of gods rest on mortal consensus, not personal whim. The tea-table debate ends inconclusively and the Bishui River flows on. The wiki identifies the debaters as Soraya and Zhongli and links the forgotten god to Zibai, the altar to the Chiwang Terrace and the ruins to Lang-Gan; these are the wiki's links, not named in the text. The English name's Chinese origin, "Biluo", is a Taoist term for blue sky, unlike the other jade-named weapons in the series.

Owners: Item text names no owner beyond a "former master" (read by the wiki as Morax) and a mortal youth who shaped the jade. No source consulted ties it to a particular playable character.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star catalyst from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 46, secondary stat HP 10.8%. Passive "Primordial Jade Regalia": for 3 seconds after an Elemental Burst or creating a shield, the wielder restores 4.5-6.5 Energy every 2.5 seconds and gains an Elemental DMG Bonus of 0.3-1.1% per 1,000 Max HP, up to 12-44%, even off the field (refinements 1 to 5).

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the story suits themes of memory and the long view of mortal history. A character may cite one side of the debate, but do not make either side the settled lore.

345.content: In the Jadefall's Splendor story, Chenyu Vale's people once lived in the crystal-veined mountains of the Chasm and fled north after a catastrophe linked to an ancient sin buried beneath their mines. Qiaoying Village elders say they brought a great jade altar and left strange ruins. Their descendants once worshipped a now-forgotten god and are now absorbed into Liyue's people.

346.content:
Kagotsurube Isshin (also: Cursed Blade, Prized Isshin Blade (reforged), Kagotsurube): Kagotsurube Isshin is a long blood-red sword bearing the Isshin name. It was forged by Akame Kanenaga, an Inazuman smith of the fallen Akame school, but made in a snowbound land to the far north rather than in Inazuma, and its journey home was marked by dark deeds. It figures in Kaedehara Kazuha's Story Quest, where the possessed sword is finally reforged and the player receives it.

Its description says it is remarkably sharp and vividly ominous, able to cleave a porous bamboo basket and the water within it before any leaks. The name is taken from Kagotsurube, a haunted sword in a kabuki play whose blade is said to leave no drop of blood on its edge.

Appearance: A long blade the colour of blood. Its hamon, seen in moonlight, appears to flow like the blood and tears of a wayfaring wanderer. In the story it appears first as a menacing blade wreathed in an ominous purple aura (the Prized Isshin Blade), then shattered, and finally as the reforged sword.

Lore: The text says people often think each blade holds a blade-spirit; a sword forged by the Tatarigami would then hold a demon of malice. Akame Kanenaga was a swordsmith who failed to become head smith. He made this blade in a snow-covered northern land, not in the land of thunder and Jade Steel.

The Akame school, in its zealous practice of "Isshin" (the stillness of mind free of distraction), had always sought a killer blade of extreme lethality. Its members grew withdrawn and venomous, and the authorities came to regard the school as undesirable: leadership of the Isshin Art, passed down from Mitsunaga, was rescinded before three generations had passed.

After that, Kanenaga was involved in the Case of the Eccentric and committed treason, so he changed his name and went north to live humbly under the rule of "imperious ice". The text records his bitter words: he had spent half his life chasing the vanity of the Isshin Art and had become another "Kaedehara". The Kaedehara clan were master swordsmiths whose work best symbolised Masagomaru's style, and the Niwa clan were humble and diligent clay-temperers. Kanenaga died amid the snow, wishing only to forge a renowned blade that would restore the name of Kaedehara and win back the people's recognition. His last hope was that a sword born in ice and frost would not be as weak as its "useless title".

According to the wiki's synopsis of Kazuha's Story Quest, Kanenaga infused the sword with the power of the Tatarigami so that it carried its own consciousness, and told it his wish on his deathbed: to show Inazuma that the Isshin Art could still produce magnificent blades. The blade's long journey home was warped by Tatarigami hatred into a desire to rival the gods; it possessed people as tools and then discarded them. Arriving in Inazuma weakened, it met Kazuha, faced its lack of power and the truth of its corruption, and chose, with Kazuha's consent, to take hold of him so that it could be forged anew at the cost of its own consciousness, hoping the Isshin Art would one day regain the Raiden Shogun's regard. Before that consciousness faded, it gave Kazuha its name. This chain of events is wiki-summarised, not item text.

Owners: Akame Kanenaga forged it. After the Story Quest, Kazuha holds the reforged sword.

The Traveler's inventory contains the sword after the quest, but Kazuha's dialogue implies it stays with him in canon. He is also shown wielding it in his Genius Invokation TCG card.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star sword obtained from the Story Quest A Strange and Friendless Road in Version 2.8; it has a single refinement rank. Base ATK 42 with ATK% as secondary stat. It was announced under the working name "Cursed Blade", which the game never uses.

Its passive, Isshin Art Clarity, makes a Normal, Charged or Plunging Attack that hits whip up a Hewing Gale dealing AoE damage equal to 180% of ATK and increasing the wielder's ATK by 15% for 8 seconds, at most once every 8 seconds. In the quest, the Prized Isshin Blade (awakened) instead releases an Accursed Spirit that heals the wielder but halves the wielder's damage; the shattered version keeps the damage reduction without the heal.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: treat the sword as Kazuha's possession and a reminder of a personal mistake in the north. Its past owner is a bitter smith, not a hero, and its former corrupted self is gone; a scene should not revive its possession unless the scenario says so.

347.content: The Akame school pursued the Isshin Art's ideal of a distraction-free mind by forging killer blades of extreme lethality; their works were keen but carried an evil that led the authorities to rescind the school's leadership of the Isshin Art within three generations. Akame Kanenaga, a later member, fled north after the Case of the Eccentric and forged Kagotsurube Isshin there.

348.content:
Kagura's Verity (also: Kagura no Shin'i, Yae Miko's kagura bells, Kagura bells): Kagura's Verity is the set of bells used for the Kagura Dance, blessed by Yae Miko, the Guuji of the Grand Narukami Shrine, and still carrying the scent of the Sacred Sakura. Its item text is Yae's voice, looking back on her long friendship with Ei and the people and spirits she has met across her life.

The Kagura bells are a short staff with tiered bells used in Shinto kagura dance. In-universe, the text says that where there were once dances before the throne, the sound of the bells still lingers.

Appearance: A staff of tiered bells in the style of a kagura suzu, with the bells glowing in turn as the weapon's passive stacks up (top bells at one stack, top and bottom at two, the full weapon and a particle effect at three). The description adds that the scent of the Sacred Sakura clings to it.

Lore: The text opens with the white silhouette of the past, which never returned and remains an unceasing dream. In Yae's recollection she was a silly little thing, nowhere near as clever as the great matriarch Hakushin. As a whelp foraging through snow she tried to catch Ei's attention; her foolhardy courage earned Ei's pity and she entered her service, warming her hands and feet, a "very great honor".

When Saiguu departed never to return and her seniors were lost for various reasons, the clumsy Yae took up the role of Miko. The unfortunate task of putting a smile on Ei's face fell to her. On the night she first performed the Kagura Dance she felt the weight of the past. The text then says the great silver kitsune, master and friend, vanished into the river of dreams; the daughter of the great kitsune lineage would take up the bells and dance for the vibrant "now".

Yae recalls her dealings with others: she bluffed a young tengu warrior (Kujou Sara) into mountain asceticism and recommended her to the Kujou clan; she lost a contest to an obstinate oni (Arataki Itto) through his sheer perseverance, after adding tricks to make it interesting; she corresponded with a half-adeptus from Liyue (Ganyu) and gifted her fresh ocean plants, though she cannot understand her "almost foolish love", asking whether it is a bondage for adepti. She revisits the moonlit imperial garden scene that the Hakushin Ring also recalls.

Her reflections on the era: in a few hundred years she has walked the earth in many guises and come to know human beauty deeply. With Ei engrossed in her dream of Eternity, someone had to look after the common folk. Yae lists the incidents she handled: quelling the resentment of the wicked oni Kuroami with a hint of her ominous power, making sport of the disturbance caused by Kosanta the Bald Tanuki, betraying the marauding pirate Rinzou over a small discordance in plans, and hoping the "blank slate" immortal eccentric Scaramouche would find his way and not threaten them all. The darkened remains of the swordmaster's soul and the beasts of catastrophe hiding in the sacred forest were wiped out. Compared to Ei's dream, these were fleeting interludes, and Yae knew time was on her side. She ends with a mock-serious refusal of a Euthymia without wind or moon, with unwithering lotuses and udumbara: the loneliness would bore her to tears.
