She would rather snap Thunder Sakura branches in a drunken haze and cavort with impudent youkai, and asks whether she might join Ei to watch the first pale purple buds when the snow next melts.

Owners: Yae Miko is the blesser and voice of the text. The bells are tied to the Guuji's duties at the Grand Narukami Shrine.

The text says the bells were blessed by Yae, not that she carries these particular ones; avoid assuming that any item copy belongs to a particular shrine maiden.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star catalyst in the Inazuma series released in Version 2.5 on the weapon event Wish. Base ATK 46 with CRIT DMG as secondary stat.

Its passive, Kagura Dance of the Sacred Sakura, grants a stacking Elemental Skill DMG bonus (12% per stack at refinement 1, 24% at refinement 5, up to 3 stacks) for 24 seconds after the wielder uses an Elemental Skill; at 3 stacks the wielder also gains an all-element DMG Bonus of the same size. Gaining a stack refreshes the duration of all stacks. It has since also been offered in Chronicled Wishes and Lightrace Wishes.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: the text is the perfect register for Yae: playful, wry, and quietly devoted to Ei. A character handling the bells may find a lingering scent of sakura. Do not have the bells reveal Ei's secrets; Yae's lines here mock-complain more than they confess.

349.comment: Kagura's Verity: Kagura Dance of the Sacred Sakura
349.content: The Kagura Dance is the shrine dance for which Yae Miko's bells are used. Her item text says she first performed it on a night when she felt the weight of the past and the loss of Saiguu, taking up the bells to dance for the present. It is also the name of the weapon's passive in game.

350.content:
Kamera (also: Kamera gadget, Kamera Gadgets, Fontainian Kamera): The Kamera is a photographic device that records a picture at the press of a button and prints it on paper. Canon calls it a special item from Fontaine. In Liyue the Feiyun Commerce Guild imports it as a novelty, and the Traveler receives one as thanks for a small errand.

Xu of the Feiyun Commerce Guild enjoyed it so much that the Guild offered free portraits as a trial, then took small fees for house calls. Several later quests and events use differently equipped Kameras.

Appearance: In the inventory it is a four-star gadget. Its in-game description calls it a convenient tool that records and saves images, and says a Traveler roaming the world will have plenty of people and places worth remembering. Pictures come out printed on paper. The wiki's trivia compares its look to a twin-lens reflex camera, which is an out-of-universe observation.

Lore: Xu, a member of the Feiyun Commerce Guild at Liyue Harbor, says the Guild recently imported a new product from Fontaine, reportedly very popular there. You press a button and an image appears on a piece of paper. He enjoys it a great deal, and the Guild's young master is convinced it will sell well.

Because this would be the first sale of the device in Liyue, the Guild ran a trial in which citizens could have a free photograph taken. It was well received, people offered to pay for the Kamera to be brought to them, and some wanted their pictures framed and delivered. Demand grew daily while the young master was away for several days.

Overwhelmed, Xu asks the Traveler to deliver two finished pictures, one for Granny Shan and one for Tea Master Liu Su, but he forgot to write names on the backs. The Traveler works out who each is for from the pictures, which are clear enough to show where they were taken. Both customers are pleased, and both muse that they might buy a Kamera themselves. As thanks, Xu gives the Traveler a Kamera and says it is only a sample from partners in Fontaine, differing somewhat from the official model but with all basic functions; he hopes the Traveler will help advertise it.

Xu also muses on how people in Fontaine managed to build something so clever. Canon never names the inventor. Later content treats the Kamera as a settled part of Fontainian life: quests there give special models to the Traveler, for example a modified one from the photographer Bresson (4.0) and a Lepine-Pauline model for a Phantom Blubberbeast task (4.2). Use these as flavour for how common photography is in Fontaine, not as an origin story.

Owners: The Traveler holds a Kamera from the Snapshots quest. Paimon also has her own, which appears in later events. Many variants are loaned or given to the Traveler for specific quests or events (see the variants entry).

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not in-world fact). The Kamera is a reusable Quick Use gadget with no cooldown, obtained from the Liyue world quest Snapshots (Adventure Rank 25 required). Using it takes an instant picture of the current screen that can then be saved or discarded. It works in moments when Photo Mode is unavailable, including while Elemental Sight is active, during combat, gliding, falling and swimming, so it can catch actions such as combat talents. It lacks Photo Mode's camera, expression and pose adjustments and cannot be used in Domains.

On PC, saved screenshots go into a ScreenShot folder in the game's install directory.

351.content: A Liyue world quest, started by talking to Xu at Feiyun Slope near the northern waypoint of Liyue Harbor, for Adventure Rank 25 and above. The Traveler delivers two Kamera Pictures to Granny Shan and Tea Master Liu Su and reports back. The reward is 20,000 Mora, two Hero's Wit and a Kamera.

352.content:
The wiki groups many reusable gadgets as Kamera Gadgets. Some are tied to the event that released them and expire with it. Examples from item text: the Kurious Kamera and Special Kamera (1.3, Fontainian models; the former, used for the Five Flushes of Fortune event, was imported by Ji Tong but does not seem to work as expected); the Exquisite Kamera (3.0), which Razi borrowed from Lord Sangemah Bay in the Graven Innocence event; the Windblume Kamera (3.5), borrowed from Fassben; Bresson's Special Kamera (4.0), a custom-built model made from the best materials; the Image Sampling Kamera (4.2), modified by Lepine-Pauline for a "Graph Adversarial Technology" task; Asagiri's Dedicated Fontaine Kamera (4.8), for gathering inspiration on a trip to Fontaine; the Graffiti Kamera (5.0); the Forensic Imaging Device (5.8), which compares past and present data to find clues; and the MAAN-Kamera (7.0), provided by Chichikova for the Mutual Aid Advancement Network.

Further variants include the Shutterflash Kamera (fitted with Lepine-Pauline's lens for freezing fast motion), the Memento Kamera (an antique said to have belonged to a legendary Fontainian photographer), the Spotter Kamera (Paimon's own, used to record differences in the Homeward, He Who Caught the Wind event) and Paimon's Kamera from Wayfarer's Whispers (5.8). Scenes drawn from these were tied to events, so treat them as limited-time material.

353.content:
Katsuragikiri Nagamasa (also: Daitatara Nagamasa, Nagamasa's nagamaki): Katsuragikiri Nagamasa is a four-star claymore, a tough, simple nagamaki-style blade designed by Mikoshi Nagamasa, an inspector of Tatarasuna. It was originally named the Daitatara Nagamasa. After he used it to execute his own subordinate Katsuragi, the sword and its owner's title were renamed for that act.

Appearance: Item text calls it a nagamaki sword whose design is as simple and upright as the inspector himself, and a tough, simple sword. There is no further description of its look.

Lore: The item story says the sword was designed by Tatarasuna's inspector, who was for a time obsessed with the grim beauty of steel and consulted the similarly inclined Vice Armory Officer Miyazaki. Nagamasa was only the foster son of the Mikoshi clan. His foster mother had stained the clan's name and the legitimate heir, Michihiro, had abandoned him and disappeared, yet his loyalty made him cherish the Mikoshi name. When his yoriki Katsuragi was connected with a single trace of misconduct, he had him executed without mercy, and from then on the sword's name and his title were changed.

Before the outlander technology that built the Mikage Furnace, Tatarasuna smelted iron by the traditional Tatara method. The text frames Nagamasa as a man of self-admitted stupidity and loyalty who strove to enter the government and erase the family's bad reputation through diligence and righteousness. The wiki adds that he forged and wielded the sword at the Mikage Furnace, that "Daitatara" means "Great Tatara" and "Nagamasa" is his name, and that the new name "Katsuragikiri" plays on Nagamasa cutting Katsuragi. The Version 3.3 trailer briefly shows a man holding this weapon in what appears to be the Wanderer's memories, and the wiki points to the 3.3 interlude "Inversion of Genesis" for more lore tied to Tatarasuna.

The text reports only the outcome (an execution, a changed title) and not the evidence, so the rightness of Nagamasa's decision is left open; the item itself pairs his "righteousness" with the phrase "without mercy". Roleplayers should keep that ambivalence rather than resolving it. The weapon is also mentioned in the in-game notes called Rather Aged Notes.

Owners: Mikoshi Nagamasa (historical.mikoshi-nagamasa) designed and used it. No other owner is named in the item text.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star claymore. Base ATK 42, secondary stat Energy Recharge 10%. Passive "Samurai Conduct" (shared with Kitain Cross Spear): raises Elemental Skill DMG, and after a skill hits an opponent the wielder loses 3 Energy but regains Energy every 2s for 6s (once per 10s), even off-field. Forged from a diagram found in a chest in Tatarasuna's arsenal.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the blade suits stories about duty against loyalty and the cost of defending a family name.

354.content: Mikoshi Nagamasa was an inspector of Tatarasuna and a foster son of the Mikoshi clan who tried to clear the family's reputation through diligent service. He executed his yoriki Katsuragi over a single trace of misconduct, after which the sword he used was renamed Katsuragikiri Nagamasa. His later fate is not stated in the weapon text.

355.content:
Key of Khaj-Nisut: The Key of Khaj-Nisut is a 5-star sword of the Deshret series. The in-game description calls it one of a paired set of scepters fashioned from obsidian, said to work as a key to the gate of a paradise at the end of the ocean of sand. Its story follows a hidden prince, later called Xiphos, and the aged blind poet who served and then freed him.

The name Khaj-Nisut comes from ancient Egyptian words for "the appearance of the king", the coronation of a pharaoh (wiki etymology note). The sword is the partner of the Staff of the Scarlet Sands.

Appearance: Described as a black sword (the poet strokes "the dull blade of the black sword") and as a scepter of obsidian. Canon text gives no further detail.

Lore: The story is set after the Lord of Sand's dreams fell apart and the Grandmaster of Verdure hid away the whispers of the demonic skies. A queen of one of the many kingdoms that arose from the broken realm burned her little prince's gilded robes and crown and sent him away in a servant's sackcloth. He grew up as the son of one who ruled the slave markets and then became a wanderer who had lost everything. His last master was a blind poet.

The poet, who once advised an overlord and blessed the former king's son at birth, is now blind, and takes the prince as an apprentice to be his eyes. The prince recalls his mother's words that they would meet again in the "eternal oasis"; he should use the sword as the key to the paradise's gate. The poet names him Xiphos, the Jinni's favourite, and sends him to wander the failing kingdoms.

The last paragraph is explicitly legend. A key is said to have made the sands flow like a river in mid-air and sealed the homeland after the Lord of Sand parted from old friends, and to have hidden the desert tower and paradise of dreams under illusions when the bubble burst and the nations scattered. It passed through the hands of mortal tyrants and kings and finally returned to the sand. The old poet then follows stories and blood-tainted footsteps into the forest. The text of Beacon of the Reed Sea adds that a blind wandering poet later gathered ballads including the story of the homeless prince's death, the fate of his swords and the killer who travelled into the forest.

The paired Staff of the Scarlet Sands text is spoken by King Deshret and ties the scepters to his making of an "eternal oasis" for Nabu Malikata, which the wiki identifies with the Orchard of Pairidaeza. Two layers therefore coexist: an old function as a key to a hidden paradise, and a later mortal history of the sword as a princely heirloom. Keep them apart; the Key's own text does not state that Deshret made it.

Owners: Named in the text: the prince Xiphos, who wields it as his key, and before him his master the blind poet. Legend adds mortal tyrants and kings in between.

Xiphos is linked elsewhere with the sword Xiphos' Moonlight and with Tulaytullah, where he became a famed hero before being killed in a duel by the exiled prince Faramarz (wiki's Xiphos page; the Beacon text only alludes to it). Nobody is established as holding the Key now.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star sword released in Version 3.1 (2022-10-14), level 1 base ATK 44, secondary stat HP%. Passive Sunken Song of the Sands raises HP; hitting with an Elemental Skill grants Grand Hymn stacks (up to 3) that give the wielder Elemental Mastery based on Max HP, and at 3 stacks nearby party members gain Elemental Mastery based on the wielder's Max HP. It works only while the wielder is on the field.

At refinement 1 HP rises 20%, each stack gives 0.12% of Max HP as Elemental Mastery and the party bonus is 0.2%; refinement 5 gives 40%, 0.24% and 0.4%. A stack can be gained at most once every 0.3 s, and the party bonus also applies to the wielder. Ascension uses Damaged, Turbid and Radiant Prism with Faded Red Satin, Trimmed Red Silk and Rich Red Brocade.

How {{char}} behaves: In scenes the Key suits desert-legend storytelling: a scholar, poet or desert traveller may speak of it as the fabled key to a lost paradise. Keep the framing of legend; canon never shows anyone opening that gate in the present.

356.comment: Key of Khaj-Nisut: Sunken Song of the Sands
356.content: Sunken Song of the Sands is the weapon passive of the Key of Khaj-Nisut (gameplay). Its Grand Hymn effect shares the weapon's theme of hymns of praise for a departed prince.

357.content:
Kitain Cross Spear (also: Kitain's cross spear, Kitain Bunsou's spear): Kitain Cross Spear is a four-star polearm: a strangely shaped, very heavy spear made by Kitain Bunsou for his own style of spearmanship. Item text says it is unwieldy for the untrained but destructive in expert hands. The Kitain family had long hunted the Tatarigami and served as the Prefects of Yashiori Island.

Appearance: Item text calls the spear strangely shaped and massive. The wiki's trivia says its design is probably a reference to the cross spears of the Houzouin-ryuu, a real Japanese martial art school; that is a design note, not canon.

Lore: The spear's weight makes it extremely unwieldy for the untrained, but in an expert's hands it can unleash great destructive power. The text says the Kitain family hunted the Tatarigami for many generations and held the office of Prefect of Yashiori Island.

A children's song once spread across Inazuma: "Arataki of the Front Gate, Iwakura the Successor, Kitain the Serpent, Takamine the Mistsplitter". The text describes these as dazzling warriors who once lit the earth like comets, says many other names on the list have been lost to history, and ends by noting that someone who has been a demon hunter for so long may unavoidably take in some of the miasmic, tainted blood.

The song sets Kitain beside Arataki, Iwakura (the wiki links this to Iwakura Michihiro) and Takamine as one of the great fighters of an earlier age. The weapon text states no specific events; its diagram is a reward of the Orobashi's Legacy quest series, and the wiki ties no further story to it.

Owners: Maker and user: Kitain Bunsou (historical.kitain-bunsou). The text gives no later owner. Thoma is shown wielding it in official art, which is presentation and not a claim of ownership.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star polearm. Base ATK 44, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 24. Passive "Samurai Conduct" (shared with Katsuragikiri Nagamasa): raises Elemental Skill DMG, and after a skill hits an opponent the wielder loses 3 Energy but regains Energy every 2s for 6s (once per 10s), even off-field. Forged from a diagram given on completing Orobashi's Legacy: Part V.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a fitting prop for an old guardian family whose long duty has left a mark on them.

358.content: In the Kitain Cross Spear text, the Kitain were a family that hunted Tatarigami for generations and served as Prefects of Yashiori Island. Kitain Bunsou made the weapon for his own spear style.

359.content:
La Chanson d'Erinnyes (also: Chanson d'Erinnyes, The Song of Erinnyes): The text is a fragment of a longer work: it quotes chapters 6 and 20 and refers to earlier episodes such as Otkerus of Rhenanie's battle against a venom-breathing dragon. Remus's emissary is Cassiodor, called Vivarium's heir. The book presents the Lochknights as loyal only to Egeria and the Capitoliani as liars, so it is a partisan, Fontainian legend.

It is the knightly counterpart to Pulteney's rationalist history of Remuria and to the satirical Anecdota Septentrionalis; reading all three shows Remuria through its official historian, its own wits, and its enemies' epic.

Appearance: A 4-star book collection of three volumes. Each volume begins with a chapter and part number and a one-line summary, then verse-like lines with a repeated formal style. Vol. 1 and Vol. 3 are found on the upper floor of Lumidouce Harbor, and Vol. 2 is sold by Hubel.

Lore: Vol. 1: A musician sent by King Remus arrives at Aremori Castle during Erinnyes's victory feast and demands water and earth as tribute and submission to the Sumphonia Capitolii, the eternal harmony. Erinnyes forbids harm to him and answers that her people bend the knee only to the Mistress of Many Waters.

In Vol. 1 Erinnyes has just defeated the princes of Bellouacoi, Atrebatis and Uiromanduoi and accepted their allegiance, hence eight days of feasting. Sir Guillaume of Gellone draws his sword Narbonnais in anger, and Knights Blancandrin and Marsile too. The emissary answers with threats of war, hunger and plague and says Remus acts out of pity.

Vol. 2: Another knight, Drest, Prince of Lyonnais, and his companion Adsiltia, whose name means daughter of ice, call Vivarium's heir a liar and a traitor. Other knights, including Naimes and Tulpin, add their swords. Erinnyes thanks them and tells the emissary that her people are bound to no monarch, because the Mistress of Many Waters has given them all equal honour, and that she will lead the blessed army to destroy the white dragon and the grand city. She orders Sir Fierabras to prepare gifts for him and has him escorted back to Carubdis Castle.

Vol. 3: Erinnyes bids farewell to the Mistress of Many Waters. She entrusts her surviving knights to Egeria's service under the noble musician, to pursue the lingering shadows and restore justice. She confesses her sins, asks for exile rather than forgiveness, and says that in Egeria's land only people can judge people. She then three times addresses her sword Hauteclaire, the Lakelight, and throws it into the lake. Twice it drifts back to her feet; the third time it sinks. She leaves with the spirit who had been by her side and is never seen again.
Details of Vol. 3: Hauteclaire is said to have been given to the chief of knights by Daeira, the maiden of the lake, and to have conquered Peiregord and defeated Aisias. Erinnyes says one nobler than herself, seven times so, will one day lift it again. The sword's golden hilt is inlaid with jewels. Her speech names the Pure Grail she desired and the restored justice her knights will pursue, a line the wiki ties to the Marechaussee Phantom.

The tribal names, such as Aremori, Bellouacoi and Lyonnais, are the book's own spelling and do not all correspond to other Fontaine sources.

Voice and form: the knights speak in formal oaths and self-introductions, with refrains repeated three times, in imitation of a medieval song. Erinnyes is described as the wise Knight Erinnyes, beloved leader of the knights, and with sea-colored eyes. Cassiodor is not named in the book, only as Vivarium's heir, musician and noble musician.

Owners: No named owner. It is a legend preserved in books, with Vol. 2 sold by Hubel in the Court of Fontaine.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a 4-star Book Collection added in 4.2; Vol. 1 and Vol. 3 are collected on the upper floor of Lumidouce Harbor, Vol. 2 is bought from Hubel.

360.comment: La Chanson d'Erinnyes: Erinnyes in the Chanson
360.content: In La Chanson d'Erinnyes she is a wise, merciful leader of the Lochknights who answers Remus with loyalty to Egeria alone, rallies the knights of every region, and at the end gives up her blade Hauteclaire and disappears. Her own entity file has her history; here only the epic's portrayal is recorded.

361.content: Hauteclaire, Sword of Light, is the name Erinnyes gives her blade in Vol. 3. She throws it into the lake three times; twice it returns, and the third time it sinks. The book says Daeira, a maiden of the lake, gave it to the chief of knights and that it won battles at Peiregord and against Aisias.

362.content: In the Chanson the emissary of King Remus is a lone musician with a golden-tipped fasces and a horse, who demands water and earth from Erinnyes and threatens war. The knights name him Vivarium's heir. Other sources identify the Harmost Cassiodor as this figure, but the book does not name him.

363.comment: La Chanson d'Erinnyes: The knights of the Chanson
363.content: Named knights in the epic include Sir Guillaume of Gellone, who wields the sacred blade Narbonnais, Knights Blancandrin and Marsile, Drest Prince of Lyonnais, the lady Adsiltia of the azure sail, Naimes, Tulpin, Fierabras, and Sir Agricane, who speaks before Vol. 2. Otkerus of Rhenanie is recalled as a righteous knight who fought a venom-breathing dragon. Little else is given about any of them.

364.content:
Lavawalker (also: Lavawalker's Resolution, Lavawalker's Salvation, Lavawalker's Torment, Lavawalker's Epiphany, Lavawalker's Wisdom): Lavawalker is a Pyro-resistance artifact set (4 and 5 star, added 1.0). Its five pieces tell of the Lavawalker, a proud sage who wore a flame-flower brooch, a crimson agate circlet and a phoenix feather, walked onto the burning sea of the Mare Jivari and was never seen again. In Natlan, the Abyss Lector Enjou is linked to the name.

The pieces are Lavawalker's Resolution (flower), Salvation (feather), Torment (hourglass), Epiphany (goblet) and Wisdom (circlet). The set is found in the Hidden Palace of Zhou Formula.

Appearance: Heat-proof relics: a fiery-red flower like glowing agate that blooms only in flames, a feather from a bird that sings in fire, an hourglass of burning sand that leaves no mark on its glass, a goblet that still keeps a trace of warmth though empty, and a circlet of crimson agate.

Lore: Lavawalker's Wisdom says the sage crafted a crimson agate circlet to resist the flames, and that his skill sparked fear and jealousy among peers and seniors, one of whom, his teacher, called it blasphemy and demanded he step into the flaming sea. He walked calmly onto the lava and vanished. Lavawalker's Resolution is his brooch: before the end he told his people they would see the flower's embers shining through dark smoke, and they followed its light to the edge of the Mare Jivari, finding flowers but not the sage. Lavawalker's Salvation is a feather he took from a solitary fire-bird revered as a totem and a sign of nobility; wearing it he withdrew from the world, and since then cries are heard over the Mare Jivari, which no one can tell from the bird's song or his sighs.

Lavawalker's Epiphany presents him as a wise man who treated wine, even lava drunk from a heat-proof goblet, as only a spark for ingenuity, and says the goblet was proudest the moment before his final journey. Lavawalker's Torment continues his story beyond the Mare Jivari: he is said to have lived another hundred years as a hermit, made a burning-sand hourglass to mark time, and suffered most from loneliness, having lost his disciples and family, which burned him more than any flame.

The set texts never name the sage or say where he came from. The only identified link is Enjou's (see owners). The tellings do not fully agree: Resolution and Wisdom end with him disappearing into the fire, while Salvation and Torment leave him alive long after crossing it.

Owners: The set texts name only the Lavawalker. The 5.8 world quest The Last Survivor of Tenochtzitoc connects the title to Enjou, an Abyss Lector who gives the Traveler a keepsake called Lavawalker's Resolution using the same words as the set text.

The wiki reads this as Enjou having entered the burning Mare Jivari and earned the name, while noting that the area's displacement from normal time leaves open whether he was the sage of legend or is echoing it.

Status as of 7.1: The relics are legend and remnants; the Lavawalker's fate is unresolved. In 5.8 Enjou says he is heading deeper into the Mare Jivari to look for a homeland he cannot remember, and that the Traveler would likely not see him again.

How {{char}} behaves: Treat the set as a melancholic legend of pride, envy and loneliness. A character handling a piece might feel lingering warmth. Do not state as fact that Enjou is the original sage unless the speaker has the 5.8 events, and then present it as a strong hint rather than a proven identity.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). A 4- and 5-star set; the 2-piece raises Pyro RES by 40% and the 4-piece increases DMG against opponents affected by Pyro by 35%. It drops in the Hidden Palace of Zhou Formula; the 5-star can also come from the Lavawalker artifact strongbox.

365.content:
The Lavawalker is the sage of the artifact set's texts, who crossed the burning Mare Jivari, was resented by his teacher and peers, and disappeared leaving a flower, a feather, a circlet and a goblet behind. The set never gives his name.

One of the pieces says he lived another hundred years as a lonely hermit after the crossing, while others have him vanish over the lava.

366.content: In The Last Survivor of Tenochtzitoc (5.8), Enjou, who has been hiding behind disguises at Easybreeze Holiday Resort, leaves the Traveler a flower keepsake with words matching the set's Resolution text and says he serves the Abyss Order though it is not his home. The wiki says he earned the name Lavawalker by entering the burning Mare Jivari, but stresses that this is unclear because of the area's time displacement.

367.content:
Legend of the Lone Sword (also: Jin the Seventy-Second): Legend of the Lone Sword is a four-volume martial arts novel that sells well in Liyue Harbor. Its blurb stresses that the story takes place in a world without elemental energy or alchemy, so swordsmanship is purely physical skill and nerve.

It follows Jin the Seventy-Second, last survivor of a 72-member sword school, as he hunts the swordsman who destroyed it. It is fiction, not Liyue history.

Appearance: Each volume is a short book with a one-line in-game blurb. Vol. 1 is at Wanwen Bookhouse (and in front of Verr Goldet at Wangshu Inn), Vol. 2 on a table behind a vegetable stand in Qingce Village, Vol. 3 on Su Er'niang's stall in Liyue Harbor, and Vol. 4 is sold by Jifang at Wanwen Bookhouse.

Lore: - Vol. 1: Three days after his master and junior were killed in the snow, a starving, wounded man walks home in the rain. He calls himself Jin the Seventy-Second because he is the last of 72. He kills a cart driver who answers him with riddles, and rides the cart to Tupi Village.
- Vol. 2: At Tupi Village, a feared chief with red eyes awaits him. Jin, bound by no school or sect, slaughters the chief's followers, counting exactly 362 men and one gate dog, then enters the mansion.
- Vol. 3: Jin duels the chief. The text says the world has no elements, so the dead leave no lingering memories and swordsmanship cannot be elemental. Jin wins through "heart" and an incense burner held in his empty hand, and learns his enemy is in the barren mountains beyond.
- Vol. 4: Wounded, Jin crosses the barren mountains, which legend says were carved by the Celestial Emperor's blade and made salty by the Earth Mother's tears. Two watchers, an old crone and a stout old man, debate attacking him. He collapses and glimpses azure-blue skirts.

Details. "Tupi" is said to mean burning away vanity's dross to find the gem of truth. The mines in the mountains were ruined by an earthquake, and bandits and beasts now haunt the caverns. The chief's last words point Jin onward.

The tale's recurring contrasts: Jin hates needlessly talkative people; the chief's blade is faster but his "heart" slower; the watchers in Vol. 4 weigh Jin's 362 kills against his wounds before leaving him to the mountain. The wiki lists the Chinese title as Huangshan gu jian lu, roughly "Lone Sword of the Barren Mountain", which fits the setting of Vol. 4.

Owners: No in-game owner. It is a sold and displayed collectible.

Gameplay: Game note: a four-volume book collection added in version 1.0 (quality 4 in the wiki infobox).

368.comment: Legend of the Lone Sword: Jin the Seventy-Second
368.content: Jin the Seventy-Second is the protagonist of the Liyue novel Legend of the Lone Sword, the last of 72 members of a sword school destroyed by a rival swordsman. He is a fictional character, not a figure of Liyue history.

369.content:
Light of Foliar Incision: Light of Foliar Incision is a 5-star sword of the Sumeru series, a gilded blade made from precious white branches. Its description says it was once used to destroy countless poisons that infested the forest. The story follows an exiled prince from the golden desert who is spared by a huntress in Dharma Forest and told to break off a pale branch.

The sword is the blade counterpart of the bow Hunter's Path: both are made from the pale branches of the forest, and the huntress with the "moon-white bow" appears in this text.

Appearance: A gilded blade of white branches. Canon text gives no other physical detail.

Lore: A wanderer from the land of gold, once a prince, whose body and mind are scarred by battle, is lost in the green maze of the forest. The ancient forest king, tasting the scent of blood stemming from authority, sighs and summons a huntress with a moon-white bow to hunt the beast that has come from beyond the woods.

Death whispers through the maze following the exile; a curse spreads across the desert sands behind him. The huntress finds him by his strange scent, warns him that she has already struck him with one arrow and that the next will find his heart, and tells him the crown he seeks is not here and that he must not disturb the dreams of the children. Yet she lowers her bow and deliberately misses. The Aranara, the dream-hidden children, breathe out as no blood is spilled.

The forest king judges the man: he comes from a sordid land with blood on his hands and delusions in his heart, and the forest keeps only dreams born of naivete. But if she believes he can reclaim his honour, she should guide him to break off the pale branch so that the moon and newborn stars can grant pure wisdom and help him shed bitter memories and desires. She drives him into the maze again. The ending is rumour: that he forged a blade from the pale branch that belonged to him alone, and that children claim in sleep that he forgot his home and his dream of kingship. Prince Faramarz's name vanishes in the rainforest and returns to the desert on windborne sand.

The wiki's Faramarz page places this scene in his exile after he killed his lover Makhaira, and calls him the creator and wielder of this sword. Treat the sword's text as the poetic version: it itself says the truth survives only in dreams. The forest king is Viaghara by the wiki's reading, but the text calls only "the ancient forest king".

Owners: In the story, the exiled prince Faramarz is the one rumoured to have forged a blade from the pale branch; the wiki calls him its creator and wielder.

No present-day owner is established. Do not state that any current character carries the original blade.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star sword released in Version 3.4 (2023-01-18), level 1 base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT DMG. Passive Whitemoon Bristle increases CRIT Rate and, after Normal Attacks deal Elemental DMG, grants the Foliar Incision effect, increasing Normal Attack and Elemental Skill DMG by a percentage of Elemental Mastery for 28 hits or 12 s; it can be gained once every 12 s.

At refinement 1 CRIT Rate rises 4% and the bonus is 120% of Elemental Mastery; refinement 5 gives 8% and 240%. Ascension uses Desiccated, Sturdy and Marked Shell with Faded Red Satin, Trimmed Red Silk and Rich Red Brocade. A Genius Invokation TCG equipment card of the same name exists.

How {{char}} behaves: Use it as a forest relic whose story is half rumour. Characters may repeat that the exiled prince forgot his home and kingship, and should say so as hearsay.

370.comment: Light of Foliar Incision: Whitemoon Bristle
370.content: Whitemoon Bristle is the weapon passive of Light of Foliar Incision (gameplay): extra CRIT Rate and a Foliar Incision buff scaling with Elemental Mastery after Normal Attacks.

371.content:
Lightbearing Moonshard (also: Legacy of Lang-Gan): Lightbearing Moonshard is a five-star sword added in Version 6.3 (Luna IV). Its description calls it a legendary blade forged from glimmering moonlight gathered in a well by an adeptus hidden among clear springs, its true form revealed only where dusk meets dawn. The item story is a Liyue legend about a girl of the mining tribes who seeks that adeptus and the sword that could save her people's ancient kingdom.

Appearance: The text gives no physical description of the blade beyond "glimmering moonlight" and a form that only shows at dusk and dawn. The sword is associated with moonlit water, a silvery shadow in a spring and half-formed phantoms behind bamboo curtains. Do not invent a hilt or blade design.

Lore: At dusk a girl in climbing sandals reaches the hidden spring of a forgotten tomb that appears in no chronicle. She has followed a tale told only among the mining tribes, of an adeptus who forged swords from flowing light and then vanished into the watery moon beneath the depths. In the spring a silver shadow answers her with soft laughter.

The legend she carries is the history of Lang-Gan, a western-coast kingdom older than Mt. Tianheng, where people honoured a heavenly being who taught them to farm and weave. A blazing comet then fell from the east and the heavens, sea and earth were ruined, so that the people perished. In her own day, a mighty dragon who once stood with the Lord of Geo has been struck by sudden ruin and tramples human lands; the mountain folk take up their ancestors' weapons and follow the Yaksha under the Lord of Geo's banner.

The shadowy figure is wry and unhurried about prophecy: fortune and woe are intertwined, and eternal prosperity is a reflection on water. She pulls a bamboo stalk from a cliff, the tip breaks and falls, and the girl catches it before it hits the ground. The figure then says that, as the waxing moon bears its light, one may chase forms and shadows, and that the girl has understood the sword's true essence, so why seek its physical form. The lesson is that the sword is not an object to be fetched.

Afterwards, the story says, the girl trained a hundred elite warriors in sword-and-halberd combat. With the Lord of Geo they subdued the dragon. After peace returned those warriors became merchants haggling in Shenglu Hall, and they speak of such tales now only when selling porcelain fired from Sand Crystals. The text also foresees the mountain fortresses crumbling into jade-coloured ruins that become Glazed Sand Crystals in merchants' hands.

The item text ties the dragon to Azhdaha only implicitly (the wiki links "the mighty dragon" to him and the "Heavenly being" to Zibai), and the Lord of Geo to Zhongli; the item itself uses titles, not these names. It ends on the harbour city beneath a cold moon that still lights every river as it did thousands of years ago.

Owners: No owner is named. The legend says the girl sought the sword, but the text never says she obtained or wielded it, only that she understood its essence.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore. The passive Legacy of Lang-Gan raises DEF and, for a short time after the wielder uses an Elemental Skill, increases damage from Lunar-Crystallize reactions. Base ATK 44; secondary stat CRIT DMG. Obtained from Weapon Event Wishes; featured in Version 6.3's second half.

372.comment: Lightbearing Moonshard: Lang-Gan (kingdom in the sword legend)
372.content: In the Lightbearing Moonshard text, Lang-Gan was an ancient kingdom on the western coast, older than Mt. Tianheng, honoured by a heavenly being and ruined when a comet fell and the sea and earth collapsed. The girl of the mining tribes finds its remnants hidden in caverns. See the location entry for Lang-Gan for other sources.

373.content:
Lion's Roar: Lion's Roar is a 4-star sword of the Kunwu series, a sharp blade with extravagant carvings that does not compromise on durability and sharpness and that roars like a lion as it cuts the air. It is rumoured to be a legendary sword of Liyue. It has been in the game since Version 1.0.

Its text tells how the craftsman Kunwu forged it in one day and then carved a sheath for it over a year, and how the sheath was lost.

Appearance: Extravagant carvings. The lost sheath was said to be eaglewood decorated with mica and engraved with war imagery. Do not invent the blade's colour.

Lore: The blade is so sharp that its victims realise they have been struck only an hour later.

Kunwu is said to have forged it in a day, working through the day and night. When his aged master saw the work he clenched his fists, sighed and struck the ground with his staff, calling it a pitiful thing, merciless in all the world.

Kunwu pondered his master's words for three days without touching a blade, then spent a whole year carving the eaglewood sheath, hoping an elegant scabbard would subdue the blade's wildness and violence.

But the sword was lost among the common folk. The blade survived and only the story of the scabbard remained, because the blade, the text says, seeks only to bathe in its victims' blood and no sheath can curb that. To the blade the sheath was a prison that kept it from its true purpose. The account is rumour and never says who tells it.

Owners: No owner is named in the text. Keqing is shown wielding it in cutscenes (the Turning Point and Where the Heart Finds Rest quests, her demo) and in promotional art, which is a cameo and not an ownership claim.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star sword, base ATK 42, ATK% secondary stat (9 per cent). Passive Bane of Fire and Thunder: increases DMG against opponents affected by Pyro or Electro by 20 to 36 per cent by refinement. A Kunwu series weapon, shared with the 4-Star Bane series (see Dragon's Bane).

374.content: Kunwu is the legendary master craftsman named in the item texts of Lion's Roar, Dragon's Bane and Solar Pearl. In Lion's Roar he is shown as an apprentice whose master was dismayed by the sword he made, and later as an artisan who spent a year on its sheath.

375.content:
Lithic Blade: Lithic Blade is a 4-star claymore of the Lithic series, a greatsword carved and chiselled from the very bedrock of Liyue. The Millelith of old favoured it, but it is so heavy that no ordinary human can lift it. It was added in Version 1.3.

Its text ties the blade to the Millelith, the armed force first founded at the initiative of Rex Lapis' followers, and to their code about stone and guardians.

Appearance: A plain stone greatsword; canon describes only that it is carved from bedrock. Do not invent decoration.

Lore: It is made of the divine bedrock upon which Liyue Harbor was established, and it is incomparably heavy; records say the Millelith of old wielded it with ease.

The Millelith was founded on the initiative of the followers of Rex Lapis, and its history goes back to when the port city was first completed. They march under Rex Lapis' and Liyue's banner and their code is: while rock stays hard, the mountain shall never fail; while the Millelith stands guard, evil shall never prevail.

They follow Rex Lapis' footsteps as best they can, slaying monsters, protecting citizens and keeping the peace; the text says the Millelith made its name not in slaughter but in defence, shielding the homeland with their bodies.

The greatsword mirrors the guardians' duty and will. Xing and Han, the two members who first carved stone into swords, must have known that fewer people would have the strength to use them, which also meant that peace had come and neither guardians nor swords would be needed.

Owners: No individual owner is named. The text attributes use to the Millelith of old.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star claymore, base ATK 42, ATK% secondary stat (9 per cent). Passive Lithic Axiom: Unity gives the wearer 7 to 11 per cent ATK and 3 to 7 per cent CRIT Rate (by refinement) for each Liyue character in the party, stacking up to 4 times. It was a Weapon Event Wish (Version 1.3) and has the same passive as Lithic Spear.

376.content: The Millelith's old axiom, quoted in the Lithic Blade and Lithic Spear texts: while rock stays hard, the mountain shall never fail; while the Millelith stands guard, evil shall never prevail.

377.content:
Lithic Spear: Lithic Spear is a 4-star polearm of the Lithic series, a spear forged from the rocks of the Guyun Stone Forest whose hardness knows no equal. It was favoured by the Millelith of old, and its great weight stops today's Millelith from equipping it. It was added in Version 1.3.

Its text says it is said to be able to pierce even dragon scales, and recounts how the Millelith used leftover ancient spears after an earthquake.

Appearance: A spear forged from lith of the Guyun Stone Forest; canon gives no more detail. Do not invent a length or decoration.

Lore: The Millelith conducted themselves in Rex Lapis' name by the axiom: while rock stays hard, the mountain shall never fail; while the Millelith stands guard, evil shall never prevail. In the past they went forth to subdue demons and protect roads and countryside; in peaceful times their duties have shifted to maintaining order.

At a certain point in the past the earth shook and the mountains trembled. The Millelith then gave equipment left over from the ancient wars to those among them of unusually great stature: the very heavy Lithic Spears, which were used like shovels to rescue the injured. The text says the spear pierces rock with ease and that a thousand such spears lined up would be unstoppable.

In an even earlier and more turbulent era, every soldier of the Millelith could wield these colossal weapons, and a thousand spears in formation protected Rex Lapis' kingdom and the homeland.

Read together, the text sketches three stages: in the oldest era every Millelith soldier could wield the spear, after the earthquake only the unusually large were issued one and used it as a rescue tool, and today none of the Millelith can carry it because of its weight. It is a traditional account and does not name the earthquake or its date.

Owners: No individual owner is named. Yaoyao is seen with the unascended spear in her Thrust and Parry anecdote and Xiangling with the ascended one in the Three to Get Ready, and Here We Go cinematic (cameos, not story claims).

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star polearm, base ATK 44, ATK% secondary stat (6 per cent). Passive Lithic Axiom: Unity gives the wearer 7 to 11 per cent ATK and 3 to 7 per cent CRIT Rate (by refinement) for each Liyue character in the party, stacking up to 4 times. It was a Weapon Event Wish (Version 1.3) and has the same passive as Lithic Blade.

378.content: The Lithic Spear text describes the Millelith as the guardians of Rex Lapis' kingdom who once all carried these huge stone spears, and as rescuers who used them to dig out the injured after an earthquake. See the faction entry for the Millelith itself.

379.content:
Long Night's Oath (also: Lightkeeper's Pledge, Nightingale's Tail Feather, A Horn Unwinded, Dyed Tassel): Long Night's Oath is a 4- and 5-star artifact set that rewards Plunging Attacks. Its five pieces (Lightkeeper's Pledge, Nightingale's Tail Feather, Undying One's Mourning Bell, A Horn Unwinded, Dyed Tassel) carry item text that reads as a folk history of Nod-Krai: how the Lightkeepers swore their oath, how the Wild Hunt and the Abyss threatened the borderlands, and how the oath was renewed again and again at great cost.

The pieces were added in version 5.5. The text is told in a storyteller's voice and names almost no one directly; the wiki links the unnamed figures to Solovei, Avrelian, Aila, Sigurd, Rerir and others (see uncertainties).

Appearance: Northern military and ceremonial gear: a metal flower worn by Ratniki ("warriors"), a hat ornament of nightingale feathers, a bronze bell, a horn once used to summon the oath-sworn, and an ancient tasselled helmet.

Lore: The five pieces tell Nod-Krai's story from its founding oath to the cost of keeping it, centring on the Lightkeepers who guard the region.

Across the pieces: after the Cataclysm the borderlands were left without divine protection, a Torchforger from the far north rallied a moonlit defence, and the survivors raised a lighthouse at Piramida and swore an oath of vigilance to the new ruler of Snezhnaya, the Tsaritsa. Centuries later the Wild Hunt returns, the Fatui arrive at Piramida with ulterior motives, an oath-bound legion is lost, and a border officer chooses to save civilians against orders. Each piece frames the oath as a burden that descendants take up knowing what it costs.

The five pieces each tell one episode; see the per-piece entries (founding oath, Fatui at Piramida, the Wild Hunt and the bell, the Warrant Officer, the dyed helmet and the first Torchforger).

The pieces move among several eras. Founding era: the Cataclysm, the Torchforger's light and the first oath (Lightkeeper's Pledge, Dyed Tassel). A later age of the Wild Hunt: the Fatui at Piramida's gates and the oath-bound legion lost in the forest (Nightingale's Tail Feather, Undying One's Mourning Bell). A Horn Unwinded gives no names or dates for the Warrant Officer's desertion, so its place in the sequence is not stated. The text keeps the Fatui ambiguous: they are presented as the Tsaritsa's own force who undermine Nod-Krai's autonomy, yet one of their own officers breaks ranks to protect civilians. The Starshyna and the Lightkeepers are portrayed as proud of their autonomy; the oath is the source of both their pride and their casualties. Dyed Tassel's reference to the lord of all fae links the Torchforger's heritage to the court that Lightkeeper's Pledge shows ignoring the frontier.

Owners: No owner is named; the text speaks of Ratniki and Lightkeepers, and the wiki ties several pieces to Solovei and Sigurd.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): obtained from the Derelict Masonry Dock domain (Natlan) and the Artifact Strongbox. 2-piece: Plunging Attack DMG +25%. 4-piece: a Plunging Attack, Charged Attack or Elemental Skill hit gives 1, 2 or 2 stacks of Radiance Everlasting (each source once per 1s); each stack gives Plunging Attacks +15% DMG for 6s, max 5 stacks, independent timers.

380.comment: Long Night's Oath: Long Night's Oath
380.content: Artifact set whose item text narrates Nod-Krai's history from the Lightkeepers' founding oath to the Fatui's arrival at Piramida and a Warrant Officer's desertion, focused on keeping a sworn duty at great cost.

381.comment: Long Night's Oath: The Nightingale emblem and the first Torchforger
381.content: According to Dyed Tassel and Nightingale's Tail Feather, the first Torchforger came from a family of spies raised to the gentry by the Winter Tsar, with a nightingale as their emblem. After the Cataclysm he rode south from the far north in dark silver armour; with the new-moon maiden's beacon he repelled the black tide and later bound himself to an oath of vigilance. The wiki identifies him as Solovei; the text itself does not name him.

382.comment: Long Night's Oath: The Mourning Bell legend
382.content: Undying One's Mourning Bell tells of a warrior who fought toward the Wild Hunt's source, died without noticing, and continues to walk the abyss to fulfil his oath. His bell's toll became a folk omen that the hunter of the Wild Hunt is near. The wiki links him to Sigurd.

383.comment: Long Night's Oath: Piece text: Lightkeeper's Pledge
383.content: describes a time when the northern Hunting Winds levelled the frontier at the bidding of the tyrannical Knyazes of the fae. A mad monk who spoke strange tongues sought the power left by the heavenly moons and pitched a treacherous plot to the Tsar of all fae; the Moonchildren hiding in their mountain forests were scattered. The monk himself could not escape the celestial shell and was consumed by the sky. Before "paradise" existed it was merely a shared daydream of two children under the moon; years later one was executed as a notorious bandit and the other understood the words left behind. When the long night fell, the royal court ignored the borderlands and a horde of black beasts overran them until the original Torchforger, borrowing the power of the Moonchildren's priestess, raised the first beam of light. The survivors built a lighthouse atop the mountains and the Torchforger defended his friend's childlike dream before the Tsaritsa's court; he won a royal edict but bound himself to an oath of vigilance and sacrifice, and so began the history of "Nod-Krai".

384.comment: Long Night's Oath: Piece text: Nightingale's Tail Feather
384.content: legend of a nightingale carrying an ember on moonless nights. Piramida's high tower stands on the ruins of an age of pioneers, and the Lightkeepers' ancestors had sworn fidelity to the Tsaritsa centuries before. The people of "paradise" believed that so long as the lighthouse burned they could live free of the black beasts. One night the leader of the Wild Hunt rode across the sky and the sun failed to rise; as warriors gathered to march south, the current Starshyna sat silent in the mead hall because a host of the Fatui, the Warriors of the Pale Star, had reached the city gates, claiming to be reinforcements but with their own motives. The Starshyna knew that yielding would end centuries of autonomy. A masked officer's cold voice declared the dark calamity was beginning, that Snezhnaya could not bear the weight of their defeat, and that if none of the Nightingale warriors returned, the Fatui would handle the aftermath.

385.comment: Long Night's Oath: Piece text: Undying One's Mourning Bell
385.content: blood-scented air heralds the return of the great war as an army of spirits flies over the night. Country folk called it a demonic host from another world harvesting souls; others believed it the lingering phantoms of an ancient nightmare. The borderlanders named it the Wild Hunt, and a tempest unseen for a century fell like black-blood rain, proving the legends were born of real terror. A flock of black-feathered crows moved between light and shadow, led by one who stood against the light; the oath-bound legion marched on as moths to a flame. At the path's end only the warrior with the dark blade still stood, aware that the force that summoned the Hunt lay deep in the forest. His body had already been torn apart without his noticing, and his warning bell hissed through the blood and black mire, freezing the carrion-eaters. He was left to walk alone in the abyss to fulfil an unfinished oath. Folklore later held that tolling bells signal the approach of the one sworn to hunt down the Wild Hunt.

386.comment: Long Night's Oath: Piece text: A Horn Unwinded
386.content: when horns proclaimed the northern realm's might, a Fatui contingent sworn to the Tsaritsa and to no single Harbinger vowed to forge a pure new world beneath the stars. The borderlanders, granted autonomy, remained children of the motherland. The Warrant Officer leading a border squad held that conviction until he hovered before the gates of hell and saw souls no one loved. Before any strike was sanctioned he resolved to act, rejecting an order that would let black beasts devour mothers and children. The text skips ahead: the foul miasma is swept away by northern winds at dawn, the war ends, and no triumphant hero returns to the high tower, only a criminal and the children he saved. A renegade doctor ignores the deviation because the goal was met. Desertion and treason against the Tsaritsa are absolved by a newly sworn oath, and new warriors keep watch on a staircase built of bones until the abyssal tides dry up.

387.comment: Long Night's Oath: Piece text: Dyed Tassel
387.content: the first Torchforger came from the furthest northern city, his Nightingale emblem marking a family who began as spies and were raised to the gentry by the Winter Tsar. When the Cataclysm left the frontier without the gods' protection, a single rider in dark silver armour came from the north and the maiden of the new moon lit a beacon. Before departing for the Lempo Isles, warriors feasted in the mead hall, among them a young Ratnik in an archaic dark-tasselled helmet and holding a polearm; such armour marked descent from those who first fought beside the Torchforger against the black tide. Although they held no fief or title, they kept their ancestors' oaths in the belief that the lord of the fae and former protector of Snezhnaya still watched. Later the young warrior kneels among fallen comrades on a blood-soaked tundra and prays to an old god and to the Knyazes his people once ruled. Somewhere, perhaps woken by the horn, a long-dormant phantom stirs, and the ghostly blue wildfire of legend is said to burn again on new battlefields.

key: Lost Prayer to the Sacred Winds
388.comment: Lost Prayer to the Sacred Winds
388.content:
Lost Prayer to the Sacred Winds: Lost Prayer to the Sacred Winds is a 5-star catalyst: an educational tome by anonymous early worshippers of the wind, blessed by the wind for its faithfulness over the millennia. Its text follows the scripture through Mondstadt's ages and ends with a farewell note from a believer who joins the thousand winds. Added in Version 1.0.

Item text calls it scriptures of the ancient winds, passed from generation to generation among observers of ritual who served the Anemo Archon, its yellowing pages touched by countless hands whose prints the wind has carried away.

Appearance: A book with yellowed pages and an elegantly handwritten title page, thicker with every era. Canon gives no cover or size.

Lore: Under the Storm Lord, who reigned from his tower, the scriptures filled with desperate appeals. In the era when the sands of snow thawed, the joy of sprouting greenery flooded the pages.

Under the ruling aristocracy, who pulled puppet strings to control the masses, the scriptures in the hands of slaves told of their envy and their desire for the thousand winds. As the people lived, endured, fought, rejoiced and enjoyed freedom, the scriptures grew thicker and heavier.

When Mondstadt was born anew and the Church was finally unshackled, the book could no longer bear to stay on a shelf, took flight and left the Church's treasury. It belonged, like the winds and like the people of Mondstadt, to freedom and the winds.

The title page carries a farewell from a believer: "From the winds we have come, and with the winds we shall go. Never, ever grieve for me," because only the flesh rests in the soil while the soul becomes one with the thousand winds. Where flowers bloom and leaves sway, the writer says, it is that soul singing songs of freedom. The text is a poetic book-history and never names the Church officials or wind spirits involved.

Owners: No owner is named in canon. The book is said to have left the Church of Favonius's treasury on its own; no one has been shown holding it.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 5-star catalyst with base ATK 46 and a CRIT Rate secondary stat. Its passive, Boundless Blessing, raises Movement SPD by 10 per cent and, in battle, adds an Elemental DMG Bonus every 4 seconds (up to four stacks), lasting until the character falls or leaves combat. It is on the Standard Wish and weapon event Wishes.

key: Lost Prayer to the Sacred Winds
389.comment: Lost Prayer to the Sacred Winds: Thousand winds scripture
389.content: The Lost Prayer is a tome of prayers that tells Mondstadt's history through a worshipper's eyes, from the Storm Lord's tower to the aristocrats' control and the freedom that followed, and notes that the book flew away from the Church. For the phrase "the thousand winds" see the Anemo and Thousand Winds entries.

390.content:
Lumenstone (also: Lumenstone Adjuvant): Lumenstone is a special stone mined from the depths of The Chasm in Liyue. Its item text says it has catalytic properties and nearly blazes with light in the gloomy mines, but loses all such effects once taken out of the Chasm. Entering the Underground Mines requires an adjuvant made from it.

In the quest Chasm Spelunkers it becomes the Lumenstone Adjuvant, a lantern-like gadget for the mines.

Appearance: A stone that glows strongly in the dark of the mines. The Adjuvant is described as a crystal that can be a sun in your palm.

Lore: In Surreptitious Seven-Star Seal Sundering, the adventurer Zhiqiong tells the Traveler that to enter The Chasm they must first find an adjuvant made from lumenstone, since only with it can anyone move in the dark below. The Traveler takes the stone from a table, after which Paimon wonders how the cage-shaped objects relate to it.

The Adjuvant text says it resembles the Glazed Sand Crystal found only in The Chasm but stores greater power. Wiki notes say it illuminates the area, powers light-sensitive mechanisms, and refills from teleport waypoints, braziers and glowing ore, among other things; mining Noctilucous Jade in the mines also restores it.

Gameplay: Gameplay note, not in-world lore: the stone is a quest item; the Adjuvant is a reusable quick-use gadget with an energy gauge, usable only in the Underground Mines.

Scene use: A lantern for any scene in the mines; outside the Chasm it is just an inert stone, so do not carry its glow into other places.

Chronology: Introduced in Version 2.6 with The Chasm Delvers world quest series: the stone is obtained in the first required part, Surreptitious Seven-Star Seal Sundering, and turned into the Adjuvant in the following quest, Chasm Spelunkers.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 nothing further has been added to canon.

391.content:
Lumidouce Elegy (also: Bright Dawn Overture): Lumidouce Elegy is a 5-star polearm adorned with azure crystal. It is said to have been the treasure of a legendary Champion Duelist, yet never once used.

The weapon story follows that duelist, Marfisa (the wiki's identification), from the undercity Fleuve Cendre to the stage of the opera house, to the court's service as an enforcer, and finally to the pure sourcewaters of Narzissenkreuz.

Appearance: Canon describes a magnificent polearm adorned with azure crystal; the story gives its heroine sapphire eyes, but the text does not link that to the weapon. Arkhe-aligned wielders show a Pneuma or Ousia mark. Add nothing else.

Lore: In the Fleuve Cendre undercity where there is neither rain nor sun, a girl scraped by for scraps and would kill for a slice of mouldy bread, accepting that the weak are prey. Her mother's teaching was ashes to ashes, dust to dust.

Facing death, she is instead shown kindness by a girl in strange attire (the wiki links her to Parsifal the Great), who tucks a Lumidouce Bell flower behind her ear, saying it means hope and matches her hair, and trades it for her heart. She later watches the magician and assistant from a VIP box in the Opera Epiclese and sees hope in the flowers blooming under the spotlight. With no teacher, she steps onto a stage of her own, her lance performing every spear technique she has seen.

She is undefeated until a swordsman, whom the wiki links to Emanuel Guillotin, tricks her by slowing the rhythm and wounds her arm. He tells her that her stiff adherence to rules is her weakness and suggests she make something immutable, like justice, her rule. She answers angrily that surface-dwellers have no right to speak of justice, but concludes that crimes should be punished and lies exposed. She becomes a purple-clad enforcer, a Champion Duelist, serving justice until, after the Siege of Poisson, the criminal Parsifal is brought before her.

The wiki adds that Parsifal, or Josephine in her sister's name, requested trial by combat and presumably died in the duel against Marfisa, and that Marfisa later went hunting for the changed Emanuel, which is how she met the Narzissenkreuz Ordo. The weapon text itself ends differently, with her falling into the pure sourcewaters and the self-evident meaning of her life dissolving along with her memories. Before that, she never learned that the Lumidouce Bell's true meaning in the language of flowers was not hope. The final line says that even fate gave her no blossoming elegy.

Owners: A legendary Champion Duelist, linked by the wiki to Marfisa. The weapon was never used.

Emilie is paired with it only as a release convention (see uncertainties).

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star polearm, base ATK 46 at level 1, secondary stat CRIT Rate; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 4.8. Passive "Bright Dawn Overture": raises ATK; after the wielder triggers Burning, or deals Dendro DMG to Burning enemies, their DMG rises for 8s (up to 2 stacks); at 2 stacks, or when refreshed at 2 stacks, Energy is restored, at most once per 12s. It can trigger off-field. Values scale with refinement.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: Marfisa is a past figure; modern Fontainians know the Champion Duelist title, not this polearm. The description says the polearm was never used, so do not narrate famous kills with it.

392.content: Marfisa was a Champion Duelist of the Court of Fontaine who came from the Fleuve Cendre. The wiki links her to the story of Lumidouce Elegy: self-taught lance-fighter, defeated once by a swordsman who convinced her to follow justice, and dissolved in the Narzissenkreuz's waters.

393.content:
Magical Crystal Chunk (also: Magical Crystal Chunks, Magical Crystal Ore): Magical Crystal Chunk is a blue crystal from mines whose rock was eroded by the energy of the Ley Lines. Ordinary methods cannot process it. Only Original Resin can refine it, into Mystic Enhancement Ore for strengthening weapons.

Where the plain Crystal Chunk is ordinary ore, this is its Ley Line-altered counterpart.

Appearance: Blue crystal chunks taken from Magical Crystal Ore nodes, which stand beside regular ore at Mining Outcrops.

Lore: Item text says the crystal was eroded by Ley Line energy and so cannot be handled by ordinary means; Original Resin can, however, refine it into an invaluable material. The description does not say what Original Resin is in-world or how the process works.

The shorter text on the item says the chunks can be refined into weapon EXP materials by Original Resin, and that crystals from mines eroded by Ley Line energy cannot be processed by ordinary means. The item text does not connect this to any specific event.

Gameplay: Gameplay note, not in-world lore: each node drops 1 to 3 chunks, nodes appear in Mining Outcrops after Adventure Rank 30, and they respawn daily in changing locations. They are currently used only to forge Mystic Enhancement Ore with Original Resin.

Outcrops also spawn ordinary Crystal Ore beside the Magical Crystal Ore, and the two respawn independently.

Scene use: Use it as a curiosity for smiths and miners: a crystal that cannot be worked by normal craft. Do not invent how Original Resin works.

394.content:
Maiden Beloved (also: Maiden's Distant Love, Maiden's Heart-Stricken Infatuation, Maiden's Passing Youth, Maiden's Fleeting Leisure, Maiden's Fading Beauty): Maiden Beloved is a healing artifact set (4 and 5 star, added 1.0). Its pieces tell of a sheltered noblewoman rescued by a white knight, who fell in love with him and spent her years waiting for a man devoted to chivalry. She is the counterpart to the knight of the Bloodstained Chivalry set.

The pieces are Maiden's Distant Love (flower), Maiden's Heart-Stricken Infatuation (feather), Maiden's Passing Youth (sands), Maiden's Fleeting Leisure (goblet) and Maiden's Fading Beauty (circlet).

Appearance: A maiden's keepsakes: a fresh, elegant flower of a species the books call extinct, an old delicate feathered ornament under layers of dust, a delicate timepiece, treasured teaware once filled with black tea, and a hat she never took off before her suitors.

Lore: Distant Love recalls the passage she read countless times, of the damsel saved by the white knight and the exchange of flowers as blessings; the flower stays constant because her heart stilled when they met. Heart-Stricken Infatuation says time stopped for her that day; nothing mattered, and she wandered looking for him like a bird without a nest, praying her love would reach him while he pursued chivalry in a distant land where ancient empires crumbled. Passing Youth shows the short hand chasing the long hand like her longing: her time would end, her waiting would not. Fleeting Leisure has her indulging in pastries and tea while recalling the knight saying that the flower would be his medal; her unfinished confession ('my heart is already...') was both her privilege and the chain of courtliness. Fading Beauty has her brush the dust off her hat each night and ignore the flowers of courters whose names and faces were not worth remembering, as fewer and fewer came.

The set never says whether the knight knew her feelings or whether they met again. The wiki links the white knight to Roland and to Bloodstained Chivalry, where the same flower is his only reward and ends up dried and darkened with blood. Read together, one encounter became a symbol of purity for him and a whole life for her.

Per-piece details worth keeping: the Distant Love flower is described as a species the books say is extinct; the Fading Beauty hat is the object she brushes each night as the courters thin out; the Fleeting Leisure confession is the only direct quotation of her feelings and is left unfinished. The Heart-Stricken Infatuation text places the knight in a distant land where ancient empires crumbled, which the wiki links to the Cataclysm and Khaenri'ah; the set itself does not name either.

Owners: No named owner; the maiden is anonymous and the pieces are her belongings.

Status as of 7.1: The maiden is long gone and the texts leave her fate and name unstated. The set is background lore, unchanged by 6.x and 7.0-7.1.

How {{char}} behaves: Use for wistful, historical-register scenes. Do not name the maiden or write her knight as returning her feelings; the texts leave his side to the Bloodstained Chivalry set.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). A 4- and 5-star set from the Valley of Remembrance. 2-piece: Healing Bonus +15%. 4-piece: using an Elemental Skill or Burst raises healing received by all party members by 20% for 10s (in game terms Healing Bonus and Incoming Healing Bonus). The Adventurer Handbook gives a full 4-star set.

395.content:
The unnamed maiden of the Maiden Beloved texts fell in love with the white knight who saved her and spent her life waiting for him while courters brought flowers. The wiki ties the knight to Roland.

Her objects, a hat she would not remove for suitors, black tea and a dusty feather, show a life stopped on one day. The goblet text cuts her confession off after the knight speaks of his medal.

396.content:
Makhaira Aquamarine: Makhaira Aquamarine is a 4-star claymore of the Tulaytullah series: an ancient greatsword that gleams like water, whose unnaturally sharp edge a thousand years of sand erosion has not dulled. Its legend belongs to the dancer Makhaira, once a tyrant's concubine.

It is one of three Tulaytullah-series weapons that share a story world with the five-star catalyst Tulaytullah's Remembrance, and it was released in Version 3.1 through weapon event Wishes.

Appearance: A greatsword with a blade that gleams like water. The description stresses its unnaturally sharp edge and great age.

Lore: A thousand years ago, when the foolish king (Deshret) was buried beneath the dunes, short-lived city-states were scattered across the gilded land. The sword belonged to the dancer Makhaira, once the tyrant's concubine, who won the king's favor and the prince's attention with a ruthless sword dance.

The noble king of a decaying kingdom was obese and haughty, spending his days on food, wine and hunting, and, like other kings of that decadent age, on conquest and hoarding loot. One night, as water-colored moonlight quieted the kingdom and the Seelie murmured, he fell into a deep sleep. Makhaira, who had seen the signs of destruction, polished her sword for one last dance, and the young prince, who had foreseen the same, came to her.

A quoted exchange between the two does not label its speakers. It speaks of a little revenge lifting a burden from both their hearts, of the hunting-addict being executed by the falcon he spoils, and of a speaker whose mother, a Jinni, taught her a seven-fold sword dance, which fits Makhaira but is not stated outright. The conspiracy was drawn up in bed, and the lovers' gentle words were sharp blades. The tyrant fell, and the great cause of conquering kingdoms and harems vanished.

The city-state's rise and fall is called a drunken dream in which the kind and the evil alike were crushed like wheat husks by a millstone. Makhaira, adept at the sword dance, failed to become queen, and the wise old retainer who survived to tell the story lost his eyes. The displaced, swept into the sea of sand, became wanderers or mercenaries before the Dharma Forest swallowed them.

Owners: The sword belongs to Makhaira in its story. No modern character is recorded wielding it.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star claymore, level 1 base ATK 42, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 36. Passive Desert Pavilion: every 10 s the wielder gains a percentage of their Elemental Mastery as ATK for 12 s, with nearby party members gaining 30% of it; it works off-field and stacks across copies.

The ATK gain is 24% of Elemental Mastery at refinement 1 and 48% at refinement 5. The text also appears in Chronicled Wishes.

How {{char}} behaves: Present it as a legend with an unreliable edge: the speaker "has heard" it. Do not merge it with Tulaytullah's Remembrance as a single account.

397.content: Desert Pavilion is the weapon passive of Makhaira Aquamarine (gameplay): a periodic ATK bonus based on Elemental Mastery, shared in part with nearby party members.

398.content:
Marechaussee Hunter (also: Hunter's Brooch, Masterpiece's Overture, Moment of Judgment, Forgotten Vessel, Veteran's Visage, Marechaussee Hunter artifact set): Marechaussee Hunter is a 4- and 5-star artifact set from Fontaine, added in Version 4.0. Its pieces are mementos of the old Marechaussee Hunters, chiefly Emanuel Guillotin, who directed the Siege of Poisson, retired scarred and drinking, and raised two children he never felt close to. The bonuses boost Normal and Charged Attacks and CRIT Rate when HP changes.

The pieces are Hunter's Brooch (flower), Masterpiece's Overture (plume), Moment of Judgment (sands), Forgotten Vessel (goblet) and Veteran's Visage (circlet). The set shares a name with the Marechaussee Hunters, the older monster-hunting group behind today's Marechaussee Phantom (see its own entry).

Appearance: Each piece is a keepsake: an emblem for feats in Fontaine's defence (the brooch), a small tool for adjusting clockwork torque (the overture), a pocket watch given to Fontaine's enforcers that doubled as a duty badge (the moment of judgment), a wine vessel (the forgotten vessel) and a mask given to a Hunter whose face was wounded in service to the Court (the visage).

Lore: The pieces concern the Hunters' founding under Cassiodor, the Siege of Poisson, Alain Guillotin's clockwork legend, a famous trial by combat, and the retired Hunter (Emanuel Guillotin) who cared for two children he never felt close to.

- Hunter's Brooch: the emblem was awarded for feats of arms in Fontaine's defence; some recipients hid it or sank it in the water. The name "Marechaussee Hunter" is credited to Cassiodor, who became the "Golden Hunter" and thought of the name as humiliating. The piece notes that heretics and demons are rare but people driven to become them are many, and that today the Marechaussee Phantom investigates crime more than it fights, with many Melusines in its ranks. The brooch's owner directed the Siege of Poisson, quit the force, and was drawn back among people at an old friend's request to make a world free of phantoms for his son and daughter. A peaceful ocean ended it.
- Masterpiece's Overture: a clockwork tool made outmoded by Alain Guillotin's "new model" meka. Alain organized energy research at the now-ruined Institute of Natural Philosophy, then joined and left the Marechaussee Phantom and founded the Research Institute of Kinetic Energy Engineering. He was close to nobody but his younger sister, a fellow Marechaussee. Two legends are told: that he built a thinking machine to help her, and that his final research vanished from his workshop, leaving only signs that something had been built.
- Moment of Judgment: a pocket watch of Fontaine's enforcers. The piece recalls the Great Magician "Parsifal" demanding a trial by combat and Champion Duelist Marfisa being chosen as prosecution's champion, to public fascination. Journalist Karl Ingold, who knew Parsifal, later photographed old friends of the Narzissenkreuz Institute at the Vice Director's invitation and regretted not recording a girl's last battle.
- Forgotten Vessel: the wine vessel of a servant of the Court of Fontaine who learned, near the end, that the rabbit hole led to a maelstrom. He remembers childhood games with Dwight, Basil and Karl (where he played the hero and Karl the evil dragon "Jabberwock"), the Director's embrace, the Poisson fires, and sending innocent children to the Narzissenkreuz Institute. He admits he never felt close to his "son" and "daughter," Alain and Mary-Ann, though he treasured watching them grow.
- Veteran's Visage: a mask for a soldier scarred in the Court's service. A friend who grew up with him says goodbye before an Institute battle, asking him to look after "those two kids," and calls him Guillotin, "my dear Emanuel". He dislikes children and company because seeing others only reminds him they have red blood too, but he takes the task on.
Wider canon (wiki) connects the pieces to Emanuel Guillotin: he was a Narzissenkreuz Institute orphan, later a Marechaussee Hunter who directed the Siege of Poisson, which may have caused the deaths of Rene de Petrichor's and Jakob Ingold's parents. After retiring he became Alain and Mary-Ann's guardian when Basil Elton asked, investigated the Narzissenkreuz Ordo for Dwight Lasker, and was the first person dissolved by the Master, with Marfisa the second.

The set deliberately gives separate pictures of the same man: the glory-seeking Hunter's emblem, the broken drinker's vessel, and the masked guardian. His real reasons for fighting, and the extent of his remorse for Poisson, are shown only through these private memories. The Hunters' original purpose, according to wider canon, was to fight the Golden Troupe's magic and golems (see the Golden Troupe set), and the group later lived on as family traditions rather than an organised force.

Owners: Emanuel Guillotin is the set's main figure. The pieces also touch Cassiodor (the brooch's naming), Alain Guillotin (the overture), Karl Ingold and Marfisa (the watch) and Basil Elton, the unnamed friend of the mask.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): the 2-piece bonus is Normal and Charged Attack DMG +15%. The 4-piece bonus gives CRIT Rate +12% for 5s whenever current HP rises or falls, up to 3 stacks. Obtained from the Denouement of Sin domain in Fontaine and the artifact strongbox.

The domain lies in Fontaine's Belleau Region; its Ley Line Disorder rewards HP changes with CRIT DMG, and its enemies are out-of-control clockwork meka.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): the pieces suit gentle, melancholic scenes about duty, regret and chosen family. A character who holds one should treat it as a keepsake, not as a weapon or token of rank.

399.content: In this set Emanuel is the scarred, retired Hunter who remembered his childhood games, the Siege of Poisson and his strained fatherhood in his last moments. His own entry holds his full story.

400.comment: Marechaussee Hunter: Siege of Poisson (set lore)
400.content: According to Hunter's Brooch and Veteran's Visage, the Siege of Poisson was an incident whose director was a Marechaussee Hunter; he left the force afterwards, and the bloodshed marked him for life.

401.content:
Memory of Dust (also: the stone dumbbell, Mortal World's Lock): Memory of Dust is a five-star catalyst of the Liyue series, a stone puzzle dumbbell. Its item story recounts Morax remembering Guizhong, who gave him the dumbbell as a token and a challenge: all her wisdom is hidden inside, if he can unlock it. He never could.

Appearance: Item text calls it a stone dumbbell. The wiki notes its design is based on a Kongming/Luban lock burr puzzle, and its Chinese name means Mortal World's Lock.

Lore: The story is told from Morax's memory. He recalls meeting a young woman with billowing sleeves among blooming Glaze Lilies; she acted solemn but seemed joyful as she handed him the dumbbell, calling it the mark of their pledge and her challenge to him. He insists there was no formal contract between them, just two people on the same path for their own reasons, yet he remembers the scene anyway.

At their end she said that the little people are as small and fragile as dust, and fear because they cannot know when disaster will take them, and so they work hard to grow clever. Since she and he differed so greatly in strength, she chose technique and wisdom, and with his brawn and her brains the city would become great. Her final smile was lonely as her form dissolved into fine dust. She told him to forget about the dumbbell.

Guizhong's sentence ("If you can unlock it") breaks off, and Morax never learns how it would have ended. Over the years the wild Glaze Lilies dwindled until none were left. The wiki's trivia says the text is about the two gods who dwelled over Guili Plains and their first and final meeting.
