Guizhong's words give a view of her motives that the item states directly: she thought mortals fragile and fearful, and chose wit over force because of the gulf in strength between her and Morax. The pledge is framed from his side as no formal contract, which preserves how each of them described the bond differently. The text is narrated through Morax's recollection, so it shows his memory rather than an objective record.

Owners: Guizhong forged it by unknown methods and gave it to Morax (Zhongli). The wiki says he presumably still has it; the text never confirms this.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore. The passive Golden Majesty raises Shield Strength and stacks ATK on hits, with a larger bonus while shielded. It shares this passive with the Liyue-series claymore The Unforged. Obtained from Weapon Event Wishes; added in Version 1.1.

402.content:
Mistsplitter Reforged (also: Kirigiri no Kaikou, Mistsplitter, Takamine's sword): Mistsplitter Reforged is a sword from Inazuma's past, one of the blades the Shogun bestowed on her Hatamoto. It was carried by the samurai Takamine the Mistsplitter, who used it against demons and Tatarigami, and who fought the dark army of the Cataclysm at the end of his life. The sword broke and was reforged from its fragments, so the "Reforged" in the name marks it as a successor bearing the old name.

Its item text says it can call on lightning to cut through mountain mist and night fog. The reforged blade has a hamon like flowing clouds. The original line of users ended with Takamine; the sword now survives mainly in stories.

Appearance: A sword that blazes with a fierce violet light (the item description). The reforging left a hamon, the temper line on the blade, that resembles flowing clouds. In play, a purple aura surrounds the weapon while its passive is active and brightens with more stacks.

Lore: The text says the sword was shattered into a thousand pieces and reforged. Its user, Takamine the Mistsplitter, appears in a children's rhyme listing famous martial artists, after Arataki of the Front Gate, Iwakura the Successor and Kitain the Serpent.

Takamine once accompanied a member of the clergy and used the blade to slay demons and Tatarigami. He learned archery from the Yougou Tengu and passed it on to a person he loved, Asase Hibiki. At the end of his life he became one of the Shogun's yoriki and fought a dark army.

He wagered his beloved bow with Asase and promised to return to claim the future as his prize; the text imagines things might have gone differently had he not left the bow with her. As the foe flooded in like mist he kept slashing with the blade that could disperse the dark night, but the sword eventually gave out before the swordsman did. He was submerged in the thick dark mist, holding the hilt of the broken sword like a spider's thread, still reminding himself that the wager was undecided. Only some fragments were retrieved and reforged so that the new weapon could inherit the Mistsplitter name.

Takamine's story links to Asase Hibiki and the bow Thundering Pulse, to the text of Hamayumi and Shimenawa's Reminiscence, and to the Storm Cage piece of the Emblem of Severed Fate artifact set, which expand on the same pair. In Kagura's Verity, Yae Miko lists among the things wiped out in the Shogun's era "the darkened remains of the swordmaster's soul"; the swordmaster is linked on the wiki to Takamine, though that item never names him in the sentence.

Owners: Takamine the Mistsplitter is the only named user. The Shogun is named as the one who gave such swords to her Hatamoto.

The text says the sword "would have no successors"; do not portray any present-day character as inheriting it. Kamisato Ayaka is shown with it in an official sticker, but that does not make it canon property of the Kamisato clan.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star sword in the Inazuma series, released in Version 2.0 on the weapon event Wish. Base ATK 48 with CRIT DMG as its secondary stat.

Its passive, Mistsplitter's Edge, grants an Elemental DMG Bonus for all elements (12% at refinement 1, 24% at refinement 5) and up to three stacks of Mistsplitter's Emblem that add a bonus for the wielder's own element (8/16/28% at refinement 1, 16/32/56% at refinement 5). One stack comes from Normal Attacks (or Charged Attacks) dealing Elemental DMG (5 seconds), one from casting an Elemental Burst (10 seconds), and one while Energy is below 100%. Each stack's duration is tracked separately.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: Mistsplitter Reforged works as a half-remembered legend. Characters in Inazuma may know the rhyme or the story of Takamine, but nobody should treat the sword as a known, available weapon unless the scenario creates a copy explicitly.

403.content: Takamine the Mistsplitter was a samurai of Inazuma's past, listed in a children's rhyme of famous martial artists. He used the sword Mistsplitter against demons and Tatarigami, learned archery from the Yougou Tengu, and made a wager with Asase Hibiki that involved leaving his bow with her. He died or vanished fighting the dark army of the Cataclysm; his own entry carries the rest.

404.content: Mistsplitter's Edge is the weapon passive of Mistsplitter Reforged (gameplay), flavoured on the swordsman who sliced through dark mist. The Japanese passive name refers to a sword worn at the hip.

405.content:
Mitternachts Waltz: Mitternachts Waltz is a 4-star bow described as painted in the color of transgression and nights of illusion. Its text is a dramatic, German-flavored tale: the Prinzessin der Verurteilung and her Night-Severing Raven, Ozvaldo Hrafnavins, recount a long journey across space and time. The wiki notes Fischl is shown with this bow in her TCG card.

The name is German for "midnight waltz". The text never says in plain words who the Prinzessin is, but it addresses her as "mein Fräulein" and the wiki links the address to Fischl.

Appearance: A bow painted in a transgressive, dream-like night color. Beyond that short description, canon gives no visual detail.

Lore: The tale opens with Oz telling the Prinzessin that not one of her tears was shed in vain on her pilgrimage. The Prinzessin and her raven, in their journey across space and time, witnessed countless stories and their endings.

In the text, every young man's rage at injustice must turn to calm, and everything must pass through the doorway of its destruction into the Prinzessin's future kingdom, where it finds sleep in her pitch-dark Nachtgarten. When Droctulf fell to the Beast of the World, having fought for a young man's dreams, the Prinzessin began to tear up, and she declared that the Sovereign of the Immernachtreich weeps not.

She then says everyone born into the world carries sin, and when the clock strikes judgment again, the struggles of men and beasts trapped under the skirt of night will be a midnight waltz. Oz asks if she still recalls a tale of two of three bright moons being shredded by a sword that tore the horizon. The text offers a second reading: the moons were reduced to dust, yet wished to stay in the Prinzessin's gaze. It ends with the Prinzessin insisting that a Prinzessin does not shed tears; the wetness was just secretion from eyes insulted by impudent grains of sand.

The piece is both epic and comic: grand talk about eternity, undercut by a proud denial of crying. Use it as in-character flavor from Fischl's persona, not as verified cosmology. For the moon and tree motifs, the wiki's links to the Three Moons and the Irminsul are interpretive.

Owners: No owner is named in the text. The wiki notes Fischl is seen wielding this bow in her TCG character card.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star bow, base ATK 42, secondary stat Physical DMG Bonus 11.3%, obtained from weapon event Wishes (added in Version 1.6). Passive Evernight Duet: Normal Attack hits raise Elemental Skill DMG for 5 s, and Elemental Skill hits raise Normal Attack DMG for 5 s, by 20% at refinement 1 up to 40% at refinement 5.

The wiki also notes it appeared in the Honkai Impact 3rd crossover event Outworld Traveler; that is out-of-universe trivia.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: voice the bow in a theatrical register with sprinkled German words, matching Fischl's persona, but keep the weapon itself an item, not a character.

406.content: Evernight Duet is the weapon passive of Mitternachts Waltz (gameplay). Normal Attack hits and Elemental Skill hits each raise the other's DMG for a few seconds.

407.content:
Moonfall Silver (also: Moonfall Silver crystal): Moonfall Silver is a silver crystal as pure and pristine as moonlight, a local specialty of Nod-Krai. Canon says it has almost perfect elemental affinity, which is why Nod-Krai craftspeople treat it as an excellent elemental conductor. It is found on Hiisi Island.

Its name comes from Frostmoon Scions tradition, which held that the crystals were a gift from the moon. Older Snezhnayan chronicles tell a different, much older story about silver woven by the Frostmoon.

It is also an object of local enthusiasm and folklore: a collector in Nasha Town runs a small appreciation event for it, and a Nod-Krai folk tale uses it as the material of an imaginary gown.

Appearance: A silvery crystal with an iridescent white sheen. Dorota, a collector in Nasha Town, praises its flawless form, smooth rounded texture and unrivaled elemental affinity. Even good samples can hide tiny flaws that only a careful eye notices.

Lore: The item text gives two traditions. In the legacy of the Frostmoon Scions, the crystals were born five hundred years ago alongside the Moon Maiden, and the Moonchanter of that time believed them a gift from the moon, hence the name. Yet older documents by Snezhnayan chroniclers say the descendants of the golden realm (Hyperborea) were already using secret silver woven by the Frostmoon thousands of years earlier. The text says plainly that how these two tales connect is unclear.

Linnea, the Adventurers' Guild advisor, tells a folk tale in the Mineral Investigation Special Lecture. A fae governor of Nod-Krai who loved rare clothes hired a young tailor in black who claimed to spin moon-glow crystals into thread. The tailor took a large quantity of Moonfall Silver and said he had woven a gown too pure for a fool or unremarkable man to see. The governor pretended to see it and paraded in it until a child pointed out he wore nothing. By the tale, the tailor was Reed Miller in disguise, who sold the silver and gave the Mora to poor townsfolk. Linnea believes real garments of Moonfall Silver once existed and the weaving art is lost, and mentions a separate tale, "The Fisherman and the Beast", that also has a moonlight gown but that she holds back from the children present.

In the world quest Mineral Research: Moonfall Silver, Dorota hosts a Moonfall Silver Appreciation Event in Nasha Town and quizzes Linnea on which of three samples is flawless, leading to a Selected Moonfall Silver kept for exhibition. In the lecture, Maisie votes Moonfall Silver the most beautiful rock in Nod-Krai, while Mikko dismisses it as a stone that looks good but does little. Linnea replies that it has quite a few uses, though less common in daily life than Rainbowdrop Crystals.

Owners: No notable owner. Collectors such as Dorota in Nasha Town keep prized samples, and Nod-Krai craftspeople use it as an elemental conductor.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore: a Nod-Krai local specialty added in Version 6.0 (Luna I). It is gathered on Hiisi Island, especially between Frostmoon Enclave and the Light-Bathed Platform, and in Silvermoon Hall, and is used for crafting and character ascension.

408.content:
Moongazer's Engraving (also: Moongazer Engraving, Stellar Blackbody message): Vol. 1 is the dragon researcher Lusalim's digest; Vol. 2 is Nin-Kiggia's annotated translation of the first message, the lament of the immortal Ysna'qurel. The script is unreadable, yet readers understand it in their own tongue.

Appearance: Both volumes are described as an ancient stone tablet found on the moon, with writing that is completely indecipherable but understood by anyone who reads it. Vol. 1 reads as a plain, hopeful letter; Vol. 2 as a long epic poem in the third person, with repeated formulae and untranslatable words in brackets.

Lore: Vol. 1 is addressed to a friend from a distant world and urges them to beware. Vol. 2 tells of Ysna'qurel, ruler of Throgg, who learns of a Dark Destroyer and sends a last messenger to warn other worlds, despite the cost.

Vol. 1 is addressed to a "friend from a distant world". The senders do not know if they will be heard, and say that if someone does hear, they were caught by some exceptional gravitational force. They warn that pitch-black annihilation, the mortal foe of all life, crosses the universe and may have reached the reader's era already, and offer their message as a small light: one ray is feeble, but while another shines out before it fades, a ray will one day pierce the night like dawn. Lusalim adds a private note to his "daughter" Ninnin (Nin-Kiggia) that the key help the moon goddesses gave their plans lies at the lunar core, reachable through fissures.

**Volume 1.** Lusalim's note says the text records the message conveyed by the Stellar Blackbody. The message is gentle in tone: it says the cold silence of a lonely universe may be eased by hearing others, that the receivers "are not alone in this vast star-filled cosmos", and it urges them to be on their guard against the darkness without knowing where they are. The final line is a hope that its light will "embolden" the reader. Lusalim's addendum to Nin-Kiggia points her to Moonheart Gap, which he calls the lunar core.

**Volume 2.** Nin-Kiggia notes that 3,655 earlier lines tell how an immortal, Ysna'qurel, defeated seven monsters (or perhaps compatriots) and brought the world under the empire's rule. The passage translated then turns: Ysna'qurel hears from another land of a "Dark Destroyer" and an impending decline, and dispatches a last messenger to warn other worlds. An assembly of rulers or kin ("the [...]", which may mean brothers, friends, rulers and servants at once) answer that sending a messenger will not save them and will draw the Destroyer's notice. Ysna'qurel, "child of Ghel'vur, Ruler of Throgg", replies that all that dies shall die and even gods must submit to that law, and that they will send the messenger, who is "nimble as Fnost" and swift as T'rinqu'oss. Ysna'qurel admits to greater fear than all of them together, and weeps for what will never be again (a partner's embrace, tales sung to the young). The text sets out the dilemma: sending the warning will make the Destroyer notice the world, and withholding it would also bring death. The decision: to warn other worlds so they may be ready. The closing lines, spoken by the dead warriors, ask the listener to "know that you are not alone" and speak of a dim light which, once heard, can be kindled anew. The final line is "We are here, looking up at the starry sky."

**Translator's notes (Vol. 2).** Nin-Kiggia's notes are the interesting layer. She explains that the species seems to have framed whatever it wished to say as long third-person narrative poems, which is why a short message is so verbose. Unknown words are glossed from context. Pairs like "merciful and good" and "zealous for war and destruction" appear to be one word. The proverb about Olmegratheen racing through flame and the third mud-candle is quoted as-is and its meaning is described as wholly obscure. A stretch of 137 lines is only a roster of names and titles, and 32 lines are skipped because they are close to a line already translated but harder to parse. She notes that the word used for light is a verb of hearing ("listen... this is our light"). Her final note refuses to claim that the Blackbody's civilization was Ysna'qurel's empire.

**The Blackbody (wiki context).** The Stellar Blackbody wiki page says it is an extraterrestrial lifeform found in Project Moongazer and an information-bearing organism that communicates by vibration, from which black filamentous "blackbody matter" was extracted and used in Project Lunar Veil. It also says the dragons took the warning as the model for their own transmissions into space, one of which reached the Traveler and their sibling, who replied that they wished to visit Teyvat. These are wiki-level syntheses of quest and interactable text; use with care.

**Reading the two volumes together.** Vol. 1 is a digest in which Lusalim has swapped unintelligible terms for ones he could understand, so it should be read as his rendering. Vol. 2 is closer to the original and reveals a more tragic frame: a civilization whose ruler chose to warn others although doing so would hasten its own end. Both converge on one message: you are not alone, be watchful, and keep a light burning. The father-daughter note at the end of Vol. 1 ties the Moongazer project to Nin-Kiggia, who later annotates Vol. 2, so the two volumes are also a handover between researchers.

**Boundaries.** Canon does not say who wrote the tablets, how old they are, or whether the senders survived. "Pitch-black annihilation" is linked by the wiki to the Abyss in its links, but the text itself uses only the words "pitch-black annihilation" and "Dark Destroyer"; do not state more than that.

Owners: No owner. Vol. 1 is credited to Lusalim and Vol. 2 to Nin-Kiggia; both are long dead as of the cutoff (the wiki lists both as deceased).

Gameplay: Game mechanics: a 2-volume Book Collection on the Frost Moon. Vol. 1 is obtained during the quest Project Moongazer (Part 1); Vol. 2 is picked up from an Edict Module in Lusalim's Laboratory.

409.comment: Moongazer's Engraving: The Stellar Blackbody's message
409.content:
A warning carried across space and recorded on stone tablets found on the Frost Moon: pitch-black annihilation is crossing the universe, other worlds should be watchful, and a light kindled by one civilization can embolden another. Lusalim's digest and Nin-Kiggia's verbatim translation survive. Whether the original senders survived is unknown.

The Stellar Blackbody is, per the wiki, an information-bearing lifeform discovered during the Moongazer expedition that speaks by vibrations. Its relation to the empire in Vol. 2 is not confirmed by Nin-Kiggia.

410.content: In Vol. 2 of Moongazer's Engraving, Ysna'qurel is an immortal, "child of Ghel'vur" and ruler of Throgg, who united the world under an empire after defeating seven monsters or compatriots. When they learn of the coming "Dark Destroyer", they choose to send a final messenger to warn other worlds, against the assembly's objection, and weep for what they will lose. Their sex, if any, is unknown.

411.content: Nin-Kiggia ("Ninnin") annotates Vol. 2 as an artificial, draconic Moongazer raised by Lusalim as his daughter. Her notes stay careful: she marks unreadable words, summarizes omitted line ranges, and declines to say whether the message's authors were Ysna'qurel's own empire.

412.content:
Moonweaver's Dawn (also: Secret Silver's Testament): An immaculate silver sword that slices armour like moonlight through an empty night; legend says it was blessed by the first Moonchanter, Aila. A 4-star sword of the Frostmoon Scion series from Version 6.0.

Its text shows Aila obeying, then ending, the last Archpriestess.

Appearance: An immaculate, sharp silver sword; canon text gives no hilt or decorative detail.

Lore: A guardian addresses her ward Aila as her heart's child and tells her the pure silver blood of their line alone is worthy of the Frost Moon's grace.

Aila is told she will bear the heir to Elysium and must not wed an outlander's son. The text says Lovia, the Archpriestess of the far north, repeated blasphemous deeds, and Aila obediently carried out her commands, including severing silver threads of fate with the blade and silencing singing voices, to purify the holy blood.

Lovia then orders Aila to guide Solovei, a man she calls a treacherous murderer who dares seek the Scions' protection, to the sanctuary and to thrust the sword through his heart from behind. Lovia reads Aila's years of silence as consent and never doubts that she resents none of it.

The blade instead pierces Lovia's back. Aila's last words are that Mr. Solovei was right and that Lovia was lying: if not, why would she bleed dawn-light crimson rather than moonlit silver when her thread was cut? The scene is set before the pitch-black calamity swept the borderlands. The text keeps Aila's thoughts private and never says what Lovia was lying about.

Owners: No wielder is named; the blade is attributed to Aila's blessing.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star sword, base ATK 44, ATK% secondary. Passive Secret Silver's Testament increases Elemental Burst DMG, with an extra bonus when the wielder's Energy Capacity is low (60 or 40 or less, depending on the tier of the effect). One copy is awarded by the quest Echoes of an Unfinished Past.

How {{char}} behaves: Present as a sacred, ominous blade whose legend is Scion-flavoured. Do not treat the stabbing scene as universally known; it is the text's depiction, and other weapon texts tell a different Aila-Lovia story.

413.content: Secret Silver's Testament is the weapon's passive; its name echoes the scene where Aila's silver blade reveals a crimson truth. Mechanics are in the gameplay section.

414.content:
Mora (also: Mora coins, Mora currency): Mora is the common currency of Teyvat, accepted in every nation. It takes its name from Morax, the Geo Archon, whom Liyue calls Rex Lapis. All of it is minted at the Golden House in Liyue. Loading-screen text calls it the one language everybody speaks.

Mora is also described as a kind of catalyst: a medium of physical transformation, which is why so many tasks, such as crafting and strengthening equipment, can only be done by spending it.

Appearance: Mora comes as small coins stamped with a triquetra, a triangular symbol. Both faces are identical, so a coin cannot be flipped without marking one side. People in Teyvat still settle disputes by flipping a coin and still say "heads" and "tails", even though neither side has a head. Larger sums are carried in bags; a huge bag of gold coins appears as a quest item, and Childe's high-value coins could be redeemed for smaller change at the Northland Bank.

Lore: In-game text calls Mora the currency accepted worldwide, whose value and standing nobody disputes. All of Teyvat's Mora is minted at the Golden House on Mt. Tianheng in Liyue, and the currency is named after the Geo Archon Morax. In Liyue he is called Rex Lapis, and Paimon notes it is considered impolite for outsiders to use the name Morax there.

Zhongli said in the Archon Quest that making Mora requires the Geo Archon's power. Having chosen to walk the earth as a mortal, he lived by mortal rules and carried no Mora of his own, and he admitted he lacked the Mora for a pricey Liyue Harbor venue. After the Geo Archon handed his Gnosis to the Tsaritsa, Zhongli told the Traveler and Paimon that existing Mora would not vanish, but the Golden House would have to cease operations for a long time. He left the resulting financial problem to the Liyue Qixing.

Neuvillette, in the Fontaine quest A Gift From the Sea Spirits, recalled puzzling over why humans used the flesh and blood of a god as a medium of exchange, asking whether pebbles or seashells would not serve. Virda suggested stones and shells break easily; Neuvillette remarked that gods do not seem sturdier. This is his view as an outside observer of human customs, not an explanation of how Mora is made.

The Fond Farewell belongs to Archon Quest Chapter I Act III, A New Star Approaches. The wiki records the Golden House as no longer minting new Mora after that act. Nothing found through Version 7.1 reverses this, but canon never says how much Mora is in circulation or how long the shortage lasts.

Spread: Mora is used in every nation. In Liyue, the Feiyun Commerce Guild's heavy bag of it was enough to buy every Cor Lapis available in the region. The Northland Bank, a Snezhnayan institution with branches across Teyvat, is described as harnessing the flow of Mora; the Fatui use bank funds when operating abroad. Branches exist in Liyue and in Fontaine's Court of Fontaine.

Gameplay: Gameplay note, not in-world lore: Mora is the main currency for shops and is spent when levelling characters, ascending, enhancing weapons and artifacts, and crafting. Sources include quests, chests, domains, Blossoms of Wealth, enemies, events and expeditions. Wiki trivia ties this to the in-world idea that the weapons consume Mora as a catalyst.

Scene use: Use Mora as the ordinary way anyone pays for anything, from a Liyue Harbor stall to a Fontaine shop. Liyue characters may mention that Rex Lapis, not Morax, is the polite name. Zhongli can be played as someone who knows exactly where Mora comes from but now lives without producing it.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 Mora remains the universal currency. The Geo Archon has given up his Gnosis, and the Golden House no longer mints new Mora, though the existing supply stays valid.

415.content:
Mouun's Moon (also: Mouun's longbow, the Watatsumi shrine maiden's bow): Mouun's Moon is a four-star bow of the Watatsumi series, the longbow of the Watatsumi shrine maiden Mouun. Item text says it shines pure white like seafoam at the tip of a moonlit wave. She befriended the monsters of the distant seas and fought with them against the thundering clouds in the war of Orobashi (Watatsumi Omikami), a path of no return that ended in tragic obliteration.

Appearance: Item text describes a longbow shining as pure white as seafoam at the tip of a moonlit wave. No further detail is given.

Lore: The text says the shrine maiden was friends with the monsters of the distant seas, and together they fought the thundering clouds for the sake of Watatsumi's "transient dream", riding the waves in the spray at ships' bows. She is quoted as accepting that Orobashi's war may have been doomed from the start, but hoping that leaving memories and "seeds of sacrifice" would make it worthwhile. Songs eulogise her unspoken bond with her twin Ayame, "Umigozen", depicting them with bow drawn and spear raised in the wave-spray of a ship.

Other songs recount her riding with Touzannou on a sea creature at night and whispering of broken tomorrows into the hero's ear. In peaceful days the twins sang in chorus with the great whale of the deep sea, telling of dismal days in the depths and the dark ever-night, and of Omikami and the radiant jade branches. She also "frolicked with that reckless young man, whose only strength was his strength". The text closes with a promised exchange: once the legendary Great Tengu's mask is brought back, "you have to keep our promise and finish that business", and the retort that a whale will raise a wave to wash that mouth clean.

Akuoumaru's text gives the other end of this exchange: its hero wished to bring the Great Tengu's mask back to Ayame and Mouun, and Wavebreaker's Fin says Mouun was consumed by a dark storm of crow feathers while the great whale sank to the sea floor. The three Watatsumi weapons therefore overlap: Mouun's Moon is the intimate account, Akuoumaru the hero's, Wavebreaker's Fin the aftermath. The nature of the "promise" and "business" is never stated; do not fill it in.

Owners: The shrine maiden Mouun (historical.mouun). No later owner is named.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star bow. Base ATK 44, secondary stat ATK 6%. Passive "Watatsumi Wavewalker" is shared with Akuoumaru and Wavebreaker's Fin: for every point of the party's combined maximum Energy capacity, the wielder's Elemental Burst DMG rises, up to a cap. Obtained from weapon event wishes.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a bow of lost friends and a lost cause. Within Watatsumi, Mouun is remembered with affection; elsewhere she is mostly an unknown name.

416.content: Mouun was a Watatsumi shrine maiden, twin of Ayame ("Umigozen"). She befriended sea monsters and fought with them in Orobashi's war; her bow is Mouun's Moon. The item texts leave her fate to inference: she was consumed by a dark storm of crow feathers in the war's final defeat.

417.content:
Musou Isshin (also: Musou no Isshin, Makoto's blade, the Shogun's sword): Musou Isshin is the legendary sword of the Raiden twins. It was created from Makoto's divine might and kept unsharpened and unused while she lived, as a symbol of true peace. When Makoto died in the Cataclysm it passed to her sister Ei, who began to use it in battle. It is the blade the Raiden Shogun draws from her heart during her Elemental Burst.

The name means roughly "a dream of one heart". Makoto gave the sword its name and wished it to witness an Inazuma as lovely as a dream, and the noble hearts of the people in it. Ei kept the name.

Appearance: A tachi, a samurai sword with a slightly longer hilt and blade than the more familiar katana, according to the Burst's talent text. The Raiden Shogun produces it from her chest rather than from a sheath at her hip. Canon gives no further description of its fittings.

Lore: The character story calls it a sword that has accompanied Ei to this day and has "witnessed both time and eternity". It was born from Makoto's divine might but never sharpened, because Makoto was not one for battle; it was a symbol, a sign of true peace.

On the day Makoto passed on, the sword was given to Ei. It was already stained with blood and, as the blade drew its first crimson, the ichor was blown aside by wild winds and blazing thunder. Ei did not change its name, because she too had looked out over the vast scene of Inazuma's beauty and it had given her a stronger, purer dream of her own. The text ends on the aesthetic of lightning: to capture what is precious amid fleeting transience.

In the Archon Quest chapter Radiant Sakura, Ei says she feels something stirring in the sword and that the blade inherited from Makoto seems to guide her. She reasons that it belonged to Makoto and may only respond with its full power when she truly understands and believes in her sister; holding it, she felt Makoto beside her again. Makoto's voice answers from the light of the sword, saying she left a faint fragment of her will in it so that she too would be released when Ei unleashed its full power.

The wiki further states that Ei and the Shogun have performed the technique Musou no Hitotachi with this blade ever since it was passed down, and that after Ei created the Shogun she transferred her consciousness into the sword and created the Plane of Euthymia, with the blade kept within the puppet Shogun. This is a summary of Archon Quest events; treat the Plane of Euthymia and Ei's consciousness as detailed in their own entries.

Owners: First Makoto, who never used it to fight, then Ei, who has used it in battle since Makoto's death. The Raiden Shogun, Ei's puppet, wields it in her Burst.

The sword is not an item anyone can pick up; it is tied to the sisters. Do not portray other characters wielding it.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): the sword is not an obtainable weapon. The Raiden Shogun's Elemental Burst, Secret Art: Musou Shinsetsu, changes her stance from a polearm to the Musou Isshin, which uses sword animations. In the Inazuma Archon Quest boss fight, the playable Raiden Shogun stays permanently in her Musou Isshin state.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: Musou Isshin is intimate, tied to grief and to Makoto. Ei is unlikely to discuss it casually. A character who knows nothing of its history would see only a graceful, unmarked tachi drawn from nowhere; do not have strangers recognise it.

418.content: Makoto made Musou Isshin from her divine might as a symbol of peace and never sharpened it. After her death it passed to Ei, who used it in battle. Makoto left a fragment of her will in the blade, released when Ei embraced its full power; Ei says the sword seems to guide her toward understanding her sister.

key: New Chronicles of the Six Kitsune
Urakusai's Chronicles of the Six Kitsune
419.comment: New Chronicles of the Six Kitsune
419.content:
New Chronicles of the Six Kitsune (also: Chronicles of the Six Kitsune, Urakusai's Chronicles of the Six Kitsune, Black Fox Itaru): New Chronicles of the Six Kitsune is a six-volume Inazuman novel sold at the Yae Publishing House in Inazuma City. It adapts "Urakusai's Chronicles of the Six Kitsune", a hit about 500 years ago, and follows the tales of Itaru, eldest of the six apprentices of the Great Kitsune Hakushin. Its last volume adds the author's commentary on the Kitsune Saiguu and why she left.

The author is unnamed: a writer who, in the Prologue, is talked back into writing for the publishing house by the chief editor (Yae Miko, as the linked text indicates) over drinks at the Uyuu Restaurant.

Appearance: A set of novels with a cover lettered in the Inazuman script. The wiki reads it as an abbreviation of the Japanese title, which is its own reading and not stated in-game. The volumes are numbered one way in the Archive and another in shops and the overworld.

Lore: The Prologue frames the book. An aging writer meets Yae Miko at the Uyuu Restaurant and is persuaded to write again; she notes she was not yet born when "she" (the Kitsune Saiguu) left, and that he is the only one still able to recite the stories she told.

Volume 2 explains the title: "new" implies an "old". Urakusai's Chronicles of the Six Kitsune was popular five hundred years ago. The story begins on Mt. Yougou, where the Great Kitsune Hakushin had six skilled apprentices.

The apprentices were skilled in magic and shape-shifting and helped manage the shrine and defend the mountain. The eldest, Itaru the Black Fox, was broad as a bear and strong as a tiger, and wild. After she wrecked a shintai representing the Shogun while drunk, Hakushin banished her for self-reflection, and she went happily looking for trouble.
- Vol. 3 (the Twin Oni of Tokaku): on the road Itaru meets two armed women in lumberjack clothes, each carrying a nodachi, kodachi and wakizashi. They attack her as a youkai, and she beats them easily, recalling that she had already beaten them the year before for harassing villagers. She recruits them to help people in need. The volume was missing from the original text, was rediscovered later and is presented edited.
- Vol. 4: the trio, resting in Konda Village, meet a mother (surname Youzan) and daughter (given name Yui), musicians from Seirai Island travelling to a festival in Inazuma City. A Lavender Melon seller has tricked them into buying overpriced melons. The hot-tempered sisters want to cut him up; Itaru stops them and goes to talk to him. The wiki notes that in the original 500-year-old tale Youzan and Yui later got their own stories.
- Vol. 5: the seller Dozaemon, a former samurai who turned to extortion in peacetime, is outwitted by Itaru when she orders chopped melon, calls his scale crooked and knocks him down with a bag of Mora. A beating makes tanuki ears appear; he is a tanuki youkai in disguise. Itaru takes his stolen wakizashi, shares his wealth among the villagers and the musicians and spares his life. The text says Urakusai wrote this volume after returning from Liyue.

Vol. 6 is the author's commentary on "ancient matters", which the text invites readers to skip. Per the author, Yae told him fragments of history over drinks. The Kitsune Saiguu left Hakushin's lands to serve at the Grand Narukami Shrine before Yae was born, so Yae grew up on stories of her, loved and respected her, and later came to the Grand Narukami Shrine herself. Saiguu doted on Yae because they were close by blood, though Yae speaks little of it. After Urakusai was driven out, Saiguu stopped living at the shrine and settled at Tenshukaku, saying a disaster would engulf heaven and earth and she must be at the Shogun's side. When she left a second time, Yae was a young girl. The Cataclysm then swept the archipelago and the meaning of her words became clear, but too late; Saiguu left a third time, "forever". The author declines to say more about Yae's past, joking about the editor-in-chief's pen.

Owners: Not a unique item. It is a published book, printed by the Yae Publishing House for general readers.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a collectible book collection. Vol. 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 are sold by Kuroda at the Yae Publishing House; one volume is in the left-hand room of the Yashiro Commission Headquarters. Added in Version 2.0.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's suggestion): an Inazuman may know the book as a popular novel with a fox heroine; only readers of the last volume or Yae's close circle know the commentary on the Saiguu. Do not present Itaru, Dozaemon or the Twin Oni as historical figures, and do not add detail to what the Saiguu or Urakusai did.

420.comment: New Chronicles of the Six Kitsune: Itaru the Black Fox
420.content: Itaru the Black Fox is the heroine of the novel: the eldest of Hakushin's six kitsune apprentices, huge, strong and unruly, banished from Mt. Yougou after destroying the Shogun's shintai while drunk. She travels as a self-described masterless youkai, takes the Twin Oni of Tokaku into her company and rights wrongs such as the Lavender Melon swindle in Konda Village. She is a character in an adaptation; the book does not say she was a real person.

421.comment: New Chronicles of the Six Kitsune: Urakusai
421.content: Urakusai is the kitsune writer of the original Chronicles of the Six Kitsune, popular about 500 years ago. Once prized by the Kitsune Saiguu for his writing and tea expertise, he made a grave mistake and was driven out; why is not recorded, though the new author says it may have been linked to the later incursion of the Abyss. Vol. 5 is said to have been written after Urakusai's return from Liyue.

key: Night Murmurs From the Far Border
Night Murmurs From the Far Border: Varcolac
422.comment: Night Murmurs From the Far Border
422.content:
Night Murmurs From the Far Border (also: Night Murmurs From the Far Border: Varcolac, Varcolac folktale): The item description calls it a collection of folktales circulating in Snezhnaya that records lesser-known fae tales; this volume covers the dangerous fae called the Varcolac. The tale is told as a legend and ends on a deliberately open note.

Appearance: A 3-star Book Collection with one volume, credited to an author named Viliana. The prose is a short horror-tinged narrative in the style of a winter tale, closing with a brief narrator's coda that steps outside the story.

Lore: Czcibor, a seasoned hunter, keeps watch in a hunting lodge after a village girl is found with her throat torn open. A monster of coarse black fur passes; he wounds its right shoulder and follows the blood to a gloomy estate deep in the forest. A pale elderly butler denies seeing it, and the master, a strikingly handsome man in his early twenties with waist-length black hair, invites the hunter to dine and stay out of the blizzard. Czcibor, raised in the Frostmoon Scions' encampment, recalls an old priestess's warning that Varcolac are the trickiest of the fae: they have two hearts, take a human and a fae form, and keep the same fur colour in both. He tests his host with pepper, garlic and his amulet, and nothing bothers the man.

At night Czcibor finds the servants asleep with odd, non-fatal scars on their limbs and sees that the organ in the house is made of bone, not of any ordinary animal. He follows the master into the snow, where the man undresses, shows the fresh arrow wound and has it begin to close as the snow hangs in the air and the glow of Frostlamp Flowers streams to him. Czcibor attacks with a dagger. The man says he is not a monster, hesitates, and is stabbed through the heart. He then turns into the wolf-like beast, laughs, and explains that Varcolac are born with two hearts; he thanks the hunter for destroying the extra one, saying it left him complete. The beast lunges for the hunter's throat and the story stops there.

**The coda.** The narrator says it is impossible to tell whether this is a legend or an undiscovered truth, notes that the Varcolac are said to be nearly extinct and often dismissed as myth, and adds a rumor that Duchess Lady Evlampiya Orlova of Snezhnaya is a Varcolac, one not covered in wolf fur. The text says that verifying this is not possible.

**Reading the tale.** The hunter is shown as competent but acting on prejudice and fear; the host protects his household and warns the guest to stay indoors, and his one protest ("I'm not a monster") is the moment the hunter presses his advantage. The book does not decide who is in the right, and does not say what became of the servants beyond the scars. Treat the vampiric hints (blood tasting, pallid servants) as the story's atmosphere, not as established facts about the Varcolac as a species.

**Names.** The wiki notes that the protagonist shares his name with a present-day NPC, Czcibor, who once vanished for many days near Barrowmoss Barrens and returned without memory. Whether the book's hunter is connected is not stated. "Varcolac" echoes a real Slavic werewolf term, and the Volkodlak variant of the word appears in A Brief History of the Pale Starborn.

Owners: No character is established as owning it. It is sold to the Traveler by Dhabit at Mimisbrunnr Books in Nasha Town.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: a one-volume Book Collection bought from Dhabit. It has no combat function.

423.comment: Night Murmurs From the Far Border: The Varcolac
423.content:
In this folktale a Varcolac is a fae with two hearts that can take a human or a wolf-like form, with the same hair or fur colour in both. A hunter's priestess warns that they are the trickiest fae. A Varcolac heals wounds by drawing on the glow of Frostlamp Flowers, and the story claims that piercing one heart does not kill it. The book says they are now nearly extinct and often written off as myth.

Only this tale describes them; no other source named in this entry confirms the two-hearts claim. Fae in general are covered by the snowland fae entry.

424.comment: Night Murmurs From the Far Border: Czcibor the hunter (folktale)
424.content: The protagonist of the tale, a veteran hunter who grew up in the Frostmoon Scions' camp and carries an amulet that shimmers in moonlight. His dagger sneak attack fails to kill the Varcolac, and the story ends as the beast lunges at his throat. He is a story character who happens to share a name with a modern NPC.

425.content:
Night of the Sky's Unveiling (also: Bloom of the Mind's Desire, Feather of Indelible Sin, Revelation's Toll, Vessel of Plenty, Crown of the Befallen): Night of the Sky's Unveiling is a 4- and 5-star artifact set added in version 6.0 that strengthens Lunar reactions. Its item text tells of Rauthvangi, a young stargazer of subterranean Khaenri'ah who glimpsed a "pitch-black Elysium" beyond the sky. For this he was exiled, survived the surface, wandered the nations, and as Rotwang, the Tsar's "mad monk", travelled to Nod-Krai to claim a hidden treasure and break out of the celestial shell.

The set links Khaenri'ah's astrology, the forbidden knowledge of the great sin, the court of the Snowland fae and the Cataclysm-era Nod-Krai. It never states his later fate; that comes from Nod-Krai quests.

Appearance: Item text only names the pieces: a flower, a feather, a bell or clock-like piece, a vessel and a crown. It gives no physical description of the set.

Lore: Rauthvangi, a novice monk in subterranean Khaenri'ah, glimpses a forbidden "pitch-black Elysium" in a star mirror, is exiled from the Universitas Magistrorum and survives the surface unharmed. He later wanders the nations, becomes the Tsar's favourite as Professor Rotwang, the "mad monk" of Zapolyarny Palace, and goes to Nod-Krai as envoy to seize a treasure and break through the celestial shell.

Item text, summarised in story order:
- Bloom of the Mind's Desire: before the Five Sinners committed their offence, the people of subterranean Khaenri'ah had never seen the sea or the real sun, yet some astrologers recorded odd star-chart phenomena as "Signs of Truth" and decided that piercing the mirror's illusions leads to truth. Long after the earthly gods fell in the Archon War and the atrous sun replaced the crimson moon, the study of stars was banned because some had uncovered the secret of the great sin; only a few chosen servants of the one-eyed ruler were exempt. A novice monk named Rauthvangi cleaned the dust from the "mirror of Apaosha" in a stargazing chamber and saw the light ringing the horizon, a beautiful and profane "pitch-black Elysium", which consumed his every thought.
- Feather of Indelible Sin: Rauthvangi never defended himself, and the court expelled him from the Universitas Magistrorum and sent him into exile. For one of outland stock, going above ground was a curse that would catch him quickly, yet he stepped into the sunlight unharmed while those beside him screamed. He took this as the cosmos choosing him and said that flame illuminates the world but also reduces it to ash, and that he was like a moth leaping into it.
- Revelation's Toll: in the golden years before the Cataclysm, the scholar read every chronicle and library of the north without finding the Elysium. He had visited every corner of the known world except the barren borderland of Nod-Krai, which the Tsar of Snezhnaya had only recently ordered explored. He went there as a last attempt, saw the truth again, and uncovered a sinful path to the Elysium. Only the gate remained to be opened by his own hands at any price.
- Vessel of Plenty: at Zapolyarny Palace the banquets never stopped, and the fae nobles called Professor Rotwang their "mad monk". He was the Tsar's favourite for alchemy and astrology. Two rumours circulated: a grand duke who tried to poison him ended up kneeling as his follower, and a fae noble who called his research a hoax saw him summon the spirit of his late wife. He never confirmed the stories, and the nobles trusted an outlander with no local ties. The text ends hinting that none of them foresaw the tragic ending.
- Crown of the Befallen: as cities and factories rose in Nod-Krai, only the Tsar's favourite knew the Tsar's ruler of the fae was planning a revolt the sublunary order would not tolerate. The mad monk, as envoy, said the Tsar thought too small and had never looked at the stars. He travelled to Nod-Krai on a secret mission for a treasure of world-turning power, wanting it for his own ends, and called on "Reed Miller" to follow him out of the celestial shell.

Cross-references the wiki draws on: the "Rauthvangi" of the first pieces and "Professor Rotwang" of Vessel of Plenty are the same man, a Khaenri'ahn exile who joined the Belyi Tsar's court; the wiki names the treasure as the Sampo Mill and the Court of Eternal Bliss as the fae ruler's "bold scheme". The text's "sunless" Khaenri'ah, the banned astrology and the "veil of the celestial shell" tie it to the False Sky and to the rest of the Khaenri'ah setting without stating how.

Details worth noting: the text calls his exile worse than death for people of his stock, describes the expulsion as evidence of the kingdom's decline, and uses his own words in each piece to show a growing fanaticism that treats other mortals as fleeting. The narrator is sympathetic to his curiosity but never calls his aims good.

Time frame: the first two pieces are set in the Eclipse-era Khaenri'ah under the one-eyed ruler (the wiki identifies him as Irmin). The last three are set in the years before and at the start of the Cataclysm in Snezhnaya and Nod-Krai. The "Elysium beyond the sky's veil" is tied to the Abyss only by the wiki and by Nod-Krai quest text, not by the artifact text itself.

Owners: No owner is named. The text follows Rauthvangi (Rotwang); none of the pieces says who owned the objects.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): 4- and 5-star; domain Frostladen Machinery in Nod-Krai (6.0) and an Artifact Strongbox. 2-piece: Elemental Mastery +80. 4-piece: when nearby party members trigger Lunar reactions, if the wearer is on the field they gain Gleaming Moon: Intent for 4s (CRIT Rate +15% with Nascent Gleam, +30% with Ascendant Gleam). Party Lunar reaction DMG is increased by 10% for each different Gleaming Moon effect among party members, and these effects do not stack. Per the wiki, Silken Moon's Serenade's 4-piece and this one together give a total of 20%, and extra copies of either do not add more.

426.comment: Night of the Sky's Unveiling: Night of the Sky's Unveiling
426.content: Artifact set whose item text follows Rauthvangi, a Khaenri'ahn astrologer and later the Tsar's mad monk, from his glimpse of a forbidden "Elysium" through exile to his mission in Nod-Krai.

427.comment: Night of the Sky's Unveiling: Signs of Truth
427.content: Per the Bloom of the Mind's Desire text, Khaenri'ahn astrologers recorded unusual phenomena in their star charts as "Signs of Truth" and decided the mirror's illusions must be pierced to reach truth. Rauthvangi's glimpse of the light around the horizon, through the dust-covered mirror of Apaosha, is the origin of his obsession with the "pitch-black Elysium".

key: Nighttime Whispers in the Echoing Woods
428.comment: Nighttime Whispers in the Echoing Woods
428.content:
Nighttime Whispers in the Echoing Woods (also: Selfless Floral Accessory, Honest Quill, Faithful Hourglass, Magnanimous Ink Bottle, Compassionate Ladies' Hat): Nighttime Whispers in the Echoing Woods is a Geo artifact set from Version 4.3. Its five pieces tell a bedtime-style fairy tale, read aloud in fragments by a little girl in an attic with her dog Pie: a witch in the Echoing Woods grants a youth's wish, and the girl he loves is given endless good luck that turns out to be a curse.

The tale is framed twice. The outer story is the attic scene (the girl, her dog Pie and her mother, who likes to tell stories); the inner story is the book. Each piece holds a page of the book and a short return to the attic.

Lore: A girl follows her dog Pie into the attic and finds a storybook with golden-winged butterflies on its cover. It says a witch in the Echoing Woods grants any wish but hides her hut in fog and echoes, so few reach her. A youth, led by a golden-winged butterfly, finds the hut and asks that the girl he loves, who loves another, have all the happiness in the world. The witch agrees; the price will come later and need not be his soul.

The witch's magic is a pen, ink bottle and other items: whatever the dipped pen writes becomes real and the girl becomes fate's favourite. Everything goes her way, everyone adores her, and she grows spoiled.

She scorns gifts, rebukes her worried mother and leaves home, living a life like an endless ball where all forgive her. Returning years later she learns her mother has long since died, and calls the gift a curse because a life where nothing is paid for feels worthless. The youth shows her a magic mirror borrowed from the witch. In the mirror she sees what follows when the luck ends: lost wealth, people turning cold, hardship, and every gift needing repayment tenfold. She still chooses the harder, real path, recalling her mother's stories in which heroes lose things on the way and so value their reward, and says she will love others sincerely even if they stop loving her. At that moment the witch's appointed time arrives, and she takes what she most wanted from what the youth had to give. The girl ends up trapped in the ink bottle; the witch muses she will make a good character in other stories, and that she may follow the girl into the bottle's many universes. In the attic the real girl decides to tell the story to her mother, while Pie runs off, perhaps hungry.

The set's recurring motifs are paying a price versus getting things free, the witch's line that "only a heart of gold may be weighed", and the attic girl's own reflection that souls seem cheap in stories while afternoon tea and her mother's bedtime tales are what she values. The pieces describe the witch's items as a butterfly brooch, a dip pen, a sand timepiece that runs very fast if the wrong incantation is spoken, an ink bottle holding everything the user can imagine, and a lady's hat that mixes solemnity and playfulness.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): 4 and 5 star set from the Waterfall Wen domain and its strongbox. 2-piece: ATK +18%. 4-piece: after an Elemental Skill, +20% Geo DMG Bonus for 10s; increased by 150% under a Crystallize shield or near Moondrifts formed by Lunar-Crystallize, with the extra ending 1s after the condition lapses. Introduced in 4.3.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the story as a fairy tale told through a storybook rather than as a historical event; do not assign it a nation, and do not decide the witch's or youth's fate beyond what the text says.

429.comment: Nighttime Whispers in the Echoing Woods: Selfless Floral Accessory
429.content:
The flower piece: a butterfly-shaped brooch worn by the witch. Its text opens the frame story (the girl, Pie, the attic, the butterfly-covered book) and the legend of the Echoing Woods witch whose fog confuses visitors with echoes.

The youth had been looking for a blue flower when a golden-winged butterfly led him to the hut. The witch cuts him off with "That's what they all say" and warns that every wish has a different price. He asks only that the girl he loves, who loves another, be happy.

430.comment: Nighttime Whispers in the Echoing Woods: Honest Quill
430.content:
The plume piece: the witch's dip pen. The girl wonders why souls are sold so easily in stories; the youth asks what could fulfil a higher happiness, and the witch says words written with the pen dipped in her ink come true and the girl will be fate's favourite.

The girl's life changes: fortune follows her, everyone loves her, and she becomes used to praise though her looks and virtue are described as ordinary.

431.comment: Nighttime Whispers in the Echoing Woods: Faithful Hourglass
431.content:
The sands piece: the witch's sand timepiece, said to run very fast if the wrong incantation is spoken. In the tale, the girl scorns blue ribbons given by guests, tells her mother she does not need a mother who does not love her like the others, and leaves home.

In the attic, the real girl muses about what she would write with a magic pen (lots of doggie biscuits for Pie). The tale notes friends forgive her rudeness the next day.

432.comment: Nighttime Whispers in the Echoing Woods: Magnanimous Ink Bottle
432.content:
The goblet piece: the witch's ink bottle. Its text has the girl return home to find her mother long dead, call her luck a curse and set out for the Echoing Woods; the youth shows her the witch's magic mirror.

The mirror shows her future ruin once the luck ends. The witch says the magic's fortune has not yet abandoned her and none will mock her weakness.

433.comment: Nighttime Whispers in the Echoing Woods: Compassionate Ladies' Hat
433.content:
The circlet piece: the witch's lady's hat. The girl chooses the harder path, the witch's appointed time arrives, the girl is trapped in the ink bottle, and the frame story ends with the girl leaving the storybook behind on the attic floor.

The witch says she exists for the girl as the girl does for her, and hopes to find a place for them in another story within the bottle.

434.content:
Nightweaver's Looking Glass (also: Looking Glass of the Nightweaver, Millennial Hymn): A flawless silver mirror said to have witnessed the Moon Maiden's birth; the Frostmoon Scions hold it a relic of unrivalled provenance. A 5-star catalyst from Version 6.0.

Its item text is a Scion-side history of Hyperborea's Archpriestesses, the first Moonchanter Aila and the hoped-for new moon.

Appearance: A mirror of flawless silver used as a catalyst; canon gives no further description.

Lore: Its story opens with a prophecy-verse: the Eternal Moon fell, the Iridescent Moon shattered, the Frost Moon ceased to turn, and the world marches toward its end until Elysium dawns.

Descendants of the Golden City of Hyperborea built a lonely temple on the tundra, forged pale crowns of secret silver and chose Archpriestesses, though their gods had departed. The first Moonchanter, Aila, was a mortal who witnessed the birth of a god.

The text presents the Scions' rituals as both a wall hiding them from the world and the sign of a people without a homeland, awaiting a sacred heir of a pure bloodline after which all sins would be forgiven as service to Elysium.

According to later generations, Aila foresaw the new moon (Columbina) and chose to abandon the old rites. The last Archpriestess, Lovia, admired her, handed her the authority to lead the people and let her seal the ancient sanctuary with her own hands. The title of Archpriestess of Hyperborea was never held again; only the Moonchanter remained.

After an ellipsis the text jumps forward through many moons. Those who dreamed of Elysium found the shadow of the axe, while those who longed for salvation were swept up in flowing light. It names the mad monk who reached for the heavens, the old master of the Pale Star throne (the Belyi Tsar), the White Emperor who fell into the black waves of the Abyss, and the silent nightingales (the Lightkeepers). As promised to the Torchforger (Solovei), the new moon's maiden spun a prayer song and laid it to rest alongside the sanctuary. The closing lines repeat the verse but end on hope: from the ashes the New Moon rises and spins the wheel of fate anew. The text is a Scion-side account with a partisan tone; each person it names has their own entry.

Owners: No wielder is named in canon; the description ties the mirror to the Frostmoon Scions as a whole.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star catalyst with Elemental Mastery as secondary stat. Passive Millennial Hymn gives Elemental Mastery after the wielder's Hydro or Dendro Skill damage and when party members trigger Lunar-Bloom; with both active, the party gains Bloom, Hyperbloom, Burgeon and Lunar-Bloom bonuses, even off-field.

How {{char}} behaves: Treat it as a Scion heirloom with ritual weight: those who know Nod-Krai religion may recognise it as sacred, outsiders see a beautiful silver mirror. Do not assign an owner, and keep claims about Aila as what the Scions say, not settled history.

435.content: Millennial Hymn is the weapon's passive. Its two named effects, Prayer of the Far North and New Moon Verse, echo the text's themes of the northern faith and the coming new moon. Mechanics are in the gameplay section.

436.content:
Noblesse Oblige (also: Royal Flora, Royal Plume, Royal Pocket Watch, Royal Silver Urn, Royal Masque): Noblesse Oblige is a 4- and 5-star artifact set (1.0) about the old aristocracy of Mondstadt: nobles who began as heroes and guides of the people and decayed into idle, grasping rulers. Its name is French for 'nobility obliges'. It drops in the Clear Pool and Mountain Cavern domain.

The pieces are Royal Flora, Royal Plume, Royal Pocket Watch, Royal Silver Urn and Royal Masque.

Appearance: A blue satin lily headdress, a hunting-hat falcon feather, a sapphire pocket watch that still keeps time, a sapphire urn with a silver noble insignia, and a silver masquerade mask inlaid with gold and gems.

Lore: Each piece pairs a virtue with its decay. Royal Flora: nobles guided subjects by conduct and wisdom. Royal Plume: hunts shared with common folk. Royal Pocket Watch: punctuality as self-discipline, a worthy noble more vigilant than his people. Royal Silver Urn: treasures that stood for the people's prosperity. Royal Masque: chieftains of humble origin who welcomed the people to banquets. Each ends with later nobles abandoning that virtue.

The texts say the early nobles were heroes of humble origins who became rulers, and that their longevity was cut short by self-indulgence. Hunts were once shared festivities in which servants and common folk took part as a sign of the nobles' benevolence; later the nobles claimed everything as their right. The pocket watch's schedule was overturned by indolent descendants and their timepieces became extravagant but lost their function. The urn lost its treasures, and luxury became vanity. Later banquets were for the nobles' own pleasure.

Canon history (the Mondstadt Aristocracy) says the aristocracy ruled Mondstadt for about 1,600 years after the fall of Decarabian's Mondstadt, going from protectors to tyrants, until the rebellion of Vennessa. The set does not mention the rebellion; it is the earlier, nostalgic view of the class.

Owners: No named owner; the relics were left behind by nobles who once ruled Mondstadt.

How {{char}} behaves: Use as a tragic parable about duty decaying into privilege. A modern Mondstadt scholar or Knights of Favonius member could cite it as a reminder.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). 2-piece: Elemental Burst DMG +20%. 4-piece: using an Elemental Burst raises the whole party's ATK by 20% for 12 seconds (multiple copies refresh but do not stack). Sources include the Clear Pool and Mountain Cavern domain and the Nine Pillars of Peace quest.

437.comment: Noblesse Oblige: The old nobles of Mondstadt
437.content: The set remembers early Mondstadt nobles as guides and hosts of the people who later fell into self-indulgence. The same class eventually became the tyrants overthrown by Vennessa's rebellion.

438.content:
Noctilucous Jade (also: Night-Staying Stone, Yepo Stone): Noctilucous Jade is a rare mineral from Liyue that glimmers in the dark. Its item text says it is a mutated gemstone condensed from the world's flourishing elements. It is found in caves and mines across Liyue, especially near Mingyun Village.

The Chinese name means Night-Staying Stone.

Appearance: A gemstone that shines faintly in dark places, which is the sense of the word noctilucous.

Lore: Beyond the item description, canon gives it no story. It is called a mutated gemstone, condensed from the flourishing elements of the world, and only said to be so. Chang the Ninth in Qingce Village gives four to the Traveler on a first dialogue branch.

Mining it in The Chasm's Underground Mines restores Lumenstone Adjuvant energy, per wiki trivia.

Gameplay: Gameplay note, not in-world lore: Geo nodes at cliff bases, caves and mines drop one to three each; they are best broken with blunt attacks. It is used in crafting and ascension.

Scene use: Use as a miner's or collector's find in a Liyue cave: a faint glow in the rock. Avoid claiming a source for its formation.

Chronology: Present since Version 1.0 as a Liyue local specialty. Its use in the Chasm's Underground Mines, as an energy refill for the Lumenstone Adjuvant, dates from the mines' addition in Version 2.6, per the Lumenstone page.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 canon adds nothing beyond the item text.

439.content:
Nocturne's Curtain Call (also: Ballad of the Crossroads, Bountiful Sea's Sacred Wine): A jade pearl wrapped in moonlight whose gentle warmth lingers like a song even on the coldest winter night. A 5-star catalyst from Version 6.3, its text a lullaby and a vision of the Moon Maiden.

It frames Columbina's memories of the three moons.

Appearance: A jade pearl shrouded in moonlight. Canon text describes only the pearl and its warmth.

Lore: The text is framed by a lullaby to a little dove, child of the moon: may the moon be with you in your slumber. Between its verses is Columbina's vision of the Moon Maiden drifting through the night.

A shattered husk falls toward Nod-Krai, the misty land that never became a moon. In a prison beyond the reach of Time and Wind, Columbina, called the one who traverses backward, watches the eternal slumber of three sisters.

A silvery vessel once patrolled between mountains and seas at the meeting of day and night, ferrying the souls of the untainted across the corrupted mortal realm to rest on the dark side of the moon. The three mistresses of the golden hall could not meet the gaze of mortals: the Lord of the Seven Calamities would not tolerate gods pitying mortal suffering, so even the three sisters, spinning silver threads of fate, were bound in threefold silence.

The three moons each walked a different path: turning against their corrupted master of old to protect the living, looking away from one another so that the ember of defiance might survive, or staining themselves with darkness to take vengeance on a tyrant. At the end of every path lay oblivion, the future once lamented by the vanished moons in the era "when three were still three". Yet in her private memories Columbina sees a golden star not of this world, reflected in a cold courtyard under the silver moon, and believes it will light her way home. In the next instant "three are no longer three": the Lord of the Crossroads (unnamed in the text) looks back at the fourth path beyond the three-way fork, and waits among honeyed veils for her appointed meeting with her companions beneath the stars. The golden star is tied by the wiki to the Traveler; the text itself only says a golden star.

Owners: No wielder is named; the text concerns Columbina but does not make her the owner.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star catalyst, CRIT DMG secondary. Passive Ballad of the Crossroads raises Max HP and, on triggering Lunar reactions, restores Energy and grants Bountiful Sea's Sacred Wine, a Max HP and Lunar CRIT DMG bonus.

How {{char}} behaves: Handle as a delicate, lullaby-like heirloom. Keep the three moons and the golden star as poetic memories belonging to Columbina's perspective, and do not state who owns it.

440.comment: Nocturne's Curtain Call: Ballad of the Crossroads
440.content: Ballad of the Crossroads is the weapon's passive, named for the three-way fork in its text. Bountiful Sea's Sacred Wine is the buff it grants. Mechanics are in the gameplay section.

441.content:
Nymph's Dream (also: Odyssean Flower, Wicked Mage's Plumule, Nymph's Constancy, Heroes' Tea Party, Fell Dragon's Monocle, Nymphs Dream): Nymph's Dream is a 4- and 5-star artifact set that boosts Hydro damage and ATK. It was released in Version 3.6, long before Fontaine opened, and its lore tells a quiet story: orphans playing heroes, wicked mages and fell dragons, a tea party that pauses the adventure, and the later scattering of the "Narzissen champions" after a catastrophe.

The pieces are Odyssean Flower (flower), Wicked Mage's Plumule (plume), Nymph's Constancy (sands), Heroes' Tea Party (goblet) and Fell Dragon's Monocle (circlet). It is the one set here that is obtained in Sumeru but belongs to Fontaine's story.

Appearance: A pocket watch (Nymph's Constancy) pieced from rejected parts of other devices, a dark green feather from a hat (Wicked Mage's Plumule) and a monocle are described, but no piece has an owner who is shown on-screen.

Lore: Told as children's play, the pieces move from a tea party that pauses the adventure, through stories of heroes, mages and fell dragons, to the Director's departure and the scattering of the champions after a catastrophe.

- Heroes' Tea Party: between adventures the champions, mages, knights and fell dragons all pause for the Vice Director's very good refreshments. A little girl arrives at a home that sees neither sun nor moon, is embraced by the tall Director and led by the Vice Director to the others.
- Wicked Mage's Plumule: where there are heroes there must be wicked mages. The children gaze at a dark green feather pinned to the Vice Director's hat and are told to get along. Before leaving on business with the Director, the Vice Director gives the feather, as a loan, to one child, who is named only by a black bar. It never becomes a mage's staff but travels with its owner to the source of the calamity of parting, then returns.
- Nymph's Constancy: a pocket watch made from rejected parts, owned by a tiny champion who loved machines, which fell, together with the person it was gifted to, into the primordial liquid that dissolves all. It carries a bedtime story of a dark empire ruled by the fell dragon Narcissus, a sleeping princess, and a pearl of water from which a tiny life was born.
- Fell Dragon's Monocle: heroes and dragons depend on which story is told, and heroes who live too long become dragons. A dragon dreams of being reborn as a new universe, while the victorious hero loses the thing he valued and thereafter imagines a kingdom run on machines not powered by the elements.
- Odyssean Flower: the kingdom's shadow came not from the dragon beating the hero but from both being lost in the world. The Director and her sisters set out to defeat the evil at its source, her assistant boarded a battle ship and slept beneath the waters, and the champions scattered. Some joined the Marechaussee Phantom or the Special Security and Surveillance Patrol; some went with explorers; some sought a path with machinery and bodies of steel; some began again in the name of the nymphs.
The wiki's Trivia states that the set's lore relates to Fontaine and the Narzissenkreuz Institute, and its Institute and Marechaussee Phantom pages cite these pieces: the play-acting, tea parties and a Vice Director with good refreshments, and the Odyssean Flower for Institute members recruited by the Marechaussee Phantom after the Director and Vice Director vanished in the cataclysm 500 years ago.

Read together with the Marechaussee Hunter set, the games here echo the "hero" and "evil dragon" childhood play that set recalls (Emanuel as hero, Karl as Jabberwock). The set itself never states a link between the two sets, and the machine-minded ending of Fell Dragon's Monocle names no person.

Owners: No named owner. The pieces speak of anonymous children and of the Director and Vice Director.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): the 2-piece bonus is Hydro DMG +15%. The 4-piece bonus grants a Mirrored Nymph stack (8s) after attacks, skills and bursts hit opponents; 1, 2 and 3+ stacks give ATK +7%/16%/25% and Hydro DMG +4%/9%/15%, and stacks from each attack type are independent. Obtained from Molten Iron Fortress (Gavireh Lajavard, Girdle of the Sands, Sumeru), whose Ley Line Disorder gives Elemental Mastery for Dendro-related reactions, and from the artifact strongbox. Added in 3.6.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the set as nostalgic and wistful, a childhood game remembered after loss. Do not name the children or confirm which Fontainian figures they became unless a canon source for that scene is cited.

442.content: In these pieces the "Narzissen champions" are children playing heroes, mages, knights and fell dragons at a home without sun or moon, tended by a Director and a Vice Director. The Institute itself is covered in its own entry.

443.content:
Oathsworn Eye (also: Oath Eye, serpent's eye jewel): Oathsworn Eye is a jewel-like catalyst that glimmers like a snake's eye. Its description calls it a national treasure of Byakuyakoku, stored in the Dainichi Mikoshi, and says that when the Serpent God came, it was used to notarize great oaths and wishes. Its item text is a short fable of the oath a lonely serpent swore with a child and with his people in the depths.

It is a 4-star catalyst that players could obtain only as a reward in the Three Realms Gateway Offering event (Version 2.5), so its in-world material is tied to Enkanomiya.

Appearance: A jewel that glimmers like snake-eyes, shown in the text as held out by the giant white serpent. Canon text describes it no further than a glittering jewel used as a witness to oaths.

Lore: The text imagines the giant white snake looking down at a child who asks him to become their deity. The snake says he fled into waters unknown because he could best neither Deus Auri nor Narukami, and warns that anyone who keeps seeking the light will suffer loss. Yet he shows a snake-eyed jewel and says: swear it upon this eye, as he did when he made a pact with his coral servants.

A speaker quotes Master Spartacus's teaching that they must never worship a god and can rely only on themselves. The white serpent says nothing, since he respects the will of the people dwelling in the depths: if vain worship were replaced by new belief, would that not dishonour those who fought? The child swears before the eye anyway, declaring that all is as it was when everything was lost.

Years pass. The island is complete, the vishaps are repelled and the Holy Soil may now be governed. The oath sworn on the eye has come to fruition, with the House of Sangonomiya, gathered Jibashiri and the vassals named as parties. The speaker sets the terms: if two or more parties are dissatisfied with the arrangement concerning Enkanomiya, or decide otherwise than they first did, the tower of the sun will hear their wishes and collapse of its own accord, destroying all that was once their past. Saying this, the serpent god took the remaining people to the surface, to fulfil his oath to the heavenly city.

The wiki identifies the white serpent as Orobashi, the island as Enkanomiya, the vishaps as the Bathysmal Vishaps, the tower of the sun as the Dainichi Mikoshi and "Master Spartacus" as Supada no Hiko; the text itself uses titles. The final line points to the serpent god's covenant with Celestia, which the Enkanomiya quests tell in more detail.

Owners: No individual is named. The eye belongs to Byakuyakoku as a national treasure, and its home was the Dainichi Mikoshi.

The text implies the original eye was the serpent's own witness-jewel for his pact with his coral servants and later with the people; do not assume that any player-obtained copy is that jewel.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star catalyst, an event weapon of the Three Realms Gateway Offering (Version 2.5, limited-time event). Base ATK 44 with ATK% as secondary stat.

Refinement uses the event material Ointment of Sight (four obtainable from the event) rather than duplicate weapons. Its passive, People of the Faltering Light, increases Energy Recharge for 10 seconds after using an Elemental Skill (24% at refinement 1, 48% at refinement 5).

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: treat the eye as a witness to promises. Characters from Enkanomiya or those who know its history may be moved by it; others see only a snake-eyed jewel. Keep the oath solemn: breaking it, in the text's wording, destroys the past.

444.content: In the item text, the serpent god's pact over Enkanomiya binds the House of Sangonomiya, the Jibashiri and his vassals: if parties are dissatisfied with the arrangement, the tower of the sun will hear their wishes and collapse, destroying their past. The story is told fully in the Enkanomiya quests.

445.content:
Obsidian Codex (also: Obsidian Codex artifact set, Reckoning of the Xenogenic, Root of the Spirit-Marrow, Myths of the Night Realm, Pre-Banquet of the Contenders, Crown of the Saints): Obsidian Codex is a 4- and 5-star artifact set from Natlan, added in Version 5.0. Its five pieces are mythic fragments, each opening with the line that many stories "were never recorded or eulogized in any human history": a dragon's gift of fire to humans, the first tribe, a contest of heroes and the crowning of a king who ended the tribes' wars. It boosts characters in Nightsoul's Blessing.

The pieces are Reckoning of the Xenogenic (flower), Root of the Spirit-Marrow (plume), Myths of the Night Realm (sands), Pre-Banquet of the Contenders (goblet) and Crown of the Saints (circlet). Together they read as one long legend told in epithets, not names.

Appearance: Only item descriptions survive. The flower is carved from black crystal and glows mysteriously at night. The plume is a feathered accessory in imitation of an ancient dragon's wing. The sands is a ritual element that is neither timepiece nor compass, with no known use. The goblet is a stone vessel shaped in a seemingly whimsical way, leaving open who could have the strength to make it. The circlet is an obsidian crown, once used in coronations by noble tribal kings.

Lore: Every piece opens with the same refrain, that many stories passed which no human history recorded. In order:
- Reckoning of the Xenogenic: a dispossessed divine envoy fell into lightless realms.
- Root of the Spirit-Marrow: the wisest of dragons carried a seed of the primal fire across a burning land and, finding no creation worthy of it, chose the weakest and most cherished of species, humans living in the shadow of ancient wings.
- Myths of the Night Realm: brave Chaac took the ever-bright kindling from the Sage of the Stolen Flame, shared it.
- Pre-Banquet of the Contenders: priests of smoke.
- Crown of the Saints: as a dark tide rose, warriors carried the Wayob's blessings into forbidden realms, the dragons were gone from the fields.
Each piece has its own entry with its full text.

Cross-references used by the wiki's lore transcription (not stated inside the item text): the wisest of dragons and Sage of the Stolen Flame is Kukulkan; the ruler and "overlord of fire" is the Pyro Dragon Xiuhcoatl; the dispossessed envoy is the Lord of the Night (Yohualtecuhtin); the "first barbarian" is Chaac; the "high king among dragons" is Nibelung; and the unprophesied hero of Crown of the Saints is Xbalanque, the first Pyro Archon. The "black tide" and foul darkness are the Abyss, the fall of heaven and earth is the War of Funerary Flame, and the citadel destroyed is tied to the Unified Civilization.

Read side by side, the pieces describe a plan that mostly worked and partly failed. Kukulkan's gift of Phlogiston let humans found tribes and meet the Night Kingdom's gods, but "evolution" was meant to produce a single strong heir for the dragons' purposes. Pre-Banquet of the Contenders shows that plan crowning the strongest hero; Crown of the Saints shows a different hero ending the tribal wars through a pact instead. The pieces never say what became of the dragon afterwards, and they do not name the heir of the prophecy.

Owners: No named owner. The text is legend, not the biography of a wearer; no character is known to have carried these artifacts.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): the 2-piece bonus gives +15% DMG while the wearer is in Nightsoul's Blessing and on the field. The 4-piece bonus gives +40% CRIT Rate for 6s after the wearer consumes 1 Nightsoul point while on the field, at most once per second.

The set is obtained from the Sanctum of Rainbow Spirits domain in Toyac Springs, Natlan, from Tribal Secret Space (from 5.2) and from the artifact strongbox (from 5.3).
The Sanctum of Rainbow Spirits' Ley Line Disorder unleashes a True DMG shockwave from an opponent's position whenever a character triggers a Pyro-related reaction on it, at most once every 5s. The same domain also drops the Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present the pieces as relics whose texts are half-understood. Ordinary Natlanians know the tribal legends of Chaac and the Wayob but not the dragons' side of the story; no one has a ready key to the epithets. Do not let a character confidently name every figure in the set.

446.content: In Myths of the Night Realm Chaac is the brave, wise hero who received the ever-bright kindling from the Sage of the Stolen Flame, shared it with fellow tribespeople, defeated a raging dragon, founded the first tribe, and called on the night realm's god on the last night of his life.

447.comment: Obsidian Codex: Sage of the Stolen Flame
