447.content: In Root of the Spirit-Marrow and its sister pieces, the wisest of dragons carries a seed of primal fire to a rugged land, grants humans the kindling of wisdom and foretells a savior of two worlds. The wiki's lore transcription links this figure to Kukulkan, Waxaklahun Ubah Kan. The pieces call his path "evolution" and note it will order human destinies as the price of civilising them.

448.comment: Obsidian Codex: Reckoning of the Xenogenic
448.content: a dispossessed divine envoy fell into lightless realms, and the newly returned ruler destroyed a blasphemous citadel. The vishap kingdom survived the collapse of heaven and earth, isolated by a sea of red soil, but its fire-wisdom had been seized by foul darkness and only a gray corpse shambled on, while its blind heirs mistook violence for law. One "human" among them foresaw the ruler's deathbed and the fall of a great civilization, and carried off unextinguished primordial kindling from the palace beneath the magma.

449.comment: Obsidian Codex: Root of the Spirit-Marrow
449.content: the wisest of dragons carried a seed of the primal fire across a burning land and, finding no creation worthy of it, chose the weakest and most cherished of species, humans living in the shadow of ancient wings. The gift would civilise them but also order their destinies, since it was the profane path of "evolution" rather than the first divine plan. The dragon told the first barbarian who climbed the floating landmass that from his heirs would come a savior of two worlds who would slay the overlord of fire and take the oldest throne.

450.comment: Obsidian Codex: Myths of the Night Realm
450.content: brave Chaac took the ever-bright kindling from the Sage of the Stolen Flame, shared it, and with his companions defeated a raging dragon and founded the first tribe. The Sage knew every answer but two: the end of the living and the homeward path of the dead. When his companions were gone, Chaac climbed a mountain on his last night, lit the first flame, and the god of the night realm answered; people heard what seemed a mother's song, the birth-cry of the first Wayob.

451.comment: Obsidian Codex: Pre-Banquet of the Contenders
451.content: priests of smoke and mist fed bonfires with the blood of other species, a hero rode a tamed beast to a fortress of huge stones with the Wayob's guidance, and reptiles feared an ancient city. The wisest dragon watched, planning that the strongest tribal hero should rule all humans, make a covenant, raise the banner of the blazing sun and take the primal fire from the living corpse on the throne. It knew foes waited in the deepest night, and that neither the gods in their heavens nor the high king among dragons would be enough.

452.comment: Obsidian Codex: Crown of the Saints
452.content: as a dark tide rose, warriors carried the Wayob's blessings into forbidden realms, the dragons were gone from the fields, and the dragon temples stood waiting for judgment. The tribes' war chiefs abandoned dragon-slaying to fight over supremacy. A hero no plan had accounted for, wearing a crown of golden flowers and carrying a great obsidian blade, visited tribe after tribe; the tribes made a pact of armistice and the sacred ones of the night realm offered him the crown. The dragon that thought itself master of evolution had not foreseen that strength would answer with something other than conquest.

453.content:
Ocean-Hued Clam (also: Ocean-Hued Clam artifact set, Sea-Dyed Blossom, Deep Palace's Plume, Cowry of Parting, Pearl Cage, Crown of Watatsumi, Sea-Dyed Foam): Ocean-Hued Clam is a 4 and 5 star artifact set from Watatsumi Island's songs. Its texts recall Omikami, the sea god the islanders worshipped; the first Divine Priestess and her twin sisters; shells and pearls given as tokens of family; and the sacrifice that ended that age. It is a healing set whose 4-piece turns healing into burst damage.

It drops from the Slumbering Court domain on Seirai Island, and came with Version 2.3. The texts are legend rather than record: they say what the islanders sing, and the Pearl Cage admits that the tale may be an ancient story that can no longer be verified.

Appearance: Five pieces: Sea-Dyed Blossom (flower, a soft sea flower with a pearl core that shimmers many colours in moonlight), Deep Palace's Plume (plume, a coral-coloured down feather said to come from a shrine maiden's ceremonial garment), Cowry of Parting (sands, a clean, flawless shell from the bottomless ocean), Pearl Cage (goblet, the ever-shining pearls shrine maidens offer), and Crown of Watatsumi (circlet, an ancient pearl-and-coral crown of a forgotten clergy, now ceremonially enshrined).

Lore: Watatsumi's people say they came out of the dark depths, and took a single shell each as a keepsake of their clan; those who had none were welcomed into another family. Omikami chose a Divine Priestess and rulers from among them, and the age ended in sacrifice.

Cowry of Parting: the ocean people left the silent glowing depths and escaped the gaze of the Dragonheirs by climbing a coral stair into daylight. Each took a seashell to remember their clan; the shells came to be called Parcels of Reunion in the old tongue, and two parties who embrace on one should not be parted by an outside force, though the bond is not eternal. The shells mark a farewell to life under the waves and the start of life under the sun.

Deep Palace's Plume and Pearl Cage: when the clans first saw daylight Omikami chose shrine maidens from the sea people. The first Divine Priestess was a pearl-gathering sea-daughter who comforted children lost in senseless fighting and old people who had lost sight of life's beauty; her songs gave the people hope for the first time. The plume comes from her ceremonial garb, pulled out by a child by mistake and kept by a worried person. Only she could sing the great song of the pearls, which the rainbow-hued clams produced in gratitude for Watatsumi's tenderness, and some said her bloodline began in those pearls. At the moment of defeat the Priestess and the twin sisters traded clothes and hid in the waves; one bright pearl was lost and sank back to the silent depths.

Crown of Watatsumi: Omikami picked its clergy from the people and gave them circlets of office; when the age of martyrdom ended, the old priesthood ended and the crowns were sealed. The people sing that pearl-and-coral crowns never stain and that whoever receives one is recognised as a ruler by Omikami. The valiant vassal lord Touzannou and the twins who crossed the waves freely (a note identifies them as the Yuna twins, Mouun and Ayame) had Omikami's tender favour and live on in the islanders' songs, and once served as the god's auxiliaries, guiding the sea people in farming, fishing and hunting. As the time of destined martyrdom came a god fell, and the crowns passed with their owners into forgotten rifts.

Sea-Dyed Blossom: songs say the flowers bloom in the pearl-lit depths, steeped in the lovesickness of diving sea-daughters and in moonlight. When conflict ceases, sea beasts will no longer weep for lonely companions, and when the moon rises over Touzan the lovely deity will rise and sing, with the lightning and storm unable to hide the moon's pearly glory.

Owners: No individual owns the set; its pieces are ceremonial and sacred items of the Watatsumi priesthood, the Divine Priestess and the Yuna twins' circle, as told in island songs.

Gameplay: Gameplay, not lore: the 2-piece bonus is Healing Bonus +15%. The 4-piece bonus makes each heal create a Sea-Dyed Foam that collects the healing for 3 seconds (up to 30,000 HP, overflow included) and bursts as Physical-type damage of 90% of the total, with one foam every 3.5 seconds and one at a time; it works off-field. The damage ignores Elemental Mastery, level and reaction bonuses, and counts healing absorbed by Bond of Life.

454.comment: Ocean-Hued Clam: Omikami and Watatsumi's faith
454.content: The Ocean-Hued Clam texts speak of Omikami as a deity who chose priestesses and rulers from the sea people, rejoiced in their love and gave pearls. Wiki summaries identify Omikami with Orobashi no Mikoto, the coral serpent once worshipped in Enkanomiya and on Watatsumi Island, who met its end near the close of the Archon War; the artifact texts themselves allude only to sacrifice and martyrdom, not to the war.

455.content: The Cowry of Parting says that in the old tongue the keepsake seashells of the Watatsumi people were called Parcels of Reunion; each person took one for their clan, and those without one were welcomed into a new family. The shell symbolises leaving the depths for daylight.

456.comment: Ocean-Hued Clam: Divine Priestess and the twin sisters
456.content: The Divine Priestess of Watatsumi is, in these texts, the first of the shrine maidens, a pearl-gathering sea-daughter whose songs gave her people hope. She and her twin sisters were favoured by Omikami and, at the moment of defeat, swapped clothes and hid in the waves. A note names the Yuna twins as Mouun and Ayame, but it is not stated whether the Priestess is one of them.

457.content:
Oratrice Mecanique d'Analyse Cardinale (also: Oratrice, Oratrice Mecanique, Mechanical Oratress of Cardinal Analysis): The Oratrice is a huge mechanical scale in the Opera Epiclese, Fontaine's court-theatre. At trials it weighed the arguments, returned the verdict the Iudex had to honour, and turned judgment into Indemnitium, the energy that powered the Court of Fontaine. Fontaine believed it was Furina's creation; in truth Focalors, the real Hydro Archon, built it and hid inside it. In 4.2 it sentenced "the Hydro Archon" to death and executed Focalors. It has not functioned since.

Its name is French, roughly "Mechanical Oratress of Cardinal Analysis".

Appearance: A towering set of scales at the back of the stage, below the judge's seat, with four lights that come on as a trial progresses. Its core sits in a chamber in the opera house basement.

A great blade hung above it; in Focalors's execution the spinning energy above her stopped and came slicing down. At the end of a trial a ticket is inserted and the Oratrice ejects its verdict.

Lore: Navia explains a trial (4.0): the arguments of both sides, testimony and even the audience's emotions are projected onto the Oratrice, whose scales tip toward whoever is winning. The Iudex's decision is fed in as a reference, and the result is treated as the will of "justice" itself.

Neuvillette's character story says children think of the judge as the Oratrice's "messenger pigeon". It acquitted Lynette and Lyney in their 4.0 trial, but later found Tartaglia guilty even after the real culprit was caught, the first time it ever disagreed with the Iudex; Furina covered the error with bravado. Lyney, sent by Arlecchino, slipped into the core chamber during his show and fled when a voice there seemed to recognise him; even approaching the core contaminated him with a large amount of Indemnitium. In 4.1 Arlecchino asked Furina what the vast store of Indemnitium was for, and Furina had no idea.

Indemnitium lit lamps and ran transport in the Court of Fontaine and powered the island of Erinnyes (4.0 Special Program). Fontaine's energy supply had long worried its people; about 400 to 500 years ago a looming energy crisis led to Alain Guillotin's Pneuma-Ousia Arkhe system for the Clockwork Meka, but the Oratrice was never wholly replaced, and Lyney believed its secrets were key to Fontaine's troubles. The viewpoint text asks how, without law, sins could be forgiven in the name of sin.

True purpose: Focalors revealed (4.2) that the Oratrice was no enactor of justice but a device built to kill the God of Justice and her divine throne. For 500 years she stored almost all its Indemnitium inside it; only a small fraction ever powered Fontaine.

The voice Lyney heard was hers: she had merged with the machine, taking Fontaine's Gnosis with her. At Furina's trial the Traveler and Neuvillette proved Furina was not a god; the Oratrice agreed she was guilty but sentenced "the Hydro Archon" to death, a sentence many had thought a myth. Neuvillette realised it was aimed at neither Furina nor Focalors but at the Hydro Archon's throne. Focalors said the stored power could have sustained Fontaine for millennia, but only that much could break a throne established by Celestia. Destroying it returned the Hydro authority to the Hydro Dragon, Neuvillette, whose verdict then made the Fontainians true humans, safe from the Primordial Sea.

Focalors admitted to Neuvillette that she was a little afraid of death, danced on her stage inside the Oratrice while Furina danced the same dance elsewhere, bowed, and the blade fell. She had also arranged for Neuvillette to be invited to Fontaine as Iudex, which he understood only then.

Status as of 7.1: Since Focalors's execution (4.2) the Oratrice no longer works. Neuvillette hears cases and passes verdicts himself.

The opera house no longer produces Indemnitium; Neuvillette's full command of Pneumousia replaces it.

Owners: Built and inhabited by Focalors. Furina publicly passed as its maker; asked to explain the Tartaglia verdict as its supposed creator, she could only bluff. It still stands in the Opera Epiclese.

Gameplay: Gameplay: a fixed object in the Opera Epiclese. In the Archon Quest courtroom sections its scales and lights track the arguments.

A viewpoint named after it is in the Opera Epiclese. It appears in quest cutscenes; it is not an item the player can obtain.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay guidance (project recommendation): before 4.2, Fontainians revere the Oratrice as impartial justice and credit it to Furina; nobody knows Focalors is inside. After 4.2 it is silent and Neuvillette judges alone; do not have it pass new verdicts or produce Indemnitium. Its true purpose is known to Neuvillette, the Traveler and Paimon, and through them a few others; the public saw only the death sentence and the end of the prophecy.

458.content:
Indemnitium is the energy the Oratrice produced from trials, drawn from people's belief in justice. It powered lamps and transport in the Court of Fontaine and the island of Erinnyes. Large doses are harmful: getting close to the Oratrice's core contaminated Lyney with a great deal of it.

Focalors stored almost all of it for 500 years to power the Oratrice's death sentence (4.2). Since the Oratrice stopped, none is produced; Neuvillette's command of Pneumousia replaces it.

459.comment: Oratrice Mecanique d'Analyse Cardinale: The Oratrice's verdict on the Hydro Archon
459.content: At Furina's trial in Masquerade of the Guilty (4.2), the Oratrice found her guilty as Neuvillette had, then sentenced "the Hydro Archon" to death, a shock because the trial had just proved Furina was not an Archon. The All-Devouring Narwhal attacked the courtroom. Inside the Oratrice, Focalors explained her plan to Neuvillette and was executed by its blade, destroying the Hydro Archon's throne and returning its authority to the Hydro Dragon.

460.content:
Padisarah (also: Padisarahs, Padisarah flower): The Padisarah is a holy, noble flower of Sumeru. It is very demanding about where it grows, and its buds are processed into valuable spices. Its archive text says it is a cultivar restored to the land by the Anahitian Blessing, after the original flower vanished.

It is a Sumeru local specialty and a cooking ingredient, seen around Sumeru City, Pardis Dhyai, the Palace of Alcazarzaray and the real Vanarana.

Appearance: Item text gives no description of the blossom beyond calling it holy and noble. The wiki's wild-growth image is the only visual reference; do not invent colours or scent.

Lore: The item text calls it a holy and noble plant with demanding growing conditions, whose flower buds become valuable spices. Its archive text adds that the name is said to come from an ancient deity. It tells of a time when three gods were on excellent terms and a great plain of lovely flowers lay in the land; people gathered the blossoms as incense to offer to their gods.

Those original flowers are no longer extant. The Padisarah is a cultivar brought back to the land through the Anahitian Blessing, a fertilizer said to be a blessing of the Dendro Archon. The wiki links the deity of the name to Nabu Malikata, though the text itself does not name her.

The Anahitian Blessing is distributed free by the Akademiya to farmers on a certain list in Sumeru City, and guarantees a good harvest if applied correctly; used wrongly it yields mushrooms instead, per the wiki's account of NPC dialogue. Nothing says the Padisarah itself grows from it by ordinary farming.

Gameplay: Gameplay note, not in-world lore: a Sumeru local specialty used in cooking. Dana at Pardis Dhyai and Jut at the Grand Bazaar in Sumeru City each give four on a first dialogue branch. It grows near Pardis Dhyai, the Palace of Alcazarzaray, Sumeru City, the real version of Vanarana, and a few spots near Vissudha Field.

Scene use: Use it as a quiet marker of Sumeru's restored past: a spice merchant praising its price, a gardener complaining how fussy it is, or a scholar reciting the story of the three gods. Keep to the archive text and do not give it magical properties.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 no later canon changes its description; it remains a cultivated local specialty of Sumeru.

461.content:
Pale Flame (also: Stainless Bloom, Wise Doctor's Pinion, Moment of Cessation, Surpassing Cup, Mocking Mask): Pale Flame is a 4- and 5-star artifact set added in version 1.5. Its five pieces read like origin stories of the Fatui: the first Fatuus (Pierro) approaches a woman consumed by fire, a heretical scholar, a moneyman and a discarded constructed being, and each takes a role in the Tsaritsa's cause. The last piece, the Mocking Mask, is Pierro's own declaration. In it he says the blood of his Khaenri'ahn compatriots cannot be washed away and that he will become a jester who mocks fate.

The set is an early long-form hint that the Fatui's founders each carry a grievance against the heavens or the old order. The first four figures are not named in the item text; the wiki reads them as Harbingers.

Appearance: The five pieces are a flower (Stainless Bloom), a feather (Wise Doctor's Pinion), a clock-like sands piece (Moment of Cessation), a cup (Surpassing Cup) and a mask (Mocking Mask). Item text gives no further physical description.

Lore: The five pieces dramatise how the first Fatuus, Pierro, recruited early Fatui: a woman consumed by fire (read as Signora), a heretical scholar (Dottore), a man seeking worldly power (Pantalone) and a discarded divine creation (the Balladeer). The Mocking Mask is Pierro's own vow: because his Khaenri'ah compatriots' blood cannot be cleansed, he will become a jester who mocks fate and serve the Tsaritsa.

Item text, summarised:
- Stainless Bloom: the first Fatuus offers a deal to a young woman whose life-flame has all but burnt out and who feels she is made of fire. She asks that glacial ice replace her erased past and quench the fire, and that pain and sin be purified by silent ice. A pure white flame still burns in her heart, and she calls herself a tool stained by the ashes of the dead. The wiki identifies her as Signora.
- Wise Doctor's Pinion: a young researcher in the seat of learning argues that people are machines that can be improved, fears being cast out as a heretic, and notes that the Akademiya's way of working blocks research. The first Fatuus finds him in the desert, and he boasts that with enough resources he could make what the nation calls a god. He is accepted as a partner and given a title that amuses him bitterly. The wiki identifies him as Dottore.
- Moment of Cessation: a man not favoured by the gods can pursue only worldly power, and money is cast as the world's lifeblood. He vows that Snezhnaya will become the heart that pumps wealth around the world and that, when the time comes, it will stop by its own will. The wiki identifies him as Pantalone.
- Surpassing Cup: a being born with a face fairer than any other, divinely made and discarded as worthless dross, wakes through an unknowable error and wanders for countless years. He decides to join the mask-wearing Fatui because they are fun. The wiki identifies him as the Balladeer (Scaramouche, now the Wanderer).
- Mocking Mask: Pierro speaks in his own name. Because the blood of his Khaenri'ah compatriots cannot be cleansed, he will be the Jester who laughs at fate. He says he could not match the sages, failed to win the previous ruler's favour, and failed to stop others tearing away the veil of sin, which brought divine wrath and cataclysm. He will therefore become a fool and a Fatuus in service to the Tsaritsa, then calls on his comrades to put on masks in mockery and rewrite destiny.

Cross-references the wiki cites: Signora says "Pale Flame" at two points in her boss fight, which supports the Stainless Bloom link; the Balladeer's "worthless dross" phrasing echoes a line in the Inversion of Genesis interlude; Pantalone's wealth supports the Moment of Cessation link; and Dottore's earlier Ruin Machine facility matches the "manufacture a god" boast. These are community inferences from matching wording, not statements in the item text.

The Mocking Mask is the key canon claim: Pierro frames himself as Khaenri'ahn and as someone shaped by the causes of the Cataclysm, but he does not name the Five Sinners or say what he did. The phrase "tearing away the veil of sin" refers to events the set leaves unexplained.

The pieces mix an omniscient narrator with quoted speech, so the recruitment scenes are best treated as a dramatised, possibly unreliable account rather than minutes of real meetings. Later canon gave several of these figures more tragic or complicated stories, so use the set as flavour about how the Fatui present their own origins.

Owners: No owner is named. The text is narrated from the perspective of the first Fatuus about his recruits and himself.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): 4- and 5-star; obtained from the Ridge Watch domain (Liyue) and an Artifact Strongbox. 4-piece: when an Elemental Skill hits an opponent, ATK +9% for 7s, up to 2 stacks, once per 0.3s. At 2 stacks the 2-piece Physical DMG Bonus increases by 100%. The wiki notes the effect applies only to the wearer, only for an on-field hit, and persists after swapping characters.

462.content: Artifact set whose five pieces of item text dramatise how Pierro, the first Fatuus, recruited early Fatui members, and state his own vow of mockery.

463.content: Pierro's own piece. He says the stain of his Khaenri'ah compatriots' blood cannot be cleansed and that he will become The Jester who laughs at fate, a Fatuus devoted to Her Majesty (the Tsaritsa), who understands his pain. He addresses his Fatui comrades, saying they carry both the fire of rage and the cold of eternal winter, have seen the callousness of the world's foundational principles, and should wear masks in mockery to rewrite destiny.

464.content:
Parametric Transformer (also: Parametric Transformer gadget, transmutation device): The Parametric Transformer is a gadget the Traveler wins in Liyue by solving an Adventurers' Guild treasure riddle. It is a mysterious device from the ruins that can "transmute" material objects: a heap of ordinary materials goes in, and different materials come out after elemental energy has charged it.

It is a placeable device, usable again after about a week. Its Archive text frames transmutation as accelerating the natural cycles of the world, and no maker or origin is given.

Appearance: In the inventory it is a four-star gadget. It is set down on a flat surface, where it shows a charge gauge. The wiki lists a "Deployed" state and a "Loaded" state. Canon does not describe its build beyond calling it a device.

Lore: Lan, who works at the Liyue Harbor Adventurers' Guild, posts a rumour about treasure near Tianqiu Valley. Nobody has found it. The Traveler follows a treasure map to Dunyu Ruins, reads a rhyming note about a giant tree, a road and a flight of stairs, opens three chests, and finds a strange box. Lan has never seen anything like it.

Lan says that, by the adventurers' code, whatever is found belongs to the finder, and that the Guild only wanted the experience of solving the riddle. Puzzled that the box was at Dunyu Ruins, a place searched many times, Lan arranges a closer search there.

The Archive description reads as a small piece of philosophy. Everything is said to be in a cycle: memories and elements surge in the ley lines, rotten fallen fruit returns to the soil, and trees born of the soil one day bear crystal fruit. The device speeds such cycles up.

Nothing in canon says who built the device, how it came to be at Dunyu Ruins, or whether it is linked to ley-line research. Do not invent one; in a scene it works best as a puzzling relic that someone has put to practical use.

Owners: The Traveler holds the only copy shown in canon. Lan hands it over as the finder's reward.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not in-world fact). The device is placed on a valid surface and loaded with non-event materials worth a total quality of 150 or more. It must be charged with Elemental damage, either from the player or from an environmental source such as an Electro Crystal. It cannot be used while in combat and is dismissed if the player wanders off or draws enemies, keeping the loaded materials for the next try. After use it has a cooldown of about 7 days. The first use grants the achievement "Transmutation Nuclide".

The wiki counts about 18 elemental hits to fill the gauge, with a 0.4 second delay between charges, regardless of how large the elemental application is. Material quality is tiered: ordinary produce and ore count as 1, and higher-tier enemy drops count as 1, 2 or 4.

Community observation (Genshin Impact Data Gathering team, not official) puts the payout at 5 to 10 sets, most often 5 to 7. Each set is drawn from groups such as 20,000 Mora, character and weapon experience materials, 3-star and 2-star character ascension materials, talent books and weapon ascension materials. The mix of materials fed in appears to shift which groups come up, but never guarantees one.

465.content: A Liyue Harbor world quest that gives the Parametric Transformer. Lan of the Adventurers' Guild passes on a treasure riddle near Tianqiu Valley. After fighting hilichurls the Traveler gets a treasure map to Dunyu Ruins, finds the Strange Note, opens three chests and returns with a Strange Box. Lan lets the Traveler keep it, with the reward.

466.content:
Peak Patrol Song (also: Halcyon Years Unending, Ode to Flowers): Peak Patrol Song is a 5-star sword: an obsidian blade of unparalleled sharpness and light as a song, modified by an artisan (linked to Xilonen) with a detachable Phlogiston device that plays records.

Its story is not about the blade but about Sakkuk, an old hero of the mines, and the songs of the Nanatzcayan.

Appearance: Canon says an obsidian blade of unparalleled sharpness, with a detachable record-playing Phlogiston device. Add no further details such as pattern or colour.

Lore: Every year, before the Embercore Flowers bloom, the mistress of the mountain mines comes alone to Tequemecan Valley to lay dew-kissed flowers for friends who never saw the dawn. Her once-hard heart has softened with age.

The sound of the mines and the artisans' songs shakes her from her bitter memories: the echoes of the Nanatzcayan have reached even this place, and she laughs.

The woman is Sakkuk, representative of the Chiefs, who has crossed the mountain's spine more times than she can count. All who could receive her warmth have long since returned to the Sacred Flame, and the once empty hills now ring with laughter that the young dreamed of while hiding from usurpers and that belongs to the future of civilization.

She sings aloud the song that "he" once taught her but that she was too embarrassed ever to sing to him, calling it a mere prank in those days. Its verse speaks of stone engraved and peaks that echo, tempered in the forge, blessing all beings; of converging and dispersing, rebirth in ashes, and a blazing dawn.

Thousands of years after authority was returned to the tribes, the ballads once kept by Sakkuk, called "Peace-Reforger", are lost. What survives is the sharp, resolute rhythm passed on with each hammer stroke on chisel: the text calls it the blood that has flowed through the mines since ancient times, and the sparks from the hammer a song for those who resist. It closes by repeating the opening questions, whether a life must wither like fresh flowers, where the heart goes when all is chaos, and the answer that nobody stays forever in this world: "here, there were once flowers; here, there was once song". The wiki gives Sakkuk the Ancient Name Baraka (blessing), which the verse echoes, and records her as the last survivor of the first heroes to join the Scarlet-Eyed Youth.

Owners: No wielder is named. The description's only person is the artisan who modified the blade, linked to Xilonen.

Sakkuk is the subject of the poem rather than an owner. Treat any statement that Xilonen wields this sword in the story as a scene invention unless the user's scenario sets it.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star sword, base ATK 44 at level 1, secondary stat DEF; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 5.1.

Passive "Halcyon Years Unending": Normal or Plunging Attacks that hit give "Ode to Flowers" (DEF and an All Elemental DMG Bonus for 6s, up to 2 stacks, once per 0.1s). When it reaches 2 stacks or the 2nd stack is refreshed, nearby party members get an All Elemental DMG Bonus for 15s that scales with every 1,000 DEF the wielder has. Ascension uses Night-Wind's Mystic materials, the Secret Source boss line and Fang common materials.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: a miner or artisan in the Nanatzcayan could connect the blade's name to the rhythm of hammers and chisels. Speak of it as a sword that sings, not as a relic of a specific hero.

467.comment: Peak Patrol Song: Halcyon Years Unending
467.content: Halcyon Years Unending is the passive of the sword Peak Patrol Song (gameplay): it builds Ode to Flowers stacks that raise the wielder's DEF and Elemental DMG Bonus, then gives nearby party members an Elemental DMG Bonus that scales with the wielder's DEF.

key: Perfect Heart of the Sacred Dragon
468.comment: Perfect Heart of the Sacred Dragon
468.content:
Perfect Heart of the Sacred Dragon (also: Clustered Storage Array): The Perfect Heart of the Sacred Dragon is a flawless piece of jade, the heart of the Dragonlord Ix Uxul Tz'ib Bolon Ch'ule-L (nicknamed Ixlel), who ruled Chichen Uctokah, the original city of Ochkanatlan, before human civilisation was kindled. The Traveler receives it at the end of the Natlan World Quest "Open Your Heart to Me". Its energy is exhausted, so it can no longer command anything.

Its alternate name is Clustered Storage Array. The Traveler gathers the three Ancient Jadestone Fragments of Ixlel's broken heart, and she pours her last energy into them to restore it. Item text calls it a quest item and a memento.

Appearance: Item text describes only "a flawless piece of jade." Canon gives no size, shape or glow.

Ixlel's own statue is a huge dragon carving, and her human guise, remembered in a ruin note, had crystal skin and turquoise eyes. Do not assume the heart looks like either.

Lore: The item text says the heart once let its owner command every device in Ochkanatlan, "the ineffable city". It is now spent. The text also remarks that, like the half-humans who chased it, the Dragonlord's quest for perfection ended in something as cold and lifeless as jade.

In "Open Your Heart to Me", Ixlel speaks through a great dragon statue in the Old Core of Chu'ulel, deep under Ochkanatlan. She says a traitor tore her heart apart, hid the pieces in devices and used her memories to hold her there, forcing her to "sing" for his empire because he did not know how to run the city. She would not die enslaved, so she asked the Traveler, the "Chosen of Dragons", to gather the fragments, let her restore the heart with her remaining energy, and then take it out.

She calls the heart a Clustered Storage Array that holds all her memories, and says that for long-lived beings memories are curses and shackles. Her life was nearly spent and she expected her consciousness to run out within thirty winters. When the fragments go in, Ixlel cries out the name Och-Kan, and chains bind her consciousness. She asks the Traveler to cut them. Secret Source platforms and Secret Source Automatons attack as the chains fall, and Ixlel remarks that these "parasites" on her life have run dry. After the last chain is cut she thanks the Traveler and her will dissipates; only silence answers Paimon afterwards, and the Traveler takes the heart.

Wiki summaries of ruin notes elsewhere in Natlan give the wider story. Ixlel was the Ninth of the Thirteen Sovereign Lords and ruled Chichen Uctokah. Och-Kan, ruler of Ochkanatlan, first accepted her as an ally, but he grew alarmed by what she taught him of the old dragon empire and resolved to strip her of her authority. He sealed her in the Old Core of Chu'ulel and took her heart apart. He had modelled Ochkanatlan's power system on that of Chichen Uctokah, so only a dragon could run it, and for a time he drew on her energy until he built a new Core of Chu'ulel he could control. These notes are the wiki's account and are not given as speech in the quest.

Owners: Original owner: Ixlel, the Dragonlord of Chichen Uctokah. It was taken from her and hidden in pieces by Och-Kan. Current holder as of 7.1: the Traveler, who keeps it as a memento after freeing her.

Gameplay: Gameplay: a quest item and memento from the 5.2 World Quest "Open Your Heart to Me".

Completing the quest also grants the achievement "Devoted to Eternal Serenity", and the Ancient Flint Key can then be placed in the new chamber to create a spiritway out of the Old Core of Chu'ulel.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the heart as a solemn keepsake of a proud ruler's chosen end, not a weapon or power source.

Ordinary people of Natlan would not know Chichen Uctokah's history. Do not have the heart grant authority over Ochkanatlan's devices; the item text says it is exhausted. Do not give Ixlel a continued voice through it.

469.comment: Perfect Heart of the Sacred Dragon: Ixlel
469.content: Ixlel, the Ninth of the Thirteen Sovereign Lords and ruler of Chichen Uctokah, was a proud dragon who insisted on her full name, and her nickname came from Paimon. Trapped for thousands of years in a statue, she asked the Traveler for a dignified release and died after the Traveler cut the chains that bound her consciousness. Her heart is the Perfect Heart of the Sacred Dragon.

470.comment: Perfect Heart of the Sacred Dragon: Ancient Jadestone Fragment
470.content: Three strange fragments scattered through the Old Core of Chu'ulel, which feel warm to the touch and are made of a material hard to identify. They are the pieces of Ixlel's torn heart. Once she restores them with her remaining life energy, they become the Perfect Heart of the Sacred Dragon.

471.content:
Perinheri (also: Hleobranto Innamorato): Sold by Hubel in the Court of Fontaine. Its author claims a Khaenri'ahn origin that nobody alive can verify, and it has grown over generations as an anthology with footnotes by later editors.

Appearance: A 3-star Book Collection (2 volumes). Vol. 2 carries two scholar's notes and a list of thanks naming contributors across 15 editions, which gives it the feel of a long-edited text.

Lore: Vol. 1: things from outside the world leak into the Kingdom, and its weapons destroy calamities that slip in. A sage tells the ruler a tale of sea people who honor shipwrecked strangers as possible gods. The Kingdom then founds an orphanage in case a being who transcends the gods arrives; orphans and outside wanderers are accepted too. Perinheri's first memory is being sent through a pitch-dark soot-filled corridor and asked 'Are you dead?', then seeing the crimson moon turn into a horrified eye. The adults tell him he is reborn. The awaited being never came, but many orphans became great knights, and Perinheri led them unless he competed with his best friend Hleobrant, whose rivalry turned deadly.
Vol. 2: Angelica arrives, claiming her priestly line's nation fell to Deus Auri. She will wed only the mightiest knight. Hleobrant is smitten and picks duels; she lists Njord, Alf, Alberich and Perinheri as the strongest. Convinced that killing Angelica would cure Hleobrant's madness, Perinheri hunts her. Outside the borders Hleobrant becomes beast-like; Angelica says it is the curse of forebears who forsook their god, while Perinheri, who drifted in, is free of it. At sunrise she reveals herself as freedom and tells Perinheri it is his to take, and he faces empty land.

The text says the ocean was used in the Kingdom as a metaphor for space projected by the stars. The editor's footnote on the black wolves of the first edition says archaeology indicates alchemically created warbeasts, mainstays of the Crimson Moon Dynasty that mechanical engineering overtook in the Eclipse Dynasty. The other footnote notes that Liyue's ancient people did not use a name like Angelica, and guesses 'Lady Miaoyin' or 'Tianwang Nu'.

Acknowledgements list Mr. Denon's archaeological studies (1st edition), Jean Figeac's refinements which gave the ending (2nd), corrections by two Figeac family members (3rd), a compilation of Karl Ingold's 'Investigations into an Abandoned City' records (13th), Karasawa's natural history help (14th) and Yun's notes on Liyue culture (15th). Wiki trivia suggests that Karasawa may be Eichi Karasawa, an Inazuman scholar turned romance novelist. It also notes the story resembles Orlando Innamorato and Orlando Furioso.

Owners: No named owner; sold by the bookseller Hubel in the Quartier Narbonnais, Court of Fontaine.

Gameplay: Both volumes are bought from Hubel; this is a collectible lore text.

472.content:
In the tale, Hleobrant is Perinheri's best friend and rival. Out of love for Angelica he grows reckless, and outside the Kingdom's borders his speech degrades into howls. Angelica attributes this to a curse on descendants of those who abandoned their god and came to the Kingdom, which she links to the pure-blooded aristocracy. The book does not say what became of him.

Compare the real-world Orlando legends, where a knight's madness over Angelica is cured by another knight; the wiki treats this as the inspiration.

473.content:
Polestar Ballet Anthology (also: Black Snow Swan, The Seabird, The Envoy, The Firebird): Each volume is an excerpted script with cast, act headings, stage directions and spoken lines, in the manner of a printed libretto. The four ballets are separate stories. Black Snow Swan is the one the game connects to other content, including the character Odette and the sword Whitelake Frostfeather.

Appearance: A 4-star Book Collection of 4 volumes. The text uses stage directions in parentheses, tempo markings (adagio, presto), named variations and curtain calls, and some acts are skipped with ellipses.

Lore: **Black Snow Swan.** Odile, a black swan among white sisters, believes her colour is a shame. Queen Myrtha says it comes from human emotion, love and passion, a poison that fate uses as a snare, and promises three spirits across three nights. Bathilde de Petrichor (Spring), a Fontainian noble betrayed in love, Hamsatti (Summer), a princess of Pragjyotishpura who destroyed the man she loved and the dancer he loved, and Tatiana (Autumn), a snow swan, each warn that love is sorrow, cruelty and weakness. In Act III Odile answers that love and passion belong to the heart, not to Fate, dances thirty-two fouettes, and refuses eternal purity. Myrtha lets her go. At dawn the black swan sets out to fly higher than any snow swan.

**The Seabird.** Act IV, in a country estate. Kostya, a composer chafing at popular taste, meets Zarechnaya, once his muse, who left with Boris for Snezhnograd and lost her voice and confidence there. She has learned to sing for the joy of singing and leaves alone to work in Svetloledovka. Kostya says he has killed a seabird; a gunshot is heard and he is seen lying on the stage.

**The Envoy.** In the reign of Emperor Monomakh, Viscount Schpekin's town panics when a dispatch from the Zapolyarny Palace announces an incognito envoy of the Pale Star. A visitor, Khlestakov, is taken for the envoy and leaves with gems, revealing himself as the thief Reed Miller. The Druzhna then arrive for the real envoy, and Schpekin turns on the audience: they are laughing at themselves.

**The Firebird.** Grand Duke Vernov's golden apples are being stolen. His third son Khramov keeps watch and sees the Firebird, Sirin. Vaselisa, a farm girl carried off by the Demon King Berstuk to his diamond castle, refuses his gifts and throws his crown at him; Khramov, with the Mirrorblade and the Firebird, defeats Berstuk. Sirin's closing lines say freedom and love are the dearest things.

**Black Snow Swan details.** Myrtha says mercy and kindness die at the slightest breath and only cold, impartial calculation lasts until dawn, and that love makes the mightiest hero kneel before Fate, a "cruel usurper". Bathilde recounts placing her golden necklace on a village maiden who danced with the hunter she herself was betrothed to. Hamsatti blames "the Lord of vaana" for the arrow that made her love, and warns that even gods once touched by love cannot escape Fate's bargain. Tatiana says the heavens have arranged all and warns that once the oath is broken the skies shall shut. Odile's reply is that love is "the blade that cuts Fate's snare" and that she wants one brief true-blue moment over an empty eternity. Myrtha says she has no right to judge her choice, and Odile says the same of Myrtha.

**The Seabird details.** Zarechnaya quotes lines she once sang on Kostya's bare stage about the earth bearing no living soul for ten million years. The seabird stands for both the bird Kostya killed and Zarechnaya. Boris has returned to Kostya's mother Polina. The line that a man chanced upon a seabird and destroyed it for want of anything else to do recurs at the end.

**The Envoy details.** The officials fall into a panic dance and each fears being slandered by an informer. Khlestakov ends by greeting the room in the name of the ravens, and the aristocrats' elegance dissolves into flight when the Druzhna enter with a decree.

**The Firebird details.** Act II is under the golden apple tree, where Khramov bathes his eyes with dew to stay awake. The cast list names Sirin as the Firebird, Berstuk as Demon King, Vaselisa as Princess, plus Forest Creatures and the Demon King's Minion.

**Links the wiki points out.** Whitelake Frostfeather's item text depicts the in-universe inspiration for Tatiana's scene. Odette's Elemental Skill "Adagio: Phantom Night Dancers" quotes Bathilde's closing lines about the candle flame of winter, and Odette's constellation names echo Odile's final speech, per the wiki. Odette shares her name with the heroine of the real-world Swan Lake, in which Odile is a character.

**Interpretive notes, treated as inferred.** The wiki compares Myrtha's poison of love with the Primordial Human's Eitr, which the Belyi Tsar calls love in An Ark That Used to Be a Soul, and the swan's blackening with the Shadow Realm spreading in the Court of Eternal Bliss. It also suggests "the Lord of vaana" refers to the Heavenly Principles. These are readings of the text, not statements in it.

**Real-world references the wiki lists.** Black Snow Swan draws on Swan Lake (Odile, thirty-two fouettes), Giselle (Myrtha, Bathilde) and La Bayadere (Hamsatti), and The Firebird resembles Stravinsky's ballet. They are out-of-universe references. Bathilde's dance is set to a minuet in the style of the Palais Mermonia.

**Use in scene.** The scripts suit a character reading, quoting or explaining a Troupe ballet, but the lines above are one printed version, and the books do not say how any staging differs.

Owners: No character is established as owning it. Vols. 2 to 4 are sold by Moes at Torchlight Books; Vol. 1 is obtained through the quest Variations on Belyi and Chernyi per the wiki.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: a four-volume 4-star Book Collection. It has no combat function.

474.comment: Polestar Ballet Anthology: Black Snow Swan ballet
474.content:
The Korolevskiy Troupe ballet in Vol. 1 of the Polestar Ballet Anthology. Odile, a black swan, is taught by Queen Myrtha and three spirits (Bathilde, Hamsatti, Tatiana) that love is a poison, then chooses love and flight over purity.

Odette, the playable character, is tied to the production by her name and kit text per the wiki. Whitelake Frostfeather's item text carries the inspiration for Tatiana's scene.

475.comment: Polestar Ballet Anthology: The Seabird, The Envoy and The Firebird
475.content: Vols. 2 to 4 of the anthology. The Seabird is about a composer and a singer who part. The Envoy is a comedy of mistaken identity in the reign of Emperor Monomakh. The Firebird has Khramov, Vaselisa and the Firebird Sirin overthrow the Demon King Berstuk.

476.content:
Primogem (also: Primogems): Primogems are the premium currency of Genshin Impact. Their item text calls them a primordial crystalline gem beyond the mundane world, shining with the condensed hopes and dreams of universes that once were. In play they are spent mainly on wishes.

Primogems are different from Mora, the ordinary currency of Teyvat. Canon never shows characters trading in them.

Appearance: A crystalline gem. The in-game description stresses that it is primordial and not of the ordinary world.

Lore: The only in-world text is the item description: a primordial gem, beyond the mundane world, containing the condensed hopes and dreams of universes that once were. Its wording echoes Genesis Crystals, whose text describes an energy crystal formed from pure potential and hope, with enough energy to create a newborn star. Neither is explained by a quest.

The related Intertwined Fate is described as a fateful stone whose glimmers can entwine fates and connect dreams. The wiki notes the Chinese name for Primogem means roughly "primordial stone", which resembles the term used for allogenes. This is a naming observation, not a canon link.

Gameplay: Gameplay note, not in-world lore: 160 Primogems buy one Intertwined or Acquaint Fate; they also replenish Original Resin and buy Battle Pass levels. Genesis Crystals convert one to one into Primogems, never the reverse.

Sources include Commissions, quests, chests, Statues of The Seven, Spiral Abyss, Imaginarium Theater, events, achievements and the Blessing of the Welkin Moon. Amounts are version-dependent.

Scene use: Treat Primogems as a game-system item. In a story they work best as a mysterious gem tied to wishing, with no stated origin; do not invent a creator.

477.content:
Primordial Jade Cutter (also: Primordial Jade sword, Pányán Jiélǜ): Primordial Jade Cutter is a five-star sword of Liyue, a ceremonial blade masterfully carved from pure jade. Item text says that when Liyue first arose, Rex Lapis once walked the land with a sword hewn from jade. It was cut as a costly gift for peace and luxury, then bathed in blood in war. It is a legend rather than a quest object: no scene shows the sword.

It belongs to the Primordial Jade weapon series, the Liyue weapons tied to the Archon War era. The wiki's reading of the series is that the sword is the weapon Morax wielded after the gift never reached its recipient.

Appearance: The in-game description calls it a ceremonial sword carved from pure jade, so polished that it keeps a sheen as if new despite age and blood, and says there seems to be an audible sigh in the wind when it is swung. Item text gives no other detail (no hilt, length or inscriptions), so avoid inventing any.

Lore: The item story is a lament. The jade edge, soaked in blood long ago, still looks new; rain washed the blood away over a thousand years, but the thoughts and grudges gathered around it linger. A friend, now long forgotten, once said that nephrite has the soul of the Bishui River's gentle heart and will in time cleanse itself of old grudges, and then asked who would ease the agony the jade feels at having become an instrument of slaughter.

The text widens into a statement about the Archon War: over many years people who once feasted together became mortal foes, while those who betrayed or fought to the death later shared a drink with their hatred gone. The sword was carved as an expensive gift for a certain someone, cut from jade out of love of peace and luxury. When wine vessels fill with blood and tender feelings are torn apart by cold ambition, the story ends, gifts ungiven and bonds unspoken become sharp blades with which to cleave former friends. The text never says who gave or received the gift.

The wiki's Primordial Jade Series page ties the sword to Morax, who used it in the Archon War after the intended gift never came to pass. That is interpretation layered on the text, which says only that "Rex Lapis" once walked with a jade sword. In Chinese the weapon is named after a famous jade, Jielü, from the State of Song; the English translation drops that allusion. The jade connection to the Bishui River is the text's own.

Owners: Item text names no owner beyond the legendary Rex Lapis (Morax, the Geo Archon, who as Zhongli appears in the game). It does not say the sword ever left his hands, and no playable character is attached to it by canon.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star sword from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT Rate 9.6%. Passive "Protector's Virtue": HP rises 20-40% and the wielder gains ATK equal to 1.2-2.4% of Max HP, at refinements 1 to 5. The bonus does not apply if the wielder has fallen or is not in the party.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the sword suits themes of a gift turned weapon, grudges outliving the people who held them and gentleness forced into violence. Treat it as a legend that Liyue scholars or antique dealers might repeat, not as a relic that anyone can show.

478.comment: Primordial Jade Cutter: Primordial Jade series
478.content: The Primordial Jade series is an unofficial grouping of five-star weapons made of jade with a green look. The wiki notes the first two released, Primordial Jade Cutter and Primordial Jade Winged-Spear, retell weapons or objects Morax made from jade for the Archon War, and that Jadefall's Splendor is a later addition with a different focus. The series has no shared passive.

479.content:
Primordial Jade Winged-Spear (also: Primordial Jade Winged Spear, Hépú Yuān): Primordial Jade Winged-Spear is a five-star polearm of Liyue. Its item story is a creation legend: at Liyue's foundation a sea behemoth called Baqiu, which the Geo Archon's own Geo Whale could not beat, drowned settlements with its waves. The Geo Archon hand-forged a black kite from jade and stone, it dove into the sea, and Baqiu sank for good.

It is part of the Primordial Jade series, the Liyue weapons of the Archon War era. Despite its polearm form the text describes the origin object as a kite (a bird), not a spear.

Appearance: Item text says only that the Geo Archon fashioned a black kite by hand from jade and stones, and that the stone bird took flight once forged. Nothing is said of the polearm's own look; the name's "Winged" and the kite are the only visual hints.

Lore: Item story: when Liyue was founded, monsters and gods still ruled the seas and the forebears lived in fear, fighting the sea with all they could. Over many ages a behemoth rose that dominated the waters; even the Geo Archon's Geo Whale could not triumph. Liyue's people called it Baqiu, a beast without rival in the ocean's deepest abyss, whose enormous waves washed away whole settlements.

The Geo Archon then made a black kite by hand from jade and stones. Once forged it took to the sky, dove into the heart of the sea and joined the battle against the behemoth and the whale. The behemoth sank into the depths to remain there, and Liyue's people were released from its thundering roars. The wiki adds that in Chinese the name Baqiu combines the characters for eight and young horned dragon, and that the weapon's Chinese name refers to a jade of the State of Chu (He's jade); the English text drops both allusions.

The wiki's series page frames the story as an object Morax made from jade for battle, plunging into the sea like a spear. Treat that as the wiki's reading: the item text describes a kite, and the connection between the kite and a polearm is not spelled out.

Owners: The item text names no later owner. In promotional art Xiao wields the ascended version in his official art and character demo; that is presentation, not a canon statement that Xiao owns this exact weapon.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star polearm in the standard Wanderlust Invocation and weapon event wishes. Base ATK 48, secondary stat CRIT Rate 4.8%. Passive "Eagle Spear of Justice": on hit, ATK rises 3.2-6.0% for 6 seconds, up to 7 stacks, once every 0.3 seconds; at max stacks DMG dealt rises 12-24% (refinements 1 to 5). The wielder must be on the field to gain stacks.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): an old Liyue sailors' and coast-dwellers' legend of the time before the harbour, useful for themes of the sea as an enemy and of a god's ingenuity. Keep it a tale; no character in canon can confirm it.

480.content: Baqiu is the sea behemoth named in the Primordial Jade Winged-Spear item text, a beast that dominated the seas around early Liyue, washed away settlements with its waves and defeated the Geo Whale of the Geo Archon. It was finally sunk by a black jade-and-stone kite the Geo Archon made. It appears only in that item text.

key: Princess Mina of the Fallen Nation
481.comment: Princess Mina of the Fallen Nation
481.content:
Princess Mina of the Fallen Nation (also: Mina of the Fallen Nation): Princess Mina of the Fallen Nation is a six-volume Inazuman adventure novel series, sold by Kuroda at the Yae Publishing House in Inazuma City. A wandering samurai in luxurious robes, accompanied by a small girl in an oversized haori, takes a princess prophesied to bring destruction on a journey to the Sky Tower at the centre of the world. The blurbs sell it as a hugely popular romantic adventure.

It is an in-world work of fiction, so nothing in it is evidence about Teyvat's real history. It is notable in Inazuma for its ironic, genre-aware voice: the narrator jokes about plot conventions.

Appearance: Six paperback-style instalments. Each volume has a short blurb of the kind used to advertise serialised fiction. The narration is chatty and self-aware. Vol. 6 includes an appendix on the setting, with the wicked overlords and monsters who did not appear in the story.

Lore: Vol. 1: after thirteen years of peace, a century-scale age of warring states begins; a wandering samurai and a girl stop at a checkpoint where the samurai quickly disposes of three ashigaru. Vol. 2: the princess asks what the samurai thinks about her prophesied destruction; he calls the prophecy an excuse for war. Vol. 3: they see the devastation the war has caused. Vol. 4: a flashback. Vol. 5: at the Sky Tower the onmyouji reveal their plan. Vol. 6: the samurai walks the desert and leaves for another world.

- Vol. 2 sets the principal tension: the princess wants to be rescued and to save the world, while the samurai says he did not rescue her since she gave him an order, and states that destroying the world is a stupid concept.
- Vol. 3 reveals that the war is fed by Nakura's Hex, a sorcery that drains life from living things and the land and gives it to powerful samurai, who are the Nakura Daimyo. The Hex was made by the Onmyouji of the Sky Tower at the world's centre. The samurai asks whether the world has not already been destroyed.
- Vol. 4: in Kogami, a wasteland, the samurai (called 'green') meets a former comrade ('pale'). Thirteen samurai once banded together to defeat the Nakura Daimyo, but Kogami did not recover and only two escaped.
- Vol. 5: the samurai tells the princess that the world cannot be saved; the Onmyouji say Nakura's Hex was made to preserve a declining world's vitality and that it can be used by whatever draws on the stored life. The princess insists that princesses are born to save the world.
- Vol. 6: it ends with the samurai deciding to destroy another world, if one exists.

- The book jokes about itself: an NPC speaks 'to push the plot forward'; a character says people would throw such beliefs into the nation of Tokoyo. These are narrator gags, and Tokoyo here is a fictional place.
- The recurring contrast is between the cynical samurai and the idealistic princess, with the samurai's past (the thirteen) as the engine behind his refusal.
- Only the premise and a handful of scenes are paraphrased from the wiki; details of the later chapters are not reproduced there, so avoid inventing the ending beyond what Vol. 6 says.
- Do not use the series as Teyvat history; Kogami, Tokoyo and the Sky Tower are story settings.

Owners: No individual owner. Kuroda at the Yae Publishing House in Inazuma City sells Vols. 1 to 4 and 6; Vol. 5 is in the left-hand room of the Yashiro Commission Headquarters.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible six-volume book collection added in version 2.1; reading is purely lore.

482.comment: Princess Mina of the Fallen Nation: Nakura's Hex
482.content: In the novel, Nakura's Hex is a sorcery created by the Onmyouji of the Sky Tower that drains life from living things and the land, passing it to powerful samurai and feeding a war that has lasted over a century. The samurai who exploit it are the Nakura Daimyo.

483.comment: Princess Mina of the Fallen Nation: The Princess Who Brings Destruction
483.content: The titular princess is prophesied to destroy the world. The samurai says the prophecy is an excuse for war; the princess wants to save the world anyway. By Vol. 6 the story ends with the samurai travelling on to another world.

484.content:
Prized Isshin Blade (also: Accursed Isshin blade, the cursed Isshin sword): The Prized Isshin Blade is a four-star sword that exists only inside Kaedehara Kazuha's Acer Palmatum Chapter, Act I ("A Strange and Friendless Road", Version 2.8). It is a blade full of Tatarigami malice that possesses a samurai and goes hunting for Kazuha, wanting to prove that the Isshin Art can beat even the Shogun. Kazuha defeats it, the curse drains out of it, and at the end of the quest it is remade into the ordinary, obtainable Kagotsurube Isshin.

It appears in two quest forms: an Awakened form while it is still dangerous, and a Shattered form once the curse has been worn down. It cannot be kept as a weapon; the lasting result of the quest is the Kagotsurube Isshin.

Appearance: The Awakened description speaks of an ominous purple aura clinging to a bizarre blade, with the power to control its wielder's heart and mind. After the curse weakens, the text says the aura's wickedness and hostility have decreased greatly. The Shattered form is described as a battered cursed blade showing its true form, its innate endowment ground to dust by its journey.

Lore: In the quest the Traveler and Paimon are attacked on Byakko Plain by a samurai who is really looking for Kazuha. Investigation leads through Ritou, the Tenryou Commission and the Amenoma Smithy to a small island off Inazuma City, where they find Amenoma Yuuya, a samurai of the Amenoma Clan, possessed by the sword. The sword speaks for itself. It says it was the prized weapon of an Isshin smith who failed the Shogun's tasks and exiled himself to Snezhnaya, and that after the smith died it began possessing people to make its way back to Inazuma and show that it was the ultimate weapon the Shogun had carelessly lost.

Its aim now is Kazuha. News that he survived the Shogun's Musou no Hitotachi has spread, and the sword wants to possess him to show that the Isshin Art is the strongest. Kazuha beats it and tells it that it cannot prevail against the Shogun, because its values run against those of the Isshin Art and it has neglected itself over the years. When it refuses to accept this and threatens Yuuya, Kazuha proposes a wager: the sword may possess him and fight; if its strength proves real it keeps its claim, and if not it must let Yuuya go. The sword agrees, and Yuuya follows them in silence.

In the former hideout of the Takatsukasa Clan, Kazuha cuts through the ronin there while the sword, now in his hand, tries to imitate him rather than control him. He notes that the blade's lack of maintenance makes it hard to use. After a Kairagi falls, the last of the Tatarigami drains out, Paimon calls it a piece of junk, and the sword realises its mistakes and apologises. It releases Yuuya, who then asks for a formal duel with Kazuha and loses. Back at the Amenoma Smithy the sword's story is told to Amenoma Tougo, who expresses regret over the sword's life. The sword wants to control Kazuha once more but chooses to give up its own consciousness and be reborn, producing the Kagotsurube Isshin, its original name, to serve as reference material for the Isshin Art. Kazuha then tells Kujou Kamaji he means to study the Isshin Art and revive it as a bladesmith, though he declines an offer to stay in Inazuma. The Tenryou Commission decides not to charge Yuuya.

Owners: Original owner: an unnamed Isshin smith who fled Inazuma for Snezhnaya (no name is given in the quest synopsis). In the quest it passes through its possessed victims, notably Amenoma Yuuya, and the quest also mentions a collector, Nagato, who was injured and later found alive. Kazuha wields it for the wager fight. The Kagotsurube Isshin that results is a normal player weapon.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a four-star sword, base ATK 42, secondary stat ATK. Passive "Wandering Striker": Normal, Charged or Plunging Attacks that hit an opponent release an Accursed Spirit for AoE Physical DMG equal to 180% of ATK, once every 8s, and the wielder's DMG is reduced by 50%. The Awakened form also restores HP equal to 100% of ATK; the Shattered form does not. In the Awakened form the secondary stat is about 41.3% at Level 90 on entering the Occupied Hold and drops to about 20.7% after the second fight, making it the first weapon with different secondary-stat values at the same level.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the sword is a warning about a craft pursued only for lethality, a blade that mistook obsession for strength. A character who has met it will remember it as Kazuha's cursed opponent that chose to be reborn, not as a weapon they could own.

485.content: The Kagotsurube Isshin is the four-star sword the cursed blade becomes at the end of "A Strange and Friendless Road". Its own item text credits the swordsmith Akame Kanenaga of the Akame School, which pursued the killer-blade ideal of the Isshin Art, and says it was forged in a snow-covered northern land rather than in Inazuma. The quest presents the rebirth as the sword giving up its consciousness so that it can serve as reference material for the Isshin Art.

486.comment: Prized Isshin Blade: Isshin Art and the Tatarigami
486.content: The Kagotsurube Isshin text explains the ideal this blade distorted: "Isshin" is a stillness of mind free of distraction that lets a smith forge tirelessly, but the Akame School pursued lethality to the point that its blades often carried some evil and the school was branded undesirable by the authorities. The Tatarigami, in the text's words, is malice by nature and resents mortal desire. The Prized Isshin Blade is the quest's example of that malice taking over a weapon.

487.content:
Prototype Archaic (also: Prototype Gǔhuá): Prototype Archaic is a forgeable 4-star claymore of the Prototype series. Its description calls it an ancient greatsword discovered in Blackcliff Forge that swings with such force it seems to cut through reality. It has been in the game since Version 1.0.

The item text credits the master craftsman Han Wu and the Yun family forge with building it as the first greatsword of a new line of designs called the prototypes.

Appearance: Understated: dull, blotchy gold that hid its true strength. Its hilt is made from a rare ore and the blade from fine steel, and it weighs close to forty pounds according to the text. Swung, it shows blinding flashes of light.

Lore: It is an ancient prototype greatsword from Liyue's arsenal. The batch number has faded and no records confirm the date of production.

After the great disaster, the Yun family forge joined forces with Han Wu to push past the limits of contemporary blade design. The result was a new series of weapon models simply called the prototypes, and this greatsword was the first built to the new design. It was weighty but not unwieldy.

Han Wu travelled north through the night to hand it to a martial artist who followed the chivalric code. In a trial swing the blade howled like wind and levelled a whole bamboo forest. The martial artist praised its antique elegance, worth as both weapon and ornament, and named it Archaic.

Because of its strength, the sword became the model for thousands of greatswords in Liyue. In the Chinese text the martial artist names it Guhua ('ancient flower'), which is why its Chinese in-game name is Prototype Guhua; the wiki suggests the unnamed martial artist may be Guhua, but this is unconfirmed.

Owners: Han Wu is its maker. The martial artist who named it is unnamed in the text.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star claymore, base ATK 44, ATK% secondary stat (6 per cent). Passive Crush: Normal or Charged Attacks have a 50 per cent chance on hit to deal extra AoE Physical damage of 240 to 480 per cent ATK (by refinement), at most once every 15s. It is obtained by forging (Northlander Claymore Billet, 50 Crystal Chunk, 50 White Iron Chunk, 500 Mora). It is the claymore of the Prototype series, whose other weapons include Prototype Rancour (sword), Prototype Crescent (bow), Prototype Starglitter (polearm) and Prototype Amber (catalyst).

488.content: In the game's story texts the prototypes are the new weapon models born when the Yun family forge and Han Wu revolutionised their craft after the great disaster. Prototype Archaic is described as the first greatsword of the line, later copied thousands of times in Liyue.

489.content:
Pyro Gnosis (also: Natlan's Gnosis, Gnosis of the Pyro Archon, Pyro Archon's Gnosis): The Pyro Gnosis is the Gnosis of Natlan's Pyro Archon, Mavuika, and the only one of the seven the Fatui never obtained. Capitano fought Mavuika for it and failed. In 6.6 she gave it away so Nahida could burn the corrupted Irminsul, and it vanished in the fire. As of 7.1 nobody knows where it is.

It also holds a terrible emergency function: it could drain every soul and memory in Natlan's Night Kingdom into a net shielding the Ley Lines from the Abyss, erasing Natlan's history. Mavuika always refused to use it.

Appearance: Like every Gnosis, a small, gleaming chess-piece-like object carried inside its Archon's chest. Holding it, the Traveler found it strangely ordinary and not heavy. Canon gives no description of its specific design.

Lore: Mavuika revealed the secret in 5.1: the Pyro Archons kept it as a worst-case contingency against the Abyss. The net would cost the Night Kingdom's dead, memories and legends, and could still corrode if the Ley Lines were not repaired.

Capitano learned the secret from his dying friend Ayizu, a former chief of the Masters of the Night-Wind, who had urged Mavuika to use it several times; she refused each time. Capitano condemned her for holding a solution she would not use.

History: - 5.0: Capitano storms the Stadium of the Sacred Flame for the Gnosis; Mavuika wounds him and he escapes.
- 5.1: Mavuika reveals its function; when the Abyss puts out the Sacred Flame, she uses the Gnosis to reignite it and hold the incursion back.
- 5.3: Mavuika learns from a letter Capitano left behind that, after their duel, he had asked the Tsaritsa to release him from the Gnosis mission, and she had agreed.
- 6.6: Mavuika gives it to the Traveler for Nahida; it sinks into the Traveler "just like phlogiston", Nahida draws it out inside Irminsul, and it becomes the fire that burns Irminsul for seven days and nights. No trace of it, not even ash, is found afterwards.

Nahida first meant only to borrow it and hoped to return it; Mavuika insisted it was a gift with no "returning". She said an Archon is not left powerless without a Gnosis, called a Gnosis "basically an Elemental energy enhancer" that she did not usually use, and said Irminsul matters to all of Teyvat. Afterwards she said she had sensed its loss and wondered whether it was a knock-on effect of Irminsul's loss on a strand of fate.

Owners: Mavuika until 6.6; then briefly the Traveler and Nahida. No known holder since. Capitano sought it for the Tsaritsa but never held it.

Status as of 7.1: Missing as of 7.1; the Tsaritsa holds the other six. In 7.1 the Traveler told her it burned with Irminsul and, per Mavuika, returned to the Ley Lines. She replied that remains of the Third Descender cannot coexist with the Ley Lines for long and expects it to resurface.

Its absence matters to her: she collects the Gnoses to fight the Heavenly Principles and to open the Third Descender's seal. The Traveler's account differs from the 6.6 dialogue (no ash found; Mavuika only sensed its loss), so its fate is open.

Gameplay: Gameplay note: a story object in Archon Quest cutscenes and dialogue only; not an obtainable item.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): after 6.6 nobody holds it. Mavuika keeps her full power without it. Its soul-net function was a closely kept secret. Do not invent its reappearance, a new holder or a confirmed destruction.

490.comment: Pyro Gnosis: The Night Kingdom soul-net
490.content:
Natlan's secret last resort, revealed by Mavuika in The Flickering Light Splits in Twain (5.1): the Pyro Gnosis can drain every soul, memory and legend in the Night Kingdom and weave them into a giant net around Natlan's Ley Lines to hold back Abyssal corrosion. The cost is the erasure of Natlan's history and culture, and the net can still corrode unless the damaged Ley Lines are repaired in time. Mavuika said the Pyro Archons had to plan for the worst case given the Abyss, but she cared about how Natlan won and refused to use it except as a last resort.

Capitano knew because Ayizu, chief of the Masters of the Night-Wind, who befriended him after he fled the fall of Khaenri'ah, told him as he died. Mavuika confirmed that Ayizu had recommended using the Gnosis several times, even before the tragedy five centuries ago. Capitano told her the Ley Lines had long been destined for ruin, that an oath made five centuries ago remained unfulfilled, and that she had not kept her promise. Unable to get the Gnosis, he had his men, helped by Ororon, search Natlan for another option; it led them to the Source Mechanism and a plan to reconstruct the Ley Lines themselves rather than weave a net around them.

491.comment: Pyro Gnosis: Capitano's duel for the Gnosis
491.content: In Chapter V Act II (5.0), Capitano led the Fatui into the Stadium of the Sacred Flame to seize the Gnosis and fought Mavuika, who wounded him with one full-power strike before Night-Wind smoke carried him off. When a subordinate later suggested taking it from the weakened Archon, he refused, counting the duel as his defeat. He later said Mavuika had held back to protect the spectators, and she called them evenly matched. He said he wanted the Gnosis chiefly to save Natlan and would only have taken it to Snezhnaya afterwards. After their duel he asked the Tsaritsa to release him from the mission and she agreed (Mavuika reported this in 5.3 from a letter he left behind); Mavuika doubted the Tsaritsa would let the matter rest, since it was the last Gnosis the Fatui lacked.

492.comment: Pyro Gnosis: The Pyro Gnosis and Irminsul
492.content: In A Tower Unto Wisdom and Folly (6.6), Nahida asked Mavuika to give the Pyro Gnosis to Sumeru, and Mavuika agreed at once, saying she had long toyed with giving it to someone who needed it more. She tossed it to the Traveler outside Irminsul's barrier. Thinking hard on their memories of Pyro and Natlan, the Traveler felt it sink into their body like phlogiston; Mavuika guessed it resonated with them because they had mastered phlogiston. In Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana, during the fight with Dottore inside Irminsul, Nahida drew it out of the Traveler and it vanished into a surge of Pyro that set Irminsul's roots ablaze, while Mavuika's voice spoke of the first, purifying flame. Per Nahida the fire burned seven days and nights, leaving only the underground parts; her connection moved to Aaru. Nahida and Mavuika found no trace of the Gnosis afterwards.

493.comment: Pyro Gnosis: The Tsaritsa and the missing Pyro Gnosis
493.content: In Light and Shadow, Intertwined (7.1), the Tsaritsa's one question to the Traveler was where the Pyro Gnosis is, as they were the last to see it. The Traveler said it was reduced to ashes with Irminsul and, according to Mavuika, returned to the Ley Lines. She said she did not doubt their honesty but was surprised: formed from the Third Descender's remains, it should not coexist with the Ley Lines for long and will one day be excised, so the Fatui will find it eventually. Paimon noted that without it she cannot yet open the Third Descender's seal.

key: Astral Whispers Beyond the Sacred Throne
494.content:
Rainbow Serpent's Rain Bow (also: Rain Bow, Astral Whispers Beyond the Sacred Throne): Rainbow Serpent's Rain Bow is a 4-star bow, an ancient ceremonial weapon passed down by the Masters of the Night-Wind, dark and forever wreathed in an unshakable chill. Its story tells of a covenant between a young priest and a rainbow-winged dragon.

It was an event reward in Version 6.2 (Soulblazers' Snowbound Journey). The story picks up after Cinder City's fall and Maghan's death, and ends with the first Iktomisaurus appearing.

Appearance: Canon description: a dark bow forever wreathed in chill. Keep to that; no added carvings or colours.

Lore: Cinder City and its usurper's dream collapsed in a blaze when the scarlet-eyed hero called down the god's fiery wrath and burned the corrupt throne to ash. Decades earlier Maghan the dragon slayer had driven the old ruler from the deep valleys.

The young priest Wagadu laid Maghan to rest in a nameless grave as he had wished, took up his bow and walked into the mist-shrouded mountains. He did not understand what "renew the covenant" and "restore peace" meant; he thought he was returning the cherished bow to the Night Realm to soothe spirits abandoned since ancient sacrifices.

Past a threefold stone stair and a labyrinthine hall with gilded runes, mist brought visions: a turquoise-eyed maiden, a serpent draped in starlight, a white spider weaving sun and moon, figures of black gold and white steel, a hare mocking a fox, a coyote struggling in tar. Then a mighty dragon with rainbow wings looked down. It said it knew Wagadu's purpose, that Maghan's blade had never been stained with ancient blood, that its king was long dead and it was weary of its kin lost in dreams. It offered secret rites so his tribes could prosper and hear the night's whispers without feeding blood to the fallen envoy of the underworld.

The price was two conditions: his descendants must treat the people it once protected as friends and equals and heed their counsel, never letting oaths become a mockery as under the Grand Alliance; and they must strike its name from every woven record so no self-proclaimed sage could uncover it and ruin the pact with foolish revenge. It added that the Wayob sheltering Wagadu had been its servant and had told him of this covenant long ago. Dazed, Wagadu nodded, the hall dissolved, and a cold, feather-light touch made him turn: legend says the first Iktomisaurus stood there, newly emerged from the Night Kingdom.

Owners: Used by Maghan in the story; carried into the Night Realm by Wagadu. No modern bearer is named.

The weapon description says only that the Masters of the Night-Wind pass it down. Do not assign it to a living character.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star bow, base ATK 42 at level 1, secondary stat Energy Recharge (10%). Event reward of Soulblazers' Snowbound Journey (Version 6.2); refinement material is Refined Heart.

Passive "Astral Whispers Beyond the Sacred Throne": ATK rises for 8s after the equipping character's attacks hit an opponent while they are off-field (28% at refinement 1 to 56% at refinement 5).

How {{char}} behaves: Masters of the Night-Wind characters treat this as tribal origin lore and may be careful about speaking the dragon's name, since the covenant asks that it be erased.

key: Astral Whispers Beyond the Sacred Throne
495.comment: Rainbow Serpent's Rain Bow: Astral Whispers Beyond the Sacred Throne
495.content: Astral Whispers Beyond the Sacred Throne is the passive of the bow Rainbow Serpent's Rain Bow (gameplay): hitting enemies while off-field grants a temporary ATK boost.

key: Records of Hanan Pacha book collection
496.content:
Records of Hanan Pacha (also: Records of Hanan Pacha book collection): Records of Hanan Pacha is a three-volume collection of Natlan folk tales about the Sage of the Stolen Flame, Waxaklahun Ubah Kan. Vol. 1 tells how he and a companion, Chaac, tricked a vain winged dragon and took the power of phlogiston. Vol. 2 tells how they raised the land of Hanan Pacha and taught people to use it. Vol. 3 tells how the people broke a taboo and were driven out. The game itself labels it a fable with no basis in historical fact.

The narrator is an unnamed storyteller who speaks to listeners and jokes with them about the plot. The books give Natlan's popular account of how humans first gained phlogiston and how the first permanent tribe came to be.

Appearance: A readable book collection in Natlan, in three volumes. Vol. 1 and 2 are found at the Scions of the Canopy (on crates near the patrolling guard Yawar, and next to Amauta); vol. 3 is in front of Battuta at the Stadium of the Sacred Flame. No author or publisher is listed.

Lore: Told in the age of dragons, when the Lord of the Night ruled the night realm and no Pyro Archon yet existed. Humans had no Visions and were at the mercy of the elements until the Sage brought phlogiston from the "red and black land".

The sage tricks a vain dragon and takes its phlogiston, raises Hanan Pacha with Chaac to teach people, then expels them after the Lord of the Night gets them drunk. Chaac goes on to found settled tribes.

- Vol. 1: A winged dragon, heir to the volcano lord Xiuhcoatl, claimed the sleeping lord's treasures, among them Pyrophosphorite, a rainbow crystal refined from the volcano's primal fire. Its glow made the dragon vain. The Sage blinded one eye with a bamboo blowdart, then he and Chaac posed as eye doctors and talked the dragon into letting them swap its eyes, fangs and claws for grainfruit.
