The dragon died, the Sage cracked open the crystal rather than give it to the Lord of the Night, and gained the dragons' power, called phlogiston.
- Vol. 2: Humans rejected phlogiston, since fire and fuel were already easy to find; the Sage argued that one day wood would run out but rock never would. Chaac's blunt idea was to raise a great stone above the mountains so curiosity would draw people. The two lifted a whole stretch of land, Hanan Pacha, above the clouds. Chaac guarded the lake and helped people ascend, and those who reached it learned phlogiston from the Sage and formed the first permanently settled tribe.
- Vol. 3: The people built a gem, feather and flower city and the Sage wished to raise the land higher, forbidding all food from the land beneath, allowing only water, since the Source of All Waters lies beyond the Lord of the Night's control. They fished and grew ball algae. The Lord of the Night, fearing humanity's departure, disguised as a tribesman and gave Chaac sweet water that was actually grain alcohol. Everyone was drunk when the Sage returned; he expelled them, they carried phlogiston across Natlan, and he set out "on the road home". Chaac then accepted the Lord of the Night's guidance and founded settled tribes on the land.
- Tone and framing: Chaac is called "the fool" and speaks casually, while the Sage is "the wisest in history". The narrator also pauses to correct rival tellings and answers a heckling listener, so scenes quoting the book should keep this storyteller's voice.
- The Sage's plan to climb ever higher is hinted rather than explained: only the phrases "Lunar continent" and "Newark Holy Stone" are given, and Chaac does not understand them. The wiki notes the second is a nod to a real-world hoax, which fits the collection's fictional-fable status.
- Related lore the book is cited for: The Upper Sanctum entry says that, according to legend, Hanan Pacha was created when the Sage and Chaac raised a tract of land into the sky and shared phlogiston there with those who passed their trials. Today it is a ring of smaller islands in the Toyac Springs area, reached through Spiritways.
- Chaac's own page cites the book for his tale: first human to receive phlogiston, founder of the first tribe, then leader of the scattered tribes after the exile.

- Names echo real-world mythology (Hanan Pacha, an Inca realm of the sky; Chaac, a Maya rain god); this is wiki etymology, not in-game explanation.

Owners: No individual owns it; the volumes lie at fixed locations in Natlan.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible book collection with no stats. Volumes are found in Natlan at the Scions of the Canopy and the Stadium of the Sacred Flame.

497.comment: Records of Hanan Pacha: Sage of the Stolen Flame
497.content: In the Records of Hanan Pacha, the Sage is the cleverest figure in history, who took phlogiston from a dragon, taught it to humans and raised Hanan Pacha, then left Natlan after the people broke his taboo. The text says his homeland is not named and implies he will one day return. The book is a fable; do not use it as proof of what he actually did.

498.comment: Records of Hanan Pacha: Hanan Pacha (legend)
498.content:
In the tale, Hanan Pacha was once a whole stretch of land floating above the clouds, visible from anywhere in Natlan. People came up through the power of phlogiston to learn from the Sage and settled there. Today the Upper Sanctum is a ring of islands, accessible only via Spiritways.

The legend says the Sage wanted to raise it higher still and demanded that its people eat only water and food grown on the islands themselves.

499.comment: Records of Hanan Pacha: The Winged Dragon and Pyrophosphorite
499.content: The fable's dragon is a vain winged creature in the red and black lands that took the treasures of the sleeping volcano lord Xiuhcoatl. Its pride rested on Pyrophosphorite, a rainbow crystal of primal fire. The Sage and Chaac blinded and tricked it with disguises and grainfruit replacements, and the Sage broke the crystal to gain phlogiston.

500.content:
Records of Jueyun (also: Jueyun Records): Records of Jueyun is a six-volume book collection of folk stories, myths and legends of Liyue by an author named Wuyuan. Each volume handles one tale: living stone beasts, a Sea God who takes brides, the haunted ruins of Wuwang Hill, the lonely seelie of the mountains, the gentle qilin, and the ancient Dunyu Ruins. The in-game blurb calls it quite a page turner.

The collection shows how ordinary Liyue people explain their landscape, and what local belief says about adepti and illuminated beasts. It is hearsay, not history: the compilers repeatedly hedge.

Appearance: Six short prose pieces in a storyteller's voice, each under a single-title heading (Stone Beasts, Palace Beneath the Sea, Wuwang, Mountain Spirits, Qilin, Hidden Jade). The narrator mixes local rumour with dry asides, such as noting that nobody has actually seen a stone beast move.

Lore: - Vol. 1, Stone Beasts: Liyue's animal statues are said to wake on cool autumn nights and wander. Qingce elders say they are illuminated beasts who fought beside Rex Lapis in the Archon War and asked him to turn their mortal flesh to lasting stone.
- Vol. 2, Palace Beneath the Sea: a Sea God collects a village bride each festival in return for calm seas. One bride is released, keeps his sea-snail shell, and years later blows it when her own daughter is to be given up; the village is drowned.
- Vol. 3, Wuwang: Wuwang Hill, north of Mt. Qingce, is haunted by spirits that lure travellers off the path.
- Vol. 4, Mountain Spirits: seelie are held to be good omens that guide travellers and Vision-bearers to treasure.
- Vol. 5, Qilin: gentle illuminated beasts of the mountains who sometimes take human form and live among mortals.
- Vol. 6, Hidden Jade: the Dunyu Ruins, north of Nantianmen and northwest of Liyue Harbor, were a walled city whose people sealed it and left.

- Vol. 1 says locals who know the land have long noted that animal statues change place and posture overnight, and that campers hear a deep sound like flowing water. Bishui River fishermen, Silvergrass harvesters of Dihua Marsh and old miners share the story. The narrator admits nobody has witnessed a stone beast moving.
- Vol. 2 ends cruelly: the Sea God's tidal embrace swallows the sleeping village and its elders, and mother and daughter ride his clam carriage into the sea. The Sea God had earlier said his palace sheltered women who were driven from their villages.
- Vol. 3 explains the name: Wuwang means prudence, so the hill is where the prudent are punished. A village lies abandoned at its foot. A Qingce children's fable says its young people threw themselves into the Bishui River, enchanted by a distant sea monster's song, and drifted to the Sea of Clouds. The text then offers an explanation for the haunting: the ley lines remember what people forget, and unconsciously recreate the dead village's past as spirits.
- Vol. 4 gives two readings of the seelie: auspicious souls of departed adepti or old benevolent gods, or echoes of friendless strangers who guide the lost home. A mountain legend adds that seelie once had beautiful bodies and great wisdom, long before the adepti, and links their ancestor to a traveller from the Sea of Stars, an oath witnessed by the three sisters of the Lunar Palace, and a catastrophe thirty days later that separated them and wiped their memories. The narrator dismisses all this as incoherent folk tale.
- Vol. 5 says that after the Archon War many adepti withdrew from society at Rex Lapis' direction, but some illuminated beasts chose to stay and help mortals, leaving unusual bloodlines in Liyue Harbor. A tale of a young qilin who ate a herb gatherer's lotus-leaf clothes at a mountain pool and took human form has two endings: she leaves a child in a basket at his door, or she stays and raises children with him.
- Vol. 6 says Dunyu means the land to which beauteous jade flees. The legend tells of a star that fell onto the plains west of Liyue and made the chasm, from which jade emerged and supported a thousand years of mining. A fragment fell in northern Lisha and later leapt back to the sky, leaving a pit where humans built fortresses. These kept good relations with Liyue Harbor until about 500 years ago, when the black calamity and the rise of the Abyss led the residents to seal the city and leave. The text says even the old adepti and yaksha are silent about why.

- Vol. 1 and the book Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti both describe illuminated beasts serving Rex Lapis: in one they become stone, in the other warriors who suffer under the lingering bitterness of defeated gods.
- Vol. 4 is explicitly framed as legend about a time before Rex Lapis, and the narrator stresses it lacks credibility. Use it for atmosphere or in-world rumour, not as confirmed history of the seelie.

- The wiki notes that Vol. 4's claim that seelie guide only Vision-bearers is misleading: seelie also guide people without Visions in other canon.
- Vol. 6's reference to the black calamity places the sealing of Dunyu around the Cataclysm, about 500 years ago. Use the Dunyu Ruins and Cataclysm entries for details beyond this book.

Owners: No individual owner. Vol. 1: Granny Ruoxin's home in Qingce Village; Jifang gives it as a dialogue reward. Vol. 2: Wuyuan gives it as a dialogue reward; Jifang also sells it. Vol. 3: a restaurant table at Wangshu Inn where Huangshan sits. Vols. 4-6: sold by Jifang at Wanwen Bookhouse in Liyue Harbor.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible book collection read for lore only.

501.comment: Records of Jueyun: The Sea God's Bride
501.content: A Liyue folk tale in Records of Jueyun Vol. 2. Each festival a village sends a bride to a Sea God in exchange for a year without storms. One bride is freed and given a conch to sound when she regrets leaving; she does so when the elders come for her daughter, and the Sea God drowns the village. The god is not identified.

key: hill where the prudent are punished
502.comment: Records of Jueyun: Wuwang Hill Legend
502.content: Per Records of Jueyun Vol. 3, Wuwang Hill is haunted by lingering spirits that imitate the voices of the dead and lead travellers astray. The book gives a Qingce children's fable and an explanation that the ley lines unconsciously replay the abandoned village's past.

503.comment: Records of Jueyun: Dunyu Ruins Legend
503.content: Records of Jueyun Vol. 6 says Dunyu is the land to which beauteous jade flees. A star fell on the plains west of Liyue, making the chasm; a fragment fell in northern Lisha, and the Dunyu fortresses were built in the pit it left. Their people sealed the city and left about 500 years ago, at the time of the black calamity; the reason is not known, even to old adepti and yaksha.

key: Mighty Redhorn Stoic Stonethreshing Gilded Goldcrushing Lion Lord
504.content:
Redhorn Stonethresher (also: Redhorn Pestle, Mighty Redhorn Stoic Stonethreshing Gilded Goldcrushing Lion Lord): Redhorn Stonethresher is a five-star claymore whose item story is a folk tale. Its full name is the "Mighty Redhorn Stoic Stonethreshing Gilded Goldcrushing Lion Lord", and it was the beloved blade of an eccentric known as the "Otogi Kongou Lion King". Because both names were too long, the village children called the weapon the Redhorn Pestle and its wielder the Otogi King.

The tale is told partly in affectionate mockery: the Otogi King was a boaster with real strength, and the weapon's legendary reputation outlived the man who never returned.

Appearance: The item story describes the Redhorn Pestle as a weapon made from an enchanted monster's horn. It does not describe colour or shape beyond that; the in-game model is a very large blade. Avoid inventing further detail.

Lore: In the children's telling, the weapon's bite made bake-kitsune, bake-danuki and evil demons beg for mercy, and even the Great Tengu Reizenbou of Mt. Yougou feared it. The children did not believe this. The text says the Otogi King really was strong, so strong that seven men together could not push him out of a sumo ring, and that he would kick a tree to bring down fruit for children who could not reach it. He also once kicked down a whole tree, a Lavender Melon tree, and was chased into the mountains by an old man.

Other tales have him crash an official autumn leaf-viewing concert while shouting that the Lion King had arrived and demons should beware, then wrestle a small oni who happened to be in the mood for a bout, with a result the text calls too tragic to watch. He never earned the right to wear the Shogun's colours, so the children doubted he could ever tame the "youkai of song". He answered such doubts with excuses, such as having had the chills after a long night of drinking, and promised to cut off the horns of the monsters and to deal with the creatures from beyond the ocean. He also told the children to follow the fox envoy and hide, saying he would come back for wrestling bouts later.

The text then reports what became of the boasts. The oni who wrestled him, remembered by the children as having flung him into the sky, later fled with her arm and horn cut off; the Great Tengu withdrew into the mountains and woods and no longer appeared before humans; and so the empty boasts attached to the greatsword came true in the end, though the Lion King himself never returned. The Lavender Melon tree he kicked down was tended and bore fruit again. The tale sits against the larger historical background of the Cataclysm (the "creatures from beyond the ocean") and the Kitsune Saiguu, but the item text never names the Cataclysm or the Saiguu outright in connection with him. Uraku Misugiri's item text gives a more concrete picture of him as someone "of the Front Gate" who loved plays, toys and fine clothes, and whose usual weapon in anecdotes is a huge blade with a long, hard-to-pronounce name, which that text identifies as this one.

Owners: Former owner: the Otogi Kongou Lion King, called the Otogi King by children. No other owner is named. The same figure is the recipient of Uraku Misugiri in that sword's text. The weapon is an ordinary player weapon in-game.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star claymore from the Otogi King series, base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT DMG 19.2%. Passive "Gokadaiou Otogibanashi": increases DEF by 28-56% and adds bonus damage to Normal and Charged Attacks equal to 40-80% of DEF at refinement 1-5. It was the event-exclusive weapon of the Version 2.3 Epitome Invocation, alongside Skyward Harp.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the weapon is a boast turned into a legend. It suits characters who tell the story with relish and a touch of teasing; anyone solemn about it will be missing the tone of the text. Do not give the Otogi King a death scene that the item does not supply.

505.content: The Otogi King is the nickname given by village children to the Otogi Kongou Lion King, a loud, eccentric Inazuma warrior who carried the Redhorn Pestle and bragged that he would send monsters packing. The Redhorn Stonethresher text portrays him as a boastful prankster; Uraku Misugiri's text adds that he loved plays, toys and clothes and went into battle in gold brocade with painted features. It also describes him as an oni who earned the villagers' nickname "The Great Idiot" and did not dislike it. His name remains unconfirmed beyond those titles.

506.comment: Redhorn Stonethresher: Redhorn Pestle and Mikoshi Chiyo
506.content: In the tale, the Otogi King wrestled a petite oni who, in the children's memory, tossed him into the sky. The wiki links the unnamed petite oni to Mikoshi Chiyo, who in the text later loses an arm and a horn and flees; the item text itself does not name her. Uraku Misugiri's text shows an Oni Chiyo dancing with a sword, linked to the same wiki page.

507.content:
Reed Miller's Cognoscenti Keepsakes (also: Proof of the Cognoscenti, Proofs of the Cognoscenti, Cognoscenti keepsakes, Memorata-Cognoscenti's Jest, Inscripta-Cognoscenti's Feather, Devocina-Cognoscenti's Sorrow, Weavenexa-Cognoscenti's Intoxication, Stratagema-Cognoscenti's Mask): The Proofs of the Cognoscenti are five quest-item relics in Nod-Krai, each "said to be a keepsake from Reed Miller", founder of the Treasure Hoarders: a silver mask, a black feather, a stopped timepiece, a goblet and a rusted flower. Legend says they point to his Great Treasure. The Traveler collects all five in East of the Moon, West of the Sun.

"Reed Miller" was an alias worn by at least three people, so the legend the keepsakes carry is deliberately tangled. The collective name used here is this archive's label, not an in-game title.

Appearance: - Stratagema-Cognoscenti's Mask: a cold, plain silver mask with no decoration but the frosty moonlight on its surface.
- Inscripta-Cognoscenti's Feather: a feather as dark as night.
- Devocina-Cognoscenti's Sorrow: a timepiece that stopped long ago.
- Weavenexa-Cognoscenti's Intoxication: a lavishly decorated goblet.
- Memorata-Cognoscenti's Jest: an artificial flower stained with rust.

Lore: Folk retellings of the master thief, mixing legend and rumour, not eyewitness history.

- The Feather recalls the old order in Snezhnaya, where nobles ruled under the Tsar, and how the master thief raised a black raven banner and called the poor and hungry to build an "Elysium" from the wealth of the high and haughty.
- The Mask describes a thief who wore a silver mask after surviving a failed execution, then took it off after the Cataclysm; rumour offers several reasons for the mask (hiding from searches, covering the executioner's marks, weariness of the crowd's love and hate). It ends with moonlight pouring from a high tower and destroying the silver and the resolve in "her" eyes.
- The Goblet tells of the thief after the mask came off: assuming many identities and soothing the people with song and wine, with a legend that grew until singer and subject blurred.
- The Timepiece (Sorrow) is a grieving, first-person meditation on fallen dreams: a prophesied ruler who never ruled, a would-be heir who could not break her bonds, a maid left with nothing, and an adopted son who failed to save the one he loved and took a commoner's forgotten name. It admits the tokens are the author's counterfeits that can still lead the finder to "our great treasure".
- The Flower records the master thief's most famous tricks (a fake medallion to empty a governor's palace, posing as the Tsar's envoy to drain a viscount's treasury), his promise to a partner named Alia not to take risks, and the execution that ended the first thief, followed by the woman who took his name and hid behind a mask. Its closing words are a defiant claim that "a murder of crows" would rise.

Read together with the Reed Miller lore page, the texts line up with three bearers of the alias. Avrelian, the original, founded the Treasure Hoarders and was executed after turning himself in. Alia, who had followed him, took the name and led the Hoarders, stealing Grand Duke Prokhor Trubetskoy's treasures in one night. Brahe, Trubetskoy's adopted son who loved her, took the name afterwards and spread contradictory legends so the name could not be used to justify harm. Tolfin, a character in the quests, estimates that about 20% of the legend comes from Alia, 30% from Brahe and the rest is invention.

The Flower names Solovei as the master thief's best friend, who regretted the execution. The Timepiece's lines on a "maid" singing beneath the nightingale's tower and a woman who "heralds the new moon" connect to Aila and the Frostmoon Scions only through the wiki's link annotations; the text itself names no one, so treat these as readings, not statements.

Owners and finding: All five end up with the Traveler, one per quest in East of the Moon, West of the Sun. The first four can be done in any order; the Flower unlocks only after the other four.

- Feather (Whisper Beneath the Waves): hidden in an Exquisite Chest beneath the Eye of Kratti, a whirlpool known for wrecking ships. Captain Grettir of the Atlas and others failed to get it and met misfortune; the Traveler restores the roots of a strange tree that grew there and reveals the chest.
- Mask (The Tale-Telling Heart): found in a treasure trove at Blue Amber Lake, kept by Papa Wrench (the new identity of the missing Mr. Shesternin). After Papa Wrench's death, Tolfin inherited it and used the Proof as bait to test Papa Wrench's son-in-law Zhorik; Zhorik overlooked the mask, and the Traveler took it.
- Goblet (The Shoemaker's Children Go Barefoot): Poruchik Raskolnikov of the Fatui's Kuuvahki Experimental Design Bureau had recovered it for Snezhnaya, but Omesov's drunken announcement in Nasha Town drew treasure-seekers into the Bureau. Raskolnikov "loses" it to the Traveler and Netochka, declaring the Fatui would spend no more resources on Proofs, and Netochka lets the Traveler keep it.
- Timepiece (Return to Sender): found in an abandoned bunker in Wavechaser Plain built against the "apocalypse" (the Abyss); an Abyssal entity inside calling itself the Ultimate Calamity believes the apocalypse still rages. The Timepiece had been left by Miller for Grazina.
- Flower (The Raven's Legacy): held by Hiljetta, Tolfin's grandmother, until a worthy successor appeared; she tests the Traveler in a friendly spar and hands it over, though she is displeased at Tolfin's withheld truth.

Before the Traveler reached Nod-Krai, the Fatui were already seeking the Proofs, which is why the Kuuvahki Bureau held the Goblet. Netochka fancies herself the next Reed Miller and gives the Traveler and Paimon roles from the legends, showing how the name has become a costume anyone can wear.

Gameplay: Gameplay (labelled): the five are quest items with no combat or stat use; the wiki styles them as flower, plume, sands, goblet and circlet pieces only for presentation.

508.comment: Reed Miller's Cognoscenti Keepsakes: Proof of the Cognoscenti
508.content:
Five relics said to be keepsakes of Reed Miller, the Treasure Hoarders' founder, that legend claims point toward Reed Miller's Great Treasure: Memorata-Cognoscenti's Jest (flower), Inscripta-Cognoscenti's Feather (plume), Devocina-Cognoscenti's Sorrow (sands), Weavenexa-Cognoscenti's Intoxication (goblet) and Stratagema-Cognoscenti's Mask (circlet). The Traveler gathers them in East of the Moon, West of the Sun. Their texts retell the Reed Miller legend, which canon shows was shaped by several people using one alias, and one text calls the tokens counterfeits.

Whether any of them is a real heirloom is left open. Do not have a character state that the Proofs are certainly authentic, or certainly fake.

key: silver mask of the master thief
509.comment: Reed Miller's Cognoscenti Keepsakes: Stratagema-Cognoscenti's Mask
509.content: A plain silver mask under frost-pale light. Its item text says the master thief wore it after surviving a failed execution, then removed it for good after the Cataclysm; rumours say he wore it to hide from the searches in Snezhnaya, to cover executioner's marks, or from weariness of the crowd. The thief scorned both gods and nobles. The last line, which switches to "her" and moonlight from a high tower, suggests the wearer at the end was a woman (the wiki reads this as Alia), but the text does not say so directly. Obtained in The Tale-Telling Heart.

510.comment: Reed Miller's Cognoscenti Keepsakes: Inscripta-Cognoscenti's Feather
510.content: A night-black feather whose text recalls Snezhnaya before the Cataclysm: nobles ruled for the Tsar, the poor were told the nobles bore "the sin of fullness" on their behalf, and the master thief raised a black raven emblem to gather the despised and promise an Elysium built on the wealth of the haughty. It is found beneath the Eye of Kratti in Whisper Beneath the Waves.

511.comment: Reed Miller's Cognoscenti Keepsakes: Devocina-Cognoscenti's Sorrow
511.content: A timepiece that stopped long ago, left by Miller for Grazina in the bunker in Wavechaser Plain. Its text mourns the failed dreams of a prophesied ruler, a would-be heir, a maid and an adopted son, and admits the tokens are counterfeit work that can nevertheless guide a finder to the great treasure. Obtained in Return to Sender (listed as added in 6.3).

512.comment: Reed Miller's Cognoscenti Keepsakes: Weavenexa-Cognoscenti's Intoxication
512.content: A lavishly adorned goblet. Its text describes the master thief after the mask: no longer chasing fallen nobles' wealth, taking many identities and spreading song and wine among both nobles and commoners until the thief and the legend blurred. The Fatui held it first; the Traveler gets it in The Shoemaker's Children Go Barefoot.

513.comment: Reed Miller's Cognoscenti Keepsakes: Memorata-Cognoscenti's Jest
513.content: A rusty artificial flower. Its text collects legendary tricks played on the powerful, notes that the first master thief "never lied" and promised his partner Alia he would not take risks, and ends with the execution and the woman who then took his name. It is the last Proof, given by Hiljetta in The Raven's Legacy.

514.content:
Reliquary of Truth: Reliquary of Truth is a 5-star catalyst added in Version 6.1. The in-game description calls it an angular box carved from gold and jade that legend says was once enshrined in a temple deep within Tulaytullah, the Sapphire City. Its story is about a young noble named Goudarz, who is given a power by a holy sage in exchange for an honest answer, and who rises as the king Saleb Dowleh, a king whose reign is built on lies.

The weapon connects to the Sapphire City and its Tighnarian people, a part of the Great Red Sand's history after King Deshret. It also links to the Lunar-Bloom reaction in its gameplay passive.

Appearance: An angular box of gold and jade. Canon text gives no more detail than that.

Lore: After the great tower of Shah Ramshahr fell, the royal power passed among states as fleeting as dew. The nobles of Tulaytullah, free of the tyrant, followed false sages into new carnage. By the time the brutal Khagans arrived on horseback, no warriors guarded the Garden of Endless Pillars, and foreign soldiers and tax collectors preyed on the weary people. People then looked back to the brief reign of King Humayun.

The young noble Goudarz enters a sacred hall beneath the sands, the palace of the Ibis King, wisest of the seven sage monks and keeper of records. The wise men of Tighnar had long fled and the sanctuary lay buried. From a dried-up spring a voice answers him and says it can grant a power never seen by prophet or proselyte, but only if he answers the riddles that the lord of flowers and oases left for the sage's master, King Deshret, who fell into a poisonous dream before answering. Goudarz asks to hear them and promises honest, mortal answers.

The sage poses a first riddle: what rises and falls endlessly, perishing at its peak and swelling again like the moon and tides, desired by wise and foolish alike. Goudarz answers that it is conspiracy and treachery, and that this weakness brought down the sapphire domes. The sage laughs without confirming the answer, and hands him the Staff of Falsehoods. Goudarz's name is lost and replaced by the title King Saleb Dowleh, a warrior who would not tell lies who gains kingly power through cunning and casts the illusion of a golden age.

The close is a reversal. Eventually even the perfect lie cannot satisfy his thirst for power and King Deshret's creations can no longer fake divine manifestation. When the Ibis King's voice repeats the question amid the laments of Gurabad, the aged king answers that all he speaks are lies and that he will fight to the death at least so as not to betray again the trust of the brothers who have come to help; whether the holy one seeks truth or falsehood, he must taste it in his own blood. The Deys of other tribes seize his power, and the kingdoms are ground to dust. The sage takes the king's last words as his final answer. These names appear in no other source gathered here, so tell the tale as the legend the item itself calls it.

Owners: No owner is named. Goudarz, later King Saleb Dowleh, receives the Staff of Falsehoods in the story; the reliquary itself is only said to have been enshrined in a temple of Tulaytullah.

The story does not explain how the weapon came to be a catalyst or who carries it now.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star catalyst released in Version 6.1 (2025-10-22), level 1 base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT DMG. Passive Essence of Falsity raises CRIT Rate; casting an Elemental Skill grants Secret of Lies (Elemental Mastery for 12 s), dealing Lunar-Bloom DMG grants Moon of Truth (CRIT DMG for 4 s), and when both are active their results are increased by 50%.

At refinement 1 the CRIT Rate bonus is 8%, Secret of Lies gives 80 Elemental Mastery and Moon of Truth 24% CRIT DMG; refinement 5 gives 16%, 160 and 48%.

How {{char}} behaves: Good for legends of rulers and sages in the Great Red Sand. The box suits scenes about truth and falsehood. As canon does not say more, keep any claims about the object itself modest.

515.comment: Reliquary of Truth: Essence of Falsity
515.content: Essence of Falsity is the weapon passive of Reliquary of Truth (gameplay): CRIT Rate, an Elemental Mastery buff after Elemental Skills (Secret of Lies) and a CRIT DMG buff after Lunar-Bloom DMG (Moon of Truth). The names echo the story of a king ruling by lies and a sage who wanted truth.

516.content:
Retracing Bolide (also: Summer Night's Bloom, Summer Night's Finale, Summer Night's Moment, Summer Night's Waterballoon, Summer Night's Mask): Retracing Bolide is an Inazuma artifact set from launch (Domain of Guyun). Its five "Summer Night's" pieces record, in a man's voice, meetings with a fox-eyed woman at summer festivals near Mt. Yougou: lost as a child, nursing a sprained ankle as a teenager, and as an adult hoping to see her again. The wiki links her to Kitsune Saiguu.

The set is framed as an Inazuma ghost story about meetings between the human and the inhuman. It is a memory of kindness and parting, not a monster tale.

Lore: At a summer festival a lost child, separated from his parents by the crowd carrying the divine palanquin, cries by the torii gates on the road to the shrine. A beautiful woman with fox-like eyes takes his hand and offers to see fireworks, throw darts and play fusen. Years later, on a festival night, the same woman sits beside him on a rock by the wayside, unchanged after ten years, and invites him to watch the fireworks with wine.

The woman never ages: in the pocket-watch piece, the teenager (hurt, with a broken watch while the girl he admired fetched ointment) meets her after ten years and she has not changed. Later, in the dart piece, he is a man whose wife is pregnant; he climbs the mountain carrying the water balloon from age seven, the fox mask from seventeen and a flower that would not wilt, and thinks he sees her in white on the same rock, but it is only a sunbathing fox that flees, leaving an old throwing dart.

The flower piece describes an undying summer flower as the last remembrance of a "foxy-eyed woman who eventually disappeared without a trace", set against the idea that life lies in change, meeting and parting. The mask piece describes masks cast in the image of a fox deity: people wear them hoping to gain her power of transformation. It says that in Inazuma's legends everything has a spirit but most spirits have been driven into the forests by the Shogun's suppression; many still believe thousand-year-old animals gain power. A note on the back, written in a lovely hand, says she left under cover of fireworks and that they will likely never meet again.

The narrator wonders why he expected to meet her again: no matchmaker introduced him to his wife, money was short and an heir took time, yet his days were full of happiness. The pieces keep it ambiguous whether the fox on the rock was her.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): 4 and 5 star set from the Domain of Guyun and its strongbox. 2-piece: Shield Strength +35% (affects only the wearer). 4-piece: while shielded, +40% Normal and Charged Attack DMG. Introduced in 1.0.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present it as a wistful Inazuma festival memory. The fox-eyed woman is kind, teasing and unexplained; do not state definitively that the fox on the rock was her.

517.content: The goblet piece: a finely made water balloon. The narrator as a child is separated from his parents at the summer festival, cries by the torii gates and is found by a fox-eyed lady who offers fireworks, darts and fusen.

518.content:
The sands piece: a stopped pocket watch. On a festival night, a young man walking to the shrine with a girl he admired hears a lost child crying, falls and breaks the watch. A masked woman sits by him on a rock and offers to watch the fireworks.

She says few know the spot, notes he has grown, and has not aged in ten years. They are to watch the fireworks with wine.

519.content: The plume piece: a wooden throwing dart. The man, whose wife is expecting, climbs Mt. Yougou with the water balloon, mask and flower; he sees what looks like the woman in white but finds only a fox that flees, leaving a dart.

520.content: The flower piece: an artificial summer festival flower that never wilts. It is the final thing left to remember the foxy-eyed woman who disappeared without a trace.

521.content: The circlet piece: a mask in the image of a legendary fox deity. People wear such masks hoping to gain her transformation ability. A note on the back apologises for leaving under the fireworks and wishes the finder well.

522.content:
Revelations of Divine Love: Its theme, per the in-game description, is the distinction between the love of the gods and human love. It concludes that compassion, friendship and romantic affection are all imbued with the sacred, since they arise from the same longing for freedom.

Appearance: A quest item with an icon and description only. No text of the poems can be read in game.

Lore: The Anemo Archon is the god of freedom in Mondstadt, so the book's conclusion ties human warmth to the divine and to freedom alike. The authorship claim is hedged ("said to have been composed"), and no priest is named.

**How it is given.** At Dornman Port, Hannelore listens to confessions and prays to Barbatos. If the Traveler has used Special Perfume: Wind's Breath and offers her a bottle, she says a sister of the Church cannot accept such gifts, because beautiful things belong to the wind and not to one person. She hands over this book as a small return gift and wishes the Traveler a road of virtue, freedom and compassion. In her ordinary dialogue she explains that Dornman Port's sanctuary was torn down by the Gunnhildr Clan after they threw a bishop sent from Mondstadt out of its tower, to break with the tyrannical Imunlaukr Clan and an aristocracy-bound Church, and that it was never rebuilt.

**Limits for portrayal.** Only the description's summary of the book's argument is canon; do not invent verses or a named author. Hannelore's refusal to keep the perfume and her gift of the book are consistent with her stated view that beautiful things belong to the wind. The English title matches a medieval real-world devotional work (wiki naming trivia), which carries no in-world meaning.

Owners: Hannelore gives it to the Traveler. No other owner is established.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: a Quest Item with no combat function, obtained through Hannelore's perfume dialogue branch (wiki: Luna VI, taken as 6.5), together with 2 Hero's Wit and 21,500 Mora.

523.comment: Revelations of Divine Love: Hannelore and Dornman Port
523.content: Hannelore is an open-world nun of the Church of Favonius at roofless Dornman Port, where she listens to the confessions of merchants and sailors. In the perfume branch she declines to keep the Traveler's gift and gives Revelations of Divine Love in return. The wiki has no further profile for her.

524.content:
Rex Incognito (also: Rex Incognito novel): Rex Incognito is a four-volume Liyue fantasy novel telling of Rex Lapis' incognito excursions among mortals. A framing story set in the antique shop Xigu Antiques, run by Min'gui, surrounds tales of a jade craftsman and a harsh fishing-boat owner. Its running theme is that rules matter less than a person's own judgement, and that a relic is worth its story.

The in-game blurbs say fact merges with fiction. Treat it as popular Liyue literature about the Geo Archon, not as history; its closing twist deliberately undermines its own claims.

Appearance: Four unillustrated chapters in alternating voices: a shop-set frame, then nested stories-within-stories. The mood is wry and playful, with an unnamed visitor who is a pedantic young expert with amber or golden eyes and dark long robes.

Lore: - Vol. 1: At night, Xigu Antiques of Feiyun Slope is visited by a black-robed young man who calls a damaged jade plaque in her shop a modern counterfeit. He argues that ancient tribes of Rex Lapis' followers carved such plaques as stand-in currency before Mora existed. The owner, Min'gui, says she can disprove his verdict with a story.
- Vol. 2: A prankish jade carver in Mingyun Village is asked by an amber-eyed woman to carve the true likeness of the Lord of Geo from what he has seen, or go unpaid. He delivers a plaque showing a woman and explains his three-day process of learning, observing and carving by heart.
- Vol. 3: A harsh fishing-boat owner in Liyue Harbor docks the pay of a new hand, a bashful youth from Qingce Village, who tells him a story about a jade plaque while someone takes the docked wages from the owner's pocket and returns them to the labourers.
- Vol. 4: Back in the shop, Min'gui argues that antiques are valued for their stories. The young noble buys the plaque, and admits his jade-currency theory was invented.

- Vol. 1 lists the shop's curios: a Fontaine timepiece, Sumeru incense, a Mondstadt aristocrat's goblet, a stool an adeptus once sat on, a teacup the Lord of Geo sipped from and a vase the Anemo Archon accidentally broke. The plaque, bought from an adventurer who brought it out of an abandoned palace deep in the abyss, cost Min'gui much of her fortune.
- The young man notes that this plaque carries a woman's image, unusual for the period, and that there is no historical record or physical evidence of Rex Lapis ever taking female form.
- Vol. 2's carver was known for contrary commissions, such as a fleeing boar for a hunter statue and an empty throne for a ruler. The Lord of Geo was rumoured to be cold and unfeeling, but trusted because his laws made trade fair.
- Vol. 3's youth asks why a person should do the work they hate most; the owner says that is how the world works, and the youth replies that perhaps that was not what Rex Lapis meant by his rules.
- Vol. 4 draws the moral that Rex Lapis never forced mortals to live by contracts as a perfect template, since the rules are a means rather than the end, and that a balance lies in people's awareness and choices.

- The Vol. 1 appraisal names Orobashi (pearls and shells), the Mistress of Chenyu Vale (jade), Zhongli (rocks) and Havria (salt) as sources of idol materials for forgotten gods. The visitor says idols were made from these materials in the likeness of each god.
- Vol. 4 finishes with its twist: after hearing Min'gui's story, the noble son declares he will take the fake, because the story is what makes it worth buying.

- Each of Vols. 2 and 3 ends as the visitor-figure begins another story (the woman "reminds me of another story"; the Qingce youth offers "a story about a certain jade plaque"), so the volumes read as stories nested inside the antique-shop argument.
- The in-game blurbs say the novel tells of Rex Lapis' incognito excursions, but the text never states that any visitor is Rex Lapis. Keep that distinction when characters discuss it.

Owners: No individual owner. Vol. 1 is on a table in Qingce Village's main plaza, Vol. 2 is at the bottom layer of the north boat docks in Liyue Harbor near the flower shop, Vol. 3 is at Wangshu Inn, and Vol. 4 is sold by Jifang at Wanwen Bookhouse.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible book collection read for lore only. A separate soundtrack piece of the same name exists and is not part of this item.

525.comment: Rex Incognito: Min'gui and Xigu Antiques
525.content: In Rex Incognito, Min'gui is the first owner of Xigu Antiques on Feiyun Slope, an antique shop open after moonrise for wealthy customers. She is a skilled storyteller who sells relics by their legends and spars with a pedantic young visitor over a jade plaque.

526.content: The central object of Rex Incognito: a damaged jade plaque showing a woman's likeness. The visitor calls it a recent counterfeit and says ancient plaques were a form of tribal currency. In the finale he admits that currency theory was his own invention.

527.comment: Rex Incognito: The Mingyun Jade Carver
527.content: In Rex Incognito Vol. 2, a prankish jade carver in Mingyun Village makes a plaque of the Lord of Geo as a woman after a three-day process of learning, observing and carving blind. He cannot explain why it came out that way.

528.content:
Rhinedottir's "Gift" (also: Rhinedottir's Gift, Rhinedottir's "Gift" quest item): Rhinedottir's "Gift" is a quest item from the world quest Old Friends and New Knowledge (Version 6.2). It is the present that Rhinedottir sent to her creation Albedo through her cat Sebas, and it carries a short riddle about a tree, its perfect fruit and a seed of dreams. Albedo's only response is that he needs to think.

It follows the completion of the final task Rhinedottir set Albedo, and it works as the start of a new problem rather than a reward in the usual sense: the item's own description calls it a new gift and a new quest.

The quest belongs to the Witch's Homework line in Dragonspine, set after Albedo has finished his master's last assignment and is finding idle time unfamiliar.

Appearance: Canon does not describe the object. Sebas only says the gift is on the table at Albedo's campsite. What the item shows is its text: two lines in the voice of Rhinedottir.

The wiki lists it as a 4-star Quest Item.

Lore: Albedo's master Rhinedottir sends the gift via Sebas, her old cat-butler, together with a spoken message. The message says that once a problem is solved, dwelling on it loses its point, and urges Albedo to pose questions of his own instead of resting on answers. The gift's text then compares a tree proud of its most perfect fruit with a "seed of dreams" that refuses to be only the king of a universe confined to its flesh.

Rhinedottir also teases that Albedo may be bored, asks him to bring questions she has never considered, and warns him not to build a "self" whose only purpose is asking questions, since she tried it and it failed. She adds that the gift should be kept well and that Sebas need not be fed.

Albedo calls Sebas a kind of family member, created by Rhinedottir long before himself, and says Sebas used to help him tidy vials and jars and sometimes modelled for his sketches. Sebas, for his part, says he runs Rhinedottir's large house as its butler. After the riddle is read, Albedo says he needs to think, and his post-quest line is simply "New questions...".

Sebas also mentions he has another message to deliver in Mondstadt to someone whose "birth" was recent and whose task Rhinedottir foresaw (a player who has completed A Child Wandering the World hears him refer to Durin instead). The riddle is never explained in the quest, so its link to Albedo's nature is left to the player.

Owners: Albedo, to whom it is addressed and delivered. The Traveler receives it as a quest reward in the game's mechanics, but within the story it is Albedo's.

Gameplay: Gameplay note: a 4-star Quest Item received on completing Old Friends and New Knowledge. The quest also unlocks Albedo's Book of Blinding Light talent. It has no combat use.

529.content:
Rhinedottir's "Gift" is a quest item from Old Friends and New Knowledge (6.2): a present sent to Albedo by Rhinedottir through Sebas. Its text contrasts a tree's perfect fruit with a "seed of dreams" that will not settle for being king of a universe confined to its flesh. Albedo takes it as a prompt to think and the riddle is never explained. The object itself is not described.

It arrives with Rhinedottir's message urging Albedo to pursue questions rather than answers, and not to create a self whose only purpose is to ask them.

530.content:
Ring of Yaxche (also: Yaxche Ring, Echoes of the Plentiful Land): Ring of Yaxche is a 4-star catalyst you forge: a jade vessel made by a hero of yesteryear, said to have shot down the giant dragon of the volcano. Its story belongs to the twin heroes Ahpub and Ixquieh.

Page 1 is their triumph and vow; page 2, unlocked later, is how the same bond ended.

Appearance: Canon says only that it is a jade vessel. Do not add shapes or inscriptions beyond that.

Lore: In the age of myth, when great dragons roamed Natlan, the lost twin heroes reunited before an evil dragon's corpse and swore, upon sacred Yaxche, to end death, destruction and pain, and to ensure the strong never again bully the weak.

Their father had died through a Dragonlord's whim and their mother sacrificed herself to protect them, and without the Collective of Plenty and the clans of the mines they could never have reunited.

They ventured out on the paths of "strength" and "blessings", the young man hot-tempered and the young woman calm, each covering the other's shortcomings. To the conceited self-proclaimed sun god they offered a duel: three lightning strikes from him, and if he failed to kill them, three blows from them. With strength beyond mortal ken they weathered the lightning and shot the false sun from the sky with a blowdart.

For the earthquake-causing great dragon they used deceit instead: they offered it a healing salve and an imitation gem forged with fire unknown to mortals, which fooled the dragon into drinking an elixir that stripped its power, and it was buried alive in the mountains. Their adventures became the origin of the traditions of the Collective of Plenty and the mines. At the crossroads they met the warrior (the wiki gives Xbalanque) and walked with him into the night wind, vowing that Ahpub's blowdarts and Ixquieh's forge-fires would be his.

Page 2 (unlocked after Serenity's Reprise) is set when the tribal banners were not yet dusty and the new King of Cinder City had not yet seized the highest authority. The twins, once inseparable, were divided by their positions: Ahpub was a warrior of vengeance and blood, while Ixquieh the flame-forging artisan viewed dragonkind differently. Ahpub had never openly opposed the hero's prohibition, but his hatred of dragons was known. When the Lord of the Cinder City ordered the fleeing wicked dragons pursued, only Ahpub among the heroes answered; as Chief he led the Collective of Plenty's warriors to the mines and demanded that the Nanatzcayan ruler hand over the "ferocious beasts hidden in the mountains" or face their blades.

After days of standoff he invited his twin sister to talk. She told him the real oathbreakers were the usurper and the new King, and warned that harming these peace-loving Saurians would make Nanatzcayan treat him as an enemy of the Alliance. Enraged, he drew his blade to her throat to cow her, but blood spurted forth and ended the talk, and he walked into the incinerating fire holding her. The beacons of war were extinguished along with the disappearance of the two Chiefs. The King sent emissaries to ask the tribes to hand authority to the Alliance until new Chiefs were chosen, while secretly noting the names of those who sheltered dragons. Sakkuk, later proclaimed the tribe's agent, was not yet aware of her fate, and the young heir of the Flower-Feather Clan was already offering the usurper more secret counsel.

Owners: No wielder is named. The ring is a jade vessel attributed to the heroes of the legend.

The text links it to Ahpub and Ixquieh in spirit but names no specific owner; the story that it "shot the dragon" is legend, and scenes that put it in a character's hands are inventions.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a forgeable 4-star catalyst of the Salutary series, base ATK 42 at level 1, secondary stat HP; introduced in Version 5.0.

Forging: Borderland Catalyst Billet plus Condessence Crystal (50), White Iron Chunk (50) and Mora (500). Passive "Echoes of the Plentiful Land": using an Elemental Skill grants the Jade-Forged Crown effect for 10s, in which every 1,000 Max HP raises Normal Attack DMG by 0.6% at refinement 1 up to 1% at refinement 5, with a cap of 16% to 32%. Ascension uses Sacred Lord Delirious materials, Will-series boss materials and mask common materials.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: a Natlanese storyteller could tell page 1 as a triumph and hold back page 2. Do not claim the legend settles whether the twins died.

531.comment: Ring of Yaxche: Echoes of the Plentiful Land
531.content: Echoes of the Plentiful Land is the passive of the catalyst Ring of Yaxche (gameplay): after an Elemental Skill it grants Jade-Forged Crown, which turns the wielder's Max HP into Normal Attack DMG.

532.comment: Ring of Yaxche: Ahpub and Ixquieh
532.content: Ahpub and Ixquieh are the twin heroes of the Ring of Yaxche legend: he a hot-tempered warrior who became Chief of the Collective of Plenty, she a calm artisan who ruled the Nanatzcayan mines. They defeated dragons together, then were divided over how to treat the peaceful Saurians, as told on page 2 of the ring's story.

533.content:
Royal Bow: Royal Bow is a 4-star bow of the Royal series, an old royal longbow of the erstwhile rulers of Mondstadt. Countless generations later its string is still tight and fires with great force. Its text is about the fall of the ruling Lawrence Clan and the Knights of Favonius exiling them.

It is the Royal series' bow, made of premium materials with master craftsmanship, which the text gives as the reason it is still as powerful as ever.

Appearance: A longbow of fine, long-lasting materials whose string is still taut after generations.

Lore: Hunting was once a pastime of the nobles. They showed their strength in the natural world and shared the spoils with the people in benevolence. Benevolence was lost, and with it their reign.

After the uprising, the Lawrence Clan that had long ruled Mondstadt was overthrown. The newly established Knights of Favonius judged long investigations unnecessary in the name of benevolent governance, and the clan was promptly cast out, never to return.

A first-person passage by a clan member recalls leaving: a father sighing at the betrayal of the people and the end of a glorious era, former subjects rejoicing in the open country, and the speaker's later realization that it was the Lawrence Clan who had betrayed the people and closed the history books.

The text names Vennessa as the last push that toppled a crumbling tower, and lists earlier flames of resistance: the phantom thief praised in secret by the people, the woman who could see death, and the Wanderer's Troupe intent on revolution. It closes that the spirit of resistance is in Mondstadters' blood. The wiki links these to Parsifal, the Blue-Eyed Spear Witch and the Wanderer's Troupe.

Owners: No owner is named; the text says only a noble who ruled Mondstadt.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star bow, base ATK 42, secondary stat ATK 9%, sold in Paimon's Bargains. Passive Focus: dealing damage increases CRIT Rate by 8% to 16% by refinement per stack, up to 5 stacks, and a CRIT hit removes all stacks.

534.content: Focus is the shared passive of the Royal series (gameplay). It stacks CRIT Rate on hits and resets on a CRIT hit.

535.content: Per the Royal Bow text, the Lawrence Clan was overthrown in an uprising and cast out by the Knights of Favonius without lengthy investigation. A clan member later concluded that the clan had betrayed the people, not the reverse.

536.content:
Royal Greatsword: Royal Greatsword is a 4-star claymore of the Royal series, an old greatsword once used by the nobles who ruled Mondstadt, made of the finest materials and described as a weapon for royals only. Its text covers the noble duty to fight monsters and the history of gladiatorial combat.

Even after being passed down for generations it is described as good as new.

Appearance: A large, finely made greatsword that has aged without losing its condition. The wiki notes Eula is shown with it in a character teaser and a Collected Miscellany video.

Lore: Combat was once a responsibility of the nobles, who protected their people from monsters. They all but forgot that duty, which turned them into the very monsters they once sought to destroy.

The text says research suggests gladiatorial combat began in a religious context during the aristocracy's rule, as a sacrificial ceremony held jointly with prayers to the gods. It was later turned into a perverted sport for the Lawrence Clan's pleasure and abolished by the Knights of Favonius, who now outlaw it.

Some texts of the original prayers survive. In one, the fighter asks the guardian winds of Mondstadt to look after themselves, their friends, their countrymen and their opponent, and hopes the clash of blades and offering of sweat and blood please them. In another, they ask the winds for strength when exhausted and wisdom to tell good from evil when uncertain.

The prayers are a useful scene detail for how Mondstadters once addressed wind in a martial setting. Keep them as surviving texts, not as a current practice, since the Knights ban gladiatorial combat.

Owners: No owner is named; the text says only that nobles used such greatswords.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star claymore, base ATK 44, secondary stat ATK 6%, sold in Paimon's Bargains. Passive Focus: dealing damage increases CRIT Rate by 8% to 16% by refinement per stack, up to 5 stacks, and a CRIT hit removes all stacks.

537.content: Focus is the shared passive of the Royal series (gameplay). It stacks CRIT Rate on hits and resets on a CRIT hit.

538.content: Per the Royal Greatsword text, gladiatorial combat began as a religious sacrificial ceremony with prayers to the gods, became a bloodsport for the Lawrence Clan, and was abolished by the Knights of Favonius.

539.content:
Royal Grimoire (also: royal mage's grimoire): The Royal Grimoire is a four-star catalyst of the Royal series. It is a wax-treated scroll that once belonged to a royal mage of Mondstadt, holding both historical accounts and spells. Its item story is mainly a bitter note on how the nobility and their mage tutors failed Mondstadt, and on an oath whose wording was lost.

Appearance: Item text describes a delicate scroll treated with wax against decay and moth damage; the catalyst is a scroll, not a bound volume. Nothing further about its look is stated, so avoid inventing detail.

Lore: The text says royal mages were charged with nourishing the water and soil, fighting monsters and tutoring the nobles, so their research covers history, governance, management and culture, and is still described as forward-looking. When the people overthrew the royals, the mages were exiled too, because they had abandoned their duty to instil virtue in the nobles and become birds of a feather with them.

The second half recalls early Mondstadt, when the Lawrence clan was led by Venerare. Under her the people raised a tall statue in the plaza to mark the Anemo Archon's descent; beneath it the leader of all the clans put an oath of protection for Mondstadt. Over the years the Lawrence clan abandoned its forebears' ideals and the statue was taken down, and the court's mages never spoke of the history or the oath again. In the age of the Knights of Favonius the statue was rebuilt, but the original wording of the oath was lost for good.

The story is told by a later chronicler and gives no date for the overthrow beyond the era of the aristocracy. It shares the oath-and-statue theme with the Royal Longsword, whose text records an ancient oath sworn after the Anemo Archon descended, but each item presents its own account and neither claims to be the lost inscription. Treat the scroll as an indictment of complicit scholarship: knowledge kept for the powerful and silence about the people's history.

Owners: Item text names no individual owner, only a royal mage of Mondstadt.

Klee is shown wielding this catalyst in her official character demo and in a Collected Miscellany video; that is presentation, not a canon statement of ownership.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Royal-series passive 'Focus' stacks CRIT Rate on damaging hits (up to 5 stacks, reset by a CRIT). Four-star catalyst, base ATK 44, ATK 6% secondary. Obtained from Paimon's Bargains. This is gameplay, not in-world lore.

540.content:
Royal Longsword (also: longsword of the old nobles): The Royal Longsword is a four-star sword of the Royal series. It was the sword of a noble who ruled Mondstadt, made of premium materials and still as sharp as ever. Its item story laments that noble swordsmanship, once meant to refine wisdom and elegance, decayed into formality, and recalls an oath of protection sworn 2,600 years ago.

Appearance: Item text calls it exquisitely crafted, with carvings and embellishments that testify to its owner's stature. No specific design is described.

Lore: Swordsmanship was once a required skill for nobles, but as a discipline for wisdom and elegance rather than for combat. Both qualities were eventually all but forgotten and the skill became a formality, even though the sword itself stayed sharp through generations.

The story then turns to 2,600 years ago, the era of Mondstadt's most ancient inhabitants, who swore a solemn oath after the new Anemo Archon descended and reformed the world. The oath has two parts: devotion to the plains, hills and forests of Mondstadt, and devotion to its lasting freedom from the blizzard (Boreas) and the tyrant (Decarabian), whose coldness and oppression the text calls one and the same.

The closing lines promise that whatever may come, human tyranny or monster infestation, and even if the tablet bearing the oath is destroyed, the oath will be carried by the winds and defend Mondstadt like a loving father. The 'as always' refrain matches the Gunnhildr clan's motto as quoted in Jean's voice-over, per the wiki; the item itself does not draw the connection.

Owners: Item text names only a noble who ruled over Mondstadt.

Albedo is shown wielding this sword in his official character demo and a Collected Miscellany video; that is presentation, not a canon ownership claim.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Royal-series passive 'Focus' (stacking CRIT Rate, max 5 stacks, cleared by a CRIT). Four-star sword, base ATK 42, ATK 9% secondary. Obtained from Paimon's Bargains.

541.content:
Royal Spear (also: noble's hunting spear): The Royal Spear is a four-star polearm of the Royal series. It was kept in the collection of a Mondstadt noble, remains as sharp as the day it was forged, and in the aristocracy's own time never left the dark. Its story contrasts noble sword-fighting with the spear as a commoner's weapon.

Appearance: The text mentions only that the spear is premium work and that the legendary one was emblazoned with a noble house's crest. It bathed only in pale moonlight in the old days.

Lore: The old nobles held that people of high blood fought with swords and that clashing blades were the chorus of lofty souls, whereas spears and bows were for plebeian gladiators and commoners. Commoners with pitchforks and sharpened poles could still threaten sword-wielding scions, which the rulers of Old Mondstadt found hard to accept, so the spear was kept out of sight.

A legend tells of a noble youth who asked a smith to make this weapon, marked with the house crest, and who, like the weapon, never earned the family's favour without bloodshed. Wanting change, the youth chose power even through an ignoble weapon, accepting that the spear-wielding shadow would only ever be seen by moonlight.

The wiki links the youth to Eberhart, a figure of the same age of rebellion against the aristocracy. The item text never names them, so this tie is recorded in uncertainties. The spear thus pairs with the Royal Longsword and Royal Grimoire as another view of the old nobility's blind spots.

Owners: No named owner. The legend refers only to a noble youth.

Rosaria is shown wielding the base version in her character demo, Collected Miscellany and the Version 1.4 trailer, and an ascended one in a birthday artwork; that is presentation, not a canon ownership claim.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Royal-series passive 'Focus'. Four-star polearm, base ATK 44, ATK 6% secondary. Obtained from Paimon's Bargains; released in Version 1.1.

542.content:
Sacrificer's Staff (also: Untainted Desire, Archpriestess's staff): A silver-white polearm, pure and without blemish, which legend says the Archpriestesses of Hyperborea used to guide their flock of Frostmoon Scions. A 4-star polearm of the Frostmoon Scion series from Version 6.1.

Its text is Lovia's turn from compassion to authority.

Appearance: A silver-white staff-like polearm. The text mentions an antlered crown worn by Lovia later, but that is separate from the staff.

Lore: A fading Archpriestess hands the staff to her kind adopted daughter Lovia, telling her only her mercy can open the eyes of the lost.

Lovia was an orphan from another land, unaware of it, and never blessed with the moon's light. The pale Frost Moon no longer gazed down and the faithful were turning away, so the frail Archpriestess put her adopted daughter on the fragile throne, hoping kindness would unite her followers.

Lovia took "right" as absolute: feeding the hungry, tending the sick, mending suspicion with sincerity. Her faith was broken when the maiden of the purest bloodline, her sister by bond, was cut down by a traitor's blade while shielding her. Lovia could not even cry out.

She concluded that the kindness of the weak was an unforgivable delusion. If the true moon would withhold hope, lies would be spun into a gentle dawn; if the new moon never rose again, absolute authority would rule the mortal dream. Those who defied her were to be washed away in blood, until her late sister's orphan was born the sacred heir. She came to don the antlered crown, "pure, defiled and illusory", wrapping herself in it like a cocoon. The text keeps the traitor unnamed.

Owners: The text passes the staff to Lovia, the last Archpriestess; no current wielder is named.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star polearm, base ATK 45, CRIT Rate secondary. Passive Untainted Desire grants ATK and Energy Recharge for 6 seconds after Skill hits, up to 3 stacks, even off-field.

How {{char}} behaves: Present it as a weapon of sad, devout rule. Do not assert that Lovia is the only portrayal; other texts give a different background.

543.content: Untainted Desire is the weapon's passive; its name fits Lovia's turn toward absolute devotion. Mechanics are in the gameplay section.

544.content:
Sacrificial Bow: Sacrificial Bow is a 4-star bow of the Sacrificial series, in the game since Version 1.0. Its item text calls it a ceremonial hunting bow petrified by time, once the property of the proud Lawrence clan of old Mondstadt, who used it in ritual reenactments of their victory over the frozen wilderness.

The Sacrificial weapons are linked to ceremonies honouring Time and Anemo together; the Bow's story is the one in which a clan's self-image decays from conquerors to overlords to kings.

Appearance: A hunting bow with trinkets still visible on it, which the in-game description says has been petrified over time. The text adds that it was once a prop with an immobile bowstring, but the string became flexible and sturdier with the passage of time. Do not invent further decoration.

Lore: The Lawrence clan used the bow to act out their ancestors' conquest of the frozen wilderness in sacrificial ceremonies, and the bow itself was said to tell the story of the pioneers and their hardships.

On the cliff facing the eastern sea, the ancestors are said to have worshipped the masters of Time and Anemo together; the item text quotes a saying that Anemo brings stories while Time nurtures them. The ceremony's first act told how the forebears took the land through wisdom and strength. The ceremony was eventually lost, but the clan kept playing the same role.

According to the item text the role became corrupted: the clan's view of itself shifted from conquerors to overlords and then to kings, and they strayed into depravity and lost the affection of Mondstadt's winds. The text is a legend-style narration with no named narrator and gives no dates.

Read with the other two Sacrificial weapons, the Bow is the cautionary member of the set: the Sword (Gunnhildr clan) keeps its guardian role, the Greatsword (Imunlaukr clan) finds something to fight for, while the Lawrence clan's tale ends in decline. How this corresponds to Mondstadt's recorded history (for example the clan's fall) is covered by the clan and Mondstadt history entries, not by this item text.

Owners: The item text names the Lawrence clan as the bow's former owners. No individual wielder is named.

Further details: Diona is briefly seen holding a Sacrificial Bow in her anecdote in the Travelers' Tales: Anthology Chapter event (a limited-time event). It is a cameo, not a story claim of ownership.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star bow, base ATK 44, Energy Recharge secondary stat. Passive Composed: after an Elemental Skill deals damage, it has a 40 to 80 per cent chance (by refinement) to end its own cooldown, at most once every 30 to 16 seconds. Obtainable from the Standard Wanderlust Invocation and from character and weapon event wishes; part of the Sacrificial series.

545.content: The Lawrence clan is the former owner of the Sacrificial Bow per its item text: a proud clan that reenacted its ancestors' victory over the frozen wilderness in ritual, and whose self-image corrupted over time from conquerors to overlords to kings, costing it the affection of Mondstadt's winds. See the clan's own entry for its history.

546.content:
Sacrificial Fragments: Sacrificial Fragments is a 4-star catalyst in the Sacrificial series from Mondstadt. Its description calls it a weathered script whose text is no longer legible, a cursed item eroded by the winds of time. Present since Version 1.0.

The Sacrificial series are props from early Mondstadt's wind-worship rituals; the wiki notes this script is the only one described as cursed and with no clan named.

Appearance: Canon describes only a weathered script whose text is illegible. As a catalyst it is shown as a book or script; no further detail is given.

Lore: Early Mondstadt built theaters atop windy cliffs and performed rituals as stories and ballads, because they believed the gods enjoyed stories.

The script is millennia old and now illegible. A long-ago war between the Lord of Storm and the Great Wolf King of the North buried Mondstadt in blizzards; a group who could not bear the cold built a clifftop shrine in the east to pray for mercy. Later generations presumed the shrine had always been for the wind alone.

The text says the wind blows for a moment, but the ravages of time are constant, unrelenting and irreversible. A god of the winds may move between pages of a book, but the merciless god of time will eat away at them until no legible word remains. Yet time's assault and the wind's often take their toll on the heart alike, which is perhaps why people forgot the shrine's older purpose.

The wiki reads the series as relics of the Thousand Winds Temple, associated with the new Anemo Archon's rise and with Istaroth, and notes that the Sacrificial Sword belonged to the Gunnhildr Clan, the Greatsword to the Imunlaukr Clan and the Bow to the Lawrence Clan, while Fragments names no clan. That interpretation is the wiki's reading of the item texts. The Lord of Storm in the text is Decarabian; the Great Wolf King of the North is Boreas, whose later Nod-Krai role is covered elsewhere.

Owners: No owner or clan is named in the item text.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore: a 4-star catalyst, base ATK 41, Elemental Mastery secondary stat (48). Composed gives a chance for an Elemental Skill that damages an opponent to end its own cooldown, with a cooldown on the effect. It can be obtained from Wishes, including the standard Wanderlust Invocation and weapon event Wishes.

How {{char}} behaves: This archive's suggested use: a relic that shows how old stories are lost, useful in scenes about forgotten worship or the slow erosion of memory. Keep it unreadable; do not supply the lost script.

547.content: Sacrificial Fragments is a 4-star catalyst of the Sacrificial series, a millennia-old Mondstadt script now illegible and called a cursed item eroded by the winds of time. It comes from the era of cliff-top theaters and wind-worship.

548.content:
Sacrificial Greatsword: Sacrificial Greatsword is a 4-star claymore of the Sacrificial series, in the game since Version 1.0. Its item text describes a ceremonial greatsword that began as a prop and was hardened by time, once belonging to the Imunlaukr clan, brave and gifted warriors who fought hard and died young.

It tells a story of war and was used to enact war tales in sacrificial ceremonies dedicated to Time and Anemo.

Appearance: A greatsword with trinkets still visible on it, described in game as petrified over time. The text says its blade, originally only a prop, was hardened by the passage of time. No other detail is given.

Lore: The Imunlaukr clan used it in sacrificial ceremonies to enact duels between brave warriors stained black with blood.

On the cliff facing the eastern sea, the ancestors are said to have worshipped the masters of Time and Anemo together; the item text quotes a saying that Anemo brings stories while Time nurtures them. In the clan's eyes, combat existed neither for protection, glory nor territory but for the amusement of the gods high in the heavens. They fought monsters and outlaws alike with no regard for whether they would return to their loved ones, and the point was to roar loud and clear in the heat of battle.

The text observes that such hot blood should not have allowed a long history, since their fight was endless and without hope of victory. Yet as the snow slowly melted and Mondstadt began to take shape, they gradually realized they had at last found something to fight for. It is a legend-style narration with no named narrator.

Compared with its siblings, the Greatsword is the one whose clan changes purpose: the Sword's Gunnhildr clan guard Mondstadt and the Bow's Lawrence clan decline, whereas the Imunlaukr move from fighting for the amusement of gods to fighting for a place. Specific people and events of the clan belong in the clan entries.

Owners: The item text names the Imunlaukr clan as former owners. No individual wielder is named.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star claymore, base ATK 44, Energy Recharge secondary stat. Passive Composed: after an Elemental Skill deals damage, it has a 40 to 80 per cent chance (by refinement) to end its own cooldown, at most once every 30 to 16 seconds. Obtainable from the Standard Wanderlust Invocation and from character and weapon event wishes; part of the Sacrificial series.

549.content: The Imunlaukr clan is the former owner of the Sacrificial Greatsword per its item text: warriors who treated battle as entertainment for the gods and died young, until they found something to fight for as Mondstadt took shape. See the clan's own entry for its history.

550.content:
Sacrificial Sword: Sacrificial Sword is a 4-star sword of the Sacrificial series, in the game since Version 1.0. Its item text describes a ceremonial sword, originally a prop and sharpened by time, that belonged to the kindly Gunnhildr clan, who enacted the defense of Mondstadt in rituals for the winds of time.

Its story is one of protection, meant to show the courage to protect.

Appearance: A sword with trinkets still visible, described in game as petrified over time. The text says its blade, originally just a prop, was sharpened by the passage of time. No other detail is given.

Lore: The Gunnhildr clan used it in sacrificial ceremonies that enacted the defense of Mondstadt.

On the cliff facing the eastern sea, the ancestors are said to have worshipped the masters of Time and Anemo together; the item text quotes a saying that Anemo brings stories while Time nurtures them. The ceremony dedicated to the winds of time had three acts, and the final act told a tale of the protection of Mondstadt, of life, and of freedom.

The text says the ceremony and its history are now lost, but that the Gunnhildr clan continues to act as guardians of Mondstadt to this day. This ties the item to the clan's real role in the city's history without adding named individuals.

Of the three Sacrificial weapons it is the hopeful one: where the Bow's Lawrence clan decays and the Greatsword's Imunlaukr clan seeks a cause, the Gunnhildr clan's ritual role and real role coincide. The Gunnhildr clan's history belongs in its own entry.

Owners: The item text names the Gunnhildr clan as former owners. No individual wielder is named.

Further details: Albedo is seen wielding a Sacrificial Sword in his official art. This is an art detail, not a statement of ownership in the story.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star sword, base ATK 41, Energy Recharge secondary stat. Passive Composed: after an Elemental Skill deals damage, it has a 40 to 80 per cent chance (by refinement) to end its own cooldown, at most once every 30 to 16 seconds. Obtainable from the Standard Wanderlust Invocation and from character and weapon event wishes; part of the Sacrificial series.

551.content: The Gunnhildr clan is the former owner of the Sacrificial Sword per its item text: a kindly clan who enacted the defense of Mondstadt, of life and of freedom in ceremony, and who still act as guardians of the city today. See the clan's own entry for its history.

552.content:
Sakura Bloom (also: Sakura Blooms, Hiou-kyuu): Sakura Bloom is a petal that has fallen from the Sacred Sakura of the Grand Narukami Shrine, and a local specialty of Inazuma found on Narukami Island. Electro energy keeps the petals floating in mid-air.

Item text says the blossoms are filled with a fondness for Inazuma, and attaches to them local legends about the Thunder Sakura.

Appearance: Clusters of pale petals drifting in the air rather than lying on the ground, found around Narukami Island and especially near Mt. Yougou and the Grand Narukami Shrine. They only come together into a collectable bloom when touched by Electro.

Lore: The description calls them petals from the Sacred Sakura at the Grand Narukami Shrine, suspended by Electro. It adds that, according to legend, the roots of every Thunder Sakura join deep underground, and that following them always leads back to this sacred tree standing guard over Inazuma.

A second legend in the same text holds that the Thunder Sakura are parts of the Almighty Narukami Ogosho, who divided her divine form so as to defend those under her rule more fully. The text presents this as one folk account among others, not as established fact.

Owners: No notable owner. It belongs to the shrine's sacred tree and is gathered freely by travellers.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore: an Inazuma local specialty added in Version 2.0, found on Narukami Island and used for cooking and character ascension. To harvest a floating cluster, a player must use an Electro ability, touch it while Electro-affected, or carry an Electrograna. In Japanese the name is written with an older character form for sakura, a detail noted by the wiki.

Its Japanese name is Hiou-kyuu (緋櫻毬), roughly "scarlet cherry ball", written with an older form of the sakura character. The Chinese name 绯樱绣球 is read by the wiki as most likely meaning an embroidered ball too, though the same word can also mean hydrangea.

Many of the blooms lie around Mt. Yougou and the Grand Narukami Shrine, so the specialty is spatially bound to the shrine whose tree the text names as its source. Wiki farm guides count 55 blooms in total on the map.

key: Chalice of Your Blood and Sorrow
553.content:
Scarlet Proof (also: Honor to Your Devotion, Glory to Your Legacy, Time Gifted Unto You, Chalice of Your Blood and Sorrow, Testament to Your Faith): Scarlet Proof is a 4- and 5-star artifact set for Stellar Swirl teams, released in version 7.0. Its five pieces are bright red Fatui keepsakes (a flower medal, a quill, a pocket watch, a wine bottle, a helmet), and each carries a short vignette about a Fatui member in the Tsaritsa's Snezhnaya: Sandrone, Pulcinella, Capitano, Dottore and Pantalone.

The tone is dry and personal: how members joined, what they quietly carry and how the organisation treats talent as fuel for its "grand ideal".

Appearance: All five items are described as bright red: a flower ornament symbolising blazing glory, a quill, a pocket watch, a wine bottle and a helmet. The Fatui recruitment poster in the Flower bears a scarlet flower, which is the medal promised to those who devote themselves to the cause.

Lore: - Honor to Your Devotion: Miss Guillotin, who had come from Fontaine after Duke Alain Guillotin's death, sits in a Snezhnograd square. In Fontaine she had talked with a branch president who praised a foreign bank; in Snezhnaya she met the Director of the Fatui, who spoke of saving the world by destroying the old. She later became Marionette, or Sandrone, and took on a Harbinger's duties.
- Glory to Your Legacy: a fae named Mirko joined the Fatui, studied under Mayor Ioanna Ivanovna and as Pulcinella watched a young man, Ajax, grow into a Fatui officer who showed him an old recruitment quill.

- Honor to Your Devotion: she watched the Adventurers' Guild window where Katheryne works, no longer surprised since learning of the Guild's deeper purpose in Snezhnaya. Sometimes she feels herself part of the Fatui's "voracious beast". The text says she had been given thermal and taste systems like a human's by Alain and wanted to test how well they would hold up in cold.
- Glory to Your Legacy: Mirko (Pulcinella) divides groups into the young, the old and the hopeless in between. He chose to apply to the Fatui to ensure a place in the coming world, and reports to Ioanna Ivanovna, Speaker of the Snezhnograd Veche, a human; observers read it as ambition or swallowed pride. He competes with Pantalone for control of the Adventurers' Guild, and eventually watches Ajax (Childe) grow. After a morning meeting, he talks to Capitano about it, and Tartaglia soon shows off a quill from the Fatui's earliest recruitment that Capitano gave him; it is several centuries old.
- Time Gifted Unto You: Pulcinella set up counselling rooms for the Fatui. Capitano, who took off his helmet there, listens to a former student, a soldier with one remaining hand, whose squad was sent to quell a disturbance in a remote region and came back shaken. Locals believed it was still the age of the Belyi Tsar. Dottore later judged that the area was suffering virus-induced mass hysteria linked to cannibalism, treated the soldiers and called it reasonable; Capitano questioned that word.
