The soldier leaves his medal, quill, bottle, helmet and watch with Capitano before retiring.

- Chalice of Your Blood and Sorrow: Dottore, under the persona Zandik, walks into an isolated, backward village in a birch forest to run a drug experiment, bringing animal scraps as a gift, and later notes that psychotropic drugs can control minds in either direction. A curious child asks about the butterfly on his bottle; he tells the child it is "a four-eyed monster", then loses interest. He then returns to the castle of Fatuus as Dottore.
- Testament to Your Faith: Pantalone sits alone in the Fatui's theatre box. He recalls being sold by his mother as a youth, being sold again, and learning how money multiplies from a foster father before reaching powers beyond the nobles. He notes the "newest Harbinger" (Sandrone) interrupts him, that he has ceded her share of the Adventurers' Guild's profits, and that Dottore, newly returned, needs a place for an experiment that Pantalone knows of.
Across the set the Fatui appear as people who joined for their own reasons, tolerated by a pragmatic system, not simply as a monolith. The Sands vignette is the set's own frame: the red items are a retired soldier's leftovers, and Capitano keeps them to pass on.

Owners: No single owner. The items are linked with the Harbingers named in each vignette; the Sands says a retiring soldier left five red items with Capitano to give to those who come after.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): 4- and 5-star set from the Inverted Glacier domain (Everfrozen Earth, Snezhnaya). 4-piece: for 10s after the wearer triggers a Stellar Swirl reaction, their CRIT Rate +16% and their Stellar Swirl reaction DMG +40%.

key: Chalice of Your Blood and Sorrow
554.content: Artifact set of red Fatui keepsakes whose item text offers short portraits of Sandrone, Pulcinella, Capitano, Dottore and Pantalone.

555.content: According to the Time Gifted Unto You text, Pulcinella arranged quiet rooms for Fatui members to talk with a companion they trust. Capitano is described as a kind of walking counselling room because colleagues confide in him. The text says Lohefalter, Dottore and Pantalone each used the rooms, or did not, in small anecdotes. Treat these as item text.

556.content:
Scion of the Blazing Sun: Scion of the Blazing Sun is a 4-star bow: an ancient longbow from King Deshret's era, carved with indecipherable ancient text and solemn patterns. Its story traces the priests of King Deshret's kingdom, their archery, and the descendants who still keep the old ceremonies in secret.

It is a Battle Pass (Gnostic Hymn) reward from Version 4.0 and belongs to the Gnostic Hymn 2 series.

Appearance: An ancient longbow carved with indecipherable text and solemn patterns.

Lore: In the era when the desert king ruled the land, authority covered it like sunlight over the dunes. The nomads' surviving songs sing of that golden age, and say the red lord once contended against the bright sun and fell to the earth like a meteorite. Some priests were not slain by the kings and princes who followed and passed down King Deshret's art of archery.

The priests' descendants call themselves the "Heirs of the Burning Sun" and continue the ceremonies of the old kingdom without ceasing. Few have the right to inherit the priests' legacy, few can read the ancient texts, and fewer still master the combat arts the priests prized: cudgel, spear and, above all, archery. The Eremites call such people "ascetics".

Some ascetics have turned their loyalty to the only surviving God King of Sumeru, while most vanished into the desert among snakes, scorpions and specters. Those loyal to the rainforest keep the habits of being hidden and silent, repaying an ancient favor, yet mourn their ancestors and King Deshret, who met with disaster millennia before. The art and ceremony of archery survive in their hands even though the meaning of many texts and pictures has been lost or corrupted.

The text ends with a darker branch: ascetics who strayed from the priests' path, grew obsessed with mirages of authority, tried to mold the nomadic tribes, and used the strict old ceremonies to train lost children as "Falcons". To help bring about a new "king" they trained mindless Falcons and dogs. The text calls this another tale, saying those with great ambition often vanish into the desert without a sound.

Owners: No in-world owner is named. The wiki notes Sethos wields the ascended bow in his character introduction, which is promotional use only.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star bow, level 1 base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT Rate 4%. Passive The Way of Sunfire: after a Charged Attack hit, a Sunfire Arrow descends on the opponent hit, deals ATK-based damage and applies Heartsearer for 10 s, increasing Charged Attack DMG the opponent takes from the wielder; once every 10 s.

At refinement 1 the Sunfire Arrow deals 60% ATK and Heartsearer adds 28% Charged Attack DMG taken; at refinement 5 these are 120% and 56%.

How {{char}} behaves: Use it as a relic of the priests' hidden tradition; keep the Falcon branch as rumor with no named culprit.

557.comment: Scion of the Blazing Sun: The Way of Sunfire
557.content: The Way of Sunfire is the weapon passive of Scion of the Blazing Sun (gameplay): a Sunfire Arrow after a Charged Attack, with the Heartsearer debuff on the target.

558.content:
Scroll of Streaming Song (also: Streaming Song): Scroll of Streaming Song is a three-volume set of torn pages from desert ruins, kept in the House of Daena. It tells how the Mistress of Pushpavatika visits a wise princess and tests her with three riddles. Scholars have added notes on its translation and gaps.

The pages were retrieved by Vahumana researchers, and Haravatat and Vahumana herbads argue in the margins about what the text means. In the end the two rulers ally. The in-game description says the author is unconfirmed.

Appearance: Torn pages in verse-like lines, interrupted by the scholars' bracketed remarks. Missing words appear as (...) and some guesses are marked with question marks.

Lore: Vol. 1: the Mistress of Pushpavatika, who calls herself a spirit created at the beginning, goes to the princess's land to test her wisdom. The princess is surrounded by attendants in a cloth no one has seen before, like stars around one moon. The Mistress offers spices, gold and gems if the princess can answer three riddles; the princess replies that knowledge is worth more.

Vol. 2: the first riddle (cold as the dead while alive, warm in death) is answered with the rose; the second (rises from earth, descends from the sky, unseen yet sees all, runs only top to bottom) with the universal law made in heaven, which only worship and not imitation may meet. Her warning is that forbidden arts bring calamity at the edge of divine knowledge.

Vol. 3: the third riddle asks what cannot stop arrows but stops destruction, cannot break armour but destroys cities, and cannot be overcome by gods or demons. The princess names endless wisdom, but most of her answer is lost to gaps. The Mistress, utterly impressed, praises her kin, and the two princesses form an alliance together with a king whose epithet is damaged (Blood? Resentment? Red Crown?). Together they lead the people of a city whose name is lost in the damage (the wiki links the gap to Ay-Khanoum) to eternal prosperity.

Margin notes: Tafazzoli says the word translated as silk should read as a textile no one had seen, so as not to suggest Liyue's silk, that the "grand palace" is a land where the divine is present, and that a place-word could mean farmland or cemetery; Yarshater dryly says they are now more confused about whom the author describes. On the lost words in the third answer, Tafazzoli offers "Mine (Ours)," "Eternity" or "All", a possible person's name or "preserved remains", and "Return", "Death" or "Rebirth".

Identity reading: The text names no one. The wiki's reading is that the Mistress of Pushpavatika is the Goddess of Flowers (Nabu Malikata), the princess the Greater Lord Rukkhadevata and the red king King Deshret, and that the princess's phrase "owner of yesterday and master of tomorrow morning" alludes to her link with Irminsul. This is inference. In A Divergence Leading to Oneself (6.6), lines from the Goddess of Flowers' song, including "a spirit created at the beginning," are shown to calm Jinn when Collei recites them; Baladhuri notes few records of the song survive. Treat the scroll as folklore about a meeting of rulers, with the identifications offered, not proved, by later material.

Owners: No owner is named. The pages were found in desert ruins and are kept by researchers of the Akademiya's Vahumana, with notes from Haravatat.

559.comment: Scroll of Streaming Song: Mistress of Pushpavatika
559.content: The Mistress of Pushpavatika is the speaker of the Scroll of Streaming Song: a spirit who says she was created at the beginning and is a flickering illusion and the shimmering light from the creator's eyes. She tests a wise princess with three riddles. Pushpavatika is a Sanskrit-derived word for a flower garden. The wiki connects her to the Goddess of Flowers, but the scroll does not name her.

key: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City
560.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City
560.content:
Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City (also: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City artifact set, Beast Tamer's Talisman, Mountain Ranger's Marker, Mystic's Gold Dial, Wandering Scholar's Claw Cup, Demon-Warrior's Feather Mask): Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City is a 4- and 5-star artifact set from Natlan, added in Version 5.0. Its five pieces belong to members of one band of adventurers: a beast tamer, a mountain ranger, a young mystic, a scholar and a warrior who set out in the Cataclysm for a legendary Abyss-repelling treasure in a ruined ancient city. It boosts Nightsoul Burst and elemental-reaction team play.

The pieces are Beast Tamer's Talisman (flower), Mountain Ranger's Marker (plume), Mystic's Gold Dial (sands), Wandering Scholar's Claw Cup (goblet) and Demon-Warrior's Feather Mask (circlet).

Appearance: The flower is a talisman of flint and Drakite with a flint paw print. The plume is a bird-feather-shaped path marker. The sands is a golden sun-like disc with draconic patterns that seem to symbolise the cycle of life and death; its needle points home. The goblet is shaped strikingly like a dragon's claw. The circlet is a feather mask with falcon-like plumage.

Lore: The five pieces, each with its own entry:
- Beast Tamer's Talisman: passed down among beast tamers of the Scions of the Canopy.
- Mountain Ranger's Marker: rangers from the spring's source left feather-shaped markers on their paths for future travellers.
- Mystic's Gold Dial: mystics from the canyon of night smoke normally train for decades to speak with the Wayob.
- Wandering Scholar's Claw Cup: a scholar who claimed to be President of the Saurian Relics Association spent his days with scrolls and strange mechanisms until war burned his work.
- Demon-Warrior's Feather Mask: Taika, once the mightiest warrior of the Flower-Feather Clan, said goodbye to his wife and unborn child to fight monsters, becoming as ferocious as a demon.
Each piece has its own entry with its full text.

Wiki cross-references that the item text does not state: the "city up in the clouds" and the "treasure" are the legendary Tonatiuh; the Python King is Och-Kan; the team reached Ochkanatlan around the Cataclysm and only Liriwu came back alive; and Taika led the party, which also included Quenin of the Flower-Feather Clan, Copan of the Collective of Plenty and others. According to the wiki, the party's tamer belonged to the Scions of the Canopy and the ranger to the People of the Springs.

The wiki's Taika and Bona pages say that the adventurers died to Waxaklahun Ubah Kan (Kukulkan) and that Taika's daughter Bona later followed his path to the same ruins. Kukulkan also spread the legend of the Jade of Return, which Bona's page says was a falsehood meant to lure strong warriors into a trap. The Mystic's Gold Dial text is the only piece that says any of the party made it back to tell the tale. Of the set's many legends, none confirm whether the real prize could repel the Abyss.

Owners: No wearer. The pieces are keepsakes of members of a single adventuring party. Named figures are Liriwu (Masters of the Night-Wind), Taika (Flower-Feather Clan), and, in the text, Taika's unborn child, Bona. The beast tamer, mountain ranger and scholar are unnamed.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): the 2-piece bonus restores 6 Elemental Energy when a nearby party member triggers a Nightsoul Burst. The 4-piece bonus gives nearby party members a 12% Elemental DMG Bonus for the elements in a reaction triggered by the wearer, for 15s; if the wearer is in Nightsoul's Blessing, they gain a further 28% for 20s.

The 4-piece effect works off-field and same-named bonuses do not stack. Obtained from the Sanctum of Rainbow Spirits domain in Toyac Springs, Natlan, from Tribal Secret Space (from 5.2) and from the artifact strongbox (from 5.3).
Per the wiki's gameplay notes, reactions that consume Dendro Cores give Dendro plus the triggering element's bonus (Burgeon gives Pyro and Dendro; Hyperbloom gives Electro and Dendro), Quicken and Aggravate give Electro and Dendro, Spread gives Dendro only, and Shatter gives none. A second reaction adds its own bonuses with separate timers. The same domain also drops the Obsidian Codex.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): these are the humble effects of ordinary tribespeople who walked into a lost cause; treat them with respect rather than as treasure. A Natlanian who finds one can plausibly recognise the tribe by its crafted style.

Do not turn them into the story of one named hero; the set is a chorus of unnamed people.

561.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City: Liriwu
561.content: In the set's text, Liriwu is a young mystic of the canyon of night smoke whose dial needle points home. The wiki says she belonged to the Masters of the Night-Wind and was the only member of the party to return alive; she was left in a safe tower, and found only shattered corpses at the camp.

562.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City: Taika and Bona
562.content: Taika was the mightiest warrior of the Flower-Feather Clan. He left his wife and unborn child to fight the demons and monsters, and died at the apex of Cinder City. If the child was a girl, he said, her name should be Bona. The wiki's Bona entry says she grew up to follow his path.

563.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City: Cinder City
563.content: In the set, Cinder City is the burned ancient city where the legendary treasure was said to lie; the beast tamer's and mountain ranger's notes call it filth-ridden and ash-laden. The wiki ties it to Ochkanatlan, which later canon shows as Och-Kan's domain.

564.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City: Beast tamers and Saurians
564.content: Beast tamers of the Scions of the Canopy focus on building friendships with Saurians and try to settle disputes peacefully, even with violent Saurians that have hurt a human, sometimes before the Saurian Hunters can act. Their ideals are sometimes incomprehensible even to their tribe.

565.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City: Beast Tamer's Talisman
565.content: a talisman passed down among beast tamers of the Scions of the Canopy, carved with the paw print said to be that of the first Yumkasaurus to bond with a human. Beast tamers befriend Saurians, even violent ones, and believe in patience. The young tamer who learned this believed beasts share human hearts until the black tide came, bringing monsters who could never be understood. He settled the survivors of his hometown and set out on a journey of no return, hoping to find a secret Abyss-repelling treasure the ancient Python King was said to have forged in the burned city.

566.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City: Mountain Ranger's Marker
566.content: rangers from the spring's source left feather-shaped markers on their paths for future travellers. When the black tide swept over their homeland, the last ranger, who knew every inch of Natlan, set out again to retake it, hoping for a golden wheel in the city of the foul dragon that could reverse time, even if it was another trap laid by a heartless spectator.

567.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City: Mystic's Gold Dial
567.content: mystics from the canyon of night smoke normally train for decades to speak with the Wayob, but in this chaotic time even fresh disciples had to guide fallen warriors' spirits home. The dial belonged to a young mystic named Liriwu. Joining a team of veterans bound for the city above the clouds, she was left behind in a safe tower; when she reached their camp she found only shattered corpses and the remains of a dragon's meal. Resolved to take word of their end to waiting families, she set out on the road home.

568.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City: Wandering Scholar's Claw Cup
568.content: a scholar who claimed to be President of the Saurian Relics Association spent his days with scrolls and strange mechanisms until war burned his work. Having read that ancient dragon ruins held weapons against demons, he rebuilt machines from the secret source to aid warriors, then found a secret in a forsaken city, hidden for thousands of years. Believing the legend that the Python King of Ochkanatlan built a sky-faring treasure ship holding a prize that could drive the Abyss out of the world, he joined an adventurers' team bound for the city in the clouds, despite public scorn after earlier expeditions never returned.

569.comment: Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City: Demon-Warrior's Feather Mask
569.content: Taika, once the mightiest warrior of the Flower-Feather Clan, said goodbye to his wife and unborn child to fight monsters, becoming as ferocious as a demon. He fell at the apex of Cinder City and, as he died, remembered telling his wife that if the child was a girl she should be called Bona.

570.content:
Serenitea Pot (also: Realm Within, The Realm Within, Teapot realm, Ode-of-Dust Teapot, Chen'ge Hu, Serenitea Pot realm): The Serenitea Pot is a small teapot the adeptus Madame Ping gives the Traveler in Liyue Harbor as thanks for helping save the city. Inside is a private pocket world made with the adeptal art of Sub-Space Creation, where the Traveler can build a house, garden and grounds and rest from the road. It is kept by a courteous finch-like teapot spirit named Tubby, who calls herself a butler.

The teapot is placed on the ground like a gadget and entered by interacting with it. The realm cannot become a full world: Tubby says it is only a moment of respite from the mortal realm, not a way of escaping it. Over time it becomes a home that the Traveler can fill with furniture, buildings and animals, share with visiting friends, and, later, with the characters they have met on their travels.

Its Chinese name is read as "Ode-of-Dust Teapot"; the same words appear in Madame Ping's adeptus name in Chinese. English and several other translations play on "tea" and "serenity", which is where the English name comes from.

Appearance: Seen from outside, it is a teapot carried in the inventory and set down on a surface. Its item text calls it a teapot from Madame Ping with "a whole realm within". Inside, the Traveler first finds a large house at the centre of otherwise empty floating ground, which the player then builds out.

Tubby appears as a small floating blue finch with orange and white stripes around her beak, and her look changes at higher Trust Ranks (4, 7 and 10). Realm layouts include floating islands, a mountain peak, an island chain in water, and layouts themed on other nations. Tubby remarks that the realm has clear, sunny skies all year, and says it could reproduce the weather outside but that she simply likes dozing in the sun.

Lore: Madame Ping used Sub-Space Creation, an adeptal ability she says was a blessing from Rex Lapis, to make a small autonomous world. The Traveler first walked through one such teapot in the Archon Quest, when she tested them while they collected the Cleansing Bell. After the Osial crisis she learned the Traveler camped outdoors and prepared a gift, with Yanfei running errands for the materials. Tubby, the teapot spirit, introduces the realm.

Ping says a teapot is a small trick compared with Rex Lapis, who moved mountains and seas; an adeptus of her sort must leave the real world to make a world of their own. Tubby explains that adepti create such realms but seldom have time to maintain them, so teapot spirits were created to guard realms and run their affairs. Anything built inside comes from blueprints and materials, shaped by thought, and the Traveler can refashion the realm as they please.

Tubby also states the limits: Sub-Space Creation is a product of adeptal power and has bounds, and the realm is not a true world, so a whole city cannot be built there. A golden-eyed adeptus once taught her this. She cannot remember who he was and has not seen him since.

After the companion quest, Tubby explains that adepti usually seal their abodes away from the world and issue a Realm Dispatch to those they invite. A dispatch carries the signature of the abode's adeptal energy and its owner, and lets the holder come and go. Before that step the Traveler's abode was incomplete, and guests could only enter and leave with the Traveler.

Ping's part of the story: Smaragdus Jadeite, an adepti treasure that is harmful to humans after long contact, was needed to finish the teapot, along with Shimmersoil from Dihua Marsh. Both had become hard to find; The Chasm had been sealed off and Blackcliff Forge had stripped its mines. Yanfei, whom Ping says counts as an adeptus (her father is one), tracks down a Snezhnayan merchant, Krosl, whose jadeite hairpins were rented to a woman named Zhiqiao. The quest becomes a contract and affidavit problem solved with Yanfei's legal skill, and ends with the jadeite delivered to Ping.

Sub-Space Creation can give objects special properties: soil with unlimited nutrition, fish ponds that stay clear and warm, hot springs that keep their temperature. Even so, canon says it cannot restore plants that went extinct after the death of the Goddess of Flowers.

Teapot spirits are used by adepti to look after spaces made with Sub-Space Creation. Only two are named in the canon read here: Tubby (adeptus name "Rain Calmer") and Chubby ("Jade Seeker"). Tubby says her title comes from a time of unending battle, when great storms swept the land and neither sun nor moon shone; Ping and their old friends longed for sunshine and gave her the name. She says this is why she always takes the colour of a blue sky, whatever form she takes. Ganyu calls her Rain Calmer in some dialogue, which suggests they met earlier.

In Version 3.7's "A Guest From Liyue", Tubby shows she is not bound to the teapot: sent by Ping, she remodels a room in The Cat's Tail, Mondstadt, tied to the Genius Invokation TCG invitation board, so invited friends can appear without a long journey. She says Chubby, whom she calls "Jade Seeker", travels far and wide to gather rare treasures, whereas she rarely leaves the realm.

Owners: The Traveler owns the pot. Ping is its maker and giver, and Tubby runs it. The Traveler can invite the playable characters they have obtained to live there, and other players can visit as guests. Characters in the realm generate Companionship EXP over time; some favour particular furniture sets and give a one-time reward when invited into them. The Traveler cannot be invited as a companion.

Gameplay: Gameplay description, not story. The Serenitea Pot is the player-housing system.
- It unlocks at Adventure Rank 28 after "A New Star Approaches", through the world quest "A Teapot to Call Home" (Part I in Liyue Harbor, Part II inside the realm).
- The Traveler builds from furnishings made with blueprints and materials, limited by a Load meter.

- Trust Rank 1 to 10 rises by crafting each new furnishing for the first time, and unlocks more areas, creation queue slots, Realm Currency and Companionship EXP storage, extra realm layouts, and the number of companions who can live there (up to 8).
- The Jar of Riches turns the realm's Adeptal Energy into Realm Currency, spent at the Realm Depot and on Chubby's goods.
- Chubby visits from Friday to Sunday; guests can buy from him on Saturday and Sunday.
- In Co-Op, friends can visit regardless of World Level, speed up crafting, and use most interactive furnishings, but cannot edit the realm.
Layouts listed by the wiki as of 7.1: Floating Abode, Emerald Peak and Cool Isle available early, then Silken Courtyard, Sublime Spicewood, Swirling Isles (4.3), Tletl Ilhuicatl (5.3) and Shadowflit Archipelago (Nod-Krai era). Later ones unlock through quests and the Realm Depot, and each comes with a themed mansion.

571.content:
Tubby is the Teapot Spirit who runs the Realm Within: a small floating blue finch with an orange and white beak, who speaks politely and calls herself a butler to the realm. She gives access to Trust Rank, furnishing creation, realm style and the Realm Depot. She mentions Tianheng Bohea, Yunlai white tea and Bishui green tea among her centuries-old stock, enjoys dozing in the sun, and says she has an adeptus name, "Rain Calmer", which she struggles to recall. She remembers a golden-eyed adeptus but not his name.

Her talk changes with Trust Rank: at low ranks she speaks of settling in and of choosing auspicious days to build, at higher ranks she invites the Traveler to sit and share tea, and at Rank 10 she tells the story of her name.

572.content: Chubby, the Teapot Traveling Salesman, is a second teapot spirit with the adeptus name "Jade Seeker". He appears in the realm from Friday to Sunday and sells furnishings (animals, Sub-Space Boulders and Radiant Spincrystals) for Realm Currency; how many goods depend on Trust Rank. Tubby says he travels widely for rare treasures and sometimes gives her rare flower teas.

573.content: Sub-Space Creation is the adeptal ability to create a small autonomous pocket world through imagination. Ping says it was part of the illumination adepti received as a blessing from Rex Lapis. It can make teapot realms like this one and larger abodes. Its limit is that such a world is not true: it offers respite, not escape.

574.comment: Serenitea Pot: Realm Dispatch and companions
574.content: After "Idle Teapot Talk", Tubby gives the Traveler a Realm Dispatch, modified so that a light tap on a friend's palm invites them. Invited playable characters live in the realm and produce Companionship EXP (Realm Bounty). Up to 8 can live there at the highest Trust Rank.

575.content: In the Archon Quest, Zhongli sends the Traveler to Madame Ping for the Cleansing Bell used in the Rite of Parting. Ping transports them into her magic teapot as a test, revealing herself as an adeptus. After Osial's defeat she prepares the Serenitea Pot as a gift.

576.content:
Serpent Spine: Serpent Spine is a 4-star claymore from the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn, in the game since Version 1.0. The in-game short description calls it a rare weapon from the ancient ocean whose swings carry the sound of ageless waves. The full text says it is a greatsword made from the spine of a great sea monster and tells of a singing sea captain who never returned from the deep.

The Skipper is the greatsword-wielding captain of the story, and the wiki notes that the book series Tales From the Waves covers the same character.

Appearance: A greatsword made of a sea monster's spine, each eerie segment of bone described as a tale unto itself. Brilliant white bone is mentioned in the story of the beached monster. No hilt or other design details are given in text.

Lore: In the stormy seas of the ancient past, those who set out often never returned. A greatsword-wielding captain, fond of drinking and merriment before voyages, sailed off on the day sea and wind aligned and neither he nor his ship came back.

The text says sailors once used the bones of sea monsters as figureheads to frighten the beasts of the deep sea, who envied land-dwellers. Carefree sea shanties of today were once farewell songs that left people silent. When questioned about his revelry the captain would laugh, say he knew himself, tell people not to worry and that once the sea and winds were right he would go, but never finish the thought, instead raising his mug.

After many days a sea monster's corpse washed ashore, a great gash from a greatsword in it and its blood long washed clean. Words attributed to the skipper speak of avenging a woman charmed by the tidal song and of sending his shanties into the deep where she dwells even if he sleeps with the fishes.

The text closes in the present: giant creatures no longer rise from storms to ravage the waves, the custom of mounting monster skeletons on ships has been lost with their extinction, but far abroad one can still sometimes hear rumbling thunder in the depths. The Skipper's bond with his Chief Mate Parsifal is expanded in the Heart of Depth artifact set, and the Skipper appears in the Tales From the Waves book series, per the wiki's trivia.

Owners: The previous owner is the Skipper, the greatsword-wielding captain of the item text. His relationship with his Chief Mate, Parsifal, is covered in the Heart of Depth artifact set.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star claymore, base ATK 42, CRIT Rate secondary stat. Passive Wavesplitter: every 4s the wielder is on the field they deal 6 to 10 per cent more DMG and take 3 to 2 per cent more DMG (by refinement), up to 5 stacks. Stacks persist when leaving the field and drop by one when the wielder takes DMG. Obtained through the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn bundle.

577.content: The Skipper is the greatsword-wielding captain linked to the Serpent Spine and the Heart of Depth artifact set: a carefree, hard-drinking sailor of the ancient stormy seas who sailed into the misty ocean and never returned. Parsifal was his Chief Mate. See their own entries.

578.content:
Severed Fragment of Ikhor (also: Fragment of Ikhor, Ikhor's Fragment, Ikhor's power): The Severed Fragment of Ikhor is a quest item found in Snezhnaya (added in 7.0). Its description calls it a piece of Ikhor's power, split off by Aksinya when a "ritual" was interrupted, and notes it has taken the form of a glowing doll.

Two copies are earned at Fellfrost Peak, one in the House of Hesperides cellar and one in the garden's great tree, while the Traveler gathers fragments to restore the Eye of Graeae's power.

Appearance: A glowing doll. The item text suggests the doll form is not natural to the power: it speculates that Ikhor's wish to fulfil the wishes of others became the strings that once controlled him, leaving him a puppet carrying transcendent power.

Lore: The description is the main lore. It credits Aksinya with splitting the fragment away when the ritual was cut short, and offers a sad reading of Ikhor as a being reduced to a puppet by a desire to grant others' wishes. It speaks of it as a reflection by the writer, not a statement from Ikhor himself.

In the world quests, the Eye of Graeae senses the fragments and guides the Traveler and Paimon to them. In House of the Soulless the fragment is in a hidden cellar beneath a room in the House of Hesperides whose bed seems to be Ikhor's; a cat helps open the passages, and Prime Ice statues must be matched to shadows in paintings. In The Sun's Gilded Apple it lies in the great tree of the Garden Bathed in Radiant Dew, which the guard Ladon says has borne no fruit since the gardener Larisa died; Paimon keeps Ladon talking while the Traveler slips in alone.

Elsewhere in the same chapter, Pavlina is shown performing rituals that draw on Ikhor's power, and Aksinya, who is working to restore the Eye of Graeae, moves to stop her. These are related background, not an account of this item's creation.

Ikhor is a quest-only figure, shown with the appearance of the young Belyi Tsar in his human form, according to a line Aksinya speaks late in the story. Aksinya's role as the one who "split off" the fragment fits her wider story as the Tsar's adopted daughter and heir to his aims, but the item text itself says no more than that. Treat any detail about how and when the split happened as unknown.

Owners: No one keeps it as a possession in canon read for this entry. The Traveler receives it as a quest reward; Aksinya is named as the one who split it off.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). A quest item with no stats. Rewards: House of the Soulless gives one, with Adventure EXP, Primogems, Mora, Hero's Wit and Mystic Enhancement Ore; The Sun's Gilded Apple gives one with similar rewards. Both belong to the Procrustes' Iron Bed series in Hesperides of Love and Hate.

579.comment: Severed Fragment of Ikhor: Severed Fragment of Ikhor
579.content: A glowing doll-shaped fragment of Ikhor's power, said to have been split from him by Aksinya when a "ritual" was interrupted. Two are recovered at the House of Hesperides in Snezhnaya during the search for the Eye of Graeae's scattered power. Its text is melancholy, calling Ikhor a puppet held by a wish to fulfil others' wishes. Nothing beyond that is established.

580.content:
Shimenawa's Reminiscence (also: Shimenawa's Reminiscence artifact set, Entangling Bloom, Shaft of Remembrance, Morning Dew's Moment, Hopeful Heart, Capricious Visage): Shimenawa's Reminiscence is a 4 and 5 star Inazuma artifact set. Its five item texts are the first-person memories of the shrine maiden Hibiki of her teacher the Kitsune Saiguu at the Grand Narukami Shrine, of fortune slips and paper-cord charms, and of the friends who were lost. It boosts ATK and trades Energy for Normal, Charged and Plunging Attack damage.

It drops from the Momiji-Dyed Court domain on Yashiori Island and has existed since Version 2.0. The theme is love of someone after they are gone: the texts return again and again to the idea that moments cannot be held, but time spent with someone is not lost.

Appearance: Five pieces: Entangling Bloom (flower, a mizuhiki paper-cord omamori said to bind wishes and their reasons), Shaft of Remembrance (plume, an old demon-slaying arrow kept with care), Morning Dew's Moment (sands, a bronze pocket watch with a shrine bell and twisted paper cord, its hands stopped before dawn on an autumn day), Hopeful Heart (goblet, a cylinder of fortune slips with a mechanism for removing unwanted ones) and Capricious Visage (circlet, a well-kept festival fox mask with a small enigmatic smile).

Lore: The narrator came to Narukami as a country shrine maiden and was trained by the Kitsune Saiguu, who spoke in riddles about entanglement, memory and loss. Years later Saiguu is gone, and the narrator holds the empty pipe and keeps a promise to someone who is not at her side.

Entangling Bloom: Hibiki arrived on Narukami from a small fishing village as a young shrine maiden, blunt and curious, doubting Saiguu's elegant sayings. Saiguu said everything in the world is entangled, so that illusory visions come from concrete reality, and that an omamori cannot grant a wish but can make it eternal through that entanglement. She teased Hibiki about a "fated one", a rude reckless brute, and noted that darkness engulfed everything in the end.

Morning Dew's Moment: on a slope on an autumn night Saiguu told Hibiki that trying to keep a moment's beauty is like grasping morning dew and that she herself had already passed away, so that what Hibiki saw was a residual vision born of her wishes. Then she tapped Hibiki's head with her pipe and said the sun was about to rise.

Hopeful Heart and Capricious Visage: years pass in the shrine. Hibiki has learned to talk like a kitsune; the Yougou Tengu has a daughter; Konbumaru has become a Hatamoto of the Shogun and will marry a high-ranking samurai's daughter. Saiguu jokes that the shrine misses children, draws Hibiki a Great Fortune, and explains that it means the missing person will become part of Hibiki's memories for ever, so she must live long. In the mask text, Hibiki says she has grown and is less foolish, but Saiguu's face seems to cloud with reluctant sorrow on a festive day that feels like a farewell, and Saiguu says that losing memories is like death in darkness before turning the talk to the "idiot Konbumaru".

Shaft of Remembrance: Hibiki reflects that evil is not an objective thing but grows from fear in cold, numb hearts. Saiguu is long gone and Hibiki holds her empty pipe; the Great Tengu went into self-imposed exile, enraged at failing to protect Saiguu, leaving Teruyo behind; Harunosuke left for another country in grief and rage; Nagamasa joined the Shogunate to clear the Mikoshi name. The man who taught her archery and listened to her naive promise under red sakura boughs will return, even blinded by blood or turned into a beast, and she will save him with their bow and arrows and destroy evil, folly and needless obsession. She imagines saying "Come see me, you idiotic problem gambler" and "don't lose your way this time, Konbumaru", still wondering who won the last throw of the dice.

Context from other sources: wiki summaries of Hibiki's story say the Yougou Three (Hibiki, Harunosuke and Nagamasa) trained under the Yougou Tengu; that Takamine later went to the Abyss with Ei in the cataclysm; and that when he returned corrupted, Hibiki shot him, believing it would save him. That outcome is not stated in this set.

Owners: The pieces are described through Hibiki's eyes: the pipe, the fortune cylinder, the arrow and the mask are tied to the Kitsune Saiguu and the Grand Narukami Shrine, and the pocket watch and charm are personal to the narrator.

Gameplay: Gameplay, not lore: the 2-piece bonus is ATK +18%. The 4-piece bonus: when casting an Elemental Skill with 15 or more Energy, the wearer loses 15 Energy and gains +50% Normal, Charged and Plunging Attack DMG for 10 seconds; it does not retrigger during that time and does not trigger on characters that do not use Energy (such as Mavuika). It drops from the Momiji-Dyed Court.

581.comment: Shimenawa's Reminiscence: Hibiki's memories of the Kitsune Saiguu
581.content: In Shimenawa's Reminiscence the narrator, Hibiki, remembers the Kitsune Saiguu as a teacher who spoke in paradoxes, drank sakura wine, and tapped heads with a tobacco pipe. The texts show Saiguu worrying about memory and loss, giving Hibiki a Great Fortune, and warning that she herself has "already passed away like the morning dew". The Hakushin Ring catalyst is narrated from Saiguu's side.

582.content: "The idiot Konbumaru" is Hibiki's teasing name in the set for a wandering, gambling man who becomes a Hatamoto of the Shogun, marries a samurai's daughter and taught her archery. The wiki names him Takamine, a servant of the tengu Reizenbou, and says he disappeared in the cataclysm; the item texts use only the nickname. His connection to the Storm Cage text of Emblem of Severed Fate is inferred from the shared setting.

583.content: The Shaft of Remembrance lists the aftermath for Hibiki's fellow trainees: the Great Tengu in exile, Harunosuke leaving Inazuma, Nagamasa joining the Shogunate to clear the Mikoshi name. Wiki summaries call Hibiki, Harunosuke and Nagamasa "the Yougou Three" for training under the Yougou Tengu; the set itself does not use that term.

584.content:
Silken Moon's Serenade (also: Crystal Tear of the Wanderer, Pristine Plume of the Blessed, Frost Devotee's Delirium, Joyous Glory of the Pure, Holy Crown of the Believer): Silken Moon's Serenade is a 4- and 5-star artifact set tied to Lunar reactions and the Moonsign. Its five pieces carry one narrator's account of the far north: the night Hyperborea's golden realm was destroyed by dark blue crystal nails, the pity of the Frost Moon's mistress, and the later suffering of the Frostmoon Scions, down to the Moonchanter Aila and her sister. It was released in version 6.0.

Four pieces open in a time before the new moon (Columbina) rose; only the Flower is set earlier, at the disaster itself. The stories are the Scions' own memory and myth.

Appearance: Immaculate northern relics: an everlasting flower, a feathered accessory said to have been forged by the first Moonchanter, a long-stopped timepiece, a silver cup from old Frostmoon Scion rituals, and a circlet imitating the antlers of the grove's envoy.

Lore: The set text has five stories, one per piece.
- Crystal Tear of the Wanderer: in a single night the golden tower fell, and dark blue crystal nails wiped out every city with any sign of life; the apostle and the gods' first messenger (wiki-linked to Anacharsis and Koitar) vanished. The gods stayed silent. Only the mistress of the Frost Moon wept for mortals; legend says she spun silver threads to guide survivors, and her tears became lilies. Hence the descendants of Hyperborea call themselves the Frostmoon Scions.
- The other four pieces follow the Scions' later decline, from the twin sisters Aila and Alia to the Archpriestess Lovia's long project of a "pure" bloodline and a manufactured faith.

- Pristine Plume of the Blessed: two sisters were born "defective products" and never expected to be blessed. They knew only their grandmother (Lovia, per the wiki link) and a faded storybook showing a white bird under a perfect moon, and promised each other they would one day fly together. Years later one of them (Alia, wiki-linked) broke the promise and left alone, into a darker night; Aila, later the first Moonchanter, endured twice the torment from then on. The last quoted lines have Aila saying she will not resent her older sister.
- Frost Devotee's Delirium: a plan carried through generations, with a bloodline purified for over a thousand years, aimed to give birth to a chosen one who would reign over Elysium. The girl chosen to bear the heir met a young officer from the northern realm, fell in love, cast down her bloodstained antler-crown and betrayed her people. A spy sent by a mad monk captured her to return her to Hiisi Island, and she killed herself with a dagger beside the wounded officer. The Archpriestess Lovia turned to a lesser branch of the bloodline, the twin sisters, a pale shadow of the lost girl. Maddened, she devised a scheme so profane that even the Frost Moon's mistress would recoil. The details are blacked out in the text.
- Joyous Glory of the Pure: after the Scions could no longer hear the heavens' teaching, they could not remake the apostle's marvels (a reliquary that tilled the sea of ice, the arrow that could pierce the false sky, creation's authority from the highest of angels). They turned to ploughshares-into-swords and, finally, to law to govern the generations until blood was "purified into holy seed". The grandmother urges the children to drink "pure moonlight" and embrace joyous pain as the apostle once drank bitter wine; they can no longer tell what fills the silver cup.
- Holy Crown of the Believer: when the heavenly moon had gone, miracles faded to prayer and the line between faith and lies grew thin. Moonchanters today say their antler crown was a gift from the Frost Moon at the moment of its obliteration, woven from moonlight. The young Lovia, then a priestess who had never witnessed a moonlit blessing, forged her circlet from cold iron, hoping that such shared fictions could still bind believers together.
Taken together the set presents the Scions' history as faith sustained through disaster, then through engineered breeding, and finally through a deliberate myth.

Details worth keeping apart in a scene: the Flower is the only piece set before the silver mirror shattered, and its tone is mournful rather than accusatory. The other four are set in the era "before the new moon rose" and read as an insider's indictment of Lovia's long project. The text says the apostle's marvels were lost, but not how. The sister who broke the promise is described only as leaving "for a faraway place alone", with no destination given. The text does not say which girl is addressed as "my most cherished child" in the Goblet. The set's tie to Columbina is limited to the phrase "the new moon"; the item text does not itself say she is any of these figures.

Owners: No owner is named. The pieces are relics of the Frostmoon Scions' heritage and are collected by the player as artifacts.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): 4- and 5-star set from the Frostladen Machinery domain (Paha Isle, Nod-Krai). 4-piece: when the wearer deals Elemental DMG they gain Gleaming Moon: Devotion for 8s, giving all party members +60 Elemental Mastery under a Nascent Gleam Moonsign or +120 under an Ascendant Gleam Moonsign (off-field works). All party members' Lunar Reaction DMG rises 10% for each different Gleaming Moon effect present; they do not stack.

Per the wiki, this 4-piece together with Night of the Sky's Unveiling's 4-piece gives a combined 20% Lunar Reaction DMG increase, and more wearers do not raise it further.

585.comment: Silken Moon's Serenade: Silken Moon's Serenade
585.content: Artifact set whose item text tells of Hyperborea's fall, the Frost Moon's mercy and the later history of the Frostmoon Scions and the Moonchanter Aila.

586.comment: Silken Moon's Serenade: The mistress of the Frost Moon's mercy
586.content: In the Crystal Tear of the Wanderer text, when the golden realm fell and the gods stayed silent, one celestial ruler alone shed tears for mortals. She was the mistress of the Frost Moon, queen of the celestial chariot and of light. According to legend she wove threads from the silver glow to lead survivors across the frozen plains, and her tears became everlasting lilies. The text adds that she acted from pity and a deeper, unspoken wish, "whatever her original intent".

587.content:
Silver Light (also: Radiance on the Water): Silver Light is a four-star sword obtained from the limited-time Version 7.1 event Silverwing in Pursuit of the Moon (part of the Moonchase Festival). Its description says it is a longsword left by Wind Reader, one of the Three Hermits of Guizang. The item story shows him as a reckless young thaumaturge humbled and gently taken in by the swallow adeptus.

Appearance: The text describes only a longsword, said to be forged from sacred silver from the heavens, that once cleaved sea water into two. Do not invent more detail.

Lore: The story begins in the youth of the man later revered as founder of Qimen Divination, before the name Wind Reader was known. He wandered as a vagabond, plucking talismans from the air, laying formations with poured wine, proud of his genius and answering to nothing but his whims. He once stole the bronze mirror of the Two Sages of Lianshan and struck down bandits. One night he burned shadow phantoms terrorising a mountain village, then mocked the villagers he had saved.

A flash of silver light followed, and the swallow adeptus (later one of the Three Beasts of Tao Dou) appeared, lamenting that he treated his foresight as a toy. He drew his sword and boasted with a rude verse, but was beaten and pinned under her foot. She did not rage. She lifted him up and invited him to walk the wanderer's path with her, since the world was bigger than the outlaws' squalor.

He called her an old hag and refused to bow as her servant, yet stayed, because in her cold eyes he saw a tenderness he had not felt in a very long time, like the mother's embrace described in ancient texts. Years later the story shifts to a dream: she asks "Or perhaps...?" by lamplight and he, normally quick with banter, cannot speak. He wakes to a burned-out lamp, untouched wine and a lingering spirit. Another full moon has come, and she has still not returned. He resolves to keep waiting in dreams.

The verse he shouts at the adeptus is boastful and crude and is best summarised, not quoted. Its claim to command the Jueyun adepti and thunder gods is bravado that he promptly fails to back up. The founder of Qimen Divination is named only by that title and as Wind Reader here, and the swallow adeptus is linked on the wiki to Zibai, though the item text does not name her. The story is a limited-event item text from Silverwing in Pursuit of the Moon.

Owners: Left behind by Wind Reader, according to the description. No later owner is named.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore. Obtained from the event Silverwing in Pursuit of the Moon (Version 7.1, from 2026-09-24). Passive Radiance on the Water grants Elemental Mastery after an Elemental Skill. Refinement material is Tea-Scented Tassel.

588.content:
Silvershower Heartstrings (also: Dryas's Nocturne): Silvershower Heartstrings is a 5-star bow, the legendary bow of the fairies, said to touch the hearts of listeners whether on stage or on the battlefield.

Its story is not about a person but about a very old Fontainian play, Dryas, and the many versions of its ending.

Appearance: Canon calls it a bow, fairy-made and later modified as a theatrical prop. It carries a Pneuma or Ousia mark for Arkhe-aligned wielders. Add no other detail.

Lore: Fontainian playwrights liken strings to hearts, and the word heartstring appears in one of the oldest plays, Dryas, though the string there was a bowstring.

The hero is Aurelius, glorious as gold, who conquered countless traitorous nations for Fontaine. He is the forerunner of the Aurelius in Coppelius's The Saga of Aurelius, yet no such figure exists in recorded history, so he is often regarded as fiction, like Ajax. In the story he falls into a foe's trap and is lost with his army in a pine forest.

As an assassin's blade is about to kill him, silver arrows fall like rain. He looks for the quivering bowstring and sees a maiden, Dryastis, who takes his hand and leads him from the bloodstained pines. She asks only that no more die in vain, that he take the conflict away from the land and stop tainting the pure waters with death.

The play has been edited for millennia. In some versions the hero accepts her bow and sounds the withdrawal, only to be killed by traitors and have his body sunk in the sea. In others he is driven by maddening love, leads his army back into the forest to find her, and she flees to the riverbank and begs her pure-water mother to save her. The ruler of the Many Waters (a title that Splendor of Tranquil Waters uses for Egeria) takes pity and turns her into a pine tree; the bowstring snaps and falls among blooming Pluie Lotuses, and the hero stares at the flowers until he falls into a deep pool.

Later natural philosophers say a barbarian tribe called Dryas once settled the area, which is why the forest has that name; the text calls such unromantic explanations irrelevant to theatre. It offers further endings: he sinks to have his will sanded down by time, or resurfaces after many years only to be killed by the new White Armada or the Marechaussee Hunters. The final paragraph says how the bow, changing hands many times, came to belong to someone who dwelled deep beneath the waters and was adapted into a prop for children's performances in that person's homeland, and calls this a different tale altogether.

Owners: No owner is named. The bow is attributed to the fairies in legend.

The bow's most recent holder is only described as a person deep beneath the waters (see uncertainties). Do not state who without a source.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star bow, base ATK 44 at level 1, secondary stat HP; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 4.7. Passive "Dryas's Nocturne": the wielder can gain Remedy stacks, one for using an Elemental Skill (25s), one when a Bond of Life value increases (25s), and one for performing healing (20s); each stack count adds Max HP, and with 3 stacks Elemental Burst CRIT Rate rises, ending 4s after falling below 3. Works off-field. Values scale with refinement.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: Fontainians know this as a theatre tale, likely from school or playbills. Let characters disagree on the ending, as the text itself keeps several.

589.content: Dryas is an ancient Fontainian play in which the fairy maiden Dryastis saves the hero Aurelius with silver arrows and begs him to end the war on her land. Its many endings are the story of the weapon Silvershower Heartstrings. No historical Aurelius is recorded.

590.content:
Skyward Atlas (also: Cloud Atlas, Wandering Clouds): Skyward Atlas is a five-star catalyst of the Mondstadt Skyward series, released in 1.0. It is a cloud atlas that symbolises Dvalin and his former master, the Anemo Archon, details the winds and clouds of the northern regions and holds the power of sky and wind. In its story it is a copy of a far older atlas of 100,000 odes, each naming one cloud or wind.

Appearance: The item text describes an atlas presented as poems and images. It gives no cover or binding detail.

Lore: The atlas pairs images with 100,000 odes, each dedicated to a single cloud or wind and calling it by name. The atlas gave the winds form and the odes gave them personality, so the formless winds became friends and family in Barbatos' eyes. Legend says that in ancient times Barbatos used the original to summon the four winds, thaw the snow, drive away vicious beasts, call rain and create Mondstadt.

He let the atlas be shared and copied among the people under the name Cloud Atlas. Time was unkind: surviving copies lack certain drawings and odes, though the knowledge lived on in ballads and legends. The histories of the thousand winds were not lost, because Barbatos still holds them. When he stood against the shadowy wings of the evil dragon Durin, he sang to the thousand winds and called the Wind Dragon, Dvalin.

The text says whoever holds the atlas wields the true names of the thousand winds and all their powers. It ends in calm: the skies over Mondstadt are blue, Barbatos and Dvalin have found a new place to call home, and the atlas has been entrusted to one worthy of the honour. The Anemo entry in this archive notes that legend credits the original atlas with recording the names of all the thousand winds; the Thousand Winds Temple in Enkanomiya uses a similar phrase with a different meaning, and the link between the two is left unresolved.

Owners: Original author or keeper: Barbatos. Copies passed among the people of Mondstadt. The item names no current holder. Mona is shown holding the catalyst in her 2022 birthday artwork, which is presentation rather than a canon statement of ownership.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star catalyst from the standard Wanderlust Invocation and weapon event wishes. Base ATK 48, secondary stat ATK 7.2%. Passive "Wandering Clouds": raises Elemental DMG Bonus (12-24%); Normal Attack hits have a 50% chance to summon clouds that seek out nearby opponents for 15 seconds, dealing 160-320% ATK DMG, at most once every 30 seconds.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): treat it as lore-rich rather than as a god's personal spellbook. Weather-lore, names and odes suit scenes with scholars and bards.

591.content: Cloud Atlas is the popular name for copies of the atlas of winds that Barbatos allowed people to share. They preserve poems and images describing northern weather and are incomplete.

592.content: The atlas ties to the idea of the thousand winds: the named, personified winds said to protect Mondstadt, whose true names its holder wields. The phrase carries other meanings elsewhere, as the Anemo entry explains.

593.content:
Skyward Blade (also: Sky-Piercing Fang): Skyward Blade is a five-star sword of the Mondstadt Skyward series, released in 1.0. It is the sword of a knight and symbolises the restored honour of Dvalin, with the Anemo Archon's blessing on its fuller. Its story is Dvalin's fight with the shadow dragon Durin and the poison that followed.

Appearance: The text puts the Archon's blessing on the fuller of the blade and calls it "the sky-piercing fang". No other visual detail is given.

Lore: The story opens with a fang that pierced the black-gold scales of the abyssal kingdom and cut the throats of the sons of ancient sinners. Mondstadt was threatened by the shadow dragon Durin, whose jealousy of the city's prosperity bred evil and poisoned the land. Hearing the people cry, the Anemo Archon descended and woke Dvalin, who rose into the sky to fight for all life.

Blessed by the Archon, Dvalin fought Durin; clouds broke and the sky burned red as if the end had come. Dvalin's blessed fangs pierced Durin's throat and Durin fell, but Dvalin was poisoned by the tainted blood and fell unconscious from the pain.

Centuries passed and Dvalin's sacrifice was nearly forgotten. When he awoke, his friend and the comfort of his lyre were gone, and those he had protected cowered at the sight of him. The text closes as a prayer: honour reclaimed, poison cleansed, ballads giving a people their forgotten memory, that Dvalin's name may be restored. The item only frames the restoration as a hope; the Prologue Archon Quest is where it plays out in the game.

Owners: No wielder is named; the sword stands for Dvalin's honour. The Traveler is shown wielding it in the cinematic of the limited-time event Moonlight Merriment Part II, per the wiki's trivia.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star sword from the standard Wanderlust Invocation and weapon event wishes. Base ATK 46, secondary stat Energy Recharge 12%. Passive "Sky-Piercing Fang": raises CRIT Rate (4-8%); after an Elemental Burst you gain Skypiercing Might for 12 seconds (Movement SPD +10%, ATK SPD +10%, Normal and Charged hits deal extra damage of 20-40% ATK).

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a symbol of redeemed reputation. Do not say the blade is Dvalin's own fang; the text says it symbolises him.

594.comment: Skyward Blade: Dvalin and Durin's battle
594.content: The Skyward weapons retell the Cataclysm-era battle from different angles. In the Blade's version Dvalin, blessed by the Archon, pierces Durin's throat, is poisoned by the blood, falls unconscious and is forgotten.

595.content:
Skyward Harp (also: Echoing Ballad, Sky-Piercing Lyre): Skyward Harp is a five-star bow of the Mondstadt Skyward series, released in 1.0. The item calls it the sky-piercing lyre: its story is how Barbatos' lyre drew Dvalin to him, held back the shadow dragon, and then went unheard by a poisoned Dvalin.

Appearance: Described as a greatbow whose sound when fired is music to the Anemo Archon's ears. The text gives no further look.

Lore: The clear tune of the lyre still echoes in the hearts of the people and in the winds, and it is said the ancient evil dragon from the abyss was drawn there by it. In ancient times Barbatos softly strummed his lyre and summoned the pure thousand winds and songs. Charmed by the free winds and songs, the high dragon Dvalin descended and swore loyalty. Barbatos, glad of a new friend, entrusted the people of Mondstadt to Dvalin, and the Archon and the Wind Dragon together forged Mondstadt's dawn.

In the final battle the lyre's floating tunes halted the shadow dragon's attack and gave Dvalin the chance to end its poisonous reign. Long afterwards Dvalin awoke to find his master gone and heard only the poisonous whispers of the Abyss Order. Unseen pain and unheard torture crushed his spirit.

Dvalin turned on what he had vowed to protect and cursed the one he had sworn loyalty to, crying that Barbatos was indifferent to his pain, a careless friend and the cruellest of the Archons. The text says the furious friend did not know that Barbatos was trying to save him, and that many memories may have been crushed by Dvalin's anguish but not that of the lyre, the Holy Lyre der Himmel. It closes expectantly: centuries of misunderstanding will soon pass, and Dvalin will hear his songs once more.

Owners: The item names no wielder. Per the wiki's trivia, Venti wields the bow in his Character Demo and a Collected Miscellany video, and in the Dvalin fight of the Prologue (A Long Shot) he uses it to help the Traveler free Dvalin from the Abyss Order's control. Tartaglia used it as a trial character in an early Story Quest, since replaced by the Polar Star.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star bow from the standard Wanderlust Invocation and weapon event wishes. Base ATK 48, secondary stat CRIT Rate 4.8%. Passive "Echoing Ballad": raises CRIT DMG (20-40%); hits have a 60-100% chance of a small AoE dealing 125% Physical ATK DMG, at most once every 4 seconds at refinement 1, down to every 2 seconds at refinement 5.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a weapon about friends who misunderstand each other. The text only says Dvalin will soon hear the songs again; it does not show the reconciliation.

596.comment: Skyward Harp: Holy Lyre der Himmel
596.content: Barbatos' lyre, named in the Harp's text as the memory that survived Dvalin's anguish. It has its own entry.

597.content:
Skyward Pride (also: Sky-Ripping Dragon Spine): Skyward Pride is a five-star claymore of the Mondstadt Skyward series, released in 1.0. It symbolises the pride of Dvalin soaring through the skies and hums deeply when swung, with the force of his command of sky and wind. Its story tells of the battle with Durin, the poison, and Dvalin's fall to become Stormterror.

Appearance: Only its sound is described, a deep hum when swung. The text says nothing of its look.

Lore: A tale of sky-shaking valour: even the vile dragon Durin, brought into the world by a sinner of an ancient abyssal nation, lost its dark, metallic wings to "Anemo's pride and joy". Durin, jealous of Mondstadt's glory, terrorised it. The Anemo Archon, woken from his sylvan slumber by the victims' cries, summoned his faithful servant, and the two rode the wind to fight.

In a battle that tore clouds from the sky, Dvalin spread his six blessed wings and cut through Durin's iron scales like a colossal blade, then struck with claws like swords of wind. He tore out Durin's throat with his teeth and the evil dragon fell. Dvalin saved Mondstadt, but the tainted blood he swallowed poisoned him and corruption seeped into his bones.

Though a hero, Dvalin suffered alone, and the stench of corruption drew evil creatures. Deceived by the Abyss, he fell and Stormterror was born. His master at last returned to calm his frenzied mind, and his faithful friend and a new companion fought to drive out the monsters and restore his honour. Over the century of his sleep his image faded from Mondstadt's memory, until the people recently saw his six-winged figure again. Now, blessed by the Archon and serenaded by Barbatos, Dvalin takes to the skies once more.

Owners: The item names no wielder. The claymore stands for Dvalin's pride rather than being something he held.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star claymore from the standard Wanderlust Invocation and weapon event wishes. Base ATK 48, secondary stat Energy Recharge 8%. Passive "Sky-ripping Dragon Spine": raises all DMG (8-16%); after an Elemental Burst, Normal and Charged Attack hits create vacuum blades dealing 80-160% ATK DMG along their path, lasting 20 seconds or 8 blades.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): suits a retelling of Dvalin as hero first and Stormterror second. Mention the poison honestly; the text insists he was a hero.

598.comment: Skyward Pride: Dvalin's battle with Durin
598.content: The Pride's version has Dvalin fight with six wings, claws and teeth, swallow Durin's poisoned blood, be deceived by the Abyss into becoming Stormterror and later be calmed by Barbatos. Dvalin has his own entry.

599.content:
Skyward Spine: Skyward Spine is a 5-star polearm, part of the Mondstadt series of weapons. Its item text is a short legend of the dragon Dvalin: he fought and killed the shadow dragon Durin in the skies over Mondstadt, but swallowed Durin's venom and spent the following centuries wounded in an ancient ruin. Added in Version 1.0.

The weapon is described as a polearm that symbolizes Dvalin's resolve, its shaft pointing at the heavens and clad in the might of sky and wind. It sits with Skyward Blade, Skyward Pride, Skyward Harp and Skyward Atlas in a set of Mondstadt weapons, but this entry covers only the spear.

Appearance: Canon text gives only the symbolic picture: an upright shaft that points toward the heavens, wrapped in the power of sky and wind. Do not invent materials, a maker or measurements.

Lore: In olden times the shadow dragon Durin envied Mondstadt's peace and came to defile it. His black wings darkened the sky and released toxic fumes that even the thousand winds could not hold back, so poisoned black rain fell on the people. The Anemo Archon heard their agony and called Dvalin to his side.

Cloaked in storm, Dvalin tore through the poisoned clouds and a whirlwind in his wake destroyed them. He seized Durin in his claws and carried him above the clouds, where the battle continued. In the end Dvalin's fangs pierced Durin's throat and his claws tore out its corrupted heart. The text calls Durin the sinners' creation and says it fell, full of regret, onto a snowy peak.

Winning cost Dvalin dearly. Durin's venomous ichor ran between his teeth and into his body; the pain withered bone and marrow, and he coiled up in the depths of an ancient ruin. The text ends with Dvalin still believing he would be reawakened, scatter the darkness and sing again to the Anemo Archon's lyre, which he calls his dear friend.

The item itself names no names beyond Durin and Dvalin; the wiki links the sinners to Rhinedottir, the snowy peak to Dragonspine and the ancient ruin to Stormterror's Lair, where the Prologue finds Dvalin. The weapon is told in one voice (loyalty and resolve), while the Dragonspine Spear presents Durin's own dying dream of the same fight.

Owners: No wielder is named in canon. The weapon is not tied to any playable character or to Venti, and no story shows Dvalin giving it to anyone.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 5-star polearm with base ATK 48 and an Energy Recharge secondary stat. Its passive, Black Wing, raises CRIT Rate and Normal ATK SPD and gives Normal and Charged Attacks a chance of a vacuum blade that deals area damage (roughly once per two seconds). It is on the Standard Wish and weapon event Wishes.

600.comment: Skyward Spine: Dvalin and Durin's battle
600.content: Skyward Spine's text recounts Dvalin's victory over the shadow dragon Durin in the poisoned skies and the venom he swallowed afterward. Treat it as legend told with sympathy for Dvalin. For the aftermath, the Abyss Order's exploitation of his pain and his freeing in the Prologue, see Dvalin's own entry.

601.content:
Snow-Tombed Starsilver (also: Snow Tombed Starsilver): Snow-Tombed Starsilver is a 4-star claymore of the Dragonspine series, in-game description "an ancient greatsword stored between frescoes" and forged from Starsilver. Its text tells of the princess of the snow-entombed mountain city of Sal Vindagnyr, who gave it to a hero from another land. Added in Version 1.2.

In game, one copy and its diagram lie in the Mural Room unlocked by the Hidden Exploration Objective Dragonspine's Glacial Secret; the weapon can also be forged.

Appearance: Canon calls it an ancient greatsword of Starsilver that can cleave ice and snow. In the text it lies between frescoes in a great hall, with black blood once dripping from its blade.

Lore: When the verdant city was sealed by cloud and mist and unending snowstorms blotted out the moonlight, a nail that fell from the azure skies pierced all life and every interrupted story. The priest's daughter gave the Starsilver greatsword to the hero from another land, Imunlaukr.

In the howling storm her words could not reach him. She told him a fourth fresco was prepared for him, where his likeness would remain, and promised to wait and pray for his return. She withered together with the grafted, barren silver branches while he was far away chasing answers.

Her last words, which never reached him, said she had not seen blue sky and green grass for a long time, did not know which colours could capture the thawing landscape her father longed for, and wished to see him again. The wiki notes the same final words appear in the description of the Princess' Box, from Dragonspine's Last Trio.

The hero ended his fruitless journey, trudged back through foreign snowy paths with tainted black blood dripping from his blade, and found only deathly echoes in the great hall. Seeing nothing left to protect, he addressed those who dwell in the heavens, said they must only wish to watch the suffering below, and offered to pass their time with a song of iron and blood. He left the Starsilver between the frescoes and descended to search for a land of war to paint red with blood. The princess's gift was meant to shatter snow and wind; the hero's own account is not given.

Owners: Owner: the hero Imunlaukr, who was given it by the princess and left it in the mural hall. Nobody is shown wielding it afterward.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 4-star claymore with base ATK 44 and a Physical DMG Bonus secondary stat. The Dragonspine series passive Frost Burial gives Normal and Charged Attack hits a chance (60 to 100 per cent by refinement, once per 10s) to drop an Everfrost Icicle for area damage, with much higher damage against Cryo-affected enemies. Obtainable by forging or from the Mural Room.

602.content: Imunlaukr is the hero from another land who received the Snow-Tombed Starsilver from the Sal Vindagnyr princess. He arrived too late, found the city silent and left to find a land at war. See his own entry for more.

603.content:
Solar Pearl: Solar Pearl is a 4-star catalyst of the Kunwu series, a dull golden pearl of unknown substance that harbours the light of the sun and moon and pulses with warm strength. It is rumoured to be a legendary orb of Liyue. It has been in the game since Version 1.0.

Its text gives Liyue's jewelers' tale of how the craftsman Kunwu made it, and Kunwu's own, more modest, account.

Appearance: A dull, golden pearl. Its substance is unknown and it pulses with a warm strength. Do not invent a size or setting.

Lore: The text says it once absorbed all the light in the world and was then kept in a wooden box for millennia, yet its power has not dissipated. Released from its container, it shines on, and a truly knowledgeable sage might unleash its power after so long.

A story long popular with Liyue's jewelers says Kunwu took the light of the heavenly bodies and sealed it in a wooden box, which he buried in a dark rocky chamber. After forty-nine days and twenty hours in pitch blackness, the pearl within had absorbed the shine of the sun and moon.

Many in Liyue still believe in Kunwu's esoteric talents. When someone asked the ageing craftsman his secret, he laughed off the notion and said it was purely the product of prolonged polishing.

His apprentice told a different story in private: as Kunwu finished polishing the pearl, the splendour of the heavens shone down and a crimson moon filled the sky. The text leaves open whether this means Kunwu received divine help or whether his ambitions were great enough to send waves through the firmament and draw a response from the heavenly bodies.

Owners: No owner is named in canon. Ningguang is shown with the ascended version in artwork of the Turning Point battle and Shikanoin Heizou in his character demo, which are cameos and not story claims.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star catalyst, base ATK 42, CRIT Rate secondary stat (6 per cent). Passive Solar Shine: Normal Attack hits increase Elemental Skill and Elemental Burst DMG by 20 to 40 per cent (by refinement) for 6s, and Skill or Burst hits likewise increase Normal Attack DMG. Kunwu and Gnostic Hymn 1 series; it comes from the Battle Pass bounty.

604.content: Kunwu is the legendary master craftsman named in the item texts of Solar Pearl, Dragon's Bane and Lion's Roar. In Solar Pearl's story he is an eccentric old man who credits polishing and not magic.

605.content:
Song of Broken Pines: Song of Broken Pines is a 5-star claymore, part of the Millennial Movement series. Its item text is a history of Mondstadt's rebel songs: how bards and a split Church of Favonius stood against the tyrant Decarabian and the ruling aristocracy, and how a folk song gained a second, defiant half when the rebellion rose. Added in Version 1.5.

The Chinese name means roughly "when the pine-sound echoes", a phrase from the song's last line; this is wiki etymology, not an in-world title.

Appearance: Canon text describes it as a greatsword as light as the sigh of grass in the breeze, yet as merciless to the corrupt as a typhoon. Nothing more is said of its look.

Lore: The text opens with a folk song urging people to toss coins to the bard, give a bouquet to a fair maiden, drink bitter wine and sing for tomorrow. Mondstadt, the text says, is a land where songs travel on the wind, so tyrants such as Decarabian and the ruling aristocrats sometimes banned certain chords and tunes, sensing resistance in the bards' music.

Songs and hymns were also used by rebels to communicate. Under the aristocracy the Church that revered the Anemo Archon split in a schism: clergy who dined at the lords' table, wrote hymns of praise and even helped overturn the archon's statues, against saints without office who walked the streets and wine cellars, blessed slaves and commoners with the original holy manuscripts and wrote forbidden songs.

When the gladiator from a foreign land, Vennessa, rose together with the re-awakened Anemo Archon and raised the banner of rebellion, the aged saint called the Nameless Shepherd mobilized the Church of Favonius's true adherents. Many shed martyr blood on the emerald fields, and together they sang the previously unsung second half of the old song: leave the keen steel to those who will die in the fight, prepare the thieves' gallows, sharpen rusted arrows, and shoot the beasts down when the music sounds.

Read this as one partial account from the rebels' side. It sets Church and aristocracy against each other and credits song with real organizing power, but it names no battles, dates or numbers. "Beasts" in the last line is a figure for the corrupt nobility; the original Chinese plays on a phrase for dressed-up beasts, per the wiki trivia, which is not an official gloss.

Owners: No owner is named in canon. Eula carries it in promotional art only; do not treat it as an heirloom of the Lawrence Clan or of Vennessa.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 5-star claymore with base ATK 49 and a Physical DMG Bonus secondary stat. Its passive, Rebel's Banner-Hymn, raises ATK and gives the wielder a Sigil of Whispers when Normal or Charged Attacks hit (at most once per 0.3s). With four Sigils, all are consumed and all nearby party members gain the Millennial Movement: Banner-Hymn effect for 12s (higher ATK and Normal ATK SPD), after which Sigils stop accruing for 20s. Different Millennial Movement buffs do not stack. Obtained from weapon event Wishes.

606.comment: Song of Broken Pines: Nameless Shepherd
606.content: The Nameless Shepherd is an aged saint of the Church of Favonius mentioned only in Song of Broken Pines. When Vennessa raised the banner of rebellion, the Shepherd mobilized the Church's true adherents, and many of them died on the fields singing the rebel half of an old folk song. Nothing else is known, including the Shepherd's real name or fate.

607.content:
Song of Days Past (also: Forgotten Oath of Days Past, Recollection of Days Past, Echoing Sound From Days Past, Promised Dream of Days Past, Poetry of Days Past): Song of Days Past is a 4- and 5-star artifact set from Fontaine, added in Version 4.3. Its bonuses reward healing: it records healing as a Yearning effect and turns it into extra damage. Its pieces tell of the people the Remurians called the "people of bygone times": the rebellion of a songstress against the golden authority, her search for a wish-granting Pure Grail, and the verses that later turned her into legend.

The pieces are Forgotten Oath of Days Past (flower), Recollection of Days Past (plume), Echoing Sound From Days Past (sands), Promised Dream of Days Past (goblet) and Poetry of Days Past (circlet). Many details are told through unnamed figures.

Appearance: Only a few images are given: a butterfly wing worn in the ear (Recollection), the tolling night bell (Echoing Sound), a golden grail brimming with primordial water (Promised Dream) and a silver flower and silver armor (Forgotten Oath and Poetry).

Lore: The pieces follow a northern songstress who unites the tribes against Remuria's golden authority as the first Lochknight, a doomed love between a musician and a woman of his tribe, a desperate search for the wish-granting Pure Grail, and later poems that turn her into legend.

- Forgotten Oath of Days Past: the golden authority swept across the sea and the iron legion made tribes submit, believing the Harmosts' new order was the rightful symphony. In the savage north the tribes united under the heir of Aremorica, a woman later eulogized as the "Lochknight". She called herself an oracle of the Queen of All Waters, not a sovereign, and her army made fellow tribes pledge themselves by the sword. Two vows run through every telling: never draw the sword on those who pledge faith in Egeria, and never compromise with evil. The war that followed burned "proud gold and untarnished silver" alike.
- Recollection of Days Past: in a short-lived seagrass tribe, a youth who did not yet know the God-King's laws put a butterfly wing on a woman's ear, a vow in their tradition not to part until death. They met again years later in the capital. He had become a musician and, disguised as a traveler, won the tournament and an audience with the King; when his identity was revealed, blades greeted him. His "artificial body" was cut to ribbons, and she, thinking an Usurper had imprisoned his soul in stone, whispered that she would free him and that the pale butterfly would guide their souls to the Many Waters. Both names are blanked in the text.
- Echoing Sound From Days Past: the tribes tolled bells for sunrise, sunset, births and deaths, and at last for the destruction of the golden empire. Survivors split: some tried to replay the old music, some gave up their names to hunt ghosts in the forests, some hid their names in song. A woman, doubtful but desperate, says that if the Pure Grail truly grants every wish, she will "drown in such fantastical delusions one last time" before stepping alone into the valley as the night bell tolls.
- Promised Dream of Days Past: tribes told of the Pure Grail, a golden vessel brimming with primordial water, said to heal wounds, restore youth, revive the dead and give wisdom to the purest. After the golden city fell in one night, the vengeful songstress was urged by an Oceanid to seek the primordial chalice that grants every prayer, which spread the heterodox belief that it grants any wish. At twilight's end she realised what the chalice actually was.
- Poetry of Days Past: when the Many Waters converged, a gentle mistress crossed the ruins and built a new city, and the golden symphony would never play again. For more than a thousand years later generations have enjoyed the Lochknights' adventures: swearing on silver armor to fight beside the Oceanids, finding the Pure Grail and welcoming back the Queen of Many Waters.
