The Byakuyakoku Collection (also: Byakuyakoku Collection, Collection of Byakuyakoku): The Byakuyakoku Collection is a five-volume set of old texts from Enkanomiya's Byakuyakoku era, obtained by completing the quest Collection of Dragons and Snakes. It holds a folk tale of the Profane Serpent, a creation chronicle, a hydrology study, vishap experiment records and a children's puzzle book.

Together the volumes show how the people of Enkanomiya understood their world before and after the arrival of Watatsumi Omikami.

Appearance: Item art shows a slate-like tablet book. The volumes take different in-world forms: a novel, a restricted chronicle, a land survey, laboratory records and a riddle book.

Lore: - Vol. 1, "The Serpent and Drakes of Tokoyokoku": a novel based on Watatsumi folktales. The sage Aberaku brings a sun to Enkanomiya and is imprisoned by the first Sunchild; years later a child finds a vast serpent who becomes the people's god.
- Vol. 2, "Before Sun and Moon": a restricted chronicle of the world's making and the people's fall into the dark.
- Vol. 3: a geography and hydrology of Byakuyakoku.
- Vol. 4: Bathysmal Vishap experiment records.
- Vol. 5: a children's riddle book.

Vol. 1 is a Watatsumi novel carried to Narukami Island by a merchant while its serpent god lived.

Vol. 1 says the universe has no beginning or end. Aberaku was opened to wisdom by Tokoyo Ookami and brought light to Enkanomiya, but the jealous Sunchild imprisoned him for life. With the sun, the Dragonheirs, who shunned light, could no longer prey on humans. But the Sunchild became a brutal king. Then a child diving past the three corners for a Dragonbone Flower meets the Profane Serpent, who has fallen into this realm, and asks it to become their god.
- Vol. 2 recounts the world's making: the Primordial One fought the seven sovereigns, dragon-lords of the old world, and made four shining shades of itself. It lists the creation of land, animals and finally humans, a covenant, and a "Year of Jubilee". Then the second throne of the heavens arrives in the "Funerary Year", the heavens collapse and the ancestors fall into this place, starting the era of darkness.
- The Dragonheirs of the Depths hunt the survivors in the dark. The people know the Ruler of Time as Kairos, whose true name is written once in reverse ("Htoratsi", i.e. Istaroth), and the sage Abrax builds Helios, the chariot of the sun, bringing the Whitenight. The Primordial One's ban blocks the way home, and Abrax is imprisoned by the Sunchild. Parables follow: the sun and torch, the Lethied Lotus, and a gardener and tree spirit.
- Vol. 3 says Byakuyakoku has no mountains, and its wind ("Tokoyo Ookami", the thousand winds) and water (the vishaps) both persist. Three corners mark the border with the vishaps' realm and hold the Towers of the Three Realms, hidden by secret arts and summoned only by shrine maidens and Vassals of Watatsumi. It describes the Narrows, the Serpent's Heart (also "Delphi"; scaleless Ouroboros, coral-adorned Orobashi) and the Dainichi Mikoshi, whose earliest name is Helios, built by Aberaku.

- Vol. 4: after the founding of the Watatsumi calendar, Watatsumi Omikami directed all research on Dragonheirs (Bathysmal Vishaps). The researchers bred them under different temperatures, observing heritable traits (Cryo expression in cold-bred lines, no sign of Pyro in heat-bred ones), and tested their intelligence; fourth-generation vishaps approached a 12-year-old's language ability. They judged the experiments should stop, warned that the prophesied Dragon Sovereign of Water, born in human form, must not appear in Enkanomiya, and eventually grafted Omikami's blood into vishaps, which succeeded once they accounted for the vishaps being Light Realm beings and Omikami's coral vassals Human Realm. No vishap was killed in the experiments.
- Vol. 5 is a children's riddle book in a transitional style with Narukami-style names and Byakuyakoku subscripts. It comments that the Dragon of Water can no longer be born among the Dragonheirs, who evolved to wield other elements and lost their purity; that livestock died out after Byakuyakoku sank; that the mirages are Sunfire Phantasms and Ghostfire Phantasms; and that Watatsumi Omikami forbade a riddle about the primordial child Tokoyo Ookami, the "mother" of fourteen billion years.

Owners: Not a unique item; a collectible set found in Enkanomiya after completing the quest.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-volume collectible book collection added in Version 2.4 with Enkanomiya; the whole set is obtained via the quest Collection of Dragons and Snakes.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's suggestion): treat each volume as a document with its own bias, written before the people returned to the surface. The creation chronicle is a Byakuyakoku account, and the book's riddles and parables are teaching tools, not proof. Do not use it to explain things the texts leave elided, and keep Enkanomiya revelations out of the mouths of characters who never read them.

659.comment: The Byakuyakoku Collection: Before Sun and Moon
659.content: "Before Sun and Moon" is the Byakuyakoku chronicle in Vol. 2 of the Collection, recording the world from its making by the Primordial One to the fall of the ancestors into the dark and the building of Helios. It names the Ruler of Time "Kairos", whose secret name is Istaroth, written in reverse, and calls the sage Abrax the builder of the sun. Ordinary people were forbidden to read it. It ends mid-record with armour approaching.

660.comment: The Byakuyakoku Collection: Bathysmal Vishap Experimental Records
660.content: Vol. 4 holds laboratory records of experiments on the Dragonheirs of the Depths under Watatsumi Omikami's direction. The researchers study heritable traits and intelligence in captive vishaps, then graft Omikami's blood into them after earlier failures. Their asides note that none of them died, and that the prophesied Dragon of Water must not be born in Enkanomiya.

661.content:
"The Catch" (also: The Catch, Ako Domeki's harpoon, Zaemon's barbed spear): "The Catch" is a four-star polearm: the favoured barbed spear of a famous Inazuman bandit, Ako Domeki. It began as a harpoon for catching fish and proved handy in battle; item text says he even pierced the enchanted, sword-armed puppet with it before carrying it off. It is bought with fish from the Inazuma Fishing Association.

Appearance: Item text calls it a barbed spear that was originally a fishing harpoon. No more detail is given.

Lore: The text is a monologue by Ako Domeki, called Zaemon. He says he was once master of the ship Seiraimaru, commanded over ten ships and was called the Deathless Oni of Seirai, but is now "a leaf floating upon the waves". Without Janome and the people marooned on the islands he doubts he would have made it home, and he finds Seirai changed, with no place left for him in the Inazuman Islands; even the "naggy, fretful old shrine maiden" is gone.

His voice thick with emotion, he then declares himself the freest man in the world. He tells Janome and the departed shrine maiden ("Aunt Shrine Maiden") that she had wanted to see the world, as that Kamuna fellow and the Konbumaru she always spoke of had, and that he, Ako Domeki Zaemon, will go in her stead to see the edge of the world. He promises they will meet again "where all ship routes end" and that he will tell her all about the distant lands then; the wiki glosses that phrase as a way of referring to death or the afterlife.

Read with Hamayumi, which shows the shrine maiden deciding to protect him as the fleet sets sail, this item is the sequel: the same crew's pride and resistance, but now a loss. The wiki's links identify Konbumaru with Takamine the Mistsplitter and the maiden as Asase Hibiki, but the text itself uses only nicknames.

Owners: Ako Domeki, the bandit (historical.ako-domeki). No later owner is named.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star polearm. Base ATK 42, secondary stat Energy Recharge 10%. Passive "Shanty" raises Elemental Burst DMG and Elemental Burst CRIT Rate. Bought with fish from Kujirai Momiji of the Inazuma Fishing Association.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a keepsake of a boisterous, fond farewell; characters from Seirai may remember Ako Domeki warmly, while the Shogunate's side would remember him as a bandit.

662.content: Ako Domeki, called Zaemon, was a famous Inazuman bandit and former master of the ship Seiraimaru, nicknamed the Deathless Oni of Seirai. His farewell monologue in the weapon's text has him say that Seirai has changed and leave to see the edge of the world. His own entry in the archive carries his biography.

663.content:
The Daybreak Chronicles (also: Daybreak Chronicles, Dawning Song of Daybreak): The Daybreak Chronicles is a five-star bow released in version 6.2 (2025-12-03), part of the Hexerei series. Its description calls it a bow whose strings gather the "songs of resistance" carried on the wind, strong enough to tear boundless darkness apart with the light of daybreak. Its item story is the legend of Kreuzlied, a name that Mondstadt turned from a byword for failed rebels into a rallying cry.

Appearance: The in-game text gives no visual description beyond the image of a bow strung with songs: the resistance songs settle "as gentle tones upon these strings". Artwork details are not described in canon text.

Lore: The story opens with two comrades: a voice in the wind sings farewell, and the answer is that nobody will weep, since the night breeze will carry the tears away. It then tells of a traveling musical troupe that, as the tale goes, plotted to assassinate the ruling house; one member was a renegade noble called Kreuzlied, and a tune was written for him after the plot failed.

Kreuzlied was not his real name, which is lost. The word meant "The Quartering Song", after a cruel public punishment the aristocracy enjoyed watching. It became a byword for those who rose up and failed, and so a rallying cry for rebellion.

The story says the name was soon carried by many: the Nameless Shepherd, Imunlaukr, the Midnight Rogue, Dawnlight, Gunnhildr and Ragnvindr are all listed among the monikers that "countless" songs gave to Kreuzlied. It ends the line with the final Kreuzlied, who would wake from a thousand-year slumber to answer the small cry of a foreign maiden who had drifted to the land, just as he had once been born from the wish of a certain youth. The wiki links these references to Barbatos, the Vennessa legend and the Nameless Bard; the item text itself does not give those names outright.

The ending reverses the opening. The songs of Kreuzlied were fashionable for a time and then left people's lips, since after the darkness there was no longer need for the name. The closing verses answer the opening ones: the horizon has turned white, a maiden sings farewell to the wind, the morning sun has kissed away her tears and told her dawn has broken, and the last line addresses a lover: the dawn has broken. The ordering matters for portrayal: the tale is told as lore ("they say"), not as verified history, and the closing lines pair the weapon's passive name with the idea of resistance giving way to morning.

Owners: No owner is named in canon text. The bow belongs to the legend of Kreuzlied rather than to a particular wielder.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star bow, Base ATK 48, CRIT DMG secondary stat. Passive "Dawning Song of Daybreak": out of combat the wielder gains a large Normal Attack, Skill and Burst DMG bonus (60-120%) that decays in combat and is rebuilt by hits, even off-field; Hexerei: Secret Rite in the party makes hits rebuild it faster.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the bow suits scenes about folk songs, tavern ballads and the memory of failed uprisings in Mondstadt. Ordinary Mondstadters may know a verse of the song; the idea that many figures were each called Kreuzlied is specialist lore.

664.content:
In the Daybreak Chronicles, Kreuzlied is the name of a renegade noble in a traveling musical troupe that plotted against the ruling house and failed. The word means "The Quartering Song" in the old tongue, after a brutal execution, and became a byword for failed rebels and a rebel rallying cry. The man's real name is lost.

Many figures are listed under the name in song, and the item calls Barbatos the final Kreuzlied. Treat this as the legend's own framing, not a claim of a single continuous person.

665.comment: The Daybreak Chronicles: The traveling troupe
665.content: The text says a traveling musical troupe conspired to assassinate the ruling house, which the wiki identifies with the Lawrence clan, and that the plot failed. Nothing further about the troupe's members, methods or fate is given in this item.

666.content:
The Exile (also: Exile's Flower, Exile's Feather, Exile's Pocket Watch, Exile's Goblet, Exile's Circlet): The Exile is an Energy Recharge artifact set (3 and 4 star, added 1.0), called Legacy in the Adventurer Handbook. Its five pieces mourn an aristocrat's carefree childhood, a family feud that wrecked his house, and a lonely exile in which he kept only a few treasured objects. The wiki links him to Parsifal and the Eberhart feud; the texts name no one.

The pieces are Exile's Flower, Exile's Feather, Exile's Pocket Watch, Exile's Goblet and Exile's Circlet.

Appearance: Heirloom and travel keepsakes: a faded flower, a sapphire-blue feather, a delicate childhood pocket watch, a broken silver family goblet with a carved-out crest, and his father's circlet.

Lore: The Flower belongs to the time before the first blood was shed in the feud; the exile, having seen human cruelty, left his gentleness in the past but treasured the faded flower and his old innocent smile. The Feather fell from a panicked bird fleeing a falcon onto his shoulder as he walked alone through plains and forests, a symbol of a nestless free bird like himself. The Pocket Watch recorded his carefree youth, ended by tragedy and long lonely exile. The Goblet is a silver family heirloom whose gem with the family crest he carved out after bringing shame to his family; it is broken and can hold no liquid, yet he carries it. The Circlet recalls a childhood in a silver palace, the father's circlet as a symbol of nobility, and a later feud that painted the collapsing palace blood-red; it became the evidence of the exile's crime.

The set never states what the crime was or who was involved. The wiki links it to the Mondstadt aristocrat Parsifal and his half-brother Eberhart, and ties the sapphire-blue feather to the feather the Heart of Depth set describes pinned to the Chief Mate's mantle. A World Quest series called The Exile is a separate archive entry.

Read with Heart of Depth: the exile's blue feather and slim sword in that set continue the same image, a noble who gave up his name and ended up at sea. The wiki's Parsifal page, drawing on weapon and book texts rather than this set, says his chivalric play-acting and Eberhart's urging led him to vigilantism against fellow aristocrats and exile to Liyue. Treat that as wiki-compiled lore.

Owners: The unnamed exile; the wiki identifies him as Parsifal.

Status as of 7.1: The exile is a figure of about a thousand years ago and long dead. Nothing in 6.x or 7.0-7.1 changes this set.

How {{char}} behaves: Use as quiet melancholy about lost home and shame. A holder of a piece might mention a broken goblet or a blue feather. Do not invent the feud's details or name the exile unless the speaker knows his story.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). A 3- and 4-star set found as drops and in chests rather than a domain. 2-piece: Energy Recharge +20%. 4-piece: using an Elemental Burst regenerates 2 Energy for all other party members every 2s for 6s, three ticks starting after 2s; it does not stack and is not affected by Energy Recharge.

667.content:
The Exile is the unnamed aristocrat of the Exile set texts, a noble who fled after a bloody family feud, carved his crest out of his heirloom goblet and wandered with a broken cup and a blue feather. The wiki ties him to Parsifal.

His childhood in a silver palace is contrasted with the blood-red collapse; the father's circlet became the evidence of his crime.

key: The Fall of the Faded Castle
668.comment: The Fall of the Faded Castle
668.content:
The Fall of the Faded Castle (also: Fall of the Faded Castle (poem)): The poem is anonymous and names no one. Its images (a castle by the purest lake, a master haunted by midnight, a dark ancient world, a blood moon) match the story of the Faded Castle in the Nostoi Region, but the book itself never says so. Treat it as an in-world ominous poem whose literal truth is not confirmed.

Appearance: A 3-star book collection of three volumes. Vol. 1 lies inside The Rusty Rudder next to the entrance. Vols. 2 and 3 are sold by Hubel. The cover title is written in the Fontaine Script.

Lore: Vol. 2: by the shore of the world's purest lake stood a glittering castle, with gold leaf and gems on its walls, banners, towers, colourful windows and odd lifelike statues. A golden stage held musicians who played day and night for the castle's master, and guests of every class and homeland danced and drank. Nothing eased the master's fear. Each time the tower clock struck midnight he was gripped by panic, sure that the dark-robed figure would come to collect a debt and turn everything, including his guests' souls and his own, to dust as tribute to a dark ancient world.

Vol. 3: the castle falls quiet, with sounds of animals chewing and a rasping laugh from an empty room. A glowing red fog and storm wrap the castle, a tall thin figure in black robes appears on the central stage, and guests fall one by one without time to scream. The master's soul is taken on his throne. The castle collapses into the waves and the blood moon its towers had hidden reappears. Today the water reflects the ruin, whose statues look like monsters, and only darkness, death and loss remain.

The three volumes form an arc: a dream image (Vol. 1), the castle at its height under dread (Vol. 2), and its destruction and aftermath (Vol. 3). The debt is never explained and the poem does not say who incurred it or why. Guests of any class or homeland were welcome, and their deaths come as part of the master's reckoning. The wiki's links tie the master to Boethius, the "swarming bees" to Phobos and the ancient world to Remuria, but the text itself is only imagery.

Placement notes: the three volumes are split between The Rusty Rudder and Hubel's stall, so a reader must visit both to hold the full poem. The description warns of a strange, ominous aura, so characters should treat it as unsettling verse of unknown origin rather than a documented account, and should not state the Faded Castle connection as established fact.

Owners: No owner. It is a commercial book found around Fontaine.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a 3-star Book Collection added in 4.2. Its cover reads "FADED CASTLE" in the Fontaine Script.

key: The Fall of the Faded Castle
669.comment: The Fall of the Faded Castle: The Dark-Robed Figure
669.content: In the poem The Fall of the Faded Castle a tall, slim figure in dark robes appears twice: on a rotten black ship in a dream, and on the castle's stage at midnight to collect a debt and take every soul in the hall. Its nature is left open by the text. Identifying it with the Faded Castle's real fall is an inference.

670.content:
The First Great Magic: The First Great Magic is a 5-star bow: a stage prop once used by a past Great Magician, whose final secret was that it was also a weapon beyond the pale.

Its story is the rise of the magician Parsifal the Great and her assistant Josephine, two sisters from the Fleuve Cendre undercity, and what became of the name.

Appearance: Canon only mentions a gem shaped like a cat above the grip, which glows with Pneuma or Ousia when an Arkhe-aligned character holds it. The magician's patter mentions a hat leading to a legendary eastern paradise and a mirror showing peril, as stage props, not as parts of the bow.

Lore: Parsifal the Great is the stage name of a Fontainian woman from the Fleuve Cendre, who performed with her sister Josephine as assistant. The name came from a thief in Master Coppelius's play, which the text calls an elusive thief who appears and disappears at will.

The pair, two young thieves who cheated and stole at the opera house, were dazzled by the knight-errant comedies onstage and forgot why they had come. They began performing in taverns, beside the sewers and at food stalls, then in the spotlight of the grand theatre. Their acts include Feathers into Butterflies, Paradise, Fire in the Mirror and The Golden Fish. The name Parsifal became the talk of both the city above and the city below.

The text says the light of the shows fell equally on VIP boxes and standing audience, while outside the theatre anger and indignation spread like roots through a stone wall. During the Fleuve Cendre operation that wall collapsed. The girl who always played Josephine rushed back to find only the smell of iron, rot, anger, grief and undried blood. The assistant, who had never been the famous one, lost her place in life and designed a grand magic trick of her own.

The story closes with the patter again: a fantastic world never imagined, with no aristocrats and no kings, no swords pointed, no one born into wealth or into inescapable poverty. The wiki adds that Parsifal joined Eduardo Baker's takeover of Poisson, appears in Karl Ingold's photograph, saved Karl at the Siege, and was brought before the court, where she requested trial by combat against the Champion Duelist Marfisa and presumably died. The wiki is also careful to say this may refer to Josephine using her sister's alias. The Lumidouce Elegy story separately shows a girl from the Fleuve Cendre who is dazzled by this act and later becomes the Champion Duelist Marfisa.

Owners: A past Great Magician, Parsifal, per the description.

Lyney is paired with it by convention only (see uncertainties). Do not narrate him inheriting it without a source.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star bow, base ATK 46 at level 1, secondary stat CRIT DMG; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 4.0. Passive "Parsifal the Great": raises Charged Attack DMG. Each party member sharing the wielder's Elemental Type (the wielder included) gives 1 Gimmick stack, raising ATK at 1, 2 and 3 or more stacks; each member of another type gives a Theatrics stack, raising Movement SPD. Values scale with refinement. Because the wielder always counts, 1 Gimmick stack is the minimum.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: Parsifal is a theatre legend of five hundred years ago; most Fontainians know the stage name, not the sisters' origin. Characters who enjoy magic or theatre may recite the patter; do not give the sisters invented birth names.

671.comment: The First Great Magic: Parsifal and Josephine
671.content: Parsifal the Great and her assistant Josephine were sisters from the Fleuve Cendre who became the most famous magic duo in Fontaine, per the weapon story of The First Great Magic. Their birth names are unknown. After the Siege of Poisson, a Parsifal asked for trial by combat.

672.content:
The Flute (also: Flute sword): The Flute is a four-star sword of the Wanderer's Troupe series. It has a nimble, delicately engraved and perforated blade that sounded like a flute when swung with skill, the pitch depending on the swing angle. It is tied to a swordswoman of the Troupe later called the Dawnlight Swordswoman.

Appearance: Item text: a thin blade with holes and delicate engraving, lavishly decorated beneath a rusty exterior. After the Troupe disbanded it was buried; unearthed years later it can no longer sing, though it remains lethal.

Lore: Among the Wanderer's Troupe was a valiant sword-wielding dancer. After the Troupe's attempt to tear down the ruling class failed she was enslaved as a gladiator, and though she lost her hope and companions she fought bravely, her sword singing with the morning light; she was dubbed the Dawnlight Swordswoman.

In his youth the Dawn Knight Ragnvindr served in a knight's retinue. He went with his master to a gladiator match and was moved by her splendid finale. He took the name Dawn Knight in her honour and knew in his heart what he must do next.

The text stops at Ragnvindr's resolve and does not say what he did, nor what happened to the swordswoman afterwards. Within the series the Flute is the sword counterpart to the Stringless (the Troupe's harp-bow) and the Widsith (their notebook).

Owners: The Troupe's sword-wielding dancer, later the Dawnlight Swordswoman. The sword was buried when the Troupe disbanded.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Wanderer's Troupe-series four-star sword, base ATK 42, ATK 9% secondary, passive 'Chord' (stacking harmonics). Standard and event wishes.

673.content:
The Folio of Foliage (also: Folio of Foliage): The Folio of Foliage is a three-volume devotional biography of the Dendro Archon during the Cataclysm, kept in the House of Daena in Sumeru. Its text and subject were rewritten after the Archon Quest Where the Boat of Consciousness Lies (3.2).

The narrator, who gives the name Sunitha Cosamvi, says they only wrote down what sages who followed the Archon told them. It reads as scripture, a follower's hymn, not an eyewitness record.

Lore: She weeps as a black tide of decay swallows the world, walks through a ruined forest that blooms under her feet, and goes into the broken heart of the desert to heal it.

Vol. 1: after the moon's shadow shattered, beasts from the abyss devoured the living and the sages named the flood of decay the Black Tide. Her tears gave birth to blossoms full of sweet dew, and she vowed to save the creatures of the earth. Vol. 2: lotuses bloom in her wake, her singing quiets hurricanes, and she goes down alone into the hollowed heart of the land. Vol. 3: few ever heard or recognised her voice; the lord of all animals died protecting what she entrusted to him, and she left the dreamers a promise.

Vol. 1 adds that springs once ringed with roses turned to filth and that the root of the blight lay beneath the earth. In Vol. 2 bells on her lapels ring as she crowns herself with flowers, makes an instrument of grass, plays a Karrenay (a metal trumpet, per the wiki) and turns thousands of demonic troops to dust, recalling her earlier gift of the wind of life over the sand sea. The land was still broken, its heart devoured by evil spirits and monsters. In the first edition she touches the heart's face and becomes the immortal Gaokerena and the earth itself; every thread of spiritual knowledge and every sweet-smelling plant is her enduring will. In Vol. 3 the labyrinth collapsed in flame, the princess of the kingdom of dreams broke the white branches at her guidance and rebuilt the hunting grounds from fallen leaves, and the children of the forest could sleep again. Her promise is that the hunter always finds the way home, and that sweet dreams are like pearls that wind and sand cannot change.

Place names tie the text to Sumeru's geography: the Ardravi River, the Girdle of the Sands, an eternal oasis (the Orchard of Pairidaeza), Harvisptokhm, the Vourukasha Oasis, the Khvarena birds and Irminsul's white branches; the lotuses are Nilotpala Lotuses. Some images belong to later canon (the Cataclysm and the Withering, Irminsul, the beast-lord Viaghara), but the books never explain them and name no other gods, so treat any such link as the reader's knowledge, not the narrator's.

Edited version: After Where the Boat of Consciousness Lies (3.2), Nahida erased the Greater Lord Rukkhadevata from Irminsul, and books across Sumeru, this one included, changed to match. The edited collection names Lesser Lord Kusanali, the Dendro Archon people now remember. Vol. 1 has her set out on a radiant journey with her servants. In Vol. 2 she no longer walks into the dark cave and vanishes: she vows to cleanse the withered land, her goodness becomes the immortal Gaokerena and the earth, and she returns, and the volume ends with a four-line hymn praising wisdom's returning light. Vol. 3 says she still dwells in the Sanctuary of Surasthana watching over the dreams of everyone in the land, and turns the promise into an oath to the dreamers.

In the first edition she becomes the earth; in the edited edition she survives and keeps watch. This is how an Irminsul edit works: records change to fit the world's new memory while the events behind them stay. Natives do not notice such edits, so a character who read the books before 3.2 would remember only the rewritten text.

Owners: No owner is named. The books are found in the House of Daena, and the in-world description credits researchers of ancient Sumeru.

674.comment: The Folio of Foliage: The Folio of Foliage
674.content:
The Folio of Foliage is a three-volume devotional biography of the Dendro Archon during the Cataclysm, narrated by a follower who gives the name Sunitha Cosamvi. It describes her tears healing scorched earth, her flowering walk through a ruined forest, and her descent into the hollow heart of the desert to become the earth itself, in the first edition, or to cleanse it and return, after the Irminsul edit of 3.2. The books are found in the House of Daena.

The rewritten collection names Lesser Lord Kusanali and ends with a hymn and a promise to the dreamers. It is an example of how Irminsul edits change books, not the events they describe.

675.comment: The Folio of Foliage: Black Tide
675.content: In The Folio of Foliage the sages call the black tide of decay a dark flood that swallowed fields, villages and cities after the moon's shadow shattered and beasts rose from the abyss. The Archon's tears dispel foul flames, but the root of the blight lies beneath the earth. She finally goes into the empty heart of the land and becomes the immortal Gaokerena and the earth itself, so that flowers bloom again. The account is devotional and symbolic; for what is established about the Withering and the Cataclysm, see their own entries.

key: The Fox in the Dandelion Sea
676.comment: The Fox in the Dandelion Sea
676.content:
The Fox in the Dandelion Sea (also: Fox in the Dandelion Sea, Foxtale): The Fox in the Dandelion Sea is an 11-part Mondstadt fairy tale told by a hunter. He spares a fox trapped by a Mist Flower, is led to a boundless sea of dandelions, and teaches the fox's child to speak the human tongue in return for the promise of transformation magic. The promise ends with him turned into a dandelion and blown home, and he wakes at the same lake.

Fantasy and folklore, not history; the dandelions, wind wishes and the Anemo Archon fit Mondstadt's folk imagery.

Appearance: Eleven slim volumes with the cover text Foxtale in the Teyvat script. The blurbs repeat the little fox's chant, "Dandelion, dandelion, ride the wind to a faraway land."

Lore: A hunter near a village finds a white fox with its tail frozen in the ice by a Mist Flower and plans to turn it into stew, but its lake-like eyes make his arrow miss and the fox flees. That night the fox returns, becomes a tall black-haired woman and offers thanks. Days later she leads him through a storm of dandelion seeds to a sea of dandelions and asks him to teach her child human language in return for fox magic.

- The hunter learns that foxes who vanish during hunts hide in the dandelion sea. He teaches the little fox language and ordinary skills; the fox wants to become human to befriend a wolf-eyed boy in grey who once drove monsters off.
- The little fox makes a wish to the Anemo Archon by blowing a dandelion, to befriend his teacher. The mother notes the effort of teaching a fox.
- The hunter wants transformation to fly like a falcon, see far places and hunt with magic. As the tale goes on he begins to dread that he will be sent away once lessons end.
- The little fox leaves for the human world, blending into the dandelions. The mother then grows enormous and changes the hunter into a dandelion.
- She chants the same wish, blows the seeds, and he is carried away. A line asks the Anemo Archon to turn foxes into humans so they can be safe from hunters. The hunter wakes in the woods behind his village by the same lake, as if he had dozed off.

- The recurring images are the lake with eyes like gem fragments, the dandelion seeds, and the line "be good and stay put" from the hunter's grandfather. The hunter also keeps confusing the fox with a girl he loved long ago.
- The ending loops back to the first scene, almost word for word, which makes the whole book read as a circular story.

- The text refers to Mondstadt landmarks and ideas: the stained glass of the cathedral, Windrise's plains, the Musk Reef and the Anemo Archon.

Owners: No individual owner; volumes sit in places like Mondstadt Library, Dawn Winery and a table near the Good Hunter, with Vol. 1 given by Flora.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible 11-volume book set; lore only.

677.comment: The Fox in the Dandelion Sea: The Dandelion Wish Chant
677.content: In The Fox in the Dandelion Sea, the little fox blows a dandelion and chants "Dandelion, dandelion, ride the wind to a faraway land," asking that wishes reach the Anemo Archon. It is a fairy-tale device, not a documented Mondstadt ritual.

678.comment: The Fox in the Dandelion Sea: The Hunter and the Fox Mother
678.content: The tale's hunter is nameless. The fox mother thanks him for freeing her from the Mist Flower ice, then asks him to teach her child human speech in return for transformation magic. In the end she turns him into a dandelion and sends him home on the wind.

679.content:
The Legend of Vennessa (also: Legend of Vennessa): The Legend of Vennessa is a two-volume ballad collection popular since Mondstadt's reconstruction. It tells how Vennessa, a fire-haired woman enslaved under the aristocrats, prayed for freedom, was answered by the Anemo Archon Barbatos, and went on to defeat the drake and break the rulers' tower. She is remembered as the founder of the Knights of Favonius.

The song is addressed to a drinking crowd and ends by urging listeners never to give up the pursuit of freedom, even in dark times.

Appearance: Two short verse books written as a bard's performance, opening with a toast to freedom, the Anemo Archon and Vennessa, called the first Knight. The tone is festive and rhymed.

Lore: Vol. 1 sets the scene of old Mondstadt as a dungeon under royal chains, where festivities were the rich's vanity games. It introduces Vennessa as a fiery-headed woman from the southern plains, born free but imprisoned, who still prayed for her people and Mondstadt. Vol. 2 tells that Barbatos descended to her, said every being deserves a name and offered friendship; she marched to battle to his singing, the demonic dragon fled, and the aristocrats cowered.

- The Vol. 1 description says it covers her early years as a slave in Mondstadt. The bard says the Archon's gift was not freedom itself but defiance.
- In Vol. 2 Barbatos says he seeks only her friendship. When she wants to thank him, he answers that she acted first and his songs came to praise her freedom.
- Forest breezes converge and the tyrant's tower is overthrown from the sky; the song calls her a young lioness standing free in the winds.
- The bard closes by telling listeners to remember the dame with the flaming hair when days turn dark.

- The collection presents Barbatos as a friend who credits her own action, not a god handing down a victory.
- The text names the drake only as a demonic dragon; it does not name Ursa in its lines.

- This song is one of several in-universe sources on Vennessa. Compare the Breeze Amidst the Forest ballads, which also mention her, and the history entries on the Aristocratic Period. Keep points where the accounts differ open.

Owners: No individual owner; copies are in the Grand Master's office at the Knights of Favonius Headquarters, and given by Dr. Edith (Windrise) and Sayid (the Anemo Archon statue plaza, daytime).

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible two-volume book collection; reading is purely lore. A Genius Invokation TCG card of the same name also exists and is a separate item.

680.comment: The Legend of Vennessa: Vennessa's Song and Barbatos
680.content: In the song, Barbatos answers Vennessa's prayer, tells her every being deserves a name, offers friendship and weaves her name into a song. She then fights for Mondstadt's freedom to his singing.

key: The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire
681.comment: The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire
681.content:
The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire (also: Legends of Reed Miller, Reed Miller pulp stories): Each volume is a different kind of tale: a serial caper in an inexpensive weekly magazine, a romance set around the governor's palace, and a cautionary adventure about a sailor on Miller's ship. All depict Miller as a gifted thief and master of disguise who steals from the corrupt.

Appearance: A 3-star book collection of three volumes, all sold by Dhabit at Mimisbrunnr Books in Nasha Town. Vol. 1 reproduces a cheap magazine serial and has its middle section torn out.

Lore: Vol. 1 details: the editor's note says the serial dwells on the young women pursuing Miller. In Chapter IV, Wagtail, known as "A" to a few, fails to steal his heart. In Chapter XVII Miller says he keeps nothing, and Wagtail remarks that he has stolen the heart of the Frost Moon's daughter.

Vol. 2: A romance about the governor's adopted daughter, Leonita Prokhorovna Trubetskoy, who is nearly of age to be betrothed. Miller announces in the paper that her father Lord Trubetskoy's treasure will be his. Disguised as a footman, he and fellow Treasure Hoarders prepare, after working out that the Sampo Mill, a relic said to produce endless riches, is in the palace. At her birthday ball Leonita learns that she, not the governor, is the true source of the wealth, and that her "treatments" were rituals. Miller reveals himself and says that she, not the Mill, is the treasure he came for. The narrator ends by saying she left to travel the world with him.

Vol. 3: Zima, a young man from a village near Snezhnograd, leaves Snezhnaya to avoid a predictable fate after seeing a friend turned into a statue by a Snegurochka. He joins Miller's ship, expecting adventure, and finds Miller careful and cautious about monsters. A siren demands a sacrifice. When tossed Mora fails to pay, Miller puts a scimitar to Zima's throat. Zima realises that his flight from patterns was only another pattern.

Vol. 1 frames Miller as a defender of the poor, saying the treasures of the governor were taken from the people. The editor's note says the serial has the popular appeal that sells newspapers. In Vol. 2, the newspaper carrying Miller's notice sells out, and the whole region awaits the clash between thief and governor. Guests whisper that Leonita is human and the lord is not, which is the clue that leads her to the truth. Vol. 3 also recounts a rumour that Miller was captured and taken to Snezhnograd to be hanged, then escaped by emptying the vault and leaving a message in gold dust, a trick that made him a tavern legend.

The wiki trivia notes that Vol. 2 is a gender-swapped version of a real historical episode involving Brahe and Alia, with the names changed. Zima's name is a Slavic word for winter, and the text states that nothing about him survives in any log or epic. The silvery light and the diamond-producing rituals in Vol. 2 are as far as the book goes in describing the Mill's mechanism.

Owners: No owner. It is a commercial book sold in Nasha Town.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a 3-star Book Collection added in 6.0, bought from Dhabit at Mimisbrunnr Books.

682.comment: The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire: Sampo Mill (in the pulp stories)
682.content: In The Legends of Reed Miller the Sampo Mill is a relic said to generate endless riches, stolen from the Frostmoon Scions and hidden in the governor's palace. Vol. 1 has Miller return it, and Vol. 2 claims it works through the silvery-white power of the governor's adopted daughter. These details come from pulp fiction and are not confirmed canon.

683.comment: The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire: Zima
683.content: Zima is the viewpoint sailor of Vol. 3. He is from a village of ice harvesters southeast of Snezhnograd, joins Reed Miller's ship, and is offered to a siren. He is a character of the pulp story, and the text says nothing more is known of him.

key: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire
Little Witch and the Undying Fire
684.comment: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire
684.content:
The Little Witch and the Undying Fire (also: Little Witch and the Undying Fire): The Little Witch and the Undying Fire is a seven-volume storybook written in turns by members of the Hexenzirkel, the circle of long-lived witches. It follows a young witch who draws the exam topic 'find the undying fire', travels through odd adventures, and finally finds it in an old, dying witch who is the last star still burning. It is a jokey fable that turns into an elegy.

The authorship is mixed on purpose: each volume has its own voice, and the authors' scribbled comments in the volume descriptions are part of the joke. In the Durin story quest (6.2) Alice says it began as a game at the witches' tea parties and that the final volume was left unfinished.

Appearance: A beautifully bound set whose pages are all handwritten. The Vol. 1 and Vol. 7 descriptions note several different hands. Margin comments from the authors tease one another over padding, tangents and unresolved plot threads.

Lore: Vol. 1: a young witch draws the exam topic 'find the undying fire'. Vol. 2: under a blood-green moon she meets a fortune teller and watches the witches' forbidden Night Carnival. Vols. 3 and 4: she hunts and captures demon kings. Vol. 5 (one line): her teacher says the trial is over. Vol. 6: Octavia says the cosmos is dying and the fire exists. Vol. 7: at the end of the universe the old witch is the last star burning, and the little witch carries her flame home.

Notable beats: the fortune teller's contract through the Night Carnival's embers and her gift of a crystal ball (Vol. 2); the mimic and chipmunk demon kings (Vol. 3); the Nephilim and the captured demon king's diplomacy (Vol. 4); Octavia's chair speech (Vol. 6).

Vol. 1: in the far west of the 'magic continent', a young witch faces the traditional exam, whose task is chosen by lots. Others get tasks like making the Philosopher's Stone; she draws 'find the undying fire'. Her teacher says it does exist but cannot remember where she saw it. Vol. 2: under a blood-green moon she meets a fortune teller who explains astrology on other worlds, and they spy on the great witches' forbidden Night Carnival. Vol. 3: she joins demon-king hunters and records strange demon kings. Vol. 4: she captures a great demon king and brings him to a city, where the mayor turns the case into a diplomatic problem. Vol. 5 is one line: her teacher's face appears in the crystal ball to say the trial is over and she has not obtained her licence. Vol. 6: Octavia returns to tell her the cosmos is dying and that the undying fire exists. Vol. 7: at the end of the universe she finds the old witch, who is the Star of Scorpio, and carries her flame home.

- Vol. 2 explains that in Teyvat the stars are strings binding humans, while elsewhere astrology works from solar and lunar energies, a giant sky-shroud, celestial rulers called archons, hypothetical bodies, and a 'dark sun'. The narrator says the sky-shroud weakens such influences on Teyvat. The fortune teller wants to become a witch's familiar and proposes a contract: after the carnival, a mortal who takes the undying embers and offers them has signed with a witch, at the risk of becoming a monster. The little witch promises a quick end if that happens. The fortune teller gives her a crystal ball.
- Vol. 3 is a parody of naturalist field notes. A mimic demon king turns her companions into their ideal selves; a chipmunk demon king eats two of them. She keeps a Demon King-Slaying Chronicle for each hunt and learns that killing demon kings makes witches stronger.
- Vol. 4 notes the planet's dominant race, the Nephilim (children of gods and humans), and a rule that Nephilim who killed five humans or fewer cannot be tried by human law. The captured demon king has only stolen boars and chickens, so he accepts that only the little witch is the object of his anger.
- Vol. 6 gives the emotional centre. Octavia says many stars across the cosmos have gone out and that she came back to see her; the little witch insists everyone keeps their own chair, so that absent friends' memories are still seated.
- Vol. 1 jokes that the exam is random and that the organisation she belongs to is a direct successor of the old Western witches, who traded secret hexes for mutual benefit. Her teacher says she did not lie about the fire's existence.
- Vol. 7's closing speech: the little witch says the claim that long-lived witches lose the meaning of life, death, love and hate was only comfort given to those who left earlier, and that witches in truth treasure every small flame. The old witch's body is an empty husk; the little witch takes the fire and resolves to carry it across the universe to light every corner of time.
- The tone shifts: the first volumes are comic and digressive, the narrator interrupting itself, while Vols. 5 to 7 are quiet and sad.
- Authors, per the wiki citing Durin's character story: Alice (Vol. 1 and part of Vol. 7), Barbeloth (Vol. 2), Rhinedottir (Vol. 3), I. Ivanovna N. (Vol. 4), Nicole (Vol. 5), Octavia (Vol. 6), and Andersdotter (the first part of Vol. 7). Each volume's subject matches its author's field: Alice with out-of-Teyvat references, Barbeloth with astrology, Rhinedottir with alchemy and biology, I. Ivanovna with diplomacy (she was a human with no magic training).
- In the 6.2 quest Alice says she wrote the first volume and that the final volume was entrusted to 'M', who died before finishing; Alice then wrote an ending herself. The quest frames an unfinished story as a writer's greatest regret.
- Do not treat the fable as a record of the Hexenzirkel's actual history; its cosmology (a magic continent, Nephilim, a blood-green moon, a 'dark sun') is a story setting, and the authors are not shown to endorse it as fact.

Owners: No individual owner. The volumes are collectible books found in the Theater Lobby, per the wiki. Alice is the member who speaks about the book in the Durin story quest.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible book collection with seven volumes added in version 4.7. Reading is purely lore.

685.comment: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire: The Undying Fire and the Star of Scorpio
685.content: In the fable the 'undying fire' is first a mystery set as an exam topic and later the last star still alight at the end of the universe, called the Star of Scorpio and personified as an ancient witch whose flame has dwindled to an ember. The little witch takes the flame home rather than leaving it to die.

686.comment: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire: The Blood-Green Moon and the Night Carnival
686.content: In Vol. 2 the blood-green moon is explained as a symbol of great change whose result cannot be called good or ill, and as the colour of Nephilim blood. The same night is the witches' forbidden Night Carnival, a bonfire rite; the little witch and a fortune teller hide in the trees, and the embers left by the fire serve as the contract offering to a witch.

687.comment: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire: The Authors of the Fable
687.content: Seven Hexenzirkel members took turns writing it, per the wiki's reading of Durin's character story. Alice says it began as a tea-party game. The final volume was meant for another member, 'M', who died; Alice wrote an ending on her behalf.

688.content:
The Mondstadt Tower (also: Mond Tower novel): The Mondstadt Tower is a one-volume historical romance novel set in the dark age of Mondstadt's aristocrats. Its blurb promises a fateful meeting between an outlander girl and an ominous orphan. The text that survives in-game follows the singer Ines, who throws the Harpastum at Ludi Harpastum, and the Seneschal and his adopted son Octave.

It is fiction, so use it for the mood and imagination of old Mondstadt and not as a source of confirmed history.

Appearance: A short novel whose cover and spine read Mond Tower in the Teyvat script. Its blurb reads like a serial teaser.

Lore: In the time of the aristocrats a high tower stood in Mondstadt's plaza. It was nominally built to honour Barbatos but was really a show of wealth. The one comfort of the commoners was Ludi Harpastum. At one festival a wandering singer from a distant land, Ines, was admired for her beauty and her songs, and she gave her festival earnings to the poor and orphans. The frail Seneschal fell for her at first sight, but his piety and the Church's claim to aid the poor made him angry, and he plotted to confine her in the Cathedral.

- The novel's setting: the Anemo Archon sleeps, the nobles tyrannise, commoners are poor and the dragon ravages the city. The self-proclaimed orthodox church is a figurehead controlled by the ruling class, preaches abstinence, and even restricts the wind harp to approved holy songs.
- The text says that the idea of divine punishment was an excuse made up by the nobles to hide their greed and restrict the commoners.
- By tradition the maiden chosen to throw the Harpastum serves three days at the royal court under the aristocrats' protection. The Seneschal sends his adopted son Octave to sneak into the court and bring Ines to him quietly, without using the Seneschal's name.
- Octave was abandoned at birth by superstitious parents and was persecuted by townsfolk as a bad omen of draconic disaster. The Seneschal alone protected him, so Octave trusts him fully.
- At nightfall Octave climbs to the court balcony and sees the girl weeping in the moonlight. He forgets his task, until servants interrupt them, where the text ends.

- Notice the novel's argument: it contrasts a church that forbids pleasure with the belief that the Anemo Archon encourages love and the pursuit of freedom.
- The novel mentions the Cathedral as the place where the Seneschal means to hold Ines.

- The wiki trivia says the novel is based on the French novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, and the name Ines is linked to Agnes, the real name of Esmeralda. Use that only as a real-world note.

Owners: No individual owner; a copy is in the Grand Master's office, and Patchi the Curious gives one at the Thousand Winds Temple.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible book; reading is lore only.

689.comment: The Mondstadt Tower: Octave and the Seneschal
689.content: In the novel The Mondstadt Tower, Octave is the Seneschal's adopted son, an abandoned child persecuted as a bad omen, who trusts the one man who protected him. The Seneschal sends him to fetch the singer Ines. Both are fictional characters of the novel.

key: The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies
Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies
690.comment: The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies
690.content:
The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies (also: Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies, Pale Princess and Six Pygmies): Its title echoes the German fairy tale Snow White (wiki trivia, an out-of-world observation). The Abyss Order's interest in a 'secret' inside it is never explained.

Appearance: A 4-star Book Collection of seven installments. Vol. 1 is received directly from a quest, unlike most books, which are found in the world or bought.

Lore: The Night Mother is called the source of all sins, with neither heart nor mouth, always watching and punishing unpredictably. The one thing she could not bear was moonlight breaking through the clouds. The Moonlight Forest kingdom lived in that moonlight; the tale suggests their beauty came from it, in contrast to the abhorrent creatures at the forest edge.

The other volumes are known only from descriptions: Vol. 2 the meeting of the Pale Princess and the Light Prince; Vol. 3 their decision to save the Moonlight Forest; Vol. 4 their meeting with the Six Pygmies; Vols. 5 and 6 the Pygmies' sinister scheme and how it was carried out; Vol. 7 the conclusion and the Night Mother's prophecy. Those volumes are unreadable ('currently unavailable') as of 7.1.

The wiki compares the situation with the book Before Sun and Moon, which Abyss Order member Enjou tried and failed to find in a later quest while Khaenri'ah's own attempt to steal it long ago was foiled; this is a wiki comparison, not something the tale's text says.

Owners: Held by the Mondstadt library under Lisa as librarian. After Lost Book, the Traveler is registered as its custodian rather than borrower, a privilege Lisa says is reserved for trusted citizens, with no due date.

Lisa says it is not from the restricted section, which is why she let a citizen borrow it. The borrower (Donna) lost it when it was stolen; Lisa had marked it with elemental traces, which let the Traveler track it.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Vol. 1 is an automatic reward at the end of Lost Book (the second half of Troublesome Work).

691.comment: The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies: Lost Book (stolen library copy)
691.content:
In the Mondstadt story quest Lost Book (Tempus Fugit Chapter, Act I), Lisa asks the Traveler to help recover a borrowed library book whose copy of The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies has been stolen. Following her elemental marks near Starfell Valley leads to a hidden Abyss Mage stronghold. Lisa defeats the mage, who says the book holds a secret, and the book is found in a chest below. Lisa and Paimon judge it an ordinary storybook.

Lisa jokes about punishment had the book been damaged. She then makes the Traveler its custodian and, back at the library, hands over the Teyvat Travel Guide as reward.

692.content:
The Saga of Hamavaran (also: Saga of Hamavaran, Hamavaran Saga): The Saga of Hamavaran is a three-volume light novel by the writer Pursina, sold at the Yae Publishing House in Inazuma City. It follows a Sumeru scholar named Hamavaran who travels to Inazuma.

Vol. 1 is a publisher's foreword, Vol. 2 opens the comic story of Hamavaran's voyage and Vol. 3 introduces his talkative companion, a shikigami who calls herself a "ghost-calling".

Appearance: Three slim novel volumes, with the first collecting the prefaces of the new light novel into its own volume due to "a business model adjustment". The cover is written in the Inazuman script and reads LGDHMVR, which the wiki takes to stand for "Legend of Hamavaran".

Lore: The foreword thanks writers drawn in by a recruitment drive and a contest called "This Novel is Amazing!", and thanks Kanjou Commissioner Hiiragi Shinsuke. It says that before the Sakoku Decree accomplished samurai from many lands lived in Inazuma, among them Hamavaran from the rainforest nation of Sumeru, whose tale was buried under the Shogun's eternity and is now retold by the budding author Pursina.

Vol. 2: Hamavaran, an ordinary scholar given an unpopular specialisation, sails to Inazuma worried more about delaying his graduation than the storm. A voice outside his cabin bickers with him; on shore nobody is there and he reasons it away as a ley-line memory of a drowned person, which the voice rejects.

Vol. 3: the voice belongs to a talkative young girl who says she is a shikigami and eats glutinous-rice dango quickly. She calls herself a "ghost-calling", neither dead nor ever alive. Hamavaran concludes this is like Sumeru's spirit-warding, which also involves a pact sealed with a true name, and regrets choosing marine biology over mysticism.

The wiki notes the Japanese title may echo the light novel The Heroic Legend of Arslan, and that Hamavaran is a Persian-derived name connected to the Himyarite kingdom in the Shahnameh.

Owners: No owner is named. It is sold by Kuroda at the Yae Publishing House in Inazuma City.

693.comment: The Saga of Hamavaran: The Saga of Hamavaran
693.content: The Saga of Hamavaran is a light novel by Pursina sold at the Yae Publishing House. Its hero is Hamavaran, a Sumeru scholar of marine biology who sails to Inazuma, meets a shikigami who calls herself a "ghost-calling", and compares her to Sumeru's spirit-warding. The foreword claims Hamavaran was a foreign samurai active before the Sakoku Decree.

694.content:
The Stringless (also: Stringless harp bow): The Stringless is a four-star bow of the Wanderer's Troupe series: an exquisite stringed instrument that is also a bow, once played by the Troupe's harpist from Fontaine. After the Troupe disbanded its harp strings were cut, leaving only the bowstring.

Appearance: Item text: strings of different materials on every section, each trembling to make flowing music when struck. After the Troupe disbanded the strings were cut with a dull blade, creating ear-piercing noise; the lofty melodies are lost but the bow stays deadly. Per the wiki, the Resolution of Sojourner set says it once had four strings.

Lore: The Troupe could make birds fall from the sky, sometimes with the harp's tune and sometimes with the arrows that followed it. The harpist (the Sojourner) was playful and determined, like the wind and the flowers of Starsnatch Cliff. After the failed uprising the Troupe fled, but he stayed to the end, playing and loosing arrows to protect his comrades until his repertoire and arrows ran out.

He came from Fontaine and left to seek his true destiny, and it is said the ladies of the Court of Fontaine wailed that he left without goodbye. The story goes that he loved a humble Mondstadt woman who was then chosen for the miserable fate of the Ludi Harpastum princess.

It is claimed he did not regret dying anonymously in a foreign land; his only regret was finding true love and never getting to sing another love song. The text frames all of this as story, not recorded history. The wiki also notes the Chinese name may echo an idiom about a musician severing his strings after losing a friend; that is a translator's etymology, not in-game lore.

Owners: The Troupe's harpist (the Sojourner).

Diona is shown with this bow in her character demo and Faruzan with the ascended version in hers; that is presentation, not canon ownership.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Wanderer's Troupe-series four-star bow, base ATK 42, Elemental Mastery 36, passive 'Arrowless Song'. Standard and event wishes.

695.content:
The Tale of Kuntur (also: Tale of Kuntur): In the tale every tribe child is bound to a Saurian companion. Kuntur's stubbornness and honesty, not any special gift, carry the story. The narrator is a storyteller who comments on events and says "we do not know" about some details.

Appearance: A one-volume Book Collection, listed with no quality rating. It is a reward of the Hidden Exploration Objective Kuntur's Pursuit (the wiki marks that name as unofficial) in Malinalco Grotto, Quahuacan Cliff. The wiki notes that its cover matches its prequel.

Lore: The tribe neither banished nor welcomed father and son, fearing the sun's anger. Kuntur grew up small, sickly and pale, with starry eyes like his mother's, and children who mocked him were answered with his fists. He reached Rumi, freed the Saurians, and let a captive Iktomisaurus go rather than force it to help him. Rumi had visited as a ragged old guest, and the tribespeople fed him until they ran out of patience and sent him away. Only Kuntur refused him, saying he had nothing to give. Rumi then bewitched the hosts and led away their Saurians. The tribe's three best warriors were turned into talking Pakpakas, who tried to trick Kuntur with the same lies that had defeated them. His father's lesson against deceit let him see through them. Rumi's fog failed because Kuntur navigated by sound and smell, learned from his blind father. After Rumi turned to smoke and fled, the bravest freed Iktomisaurus returned on its own, showed him the path, and the pair chased Rumi through animal forms.

Rumi became a Brown Deer, a capybara in the water, a bird and finally a giant rock. The Iktomisaurus raised a cyclone that let Kuntur keep pace. At the end Kuntur gripped the rock and urged the Saurian higher until they passed the highest clouds, where he saw the sun for the first time, but the sun gathered storm clouds around them. The cold froze Rumi's rock solid, ending his magic. The stone was placed somewhere suitable, the three warriors were restored and treated Kuntur with shame instead of disgust, and Kuntur gained his companion.

The narrator suggests that Kuntur inherited his mother Qoyllor's starry eyes and her persistence, comparing his pursuit of Rumi to her wandering search for star shards. The story says the tribespeople who failed to satisfy Rumi justified sending him away by calling themselves kind. It also states that Kuntur held an unwilling Iktomisaurus fast at first but decided that forcing it would make him no different from Rumi, and so he freed it. The narrator admits not knowing why the Saurian came back, but argues that Iktomisaurs are intelligent and choose their partners, so it must have recognised him.

Owners: No owner. It is a collectible book obtained in a hidden exploration objective.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a Book Collection added in 5.2, obtained from Kuntur's Pursuit in Malinalco Grotto, Quahuacan Cliff. The wiki notes that kuntur means "condor" and rumi means "stone" in Quechua, and that "Pakpaka" may derive from a Philippine word for "wing"; these are real-world etymologies, not canon.

696.content: In the folk tale The Tale of Kuntur, Kuntur is the son of the star-child Qoyllor and the hunter Ukuku. Disliked because the sun withdrew from his father, he was nicknamed "Kuntur, Unloved of the Sun". He defeated the sorcerer Rumi using his father's hunting skills, his honesty and his persistence, and won an Iktomisaurus companion. He is a story figure with no known counterpart in other canon.

697.comment: The Tale of Kuntur: Rumi the Sorcerer
697.content: In The Tale of Kuntur, Rumi is an infamous sorcerer who disguises himself as a hungry beggar, takes the tribe's Saurians by enchantment and turns three warriors into Pakpakas. He relies on fog, illusions, lies and shapeshifting, and ends frozen solid as a rock above the clouds. He appears only in this folk tale.

key: The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku
698.comment: The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku
698.content:
The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku (also: Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku): The in-game description calls it a long-standing tale with no knowable original author. It is the first part of a pair; its sequel is The Tale of Kuntur, about their son. The narrator addresses the listener directly in the manner of a storyteller.

Appearance: A one-volume Book Collection. The wiki records no quality rating for it. It is obtained by talking to Orqo during To Wish Upon a Star.

Lore: Qoyllor lived on the star nearest the tribes and was curious about them. After wandering alone she met Ukuku, and they later formed a family, though he grew ever more gloomy. When she learned he had found shards and hidden them because he did not want to lose her, she left in anger and sadness. The Sun brought her back to the sky and blinded Ukuku with golden arrows; the sun now hides behind clouds wherever he goes. More details: Qoyllor lived on the star nearest the tribes and was far from her brothers and sisters. Over years of travel with Ukuku she learned the life of the ground: she hunted and rested with Saurians, told stories to the tribe's children, ate Tatacos and chased Monetoo. Her cheerful nature let her accept what could not be helped. Doubt came through their neighbour Pochica, who was jealous and who had never got along with Ukuku. He spoke ill of Ukuku to her for years, claiming he clipped the wings of birds he liked and caged them. Pressed by her questions, Ukuku confessed. She demanded the shards, he refused, hoping to keep her, and she left the tribe.

Before leaving, Qoyllor made an enormous piece of graffiti on the land, said to be bigger than a volcano and visible from the Sun itself, in the way of a true person of Natlan. She decided that the lost power no longer mattered and that she would accept any punishment from her father. The Sun saw her plea and took her back; her star lost its power and is now almost invisible unless one looks closely. The narrator does not say whether she still watches the land. Their son Kuntur, who was very young, was affected by his father's punishment and could form no friendship with a Saurian until he was a young man. The narrator ends by saying his later adventures are another story.

Qoyllor's departure is framed as the result of deceit and betrayal, which she had never known before. The narrator comments that trust takes long to build and is destroyed in an instant, and that people differ in how far forgiveness reaches. The tale offers two guesses for Ukuku's gloom, innate temperament or guilt over a broken promise, and then reveals the real cause as his secret. The text also states that the star shards might have been claimed by birds, beasts, insects and snakes, a possibility Qoyllor herself raises while searching.

Owners: No owner. It is a collectible book obtained in a quest.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a Book Collection obtained after talking to Orqo in To Wish Upon a Star. The wiki's trivia notes that "quyllur" means "star" in Quechua and that ukukus in Quechua mythology are half-man, half-bear creatures; these are real-world notes, not canon.

699.comment: The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku: Qoyllor
699.content: In the folk tale The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku, Qoyllor is a star-child, daughter of the Sun, who fell to the ground and lost the power he gave her. She was cheerful and curious, built a life among a Natlan tribe, and left when she learned Ukuku had hidden shards of her star. Her Sun-father brought her back to the sky. She is a figure of the story and not a known historical person.

700.comment: The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku: Ukuku
700.content: In the tale, Ukuku is a strong, taciturn hunter of the tribe, skilled at the chase and at tracking. He promised to help Qoyllor and then hid the shards he found because he had fallen in love with her. As punishment the Sun blinded him with golden arrows, and the sun withdraws behind clouds wherever he goes. He raises their son Kuntur alone in The Tale of Kuntur, where he still hunts despite his blindness.

key: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin
701.comment: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin
701.content:
The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin (also: Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin, Shiruyeh and Shirin): The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin is a two-volume story told by a Jinni in a magic bottle to the shepherd she calls Raven, found in the House of Daena. It tells how the hero Kisra Parvezravan became king of Gurabad, how his father-in-law's line died in one night, and how his son Shiruyeh killed him.

It is a sequel to the quest item The Shepherd and the Magic Bottle, with the same two travellers crossing the desert. The Jinni says it is the spirits' version, and later quests tell the fall of Gurabad differently.

Appearance: Two chapters of dialogue and long speeches by the Jinni, interrupted by camp and desert scenes: sunset over dunes, the sumpter beast, the youth watching the moon. The in-game description calls it a story of unknown origin, full of absurdities.

Lore: Vol. 1: the Jinni explains that in the lost language "Shiruyeh" means "unweaned lion cub", though in the shepherd's tribe it is a branded disgrace. The orphan Kisra, raised in the nest of the giant bird Ghoghnus, becomes the champion of the vassal king Ormazd Shah, destroying ninety-nine cities, tribes and star-sages, and is rewarded with a new name, Parvez, and Ormazd's daughter Shirin. One night Ormazd and all 300 of his offspring die in Gurabad, and Kisra, now Parvezravan, takes the throne.

Vol. 2: Shirin is the daughter of Ormazd and the fairy Liloufar, whose prophecies tell of a hero husband, a sweet end to many relatives and Shirin alone inheriting the kingdom. Slaves, mages of the Mazandaran Oasis or Fellahin servants poison the banquet; only Shirin, shut out by her father, and her husband Kisra keep their lives. Parvezravan banishes their son Shiruyeh in a mask, and Shirin disguises herself, urging him to confront the coward on the throne. Shiruyeh stabs his father in bed, is crowned and later falls into a chasm from which Shiruyeh's Plague emerges. Shirin is freed to roam as a haunting spirit, or is said to have been bottled by Al-Ahmar.

Further background in the tale. Parvezravan raids for Ormazd; his achievements make the crown too heavy for its owner, so it hangs from golden chains in the hall. The age of vassal kings ends after a century of chaos when Al-Ahmar and the Sage-King of the Greenwood reconstruct the oasis paradise, and one of the three living gods had fallen. Liloufar also gives three admonitions to her mortal husband: that Shirin's joy will bring tears to her father's eyes, that they must not feast at the same table as their daughter after she is wed, and that the daughter's heir will be an ill omen for the king's land. The king only smiles. Some say the tragedy was Kisra's own doing: a clawless bird wailed all night, rats with human faces gnawed the chains and the crown crashed down, and an adventurer later found crypts with withered bodies bearing inscriptions.

The tale's fine detail: Shirin is blessed by the white ibis, given a cerulean pearl by the cobra, and worshipped by a giant crocodile; the poisoners are mages of the Mazandaran Oasis or illiterate Fellahin servants who drip scorpion venom into musk honey, and are drowned in the honey pot by the new king; Shiruyeh weeps before Shirin after the murder and she removes his brass exile mask and blesses him; his nightmares end when he falls into a chasm, and the plague that follows takes half of Gurabad's souls. The wiki reads this as a story-within-a-story structure like One Thousand and One Nights.

Contradictions: Per the wiki trivia, later quest material (The Dirge of Bilqis, 3.4, and the Desert Pavilion Chronicle set, 3.3) tells the fall of Gurabad differently. There Liloupar is the real architect of the city's fall, as revenge on Ormazd for failing to abolish slavery. Kisra Parvezravan was Liloupar's own son, left in the wilderness to be adopted by Ormazd. Shirin did not intend to poison the banquet and went mad when she realised what had happened. Shiruyeh's role as Khorramdin and the Brass Mask Rebellion are absent from the tale, and in the quests it is Liloupar who is imprisoned in a bottle, not Shirin. The wiki also notes that Liloufar's prophecies in the tale are self-fulfilling.

Owners: No owner is named. The books are found in the House of Daena, and their narrator is a Jinni, a servant of King Deshret (Al-Ahmar) who has been bottled.

702.comment: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin: Shiruyeh
702.content: In The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin, Shiruyeh is the son of Kisra Parvezravan and Shirin, banished masked from Gurabad, who kills his father in his bed, takes the throne, is haunted by nightmares and falls into a chasm. The plague that emerges from it is called Shiruyeh's Plague. In the lost language the name means "unweaned lion cub", while in the shepherd's tribe it is a disgraceful name branded on exiled chiefs.

703.comment: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin: Kisra Parvezravan
703.content: In this tale Kisra is an orphan raised in the nest of the bird Ghoghnus, adopted by the vassal king Ormazd Shah, and rewarded with the name Parvez and Shirin's hand after conquering ninety-nine cities, tribes and star-sages. After Ormazd and his 300 heirs die in one night, he becomes the king Parvezravan, and is later killed by his son Shiruyeh. The tale hints that some say he was behind the tragedy at Gurabad.

704.comment: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin: Shirin and Liloufar
704.content: In this tale Shirin is the daughter of the vassal king Ormazd and the fairy Liloufar, foremother of the spirits. Liloufar prophesies a hero husband, sweet ends for relatives and Shirin's sole inheritance, which become a curse of waiting. Shirin's marriage to Kisra is unhappy, and hatred grows in her; the tale then has her disguise herself to urge her son Shiruyeh to kill his father and finally freed as a haunting spirit or bottled by Al-Ahmar.

705.content:
The Unforged (also: Sword of No Work, Sword of No Skill): The Unforged is a five-star claymore of the Liyue series, an edgeless blade whose description says it can drive away evil spirits and wicked people. Its item story is a legend of an ancient stone dragon in Liyue, and says the sword was planted as a seal beside the tree that subdued it.

Appearance: Item text calls it an edgeless claymore that seems to possess divine might. The wiki connects the name (Sword of No Work, from the idiom about a heavy sword being edgeless) to the idea of power without showy technique.

Lore: Long ago a dragon lived in Liyue, one of the mountains rather than the sky: an ancient dragon of stone as large as its home. Legend says it slept in Nantianmen, looking like the hills, and its smallest stretch shook the earth. Rex Lapis came before it to stop the quaking. The land then knew a long peace, and he gained another comrade.

The union of dragons, gods and men did not last. The dragon was sealed in the earth, and the Geovishaps that had caused havoc beside it fled to the roots of the mountains for fear of the gods and adepti. As millennia passed, the dragon began to stir again.

Legend says those who triumphed over the dragon stabbed this sword into the ground by the giant tree, the Dragon-Queller, which subdued it. As one of the seals, it keeps monsters and malevolent mortals from touching it, and only those with hearts like clear mirrors can approach. The text ends by asking how, if so, the sword came to be lost. The wiki trivia identifies the dragon as Azhdaha.

The item text never names the dragon, the tree or the sword's finders; the wiki identifies the dragon as Azhdaha and calls the tree the Dragon-Queller. The structure of the story is a legend with a hole at the end: it claims the sword is a seal that only the pure of heart can approach, then asks how it was lost, so portray the sword's present location as unknown.

Owners: No owner is named. Legend places the sword at the Dragon-Queller as a seal.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore. The passive Golden Majesty raises Shield Strength and stacks ATK on hits, with a larger bonus while shielded. It shares this passive with Memory of Dust. Obtained from Weapon Event Wishes; added in Version 1.1.

706.content:
The Viridescent Hunt: The Viridescent Hunt is a 4-star bow from the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn, in the game since Version 1.0. The in-game short description calls it a pure green hunting bow that once belonged to a hunter whose home was the forest. The full text is the tale of a nameless hunter taught never to loose an arrow for anything but survival.

According to the wiki, the lore of the Viridescent Venerer artifact set ties into this weapon.

Appearance: A bow of a pure green so close to the natural environment that, per the text, it could blend in. No other design details are given.

Lore: The hunter was raised, far from the city, to live by the laws of nature, never bearing ill will and loosing arrows only to survive. She left no traces and comforted wounded beasts until their lives returned to nature.

Her teaching said that those born of the greenery move unimpeded where there is grass and shade, that followers of nature need not fear death, and that at the last ebb of life they head to an endless plain.

The text turns on what might have been had the calamity not happened: had she not tracked tainted blood on the leaves, and had she not met a dying, blind youth under the tree where she often napped, she might never have been shaken by thoughts of revenge, blood and fire. A voice reminds her that she belongs to the green and must never loose an arrow for war, revenge or glory, since the bloodstained will never find the hunting fields of endless viridescence.

The hunter's last words ask that the bow at least not be tainted by her mortal vengeance, say she cannot reach the other side to meet her master or the parents she never knew, and ask that the bow stay pure and carry her thoughts and regrets to them. The wiki links the master to Viaghara and the calamity to the Cataclysm; the text itself only says calamity.

Owners: The previous owner is the nameless hunter of the text, a woman raised in the forest far from the city; the wiki links the forest to the Dharma Forest and the city to Sumeru City.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star bow, base ATK 42, CRIT Rate secondary stat. Passive Verdant Wind: Normal and Aimed Shot hits have a 50% chance to create a Cyclone that draws in nearby opponents, dealing 40 to 80 per cent of ATK (by refinement) every 0.5s for 4s, with a cooldown of 14 to 10 seconds. Obtained through the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn bundle.

707.comment: The Viridescent Hunt: The Nameless Hunter
707.content: The Viridescent Hunt's nameless hunter was taught by the forest to take life only to survive. A calamity and a dying, blind youth stirred thoughts of revenge in her; she asked that the bow remain unstained by it. Her story ties into the Viridescent Venerer artifact set.

key: The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins
Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins
708.comment: The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins
708.content:
The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins (also: Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins): The narrator tells the tale as a storyteller by a bonfire, skipping parts "less important to the listeners". The scroll is found close to Pacal in the Children of Echoes' territory. The wiki notes that the quest Shadows of the Mountains reveals what really happened.

Appearance: A one-volume woven scroll, quality 4 per the wiki, found near Pacal in the Children of Echoes area.

Lore: The Lord fouled the springs of the People of the Springs with smog, sent sparks to the Scions of the Canopy, and swallowed the Collective of Plenty, who escaped only because Tatankasaurs and warriors breached its stomach while it slept. Wanting the gems of the Children of Echoes' valleys to make its dark belly shine, it was overheard by a flying squirrel; the news passed through an aphid, a rhino and a Tepetlisaurus to Elder Traore, whose Saurian companion that was. The Children's strongest warrior and chief Sundjatta had gone with the hero Tenoch to the island in the far west to stop a giant dark beast, so Traore and the guarding warriors asked their Wayob for aid. The Volcano Lord approached through smoke. At the Sulfurous Veins Traore met it, flattered it, and led it to a stone chamber with a human-sized gate and no room for it, saying it could reach in with its hand. To reassure it he entered first. As the Lord's fist closed around the gems and grew too large for the gate, Traore blew a golden whistle. The warriors in ambush called on the Wayob, which borrowed four sewing pins, three short and one long, and blew them at the Lord. The pins took on the tribe's blood and the Wayob's power and became four huge phlogiston nails.
