Three pinned the black arm to the Sulfurous Veins, and the Lord severed its own arm and fled before the longest could fall.

The severed arm remained pinned like a shadow, hence the name Shadow Pins for the crystalline pillars. The longest pin never fell fully and hangs above the Sulfurous Veins, and the tale says that while it stays there the Volcano Lord will never dare approach the Children of Echoes again. The narrator notes that old tales confused salamanders with dragons, though everyone now knows a salamander is just that. Traore boasts that his tribe fears death and loves life almost as much as gems, which persuades the Lord that no trap could be intended. The tale does not explain how Traore escaped from the chamber blocked by the arm.

Per the wiki trivia, the quest Shadows of the Mountains presents a truer account: Traore escaped with help from the Khaenri'ahn warriors Zephaniah and Irizar, who gave their lives holding back the Abyss so he and his people could flee. In the legend neither is mentioned and the enemy is only the Volcano Lord, so the scroll and the quest differ in what they say happened. This entry has not checked the quest text itself.

Owners: No owner. It is a collectible scroll found in the world.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a 4-star Book Collection added in 5.0, found near Pacal at the Children of Echoes in Natlan. The wiki lists a video guide for locating the series.

709.comment: The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins: The Volcano Lord
709.content: In the legend The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins, the Volcano Lord is a dark giant like a black-and-purple salamander that seized the Great Volcano of Tollan and harried Natlan's tribes. It was tricked by Elder Traore, lost an arm to the Wayob's phlogiston nails and fled. The wiki links this being with the Abyss, which the scroll itself does not say.

710.comment: The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins: Shadow Pins
710.content: In the legend, the Shadow Pins are the long crystalline pillars of the Sulfurous Veins, said to be the phlogiston nails that pinned the Volcano Lord's arm like a shadow. The longest is said to hang suspended, keeping the Lord away from the Children of Echoes. They are a real feature of the area, and the origin story is a legend.

711.content:
The Widsith (also: Widsith notebook): The Widsith is a four-star catalyst of the Wanderer's Troupe series: a heavy notebook of hand-written musical scores and travel journals, moth-eaten and worn, that the Troupe shared. It records their experiences and still carries power drawn from their performances.

Appearance: Item text describes a heavy notebook filled with musical scores, suffering moth damage and wear but with much power in the hand-written words.

Lore: The notebook was passed among the Troupe's members and holds scores and travel journals about the lands they roamed. It siphons power from the records of their performances and the cheering of the crowds. The Troupe's history was lost because it disbanded before Mondstadt was rebuilt.

The Troupe was founded in the aristocracy's reign. Many called it the Swordsman's Troupe, some from hope and some from fear, in an era that denied even poems and songs freedom. For flutes they had swords and for harps they had bows, and their song was an anthem of rebellion. Their final act was an attempt to storm the city and execute its tyrannical rulers.

The text closes by saying the Troupe and the memory of its rebellion are gone, but the spirit of resistance they embodied runs in Mondstadters' veins. The name comes from the Old English poem Widsith ('far traveller'), and the passive's song names (Recitative, Aria, Interlude) are opera terms, per the wiki; these are real-world naming notes, not lore.

Owners: Shared by the members of the Wanderer's Troupe; no single owner is named.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Wanderer's Troupe-series four-star catalyst, base ATK 42, CRIT DMG 12% secondary, passive 'Debut' (Recitative/Aria/Interlude buff). Standard and event wishes.

712.content:
Thundering Fury (also: Thundering Fury artifact set, Thunderbird's Mercy, Survivor of Catastrophe, Hourglass of Thunder, Omen of Thunderstorm, Thunder Summoner's Crown): Thundering Fury is an Electro artifact set (4 and 5 star). Its five pieces tell, in fragments, of an ancient tribe that worshipped the Thunderbird, a violet-lightning bird. A young lad who sang to the bird became a blood sacrifice, and the enraged Thunderbird destroyed the tribe. The set is earned in the Midsummer Courtyard domain.

The set's pieces are Thunderbird's Mercy (flower), Survivor of Catastrophe (plume), Hourglass of Thunder (sands), Omen of Thunderstorm (goblet) and Thunder Summoner's Crown (circlet). The tribe is the one now called the Thunderbird Civilization, of Tsurumi Island in Inazuma.

Appearance: - Thunderbird's Mercy: a purple wild flower charged with lightning, said to have survived the ash.
- Survivor of Catastrophe: a lightning-charged feather the Thunderbird lost, still flickering.
- Hourglass of Thunder: a costly hourglass of amethyst and amber gold that belonged to a shaman.
- Omen of Thunderstorm: a golden ritual goblet that held the blood offered to the bird.
- Thunder Summoner's Crown: a crown worn by the tribe's elder shamans.

Lore: The tribe feared the Thunderbird and thanked it for its blessings, and shamans offered blood to it for protection and forgiveness. The texts insist the bird was a monster that did not care for human worship, and the tribe took its unpredictable moves for divine revelations.

One stormy season a young lad sang fearlessly in the mountains, and the proud bird landed beside him. He said he had been told he could bring peace to thunder and storms, and the bird, moved by his song, said nothing. That was their only meeting. The next time the bird saw him was as blood in the golden goblet on the sacrificial altar. At the tribe's last festival, where the hourglass counted down to the bird's arrival, the frenzied Thunderbird blew away the altar and destroyed the tribe in vengeance for the singer. The text adds that the lad himself saw his death as an offering for the tribe's good.

The Survivor of Catastrophe text records that the lad kept a feather the bird dropped and promised to sing another tune when it came again with thunder and rain. The Thunderbird, driven mad by the broken promise, left the mountain in cinders. Years later it was hunted down and killed as a monster, the land slowly recovered, and the feather lay buried in the growth; the story of the bird and the lad nearly perished with the tribe. The lone flower is described as the sole survivor of the day of disaster.

The quest 'Through the Mists' (Tsurumi Island, 2.2) retells the same events through the ghost Ruu, who is identified as the sacrificed boy; there the bird is named Kanna Kapatcir, the name Ruu gave her. The wiki attributes her killing to Ei and says she was sealed away on Seirai Island. Those details come from the quests and other pages, not from the set's texts, which never name the bird, the boy, the island or the killer.

Owners: No named owner. The texts attribute the hourglass and crown to the tribe's shamans, and the goblet to the sacrificial rites; they belonged to the Thunderbird Civilization, not to a living character.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 2-piece bonus of +15% Electro DMG. The 4-piece bonus boosts Overloaded, Electro-Charged, Superconduct and Hyperbloom damage by 40% and shortens the Elemental Skill cooldown by 1s when the wearer triggers Quicken or those reactions (once per 0.8s); the set also boosts Aggravate, Lunar-Charged and Stellar-Conduct by 20%. The set drops in the Midsummer Courtyard domain.

The wearer must apply their element second to trigger the cooldown reduction, and it does not work for an off-field wearer. The damage bonus still applies off-field.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): use the set as a grim, quiet relic. Show purple lightning clinging to the pieces, and treat it as a remembered tragedy rather than a trophy. Do not give it to a canon character or make it grant powers.

713.content: Thundering Fury texts describe a tribe on Tsurumi Island that worshipped the Thunderbird and offered blood to it. A singing lad was sacrificed, and the Thunderbird annihilated the tribe in anger. The bird was hunted down and killed years later.

714.content:
Thundering Pulse (also: Rule By Thunder, the Shogun's bow): Thundering Pulse is a five-star bow, a longbow with eternal lightning crackling around it that the game calls a gift from the Shogun. Its item story follows the samurai Takamine the Mistsplitter, who won it from a Great Tengu in a gamble, learned Tengu archery from it, and left it as a wager with a shrine maiden when he went to face the disaster from across the sea. He did not return as himself.

The bow keeps its sheen despite having been soaked in thick darkness, a detail the text uses to mark that it outlasted both the Cataclysm and its owners.

Appearance: The text describes a bow that crackles with thunder and retains its luster even though it was soaked in thick darkness. The game description calls it a longbow with eternal lightning around it.

Lore: When disaster came from a distant sea, the bow was the favourite weapon of a great swordsman, Takamine. In his youth he wandered the mountains and met a great Tengu, with whom he wagered his young, strong body against a bow given by the Shogun. The wager was a draw, three wins each; he became the Tengu's servant but won the bow. The Tengu gave him the ridiculous nickname Konbumaru and showed him Tengu archery, a fierce, unpredictable and elegant form of fighting, loosing thunderbolts with every bowstring's pulse.

Years later the Tengu sent him to the Shogunate with a recommendation letter. He grew in skill, made friends and enemies, and kept his wanderlust, becoming more fearless with the bow. Before leaving for the Abyss he proposed another wager to the shrine maiden who had inherited the essence of his archery: if he returned alive, the bow would be his again; if he lost, she could keep it. When peace returned and the swordsman had not come back, the Shogun's bow went to the maiden as the prize. Later, in the forest where the Kitsune Saiguu would no longer appear, at their promised meeting place, a lone returnee stumbled back from the Abyss and met the shrine maiden again, though she could no longer be called young. His dull eyes, stained with dried blood and tears, regained their radiance and were pierced by a barbed arrow glowing with power.

The wiki's lore section puts the chain of ownership plainly: forged by the Shogun, given to the Great Tengu Reizenbou, won by Takamine, entrusted to Asase Hibiki as a pledge, and used by Hibiki against him when he came back corrupted by the Abyss. It also links the bow to Mistsplitter Reforged, both having been Takamine's. The same wager appears in the Sunny Morning Sleep-In story, told from the shrine maiden's side: the man bets his bow that he will return alive, she thinks him a hopeless gambler despite his fame as a swordmaster, and the hawk of her good dream is never seen again.

Owners: Forged by the Shogun (not specified which one) and given to Reizenbou. Then Takamine the Mistsplitter, who won it in a gamble. Then Asase Hibiki, who received it as a wager prize and is its last known owner. Kujou Sara is depicted with it in artwork, which is not an ownership claim.

It is the same type of bow as Hamayumi in gameplay terms, sharing ascension materials with it; the wiki notes this as trivia, not as lore.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star bow from the Inazuma series, base ATK 46, secondary stat CRIT DMG 14.4%. Passive "Rule By Thunder": ATK +20-40%, plus the Thunder Emblem, which gains a stack on each Normal Attack hit (5s) and each Elemental Skill cast (10s) and disappears when Energy is full; stacks 1/2/3 boost Normal Attack DMG by 12/24/40% up to 24/48/80% at refinement 1-5. It was the event-exclusive weapon of the Version 2.0 Epitome Invocation, alongside Skyward Blade.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a sad inheritance, a bow that stayed whole while its people were lost. Anyone who knows its full story will treat the wager with wry fondness and the ending with restraint; most Inazumans know the bow only as a fabled weapon of the Shogun.

715.content: Takamine is the great swordsman of the item stories, the one-time servant of the Tengu Reizenbou who won this bow and later owned Mistsplitter Reforged. The Thundering Pulse text gives him the nickname Konbumaru from his time as a Tengu's servant and tells of his wagers. His own entry carries the rest of his story.

716.content: Hibiki is the shrine maiden who inherited Takamine's archery and holds the bow after the wager. The Thundering Pulse text leaves her unnamed in the story passage; the wiki links the figure to her name and gives her as the last known owner. Her dreams are the subject of the Sunny Morning Sleep-In story.

717.content:
Thundersoother (also: Thundersoother's Heart, Thundersoother's Plume, Hour of Soothing Thunder, Thundersoother's Goblet, Thundersoother's Diadem, Flower of Thunder): Thundersoother is an Electro artifact set from launch (Midsummer Courtyard domain). Its five pieces recount a legendary hero, "the Thundersoother", who conquered thunder and lightning, killed the tyrannical Beast of Thunder, and later lived and died alone.

The story is told in legend-like fragments with no names, dates or places.

Lore: The Beast of Thunder once enslaved people with its lightning. The Thundersoother, who plucked the purple Flower of Thunder with reverence and wore it on his chest, fought the beast without wavering and defeated it in a lightning storm, beheading it and claiming a diadem as his trophy.

He made tools from amethyst and Electro shards: an insignia shaped like the plume of a falcon that fearlessly crossed storms and a burnt woodland, and an hourglass of Electro shards that shatter and merge as time passes. Watching it taught him about the cycle of life and death, which helped him defeat the beast. His goblet is said to have held the wine for the sacrificial slaying of his family, the courage for entering the beast's cave, and his only company in his last years of solitude.

The Thundersoother is called a mere mortal with human feelings, and the goblet witnessed his sorrow as well as his deeds. The Heart piece says the flower grants courage to travellers in storms; for him, the text suggests, wearing it may have been mere whimsy. The Diadem piece ends: "the past can never be fully pacified". The beast's might vanished as quickly as its lightning.

The texts never name the family sacrificed, the nature of the sacrifice (a slaying, apparently ritual), or the cave where the beast lived. The Hourglass piece notes even he could not conquer the flash of time.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): 4 and 5 star set from Midsummer Courtyard and its strongbox. 2-piece: Electro RES +40%. 4-piece: +35% DMG against Electro-affected opponents; it does not trigger on the hit that applies Electro, still works off-field, and stacks additively with other DMG bonuses. Introduced in 1.0.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): tell it as an anonymous legend of a solitary, grieving hero. Do not name him or connect him to a nation or to the Thundering Fury set.

718.content: The flower piece: a purple flower that blooms only in thunderstorms and never withers in the rain. The Thundersoother knelt to pluck it and wore it on his chest; for travellers, it gave unfaltering resolve against thunder.

719.content: The plume piece: an amethyst insignia in the shape of a falcon's feather. The falcon left it in burnt woods after flying through storms and volcano; the Thundersoother, like it, conquered both thunder and flame.

720.content: The sands piece: an amethyst hourglass filled with Electro shards that shatter and merge as time passes. The hero learned about the cycle of life and death from it.

721.content: The goblet piece: his cup, said to have held the wine for the sacrificial slaying of his family, the courage for the beast's cave and the only company of his solitary final days.

722.content: The circlet piece: a very ancient diadem that shines with the light of pacified lightning, taken as a trophy from the Beast of Thunder after the storm fight.

723.content:
Tidal Shadow: Tidal Shadow is a four-star claymore of the Beaumont series, forged in Fontaine. The description calls it an exquisitely crafted standard-model sword for the high-ranking officers and flagship captains of Fontaine's old navy. Its story recalls the white ironclad flagship Sponsian and Admiral Basil Elton, whose blue-and-white blade is all that remained of the fleet's legend.

The Navy was disbanded after the armada ceased to exist. The Admiral's First Mate, Nathaniel Pickman, spent his later years trapped by a false heroic reputation.

Appearance: A blue and white blade (the text uses the word epee) of the old Fontaine navy's standard officer pattern. For wielders with Arkhe it shows Pneuma or Ousia alignment indicators.

Lore: In the glorious past the pure white ironclad flagship Sponsian was the pride of Fontaine's Navy, and the Court of Fontaine's darlings were its metal warships with heavy cannons and ramming prows. Basil Elton could be seen on its bridge before her retirement. Afterwards Pickman petitioned the Court for years to salvage and rebuild the Sponsian, but he failed, and the families of the fallen suspected he was fishing for glory.

A short exchange recalls the ship's naming: Elton calls Sponsian an awful name, Pickman half-jokes it was a usurper's, and Elton relents, saying she likes that sense of unreal reality. Legends of the Sponsian and the White Armada were staged at the newly rebuilt opera house on Erinnyes until an accident ended such shows, the best remembered being the armada's final battle with ten battleship cannons onstage, reconstructed from Pickman's records.

The text speculates that Pickman omitted an absurd detail, or that writers cut it as undermining the epic tragedy: Elton boarded the flagship once more after years away and told Pickman and the sailors that this time they could finally fire on their enemies. Only then does she smile and call out, as in the opera, to the sailors, promising tea later and telling them to first send the 'oversized punk' Elynas back to the bottom of the waterfall.

Owners: Admiral Basil Elton, whose sword the story says it was.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not story. Passive White Cruising Wave raises ATK for 8 seconds after the wielder is healed, and can trigger when the character is off-field. Base ATK 42, ATK 9% secondary stat.

724.content:
Tome of the Eternal Flow (also: Aeon Wave): Tome of the Eternal Flow is a 5-star catalyst: a manual once passed down from generation to generation within an underwater priory. Today none know of its existence.

Its story is the oath of the priory's watchers, who guard the capital of water against a flood and a breach, and the slow decay of the order.

Appearance: Canon gives only that the tip of the tome's spine glows with Pneuma or Ousia when an Arkhe-aligned character holds it. Add nothing else.

Lore: The first watcher led new recruits to recite an oath: remember the oath of a thousand years, defend the foundation of the capital of water, and never forget the sin that was once tempting as honey nor the responsibility that may feel like fetters.

These shackles stand for the deity's honey-sweet grace and faith in them (the text links the deity to Egeria). The watchers are the shield against the flood, the line of defence against the breach. Those who join have succumbed to the euphoria of violence or to greed; the vow is the recompense of justice and their last chance at redemption. There is neither sunlight nor family, so they must find a semblance of joy.

The first watcher sometimes wondered whether the sinners swore on their own accord or only uttered meaningless syllables, yet hoped the wild joy he felt when the deity entrusted him would light the way for his brothers and sisters. If the harbinger of the apocalypse, which the wiki links to the All-Devouring Narwhal, one day arrived, the flood would wash everything away, and the watchers would fight with duty and joy in their hearts. When his duty was done he left the duty to the others and was buried between splendid mineral veins, the place most filled with light.

The flood never came, as the text says fate rarely grants would-be heroes an honourable death. Instead an inaudible trickle began to corrode the priory like a thief in the shadows. The number of those forced to join and live underwater grew, while those who swore the oath, understood it and knew the teachings declined. Many years later a fortress rose from the seabed, and the last brother who called himself a watcher and bore a god's expectations left a grave known to none. The text ends on a hopeful note: the other suppressed breach was eventually found by someone who set out to reveal its secrets.

Owners: No owner is named; it was passed on within the priory.

Neuvillette is paired with it only by convention (see uncertainties). Do not claim he owns or found it without a source.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star catalyst, base ATK 44 at level 1, secondary stat CRIT DMG; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 4.1. Passive "Aeon Wave": raises HP; when current HP increases or decreases, Charged Attack DMG rises for 4s (up to 3 stacks, once per 0.3s); at 3 stacks, or when the third stack refreshes, Energy is restored, once per 12s. Values scale with refinement.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: the tome is a forgotten relic; characters would speak of the watchers as lost folklore, not as a known institution. Do not name the priory's location or leaders.

725.comment: Tome of the Eternal Flow: Underwater priory watchers
725.content: In the weapon story of Tome of the Eternal Flow, an underwater priory's watchers, sinners given a second chance by a deity, swear to guard the capital of water against a flood and a breach. The order decays over time, and the last watcher's grave is lost.

726.content:
Toukabou Shigure (also: Toukabou, the cursed parasol): Toukabou Shigure is a four-star sword of the Youkai series, designed as an umbrella and obtained during the Version 3.3 event Akitsu Kimodameshi. Its text is a ghost story ("kaidan") told by a woman from Fontaine: a dancer's cherished umbrella becomes cursed after two deaths, turns into a one-eyed, one-legged, long-tongued youkai, and is finally washed and enshrined by a young shrine maiden.

Appearance: The sword is an umbrella, in the manner of the kasa-obake umbrella youkai. The wiki notes its icon and 3D model are oriented differently from other swords (handle at the bottom left); item text itself describes Inazuman umbrellas in general as exquisite artistry rather than describing this one.

Lore: The narrator is introduced as a visitor who is moved by Inazuman umbrellas. Hundreds of years ago, at a festival season, a girl danced with an intricate umbrella and drank the Oni clan's wine, cheered by humans and youkai alike, until she went to war with the army and died; her subordinates offered the umbrella to a shrine. A martial family's daughter bought it at full price, but before she could use it a message announced her husband's death in battle; she fell ill and died, and her parents returned the umbrella to the shrine to be sealed as cursed.

Months later a youkai was rumoured to stalk the streets on rainy nights: an umbrella taller than a man with a single eye, a single leg and a long tongue that licked passers-by. It seemed more of a prankster, but people worried, young women stayed home and the elderly said the wise and powerful would have dealt with it easily if they were not absent. A young shrine maiden washed the umbrella from the tip with a wooden spoon, wiped it with silk, and told it that tomorrow and the day after would still come even if yesterday's rains ceased, and that if its noble owner were alive it would surely not be in this state. She had it enshrined in an annex and it was never heard of again.

The narrator closes by saying that she searched the shrines of Narukami and found no mention of such an enshrined umbrella; her Inazuman friend laughs and asks whether she takes kaidan to be true. This frame matters: the text is explicitly folklore passed through a foreigner's retelling. The wiki's trivia says the design is based on the kasa-obake, a real Japanese umbrella yokai.

Owners: No owner is named: the umbrella passes from the dancing girl to a martial family's daughter to a shrine, in an unverified story.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star sword of the Youkai series. Base ATK 42, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 36. Passive "Kaidan: Rainfall Earthbinder": after an attack hits opponents, one of them gains Cursed Parasol for 10s (once per 15s); the wielder deals extra damage to that enemy, and if it is defeated the cooldown refreshes. Obtained during the 3.3 event "Akitsu Kimodameshi".

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a prop for ghost-story nights; keep the "hearsay" framing, and let characters treat it as a spooky tale rather than fact.

727.content: In the Toukabou Shigure text, a once-beloved umbrella is sealed in a shrine as cursed, becomes a rain-night youkai and is finally washed and enshrined by a shrine maiden. The story is told as a kaidan by a Fontainian who could not verify it.

key: Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi
728.comment: Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi
728.content:
Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi (also: Shinkageuchi, Chouken Shinkageuchi): Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi is a one-volume traditional Inazuman novel sold at the Yae Publishing House in Inazuma City. Also called "Shinkageuchi", it was once restricted. It tells a fantastical story of the first Shogun and her kagemusha, praising the first Shogun's wisdom and the kagemusha's valor.

It was published in a haphazard way because another book, informally called "Raiden Reincarnation", made readers hungry for this kind of story.

Lore: The book opens with the Goshintou ceremony. When Narukami came to her people she brought the craft of swordmaking; after thousands of years mortal smiths could make swords that pleased her. The Grand Narukami Shrine and the Shogunate therefore gather the finest swords and offer them to the shrine, naming them "Goshintou".

Behind the ceremony, the book says, a master smith never forges just one blade. The finest work, the "Shinuchi", is given a lovely name and offered to the smith's lord or deity; it is not meant to take lives and stays pure. The others, "Kageuchi", go to retainers as weapons, are used in bloodshed and become stained.

It then parallels the swords with the Shogun herself. From the day Narukami Gongen, the First Shogun, ruled Inazuma, she was accompanied by her younger twin sister, "Shin" and "Kage", light and dark. The younger was named Ei, a name that would be written plainly as "shadow", and she would become the successor. After the Archon War, from which only The Seven emerged, the Shadow Shogun, divinely skilled with the blade but doubting she understood mortal hearts, gave up her body so her sister could ascend to Celestia and take dominion over Inazuma. The True Shogun, Makoto, then established the Shogunate and, remembering their bond, restored Ei's divine will and reforged her body, so that her sister returned to her side as her kagemusha.

The book is an in-universe novel and idealizes. Per the wiki's note on Ei's voice-over, Ei calls it fairly accurate for the events up to the war against Orobashi and idealized for her motives and actions after that. Treat it as a flattering retelling by a writer, not an official history, and do not use it to settle what the Shogunate or the Narukami shrine later did.

Appearance: A single book. According to the wiki, its cover bears the same pattern as the Raiden Shogun's namecard.

Owners: Not a unique item; published for sale by the Yae Publishing House.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a single collectible book sold by Kuroda at the Yae Publishing House. Added in Version 2.2.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's suggestion): use it as a popular, slightly sensational Inazuman novel, and as a source of flavour about Shinuchi and Kageuchi swords. Characters who know the real events (such as Ei) may remark that parts are idealized. Do not claim the novel states the full truth of Makoto and Ei.

729.comment: Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi: Shinuchi and Kageuchi
729.content: In the novel's account of Inazuman swordsmithing, a master smith's finest blade is the Shinuchi, named and offered to a lord or deity and kept pure, while the other blades made at the same time are Kageuchi, given to retainers to use and stained by bloodshed. The novel links the pair of terms to the first Shogun and her shadow sister Ei, and ties it to the Goshintou ceremony.

730.content:
Tulaytullah's Remembrance: Tulaytullah's Remembrance is a 5-star catalyst: a bell of deep sapphire and sterling silver whose echoes are "as crisp as they are distant". Its story recalls the Sapphire City Tulaytullah, home of the Tighnarians, and the farewell of the court dancer Makhaira to her golden-eyed lover Xiphos, and what became of both of them.

The bell's design is based on a ritual bell, the Tibetan drilbu with a vajra handle (wiki trivia on design), which fits the City's ceremonial tone.

Appearance: A catalyst in the form of a sapphire-and-silver bell with a vajra-style handle. The in-game description names only sapphire and sterling silver.

Lore: Once, on the silver dunes, a woman danced with the three sisters of the moon; blood and tears mingled to form a garden spring. The Lord of Flowers grieved, and a sapphire city rose from her tears, where the Tighnarians grew proud and bred generations of wisdom. Tulaytullah was said to be her most precious jewel, and in the golden age even the moon looked amber.

In the gardens bloomed dream-violet Padisarahs and singing pomegranates, and canals shimmered; even passing deities would not see them buried in sandstorms. In a farewell speech Makhaira tells Xiphos, the exiled high-born and Blade of Tulaytullah, beloved of the Jinni, that tomorrow she must leave because the scholars have sold her to the court of Badanah, whose forefathers destroyed her homeland and enslaved her people. She will dance and speak honeyed words among her enemy and asks him to keep her name in his heart for the night.

To please the waning vassal king, the scholars who ruled Tulaytullah paid tribute, and Makhaira, a court dancer, became part of it. The story says the rest has been diluted by too many tongues. She is said to have taken vengeance and brought low a kingdom thought invincible, but an adder devoured her life and she sleeps beneath gilded sand. Xiphos earned esteem among his kindred yet died in vain protecting nobles who feared him, killed by another exiled princeling whose banishment the serpent-hearted dancer, a Jinni's daughter, had delivered. All, good or evil, are ground by fate, and the sapphire city faded like tears in the sun.

In the surrounding wiki accounts (Xiphos, Faramarz), Makhaira is the concubine of King Badanah who conspired with his son Faramarz to kill the king, and later Faramarz poisoned her with a viper's venom. The bell's text is the dancer's side and Xiphos's side of that arc, ending before the wiki's detailed political narrative. Where sources differ in detail, keep both accounts attributed.

Owners: No owner is named; the bell is a memory-object of Tulaytullah. Xiphos and Makhaira are the people the story is about.

The wiki page records no character wielding it in promotional material, so avoid assigning it to a specific character in scenes.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star catalyst released in Version 3.3 (2022-12-07), level 1 base ATK 48, secondary stat CRIT DMG. Passive Bygone Azure Teardrop raises Normal Attack speed; after the wielder uses an Elemental Skill, Normal Attack DMG increases every second for 14 s and again with each Normal Attack hit (once every 0.3 s), up to a cap. The buff ends when the wielder leaves the field and resets with the next Elemental Skill.

At refinement 1 Normal Attack SPD rises 10%, +4.8% per second, +9.6% per hit, capped at 48%; refinement 5 gives 20%, 9.6%, 19.2% and 96%. Ascension uses Inactivated, Dormant and Robust Fungal Nucleus with Fungal Spores, Luminescent Pollen and Crystalline Cyst Dust.

How {{char}} behaves: Use the bell as a mourning symbol of Tulaytullah's golden age. Speakers of the story should treat the details as legend, as the text itself does.

731.content: Bygone Azure Teardrop is the weapon passive of Tulaytullah's Remembrance (gameplay): a Normal Attack speed bonus and stacking Normal Attack damage after an Elemental Skill. It echoes the Sapphire City as a city born from tears.

key: Mourning Bell of the Undying One
732.content:
Undying One's Mourning Bell (also: Sigurd's bell, Mourning Bell of the Undying One): The Undying One's Mourning Bell is a bronze bell carried by Sigurd, a Lightkeeper warrior who fought the Wild Hunt in Nod-Krai and, in the item's words, walked through the dark abyss. Its peal is said to be heard on pitch-black nights. The Traveler recovers it as a quest item and returns it to his grave, and it also exists as the Sands piece of the Long Night's Oath artifact set.

Beasts are said to flinch at the sound of Sigurd's warning bell. The Lightkeepers still try to carry on the work he left unfinished.

Appearance: A bronze bell. The item text adds only that it is Sigurd's and that its peal can be heard on pitch-black nights; no further design is described.

Lore: Sigurd was a formidable Lightkeeper who fought the Wild Hunt to the end. The bell is the sound of his stubborn watch: folk tales hold that whenever mournful bells toll, the one who swore to hunt the Wild Hunt is near.

The artifact text describes a terrible storm of black rain and a host of spirits crossing the night sky, which people of the borderlands call the Wild Hunt. A black-feathered flock of crows and an oath-bound legion pushed forward against it. Sigurd, the last one standing with a dark blade, reached the edge of the forest where the Hunt's source lurked, but his body had already been torn apart; the bell he carried kept ringing amid the blood and black muck, and the carrion feeders around him faltered. He was left to walk alone in the abyss to fulfil an oath not yet kept.

Per the wiki's reading of Sigurd's story, he disappeared about a decade before the game's events in a great battle that also took the family and village of Illuga. The surviving Lightkeepers built an empty grave for him northeast of the Barrowmoss Barrens, and Nikita succeeded him as Starshyna. The Abyss's corrosion and his refusal to stop defending his homeland left him as a lingering, corrupted fighter.

Sigurd was close with Chicherin, and the two once saved a young Malusha, whom Chicherin took in. The Local Legend that bears his name, "The One Who Swore to Hunt the Hunt", reveals him as a corrupted Wilderness Ghoul and ends with the words that it is finally over. Flins and Illuga can also meet him through the exploration objective Secrets of the Tideseal Stones.

Quest use: In The Bell of Mourning Echoes (World Quest, Nod-Krai, Version 6.0), the Traveler and Paimon clear Wild Hunt corruption at Tideseal Stones with a strange, Lightkeeper-clad figure fighting beside them. Cleansing three stones yields this bell, A Horn Unwinded and a Dyed Tassel. Lushne and Sukhovykh in Nasha Town recognise them as Sigurd's.

Sukhovykh asks the Traveler to take the relics to Sigurd's grave near the eastern battlefield ruins on Lempo Isle, hoping his spirit may rest. The grave is inscribed with the Latin motto "Pro aris et focis" ("for hearth and home"). When the Traveler returns the three relics, a voice asks whether they pursue the Wild Hunt or hunt with it, and the Sigurd Local Legend appears; the quest earns an achievement of the same motto name.

Owners: Sigurd carried it in life. After the quest the Traveler returns it to his grave; in the artifact system it can be equipped by any character.

Gameplay: Gameplay (labelled): as a quest item it has no use in play. As an artifact it is the Sands of Eon piece of Long Night's Oath, whose 2-piece bonus increases Plunging Attack DMG by 25%.

The 4-piece bonus grants "Radiance Everlasting" stacks after Plunging Attacks, Charged Attacks or Elemental Skills hit, raising Plunging Attack DMG by 15% per stack for 6 seconds, up to 5 stacks. The set drops at the Derelict Masonry Dock.

733.comment: Undying One's Mourning Bell: Undying One's Mourning Bell
733.content: Sigurd's bronze warning bell. Beasts and Wild Hunt creatures are said to flinch at its peal. The Traveler recovers it and two other relics in The Bell of Mourning Echoes and returns them to his grave on Lempo Isle. It is also the Sands piece of the Long Night's Oath artifact set.

734.comment: Undying One's Mourning Bell: The Bell of Mourning Echoes
734.content: A Nod-Krai World Quest begun by collecting Sigurd's relics from three Tideseal Stones. Lushne and Sukhovykh of the Lightkeepers in Nasha Town identify them, and the Traveler lays them at his grave, which triggers the Sigurd Local Legend. Not a Treasure Hoarder or Reed Miller matter; it is about the Lightkeepers' dead.

key: The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched
735.content:
Unfinished Reverie (also: Unfinished Reverie artifact set, Dark Fruit of Bright Flowers, Faded Emerald Tail, Moment of Attainment, The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched, Crownless Crown): Unfinished Reverie is a 4- and 5-star artifact set, added in Version 4.6, whose lore belongs to Natlan. Its pieces tell of the scarlet-eyed youth who gathered heroes against an insane king, and of a young girl, twin heroes, a taciturn warrior and a scarred craftsman who helped him. The final piece shows the girl grown old and erasing the craftsman's name. Its bonuses reward fighting Burning enemies with off-field damage.

The pieces are Dark Fruit of Bright Flowers (flower), Faded Emerald Tail (plume), Moment of Attainment (sands), The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched (goblet) and Crownless Crown (circlet). The set is a Natlan story that was released before Natlan itself, in Version 4.6.

Appearance: The flower is grey stone covered in gold foil, said to have marked friend from foe in a war. The plume is a tail-feather ornament whose lustre has faded, its patterns said to be the work of a skilled artisan. The sands is an ancient sundial with tiny marks visible only on close inspection. The goblet is a three-legged cup. The circlet is a golden crown decorated with turquoise and emerald feathers that has never been used in a coronation.

Lore: - Dark Fruit of Bright Flowers: as the tribes' banners faded, a half-man holding a cracked ring played on the throne and ordered that none heed the instructions of the ancestors and first ascended.
- Faded Emerald Tail: the girl, bonded to the youth, searched the city for the renowned craftsman among the nobles and found nothing, until a hooded drunkard at a dilapidated tavern told her the story of the feather ornament.
- Moment of Attainment: researchers puzzle over identical burin marks in the same spot on the sundials in the city's ash.
- The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched: the craftsman told the youth and the heroes how the king of the ineffable city had gathered tribal artisans to dig up huge beast-shaped constructs.
- Crownless Crown: the girl, grown old as the mistress of the mines, had promised a turquoise crown to the craftsman once the ancient kingdom fell.
Each piece has its own entry with its full text.

Wiki cross-references that the text leaves implicit: the red-eyed youth is the scarlet-eyed youth, later the second Pyro Archon, said by the wiki to have asked that his own name be erased; the girl and later mistress of the mines is Sakkuk, chief of the Children of Echoes; the taciturn warrior is Yupanqui; and the twins are Atawallpa and Waskar. The insane king is Och-Kan, the Sacred Lord and Python King, whose city is Ochkanatlan. The blind old woman is not named in the item text.

The set is framed as a puzzle: researchers find the same burin marks on many sundials, and Moment of Attainment says unofficial histories credit an unnamed artisan with the plan. Crownless Crown shows the tribes swearing to erase his name, and the wiki's Scarlet-Eyed Youth page adds that the youth himself asked Sakkuk to remove his own name from history. The pieces are best treated as legend about a rebellion, not a verified chronicle.

Owners: No wearer. The only named people in the text are Sakkuk, Yupanqui and Atawallpa; the set contains no keepsake attributed to a living owner.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): the 2-piece bonus is ATK +18%. The 4-piece bonus gives +50% DMG after leaving combat for 3s; in combat the bonus drops by 10% per second after 6s without a nearby Burning opponent, and climbs 10% per second to 50% while a Burning opponent is nearby. It still works if the wearer is off-field.

Obtained from the Faded Theater domain (listed on the wiki in the Nostoi Region of Fontaine) and the artifact strongbox. Added in Version 4.6.
The Faded Theater's Ley Line Disorder gives a stacking All Elemental and Physical DMG Bonus whenever a Bond of Life gains or loses value. The wiki's trivia notes that the set's lore relates to Natlan, citing the Saurians and names such as Sakkuk, Yupanqui, Atawallpa and Waskar, which echo Maya and Inca figures.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present the pieces as bittersweet relics of a rebellion told by those who loved its unsung planner.

Characters in the present would know little of the craftsman, because the tribes deliberately erased his name; do not give him a name or face beyond what the text allows.

736.content: Sakkuk appears as the daughter of the mines who sent wandering spirits back to the night realm and later as the long-lived old mistress of the mines who bought the craftsman's works and erased his name. The wiki identifies her as the first hero to join the scarlet-eyed youth and as a chief of the Children of Echoes.

737.content: In this set the scarlet-eyed youth returns from the kingdom of flowing light to gather heroes against the insane king, summons a god's fiery wrath to burn the corroded city and returns to the sacred flames after completing his calling. Wider canon names him as the second Pyro Archon; the pieces only call him a youth and a hero.

738.content: The pieces describe a burnt-faced beggar who made the feather ornament and planned the uprising, saw visions in the fire that nearly killed him, and was later erased from history. He is never named in the text.

739.content: The twins are described as the elder, whose lips and teeth were sharper than any blade, and the younger, whose back bore the tyrant's lash. Atawallpa rekindled the desire for past glories in Moment of Attainment. A surviving twin mourns him in Crownless Crown.

740.comment: Unfinished Reverie: Dark Fruit of Bright Flowers
740.content: as the tribes' banners faded, a half-man holding a cracked ring played on the throne and ordered that none heed the instructions of the ancestors and first ascended. When darkness seized the depths, a red-eyed youth returned from the kingdom where water flowed as rays of light to the ineffable city. A blind, stooped old woman warned him to seek the truly righteous, those who still stand in the cold night and throw themselves on the fire. A young girl came first, then the hero twins (the elder sharp-tongued, the younger scarred by the tyrant's lash), then a taciturn warrior who hoped Saurians and humans could live in peace. The youth needed someone who knew the city's secret and open paths and could handle mechanisms like toys, and the warrior named a craftsman.

741.content: the girl, bonded to the youth, searched the city for the renowned craftsman among the nobles and found nothing, until a hooded drunkard at a dilapidated tavern told her the story of the feather ornament. He was a beggar whose face was burnt away on one side. She had lost her father, condemned for protecting the tribe's Saurians, and he saw the same hatred in her eyes. He offered his service before she asked.

742.content: researchers puzzle over identical burin marks in the same spot on the sundials in the city's ash. Those who came from the canyons thought it a time to relight the obsidian pillars, and Sakkuk, daughter of the mines, sent wandering spirits back to the night realm. Those from the hanging trees renewed the contract with the Saurians of the six tribes, and Yupanqui shattered the shackles on a Saurian's neck. Those from the spring's source heard again the echoes of the waves, and Atawallpa rekindled the desire for past glories. Those from the mountain peaks returned to freedom, and the scarlet-eyed hero summoned a god's fiery wrath to burn the corroded city and restore the tribe. According to unofficial histories, a skilled artisan with no recorded name planned the overthrow of the insane king, then vanished from the old stories.

key: The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched
743.comment: Unfinished Reverie: The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched
743.content: the craftsman told the youth and the heroes how the king of the ineffable city had gathered tribal artisans to dig up huge beast-shaped constructs, and burned everything and everyone to bury the secret behind a stone gate. A golden tear from a stone head fell into the craftsman's eye as he lay dying, and he saw the machines, shadows climbing to the moon, golden patterns and an alternate escape route, and the iron laws that built the empire. The twins laughed it off as a tale. He hoped that, once the dust settled, he could design a brilliant imperial wall for the new king.

744.content: the girl, grown old as the mistress of the mines, had promised a turquoise crown to the craftsman once the ancient kingdom fell. After she saw his corpse hunched beneath a black beast's butcher's blade, the crown waited alone for a master who would never attend a coronation. She bought his genuine works and forgeries alike, at any price in gems, so the fakes would not stain his name, and she dealt harshly with cheats. Outliving the youth, who returned to the sacred flames, the warrior who fell into the ruler's flames, and the twins, she took the last of his true works into the dark night and never returned. Next day, the tribes swore beneath the tree where the crown lay to follow her last order, to blot the craftsman's name from history.

745.content:
Uraku Misugiri (also: Misugiri, Brocade Bloom, Shrine Sword): Uraku Misugiri is a five-star sword made by the renowned literato Urakusai, a Kitsune. Legend says that in hundreds of years it has never cut any living creature. The name comes from an episode where a drunken Urakusai sliced the gold-lacquered stage curtains of the bake-danuki in a dance, and the sword was later given as a reward to the man known as the Otogi King, "he of the Front Gate".

The item story adds a second, oral account from the oni: the Otogi King traded the blade to a young tailor for her scissors, and she later wove a scroll of him with two swords.

Appearance: The text calls it a great golden blade, "Misugiri", of famous make. Its owner is pictured in golden brocade threaded with autumn grass and clouds, with painted features; in some scrolls he holds one large and one small sword. The sword's own look is not detailed beyond its name and size.

Lore: Urakusai once earned the bake-danuki's undying enmity by cutting the gold-lacquered stage curtains in the forest during a drunken reverie. That gave his sword its name, and his blade-wild dance under the moon became a tale told by everyone but the bake-danuki. He later apologised to the performers and gave them his tea set and other treasures. The man "of the Front Gate" had met him only once before, and received the blade as a reward for mediating between the parties.

The recipient was unlike the rumours: a strange character who fought a vicious battle against Lavender Melon trees, yet had a sense of elegance and loved plays, toys and clothes. In battle he wore golden brocade and painted his face. Ancient texts and folk tales never show him wielding Misugiri in his final battle; his weapon in anecdotes is always the prodigiously large blade with an equally long name, which the Redhorn Stonethresher text names. The "Anthology" of the time records that Misugiri was lost by him one summer before the disaster. The oni tell a different story, preserved only in song and chant. After a festival wrestling match he gave the blade to a tailor from a non-martial family: a young girl who had patched a golden flower loose from his haori, and who refused a reward.

He insisted on a swap of the sword for her scissors so it would not count as a reward, claimed a long blade would cut cloth better, and said he was giving it away because its owner had been long-winded and he did not want Urakusai visiting every few days to ask after it. He then drew it, cut off one of his own sleeves cleanly, and handed over sleeve and sword, frightening the girl by his sudden seriousness before laughing and leaving. The villagers called him "The Great Idiot" and he did not mind. Later, he was said to have sighed while cleaning the sword, blaming Urakusai for leaving such a treasure to a man like him and saying it should enjoy the beauty of the world rather than be tainted with slaughter. The tailor, wracked by guilt for never being able to return the blade to help him fell his foes, later designed the scroll showing him with two swords cutting through the tide of black monsters. The text ends before that scroll, with the oni Chiyo dancing with a sword in her resplendent juunihitoe, and says Urakusai first had years of grieving the scattered, wandering people.

Owners: Maker: Urakusai. Recipient: the Otogi King, "he of the Front Gate". According to the oni account, he gave it to a young tailor of common birth, who is unnamed in the text. The item is an ordinary player weapon in-game.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star sword from the Otogi King series, base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT DMG 19.2%. Passive "Brocade Bloom, Shrine Sword": Normal Attack DMG +16-32% and Elemental Skill DMG +24-48%; after a nearby active character deals Geo DMG, those bonuses double for 15s; the wielder's DEF rises by 20-40% (refinement 1-5). It was one of two event-exclusive weapons in the Version 4.5 Epitome Invocation (2024-03-13), alongside Redhorn Stonethresher.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the sword suits a theme of a treasure refusing to be only a trophy. Characters who tell its story should keep both accounts, the Anthology's and the oni's, and not pick one as the truth.

746.content: Urakusai is the renowned Kitsune literato who made the blade. The item story shows him as a refined drinker who offended the bake-danuki, made amends, and later grieved for the scattered, wandering people. His own entry carries what else is known.

747.comment: Uraku Misugiri: The Great Idiot of the Front Gate
747.content: The man "of the Front Gate" is the oni warrior of the oral account, the same figure as the Redhorn Stonethresher text's Otogi King by the weapon connection the Uraku Misugiri text draws. Villagers called him The Great Idiot; he was quick to laugh and anger, made many friends and protected many lives. The text states he was neither exceptionally long-lived nor short-lived.

key: Many Oaths of Dawn and Dusk
748.content:
Verdict (also: Many Oaths of Dawn and Dusk): Verdict is a 5-star claymore of Fontaine, released in Version 4.3 alongside Navia. Its item text tells of Leticia, the eldest daughter of the noble House Randolph, who slipped into the underground Fleuve Cendre in disguise, fell in love with a young man there, and eventually abandoned her family name to live among its people. The weapon is described as stained with the blood of enemies and loved ones alike.

Its passive is named Many Oaths of Dawn and Dusk, echoing the oaths in the story. The weapon's text is one of several Fontaine item stories about the Fleuve Cendre and the events leading to the Siege of Poisson.

Appearance: Canon text does not describe the blade beyond calling it a claymore; the story mentions an axe in Leticia's hand years later, though the text does not say the axe and the weapon are the same. Unusually, the weapon's inventory icon shows the handle at the bottom left rather than the top right, unlike most claymores.

Lore: A young noblewoman, Leticia, is told by her father that as the eldest daughter of House Randolph she must keep a composed, pure bearing, because when nobles fall they drag many common homes down with them. She still disguises herself and goes down to the Fleuve Cendre, the sunless subterranean city. A man there sees through the disguise and invites her to see how its people live.

Her guide is a young man she already knows by name; he explains that her father, brother and servants need not learn of this place, quoting the Boss's saying that the sun's light belongs to others and the Fleuve Cendre to them. He later tells her he adores her noble soul and that if he is ever lost, her hand will decide his fate. Years pass; when she meets her father again she has taken on the name of the rose and is used to the weight of an axe rather than fine dresses. She tells him she has made a pact with her beloved and an oath to those she loves, and that she will not let the Randolph name be stained on her account. He answers that he lights a candle for her every day, asks her to come home, says her child is innocent and he will not abandon it, and hints that Randolph influence could be used for her husband too.

The text closes in a dream: she remembers that naval cannons had not shaken them, yet no outsiders should have known the secret paths the hunters used to infiltrate. This links the story to the Marechaussee Hunters' assault on the Fleuve Cendre and Poisson. The wiki deduces, from this text together with the Fleuve Cendre Ferryman text, that Leticia and her husband are the Rosa and Thompson Reed of Eduardo Baker's faction at the Siege of Poisson. Verdict does not state this outright (see uncertainties).

Reading notes: the text's timeline begins several years before the Siege of Poisson, which the wiki dates to over 500 years before the present, before the cataclysm. Her father's closing offer (return home, with her child sheltered) is made in the early days of the siege per the wiki's reading; the item text itself gives no dates. The Fleuve Cendre Ferryman text, by contrast, names Baker's companions in the faction, which is why the Reed identification rests on combining the two items. Keep the Boss's saying and the lovers' oaths as the emotional core; avoid stating how the story ends.

Owners: The text names Leticia as the weapon's former user ("a young maiden who forsook her family name"). No present-day character is established as owning the original.

Leticia appears by name only in her father's words; she herself later goes by the rose. Do not assume Navia, whose organisation, the Spina di Rosula, uses rose imagery, carries or inherited it.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star claymore released 2023-12-20 (Version 4.3) in the weapon event Wish, later also in Chronicled Wishes. Base ATK 48 with CRIT Rate as its secondary stat.

Passive Many Oaths of Dawn and Dusk raises ATK by 20% to 40% by refinement. When party members gain Elemental Shards from Crystallize, or trigger Lunar-Crystallize, the wielder gains a Seal that boosts Elemental Skill DMG (18% to 36% per Seal at refinements 1 to 5), lasting 15 seconds, with up to 2 Seals; Seals vanish shortly after the wielder's Elemental Skill deals damage, and Lunar-Crystallize grants at most one Seal per second. The Lunar-Crystallize clause belongs to the Nod-Krai era of the game and is not part of the weapon's original 4.3 text as far as verified. Ascension uses Ancient Chord materials, Rift Core line boss materials and Meshing Gear common materials.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: the weapon works as a Fontainian relic of an old, tragic love and defiance of class. Treat links to Navia, the Spina di Rosula or the Reeds as possibilities the user or scenario may introduce, not as canon fact.

749.content: Leticia is the eldest daughter of House Randolph in Verdict's story, who disguised herself to visit the Fleuve Cendre, fell in love with a man there, and later took on the name of the rose and cut ties with her family. See Verdict's lore for the full account; her possible identity as Rosa Reed is an inference and not stated in the text.

750.content:
Vermillion Hereafter (also: Flowering Life, Feather of Nascent Light, Solar Relic, Moment of the Pact, Thundering Poise): Vermillion Hereafter is a 4- and 5-star artifact set that boosts ATK after an Elemental Burst. Its five pieces (Flowering Life, Feather of Nascent Light, Solar Relic, Moment of the Pact, Thundering Poise) have item text about the Chasm in Liyue: the mountain tribes' plea to a four-armed yaksha, the Millelith soldiers who marched into the abyss, and the battle that ended with the yaksha and many soldiers lost.

Added in version 2.6. The text is legend told by miners and merchants; no one is named, and the set is a companion to the older Tenacity of the Millelith set.

Appearance: Relics of the Chasm story: a small flower given as a memento, a dim eagle feather, an ancient solar timepiece, a crystal-sand wine cup, and a fearsome mask.

Lore: Mountain tribes ask a four-armed yaksha for help; he drinks their wine, promises nothing and goes east into the Chasm, while Millelith soldiers march into the abyss beside him. Both are lost, and the pieces insist the land will remember.

Flowering Life: a Millelith soldier, sworn to Rex Lapis, tells a mountain tribe's daughter he will go with the four-armed yaksha into the depths and leaves her a small flower, asking not to be forgotten. Feather of Nascent Light: a hero who plucks an eagle's feather from the Chasm's highest cliff is said to earn the right to die beside the adepti; soldiers' doubts about being forgotten are described before the battle ends and the land remembers them. Solar Relic: a story about a fallen solar chariot and glowing sand crystal, said to come from Millelith who held out in the lightless abyss five hundred years ago. Moment of the Pact: mountain tribespeople offer wine to the four-armed yaksha and beg for help; he drinks it all, promises nothing and walks east, and the cup remains as a testament of the pact. Thundering Poise: a verse about the yaksha's battle at the Chasm, ending with the vortex and the lament of birds.
Details across the pieces. The tribes in Moment of the Pact say Rex Lapis's grace keeps their lives free of terror and that a dark shadow now clouds the blessing of the fallen star. Flowering Life says the Millelith stood guard when dark demons threatened, and the soldier speaks of braving crystal halls and twisted beasts. Solar Relic notes the Millelith gathered glowing sand to light their way, resembling pale moonlight, and kept a timepiece to mark their time in the abyss; it is described as proof that others later took up the duty of those who fell. Feather of Nascent Light states that the cries of the dark forces were silenced and many soldiers rest in the cavern.

Several pieces carry deliberate doubt. In Feather of Nascent Light the soldiers voice despair, saying that dying unremembered, like feathers in a whirlwind, makes saving and defending seem meaningless; the narrator answers that the land will remember. Solar Relic frames the sun-chariot story with a sceptical merchant's warning not to trust folktales, and ties Shenglu Hall's merchants to the sand crystal trade in the same hedged way. In Thundering Poise the yaksha is called a hero who sinks into the vortex, a loss mourned as a life spent for the dawn. Compared with Tenacity of the Millelith, which centres on the Millelith's ceremonial customs, Vermillion Hereafter centres on the yaksha and the tribes who asked for help.

Owners: No owner is named. The pieces speak of a four-armed yaksha, Millelith soldiers and mountain tribespeople, all unnamed.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): obtained from The Lost Valley domain and the Artifact Strongbox. 2-piece: ATK +18%. 4-piece: after an Elemental Burst, the wearer gains Nascent Light (ATK +8% for 16s); each time their HP decreases, ATK rises another 10%, up to 4 times, at most once per 0.8s. It is dispelled when they leave the field, and a new Burst replaces it.

751.content: Artifact set whose item text tells legends of the Chasm: the tribes' plea to a four-armed yaksha, the Millelith's march into the abyss, and the battle in which both fell or vanished.

752.comment: Vermillion Hereafter: The yaksha's pact with the Chasm tribes
752.content: In Moment of the Pact, the mountain tribes' elders offered wine and asked a lone four-armed traveller for help against a shadow troubling the Chasm. He drank it, promised nothing and went east; what followed is left to the listener's knowledge. In Thundering Poise he enters the Chasm with a blade and is lost in the collapse. The text never names him.

753.comment: Vermillion Hereafter: The Millelith soldier's flower
753.content: Flowering Life records a Millelith soldier's farewell to a daughter of the mountain tribe, pledging to follow the four-armed yaksha into the glowing depths. He leaves her a small flower and asks not to be forgotten if he is buried in some nameless place. Neither person is named.

754.content:
Viridescent Venerer (also: In Remembrance of Viridescent Fields, Viridescent Arrow Feather, Viridescent Venerer's Determination, Viridescent Venerer's Vessel, Viridescent Venerer's Diadem): Viridescent Venerer is an Anemo artifact set from launch (Valley of Remembrance domain). Its five pieces tell of a legendary huntress, the "queen of hunters", who moved silently through the forest, stopped hunting animals at a boy's request after disaster struck an ancient kingdom, and hunted monsters instead.

The huntress is nameless apart from her title. The set's story continues in the lore of the bow The Viridescent Hunt.

Lore: In the days when monsters had not yet appeared, the Viridescent Venerer hid her human scent with a white wild flower, and was sought by walking barefoot through the forest. The one who found her was a boy, when disaster had just befallen an ancient kingdom. She had once let the grass and mud tell her what birds and roots perceived, but when the God of the Woods died in the disaster the plants stopped speaking, so she used a wayfinding device. At the boy's request she stopped hunting birds and beasts and hunted the monsters that brought suffering instead.

Her arrows once brought death gently: she stroked her prey so its life force returned to nature, and believed she would meet the departed at an endless hunting ground. But she killed the monster that had slain the boy out of vengeance, and believed that hunting ground was then lost to her. The Chinese text ties this to avenging those the monsters hurt on the boy's behalf. Her vessel held the laughter of a campfire she once overheard; she had forgotten human speech, and even after joining the humans no one heard her say a word or saw her leave a trace.

The English text says that "disaster" came, while the Chinese original specifies the ancient kingdom, and the wiki reads this as Khaenri'ah and the Cataclysm; the God of the Woods is said to have died with it. The diadem piece quotes the hunters' rule, "Never become the foe of the earth and the forest", says a bird nested in her hat, and notes none could crown her since only nature was above her. After the crisis her hunter's hat became a frightful sight for monsters.

She replayed the stored voices for years whenever she felt lonely. A translation note says the original gives her a believed place at a "fenceless range", lost because she took revenge, not because she saved the boy.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): 4 and 5 star set from Valley of Remembrance and its strongbox. 2-piece: Anemo DMG Bonus +15%. 4-piece: Swirl DMG +60%, Stellar Swirl +20%; lowers the enemy's RES to the swirled element by 40% for 10s, and Cryo RES too on a Stellar Swirl; same-element debuffs don't stack. Introduced in 1.0.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): portray her as silent, gentle and grieving. Do not name her or the boy, and do not state more about the disaster than the items imply.

755.comment: Viridescent Venerer: In Remembrance of Viridescent Fields
755.content: The flower piece: a white wildflower that once covered the land, worn by the huntress to hide her scent. The silent huntress could be found by walking barefoot through the Dharma Forest following its fragrance; the one who found her was a boy, as the ancient kingdom suffered disaster.

756.content: The plume piece: a falcon feather, once fletching on her arrow. She comforted prey so its life force returned to nature, expecting an endless hunting ground, but believed her vengeful killing of the monster that killed the boy cost her that.

757.content: The sands piece: a wayfinding device that points to prey. She once learned what birds saw from the grass and what roots heard from the mud; after the God of the Woods died, the plants fell silent, and at a boy's request she began hunting monsters.

758.content: The goblet piece: a leakproof water pouch she used to store the laughter of a campfire. She had forgotten human speech; no one ever heard her speak or saw her leave a trace.

759.content: The circlet piece: a bloodless hunter's hat, from folklore of the uncrowned queen of hunters, who held to the rule never to become the foe of the earth and forest. It became a frightful sight for monsters in the crisis that followed.

760.content:
Vivid Notions (also: Falling Rainbow's Wish, Dawn's First Hue, Twilight's Splendor): Vivid Notions is a 5-star catalyst: a trophy of gemstones from the Collective of Plenty and crystals from the Flower-Feather Clan, said to have belonged to a legendary wrestler.

Its story concerns a woman of the Collective of Plenty who stepped into the hero's role when the tribes fell into a succession quarrel.

Appearance: Canon says only that it is a trophy of gemstones and crystals. The story speaks of a hero's prop or mask, which is not the same object; keep to a glittering trophy.

Lore: After the six heroes of the blazing sun had stepped into the night wind, the tribes quarrelled over the empty throne. A girl who had stood silently in Wanjiru's shadow burst into the council chamber and drove a half-broken bone blade into the long table, ending the quarrel.

Fietena, born of the Collective and married into the Flower-Feather Clan, then led the united tribes against the Abyss's black tide.

The tribes had been scheming for the authority left behind while the calamity loomed. Fietena had never received an Ancient Name nor been expected to become a hero; she had huddled by campfires listening to Wanjiru's legends. She now wore a hero's mask and rallied the tribes. With Traore, an orphan of the mines, she carved through rocks to channel lava into protective rivers, and with Nzambe, a priest of the deep valleys, she set a trap that unleashed a hurricane across the corrupted swamp.

In the end a mortal is only a mortal: when the calamity finally waned, the withering tide had permeated Fietena's bones. As the last shadow crumbled she removed her mask and gave the prop she had played the hero with for many years to Taika, a young follower from the Flower-Feather Clan. Her final words, as told, are that when the storm passes a rainbow will shine, but its false colours are illusions in the mist; whether a true hero or merely acting the part, each person's turn to bow out comes, as with a wrestler; and Taika should let the mask witness the journey ahead. The wiki's Fietena page adds that she was a renowned wrestler and calls the mask the Demon-Warrior's Feather Mask.

Owners: The description says the trophy once belonged to a legendary wrestler; the story is about Fietena.

No wielder is named; Taika receives Fietena's mask, not necessarily the trophy. Treat any scene in which a character carries the trophy as invented.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star catalyst, base ATK 48 at level 1, secondary stat CRIT DMG; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 5.5.

Passive "Falling Rainbow's Wish": ATK is increased by 28% to 56%. A Plunging Attack grants "Dawn's First Hue" (Plunging Attack CRIT DMG up by 28% to 56%), and using an Elemental Skill or Burst grants "Twilight's Splendor" (up by 40% to 80%). Each lasts 15s and is cancelled 0.1s after the ground impact hits a target.

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: a Natlanese wrestler or storyteller can use the story to talk about being a hero as a role that mortals take up and later put down. Avoid claiming the trophy's exact history.

761.content: Falling Rainbow's Wish is the passive of the catalyst Vivid Notions (gameplay): an ATK boost, plus Dawn's First Hue and Twilight's Splendor, which raise Plunging Attack CRIT DMG until the plunge lands.

762.content: Fietena was a Collective of Plenty woman who married into the Flower-Feather Clan and, with Traore and Nzambe, protected Natlan for about a decade after the Pyro Archon went into the Sacred Flame. She wore a hero's mask, was a renowned wrestler, and handed the mask to Taika as she aged.

763.content:
Vortex Vanquisher (also: Guànhóng zhī Shuò, Rainbow-Piercing Lance): Vortex Vanquisher is a five-star polearm of Liyue and the weapon Zhongli is shown with. Its item story is a sailors' legend from the days when ships sailed beside sea monsters: Rex Lapis once wielded a spear that pierced the rainbow and pinned a churning vortex in the middle of the deep sea, and whales and dolphins still gather there to sing.

Folklore adds that the vortex is not dead, only stilled, and that one day it will wake and bring a hurricane. The text asks who then will be able to subdue That Which Lies in the Deep.

Appearance: Item text gives no look for the spear apart from its power to pierce a rainbow. Zhongli appears with its ascended version in his portrait art and the Version 1.5 trailer, and the plain version in his demo.

Lore: In ancient times Liyue Harbor was not at peace because of creatures from the deep. A great shadow dwelt in the oceanic abyss and used great vortices and whirlpools to smash even the strongest ships and drag prey into the sunless depths. Sailors also told of a divine island, rainbow-clad and fog-shrouded, that rises from the sea with treasure for whoever sets foot on it, though others said the island was itself a monster in torpor.

Most such legends are bizarre, but sailors and skippers all believe one: Rex Lapis once wielded a spear that pierced the rainbow and pinned the vortex at the heart of the deep sea. Since then dolphins and whales are often seen gathering there, singing. Some say they mourn the god they revered; others that they are awed that he could pierce the rainbow and bring the sun down to them.

Folk legend adds that the vortex, held in a dead stillness by the spear, will one day wake; the omen is wind carrying the stench of the deep ashore, followed by a hurricane as big as a nine-headed hydra. The wiki links the great shadow to Osial, the Overlord of the Vortex, though the item text does not name him. The Chinese name, "Rainbow-Piercing Lance", is wordplay on an idiom about a white rainbow piercing the sun; in the lore it is Osial's rainbow that is pierced.

Owners: The story credits the spear to Rex Lapis (Morax). In play it is Zhongli's weapon; the wiki notes that in some one-time story domains and trials he swaps it for the Staff of Homa, which is presentation only.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star polearm from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 46, secondary stat ATK 10.8%. Passive "Golden Majesty", shared by the Liyue series: Shield Strength +20-40% and scoring hits raises ATK 4-8% for 8 seconds, up to 5 stacks, doubled while under a shield (refinements 1 to 5). A shield-friendly passive suits Zhongli's shielding.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the story is a sailors' tavern tale with deep-sea dread and awe at a god's power. Present it as legend; do not state that the vortex is about to wake.

key: That Which Lies in the Deep
764.comment: Vortex Vanquisher: Overlord of the Vortex
764.content: The Vortex Vanquisher legend speaks of a great shadow in the oceanic abyss that used vortices to wreck ships. The wiki connects it to Osial, but the item story only calls it a monster of the deep that Rex Lapis pinned with a rainbow-piercing spear.

765.content:
Vourukasha's Glow (also: Stamen of Khvarena's Origin, Vibrant Pinion, Ancient Abscission, Feast of Boundless Joy, Heart of Khvarena's Brilliance): Vourukasha's Glow is a Sumeru artifact set (Version 3.6, Molten Iron Fortress domain). Its five pieces trace the Khvarena, a daughter-like shard of life made by the Goddess of Flowers: she is entrusted to the queen of grass and trees, forged into the divine bird Simurgh, and finally shatters into the countless flowers of the Vourukasha Oasis. The set is a farewell, not a chronicle.

Its images are verdant: a pilgrim's flower insignia, a feather alive with leaves, a pure liquid timepiece, a wine goblet that was once full of nectar, and earrings of a hundred flowers. The speakers address a daughter or a friend, never an audience.

Lore: A mother warns her "innocent daughter", the Khvarena, of a faceless nightmare in her dreams and sends her to "another mother", a verdant queen of grass and trees whose light is brighter than her own. The Khvarena will face division and death before becoming immortal, and the lord of sweet dew and the lord of grass and trees will lose their divine forms and be forgotten.

Before the Cataclysm's dark tide, the queen of grass and trees forged the Khvarena into a divine bird to guard the border between birth and death. The bird slept among pines and snow-lotuses until disaster woke her. When the dark tide struck, the former leader of the water realm was slain and her body became a sea of pure dew, the Amrita, which would dry up under the Abyss. To cleanse it the divine bird, Simurgh, shattered her own form. The scattered Khvarena fell upon the water mistress's remains and became a sea of flowers; spirits dwell there, singing of the three mothers (verdure, sweet dew, flowers).

Each piece speaks a different voice. In Ancient Abscission, a friend gives the queen of trees a shard of Khvarena to protect, fearing the "chaotic darkness" more than any predictable disaster. After the mistress of flowers withered and the master of the desert was led astray by a false dream, the queen fulfilled the pact and gave the Khvarena a beautiful form: Simurgh, whose song held countless flowers' songs and whose body hid the sea of flowers. In Feast of Boundless Joy, the queen of grass and trees cuts ties with the sea of sand after the mistress of the orchard dies and returns to the rainforest to defend life. Simurgh is born from the Khvarena of the flowers and declares herself "the final remnant of my mistress", ready to burst into rays of light like a pomegranate. The wiki identifies the mothers as Nabu Malikata, Greater Lord Rukkhadevata and the Hydro Archon Egeria, and says Simurgh's shattering gave rise to the Pari of the Vourukasha Oasis.

The Heart of Khvarena's Brilliance supplies the set's philosophy: life walks with death and forgetting is the lover of remembrance; without the threat of death no life would matter, and without waves of forgetfulness no history would be worth recording. It adds that one night "the daughter must leave the embrace of the three mothers" and sacrifice herself because the world's impurity has grown. The Plume says even the pure sea would dry in the Abyss-devastated land, so the queen of grass and trees, who had no time to mourn, had to tend the mother-tree of numberless seeds. The Stamen piece adds that the lord of sweet dew and the lord of grass and trees will be forgotten and only the memory of the daughter's sacrifice kept.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a 4- and 5-star set from the Molten Iron Fortress domain and the Vourukasha's Glow strongbox. 2-piece: HP +20%. 4-piece: Elemental Skill and Burst DMG +10%; after the wearer takes DMG, that bonus rises by 80% for 5s, up to 5 independent stacks, even off-field. Released in 3.6; no later change is listed.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): the set suits quiet, elegiac scenes about the Vourukasha Oasis. Keep the mothers unnamed unless a character knows the Khvarena story.

766.comment: Vourukasha's Glow: Stamen of Khvarena's Origin
766.content:
The flower piece of Vourukasha's Glow: a small flower insignia once worn by pilgrims. A mother tells her daughter, the Khvarena, that she is being sent to another mother, because the speaker dreamed of a faceless nightmare and separated her daughter from her body to hold it off.

The mother predicts division, death and a harder immortality, and says the lord of sweet dew and the lord of grass and trees will be forgotten. She asks her daughter not to let her Khvarena dim and not to disgrace her mother.

767.content:
The plume piece: a feather-shaped ornament whose colours shimmer like leaves and flowers. It tells of the night before the sandstorm of tragedy, the dark tide, the queen of grass and trees forging Khvarena into a divine bird, the slain water leader whose body became the Amrita, and Simurgh's decision to shatter her form and cleanse it.

The text says new plants and beasts united with mortals to push back the dark tide. The queen of grass and trees had broken ties with the lord of the red sands in the "lonesome years" before. All beautiful things born of the Khvarena must wither and fall in the mud, then be reborn from the Amrita as beings of the flowery sea.

768.content:
The sands piece: an ancient timepiece with Khvarena's light and a living pure liquid inside. A friend entrusts a shard of Khvarena to the queen of grass and trees, calling it a drop of light in a sea of dew; later the queen shapes it into Simurgh, whose body hides the sea of flowers.

The giver foresees mortals wandering lost like infants unswaddled, strong enough to defeat wind and flame and their own flaws, but threatened by chaotic darkness. When the mistress of flowers withered, the desert master was misled by a false dream, and the gilded sand devoured the old paradise, the queen kept the covenant.

769.comment: Vourukasha's Glow: Feast of Boundless Joy
769.content:
