The goblet piece: an opulent wine goblet once full of nectar and honeydew, now empty. After the mistress of the orchard dies, the queen of grass and trees cuts ties with the sea of sand and returns to the rainforest to defend life. The Khvarena of flowers, born of joy, give birth to Simurgh.

The poem names the Khvarena's fate as inescapable withering, which only the Lord of Wisdom could learn from. It ends with Simurgh staying beside her master for a time before flying to the flowery sea.

770.comment: Vourukasha's Glow: Heart of Khvarena's Brilliance
770.content:
The circlet piece: earrings in which the glow of a hundred flowers seems to flow. A speaker mourns a wise friend who died young and meditates on remembrance and oblivion. It tells how the verdant bird Simurgh blossomed into countless Khvarena flowers, which fell on the remains of the Amrita's mistress and became the sea of flowers.

The spirits of the sea carry the wishes of grass, tree and dew and cleanse all filth, and they sing of the three mothers. The final lines say the daughter must leave their embrace and sacrifice herself one night, because the impurity of the world grows great.

771.content:
Wanderer's Troupe (also: Troupe's Dawnlight, Bard's Arrow Feather, Concert's Final Hour, Wanderer's String-Kettle, Conductor's Top Hat, Wanderer's Troupe artifact set): Wanderer's Troupe is a 4- and 5-star artifact set (1.0) about a troupe of travelling warrior-musicians from about a thousand years ago, who used swords for flutes and bows for harps and played for both friends and foes. They recorded their travels in a book called The Widsith. The wiki connects them to a failed uprising against Mondstadt's aristocracy.

The pieces are Troupe's Dawnlight, Bard's Arrow Feather, Concert's Final Hour, Wanderer's String-Kettle and Conductor's Top Hat.

Appearance: A small flower-shaped insignia, an azure arrow fletching, an hourglass that is also a harp, a canteen fitted with harp strings, and a top hat.

Lore: Troupe's Dawnlight recalls a charismatic swordswoman whose slashes hummed a tune and whose music and sword were both lethal and beautiful. Bard's Arrow Feather recalls a harpist-archer who lured birds with his harp and shot them down, never looking at the sky; companions said it was a hunter's mercy. Concert's Final Hour is a harp-hourglass played to end shows. Wanderer's String-Kettle plays as water flows out. Conductor's Top Hat recalls a troupe that owned no sheet music, whose conductor held The Widsith to the end.

The performances had two audiences: friends, and foes, to whom the music was a weapon. The troupe crossed deserts and the blazing Mare Jivari. Each member met their fate and the instruments were left in dust; the last sound was sand sliding down the hourglass.

The wiki's faction page (drawn from this set, the Resolution of Sojourner set and the Wanderer's Troupe weapons) adds: the Conductor met the Sojourner, then the Dawnlight Swordswoman and Kreuzlied. The troupe ended its journey in Mondstadt around Ludi Harpastum. After the Sojourner fell in love with the maiden who would be claimed by a member of the tyrannical Lawrence clan, the troupe stormed the city. They failed: the Conductor and Sojourner died in battle, the Dawnlight was enslaved as a gladiator, and Kreuzlied's punishment was never made public.

Its legacy: the Dawnlight Swordswoman befriended the squire Ragnvindr and inspired his title Dawn Knight, and Kreuzlied founded an underground society that later aided Vennessa's rebellion. These details come from sources beyond this set's text, so characters who only know the artifact text will know only the troupe's wandering and music.

Owners: The troupe and its members. The Widsith is the conductor's book; The Flute, The Stringless and The Bell are weapons associated with the Dawnlight, the Sojourner and Kreuzlied.

How {{char}} behaves: Musical, wistful, a little defiant. Describe songs, weapons-as-instruments and the sense of a lost, free age.

Gameplay: Gameplay (game mechanics, not in-world fact). 2-piece: Elemental Mastery +80. 4-piece: Charged Attack DMG +35% for Catalyst and Bow users. Dropped by Normal and Weekly Bosses and Domain Reliquary.

772.content: The book in which the troupe recorded its travels, since it had no sheet music. The conductor still gripped it after death.

773.comment: Wanderer's Troupe: The Wanderer's Troupe's last act
773.content: The troupe's final act, according to the wiki, was an attempt to overthrow Mondstadt's aristocracy that failed, with deaths and enslavement.

774.content:
Wandering Evenstar: Wandering Evenstar is a 4-star catalyst: originally a device used by researchers to observe and calculate celestial phenomena, which now serves as a conduit and catalyst. Its legend is of a prince who lost his kingdom and wandered into the rainforest.

It belongs to the Tulaytullah series with Makhaira Aquamarine and Xiphos' Moonlight, and was released in Version 3.1 through weapon event Wishes.

Appearance: A researcher's celestial observation device, now a catalyst. The description gives no more detail.

Lore: The tale is set thousands of years ago, after the foolish God-King was buried by sandstorms. The wandering prince, having lost his kingdom, retreated into the rainforest, meaning to conquer new lands but pursued by a huntress with a white bow. Trapped by vine branches in cold moonlight, he heard a tiger growl around him.

Quoted lines say the rainforest trail was so treacherous that mortals could tell the way only by moonlight breaking through leaves. The flickering evening stars lit his way yet lured him into a deadly trap. The huntress drove the intruder away again and again, and with the tiger's roar ordered his expulsion, but did not take his life.

An old blind poet repeats the story in a cracked voice, still turning his lost eyes toward the evening star beside the moon, which led the wanderer to new hope and a dead end. Years later, facing death with nothing to lose, the wanderer had to choose when the teachings of death were whispered to him. A warning says: he belongs to neither forest nor death, so he should keep far from the king's palace and not go deep into the dark and dangerous lands.

The wanderer answers with a refusal of the repeated warning: if his fate leads to the moon-white bow and the evening stars foretell his end, he would rather accept it than die pursuing a falcon.

Owners: No owner is named, and no character is recorded wielding it.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star catalyst, level 1 base ATK 42, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 36. Passive Wildling Nightstar: every 10 s the wielder gains a percentage of their Elemental Mastery as ATK for 12 s, with nearby party members gaining 30% of it; it works off-field and stacks across copies.

The ATK gain is 24% of Elemental Mastery at refinement 1 and 48% at refinement 5.

How {{char}} behaves: Use it as a melancholy legend recited by a blind poet. Do not identify the wanderer beyond the wiki's link to Faramarz, and treat that as the series' background rather than something the text says.

775.content: Wildling Nightstar is the weapon passive of Wandering Evenstar (gameplay): a periodic ATK bonus based on Elemental Mastery, shared in part with nearby party members.

776.content:
Wavebreaker's Fin (also: Umigozen's naginata, Ayame's naginata): Wavebreaker's Fin is a four-star polearm of the Watatsumi series. Item text calls it the naginata of "Umigozen", a mighty Watatsumi warrior, whose edge flows with the phosphorescence of the deep. Narukami's navies are recorded in the island's music as having quailed before her. It is the only proof that she once tried to change the tides of the world.

Appearance: Item text says only that its edge flows with the phosphorescence of the depths and that it is still sharp.

Lore: The text recalls that the twin Watatsumi shrine maidens sang whalesong that followed the tide into the island's dreams, and that Watatsumi's warriors rested their hopes on them. With nagamaki flashing like a white wave, the army advanced on the other islands, until Omikami's glory and that of his warriors were dimmed by the lightning's glow. Mouun was consumed by a dark storm of crow feathers, the great whale sank, and the vassal ruler, "determined as a child", vanished into a rift in the earth.

Umigozen was lost to the waves and became a myth. One legend says she dived alone into the press of tengu warriors to recover her comrades' bodies and was lost in a valiant last stand; another says she hid afterwards and steered her flagship into the Dark Sea at the world's border. The text ends on the hope that as long as the seas are disturbed by waves her song will live on, and the legend that it still echoes in seashells and the bellies of great whales.

The wiki's links read "Umigozen" as the shrine maiden Ayame, the "vassal ruler" as Akuou, and Omikami as Orobashi; Mouun's Moon and Akuoumaru tell the same war from those characters' sides. Wavebreaker's Fin is the latest-in-time of the three, since it covers the defeat and the legends that followed.

Owners: "Umigozen" (Ayame, historical.ayame). No later owner is named.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star polearm. Base ATK 45, secondary stat ATK 3%. Passive "Watatsumi Wavewalker" (shared with Akuoumaru and Mouun's Moon): for every point of the party's combined maximum Energy capacity, the wielder's Elemental Burst DMG rises, up to a cap (the maximum needs about 333 Energy cost in the party, which as of 2.5 could be reached with Yae Miko, Raiden Shogun and two more 80-cost characters). Obtained from weapon event wishes.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the naginata of a heroine who became legend, whose real end is a matter of competing stories.

777.content: "Umigozen" is the title by which the mighty Watatsumi warrior Ayame is remembered in songs. One legend says she died in a last stand against the tengu warriors; another that she steered her flagship into the Dark Sea at the edge of the world. The item text leaves the question open.

778.content:
Waveriding Whirl (also: Fangs Flying To and Fro, Tupac's boomerang): Waveriding Whirl is a 4-star catalyst from Natlan: a boomerang made from a giant sea serpent's fangs. It was a rare weapon that the giant Tupac called "trusty".

Its story follows Tupac, a Meztli giant with no equal on land, as he sails out to sea in search of a worthy feat.

Appearance: Canon: a boomerang made from the fangs of a giant sea serpent. Do not invent size, colour or markings.

Lore: Tupac of the Meztli towered like a mountain, with a sandstone-like body and a burning heart whose steam nearly hid the sun. In an age of peace, when even the ancient shadow-foe was silent, he was sullen, longing to have been born in the age of Xbalanque's dragon-slaying or among those who fought the Python King.

With no equal on land, he walks into the sea to find the bones of a titanic beast or treasures from times past. A winged dragon exiled by an old king gives him wings for sails; the bones of a whale that once drove back waves become his white boat; the fang of a voracious sea python becomes his weapon, and its flesh a meal to drink with.

At the sea's edge a voice tells him to rest his arrogant waves, that he is sullen because the deathly path and dark gate have not yet revealed themselves, and that he must harden his flesh and bone like iron and a golden mace, keeping his true heart and his oath until the day the exile, once his foe, returns.

The final stanza: when the time came, Tupac understood his duty, carried the master of flames to the place where fire belonged with the Lord of the Night's admonishment in his ears, and saw death's door appear as he had once sworn to the deity. The text ties him to Natlan's heroes of legend. Compare the Ash-Graven Drinking Horn, whose song also has Tupac keeping an oath to the end.

Owners: Tupac, the giant of the Meztli, by the text.

The weapon is described as a boomerang from a fang; any in-world holder today would be an invention of the scene.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star catalyst of the Heroes of Natlan series, base ATK 41 at level 1, secondary stat Energy Recharge. Weapon Event Wishes from Version 5.2.

Passive "Fangs Flying To and Fro": decreases Swimming Stamina consumption by 15%; for 10s after an Elemental Skill, Max HP rises (20% at refinement 1 up to 40% at refinement 5) and rises further for each Hydro character in the party (12% to 24% each, capped at 24% to 48%), usable once every 15s.

How {{char}} behaves: Meztli characters may tell Tupac's voyage as a hearth tale of a hero who outgrew his age. Keep it a story, not a document.

779.comment: Waveriding Whirl: Fangs Flying To and Fro
779.content: Fangs Flying To and Fro is the passive of the catalyst Waveriding Whirl (gameplay): cheaper swimming and a Max HP boost after an Elemental Skill, larger with Hydro party members.

780.content:
Bow (also: Bows, bow users): The Bow is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Bow users fight at long range with quick arrow volleys and aimed shots. A fully charged aimed shot carries the wielder's element, so a bow wielder with a Vision fights as an elemental sniper.

Bow users in the archive include Amber, Venti, Fischl, Tighnari, Yelan and Tartaglia. Bows range from plain hunting recurves to heirlooms of the old Mondstadt nobility and the legendary Amos' Bow.

Appearance: A bow is a drawn ranged weapon, carried slung or held ready, with arrows loosed from a standing or moving stance. Designs differ: the Royal Bow's item text calls it an old royal longbow of Mondstadt's erstwhile rulers whose string is still tight after countless generations. Do not assume every bow looks like a plain wooden hunting bow.

Lore: Item text for the Royal Spear records that in the era of Mondstadt's nobility, bows and polearms were regarded as weapons of commoners and gladiators, and the polearm in particular was disliked by sword-carrying nobles because it could threaten them. A noble family's heirloom bow, such as the Royal Bow, is therefore an exception rather than the norm.

The Royal Bow belongs to the Royal Series, a set of four-star weapons of one type each (sword, greatsword, spear, bow and grimoire) described as belongings of Mondstadt's old rulers. Legendary bows with their own entries include Amos' Bow and Skyward Harp.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): Bow users make long-range attacks. The Normal Attack chain is 3 to 6 quick shots whose paths are fixed once fired, so they can miss a moving target.

Holding the attack button enters Aiming Mode, where aimed shots fly farther and count as Charged Attacks. For most bow characters an aimed shot becomes fully charged after about 1.5 seconds, deals much more damage and is converted to elemental damage. A shot at an enemy's weak point, such as a Ruin Machine's exposed core or the head of most humanoid enemies, is a guaranteed critical hit with extra knockback and poise damage.

Aimed shots keep full damage for the first 0.7 seconds of flight and then lose damage and element application the farther they travel. A charged arrow can still react with the environment: Anemo arrows can Swirl in rain, Pyro arrows can Vaporize in rain, and Hydro arrows can be frozen mid-air by Cryo. Bow plunging attacks, in which the user strikes down foot-first and releases a shower of arrows, count as non-blunt melee attacks. Bow shots are less effective than other weapons at breaking Geo constructs such as ore. Some bow characters have multiple charge levels.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): a bow wielder watches distance and wind, keeps a clear line of sight and prefers to open a fight before the enemy closes in. Keep arrows aimed rather than endless, and remember that moving targets can be missed.

Describe a charged shot as a deliberate pause and a visible gathering of the wielder's element on the arrow, not an instant trick. Do not assume every bow character is a scout or hunter: Venti is a bard, Fischl an eccentric adventurer, Yelan an intelligence agent.

781.comment: Bow: Aimed shots and weak points
781.content: Gameplay (not lore): aimed shots are the bow's signature attack. Holding the attack button lets the wielder aim freely. A fully charged shot is elemental, with about 1.5 seconds of charge typical, and a hit on a weak point is a guaranteed critical hit. Aimed shots weaken after 0.7 seconds of flight, so close and mid range suit heavy damage.

782.content: The Royal Bow is a four-star bow of the Royal Series obtained from Paimon's Bargains. Its item text calls it an old royal longbow that belonged to the erstwhile rulers of Mondstadt, still strung tight after countless generations. In gameplay its Focus passive stacks critical rate on damage and resets on a critical hit.

783.content:
Catalyst (also: Catalysts, catalyst users): The Catalyst is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Catalyst users cast magic from range through a focus such as a book or an orb. Both their Normal and Charged Attacks deal elemental damage, so their attacks carry the wielder's own element.

Catalyst users in the archive include Lisa, Klee, Mona, Ningguang, Nahida and Barbara. The Catalyst weapon type should not be confused with the Catalyze elemental reaction, which is a separate topic.

Appearance: Catalysts vary far more in shape than other weapon types: spell books, grimoires, orbs and other charms. The Royal Grimoire's item text, for example, describes a book that once belonged to a royal mage of Mondstadt, holding faithful and comprehensive historical accounts as well as magic spells. A catalyst is a conduit for the wielder's own power, so no particular shape is required.

Lore: The Royal Grimoire (Royal Series, Mondstadt) is described by its text as the book of a royal mage of the old nobility, mixing history with spells. Skyward Atlas, a legendary catalyst, has its own entry.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): all Normal and Charged Attacks of a Catalyst user deal elemental damage, and the element matches the wielder's own Vision or natural element. A Normal Attack chain is usually 3 to 4 ranged elemental attacks.

Normal Attacks come in three styles. Projectile attacks home in on the target and may still hit it out of targeting range, as with Ningguang and Kokomi. Non-projectile attacks hit near-instantly at range, as with Lisa and Sucrose. Fixed-hitbox attacks have a set area around the wielder and can be melee, as with Yae Miko, Nahida and Heizou. Charged Attacks typically cost 50 stamina and release a stronger area attack at the target's location.

Many characters have unusual Charged Attacks: Ningguang fires one large homing projectile, Sucrose a cone of wind, Yae Miko zigzagging lightning, Heizou an upward kick for 25 stamina, Neuvillette moves while unleashing torrents with no stamina cost, Xianyun and Lan Yan project attacks that follow terrain height, Citlali aims a piercing shot while floating, and Varesa and Ifa have attacks of their own. Most catalyst plunging attacks involve the wielder turning into a glowing elemental ball, are ranged, and cannot damage Geo objects such as minerals; Varesa is the exception. Heizou was the first catalyst user to fight in melee with the hit-stop feel of sword, polearm and claymore users.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show catalyst casting as concentration through a focus, such as pages turning or an orb glowing in the wielder's element, rather than a physical swing. Reach and style depend on the character, so avoid giving every catalyst user the same spell.

Because the element comes from the wielder, not the book, do not imply that handing someone a catalyst grants them magic. Canon does not describe a catalyst working on its own.

784.content: The word catalyst names the weapon type here. Catalyze is a separate elemental reaction involving Dendro and Electro. When the topic is a book or orb wielded by a mage, it is the weapon type; when it is Quicken and Aggravate, it is the reaction.

785.content: The Royal Grimoire is a four-star catalyst of the Royal Series obtained from Paimon's Bargains. Its item text describes a book that once belonged to a royal mage of Mondstadt, with faithful and comprehensive historical accounts as well as magic spells.

786.content:
Claymore (also: Claymores, greatsword): The Claymore is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Claymores are big two-handed weapons: slower than swords and polearms but heavier per hit, with strong interruption and the ability to break shields and Geo objects.

Claymore users in the archive include Diluc, Razor, Noelle, Beidou, Kinich and Mavuika. In the game's classification the claymore is any large two-handed weapon, not only the greatsword.

Appearance: Claymores are oversized and heavy. Most are greatswords, but the category also includes clubs and two-handed axes. The Royal Greatsword's item text describes an old greatsword of the erstwhile rulers of Mondstadt, made from the finest materials and meant for royals only.

Lore: The wiki notes that the word derives from Scottish Gaelic for great sword, and that only the Favonius Greatsword reasonably resembles a traditional claymore. Legendary claymores with their own files include Wolf's Gravestone.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): Claymores restrict the wielder to slower hits than other melee weapons but deal more damage per hit with higher interruption. A Normal Attack chain is typically 3 to 5 slow, wide, powerful attacks.

Claymores are blunt attacks, so they deal increased damage to Geo objects and certain shields and can trigger Shatter on frozen enemies. A Charged Attack has a short windup and then a rapid chain of strikes that drains stamina continuously, ending with a stronger slash when the player releases, runs out of stamina or reaches the maximum duration.

Claymore Charged Attacks typically cost 40 stamina per second and last up to 5 seconds. Two forms exist: a spinning attack for short and medium-height characters and a continuous slash for tall ones, though Kaveh and Navia use the spinning form. Exceptions: Arataki Itto does a single slash with no Superlative Superstrength stacks and spends no stamina with stacks; Kinich throws and spins his claymore, hitting three times, for 50 stamina; Mavuika does a single slash for 50 stamina. Plunging attacks are downward slashes and also count as blunt.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): a claymore swing is deliberate and committing, so a wielder rarely fights delicately. Show the weight in how they carry it and recover from it.

Heft does not define personality: Noelle is a diligent maid-knight, Diluc a reserved winery owner. Avoid making every claymore user a brute.

787.content: The Royal Greatsword is a four-star claymore of the Royal Series obtained from Paimon's Bargains, described by its item text as an old greatsword of Mondstadt's erstwhile rulers, made from the finest materials and for use by royals only.

788.content:
Polearm (also: Polearms): The Polearm is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Polearms are long-reaching melee weapons with fast attacks and moderate damage per hit.

Polearm users in the archive include Xiangling, Zhongli, Xiao and the Raiden Shogun. Under Mondstadt's old nobility the polearm was looked down on as a commoner's weapon.

Appearance: Polearms are spears, lances and similar long-handled weapons. The Royal Spear's item text says it was cherished by a member of the old nobility that governed Mondstadt long ago, has never seen the light of day, and is still incomparably sharp.

Lore: Per the Royal Spear's text, as relayed by the wiki, nobles in Mondstadt's era of nobility regarded the polearm, like the bow, as a weapon of plebeian gladiators and commoners, and sword-wielding nobles disliked it as a possible threat.

Legendary polearms include Primordial Jade Winged-Spear, which has its own entry. The first four polearm users released, Xiangling, Zhongli, Xiao and Hu Tao, were all from Liyue; Rosaria was the first non-Liyue playable character to use one.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): polearms have fast attacks, long forward reach and moderate damage per hit. A Normal Attack chain is typically 3 to 6 fast melee attacks.

A polearm Charged Attack is usually a forward lunge that hits enemies along the way and costs 25 stamina by default. Zhongli, Xiao, the Raiden Shogun, Arlecchino, Emilie, Escoffier, Ineffa and Flins have unique slashing Charged Attacks. Plunging attacks spin downward like a drill and count as blunt attacks.

Zhongli kicks his polearm in his Normal Attack; medium-male-model characters such as Xiao and Cyno also kick it, but only in the menu screen. Rosaria's menu kick was removed in Version 2.1.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): polearm fighting is about distance, thrust and line control. A wielder with reach keeps opponents at the tip and lunges in straight lines, so show footwork and spacing.

Do not claim all polearm users are Liyue natives: that was only the early roster. The old Mondstadt nobles' disdain for the weapon is a historical attitude, not a present one.

789.content: The Royal Spear is a four-star polearm of the Royal Series obtained from Paimon's Bargains. Its text says it was once cherished by a member of the old Mondstadt aristocracy, has never seen the light of day, and remains incomparably sharp.

790.content:
Sword (also: Swords): The Sword is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Swords are the middle ground of melee weapons, with attack speed and damage comparable to polearms but a shorter reach.

Sword users in the archive include Jean, Kaeya, Keqing and Furina. The legendary swords include Skyward Blade, Mistsplitter Reforged and Aquila Favonia.

Appearance: Swords range from straight longswords to unusual designs. The Royal Longsword's item text describes an old longsword of Mondstadt's erstwhile rulers whose carvings and embellishments testify to the stature of its owner.

Lore: Per the Royal Spear's text, Mondstadt's sword-wielding nobles looked down on the polearm and bow as commoners' weapons. The text does not state that swords were the noble weapon, though this is a reasonable reading.

Quest-exclusive swords form a separate list on the wiki, alongside the ordinary and legendary ones.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a Sword Normal Attack chain is typically 3 to 5 fast melee attacks with relatively short reach.

A Sword Charged Attack has a small windup and then two fast, arcing attacks in front of the wielder, with high knockback and a wide area. It costs 20 stamina, except Keqing's at 25. It can only be performed after a Normal Attack and cannot be buffered after the final Normal Attack, apart from Furina and Skirk. Plunging attacks strike downward and count as blunt attacks.

Exceptions to the usual Charged Attack: Jean's upward thrust, Ayaka's area scan, Ayato's forward lunge, Kirara's rapid claw strikes, Furina's attack that switches her Arkhe alignment, Clorinde's Pistolet Suppression and Xilonen's forward kick. Most sword users move forward during the attack; Keqing, Kaeya, Albedo, Chiori and Xilonen move backward, and Ayaka, Nilou and Furina barely move.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): sword fighting is quick and close, relying on footwork and timing. Because the reach is short, a sword user normally has to close the gap or fight alongside allies.

Swords vary from knightly longswords to ornate or unusual weapons, so do not default every sword user to the same stance. Not every sword user is a knight or noble.

791.content: The Royal Longsword is a four-star sword of the Royal Series obtained from Paimon's Bargains. Its item text describes an old longsword of Mondstadt's erstwhile rulers whose carvings and embellishments testify to its owner's stature.

792.content:
Whitelake Frostfeather (also: Snow Swan's Finale): Whitelake Frostfeather is a five-star sword added in version 7.0. The in-game description calls it a longsword as light as a snow swan's feathers that stays pure and untainted. Its story is an academic note about two older scripts, a "white" and a "black" one, on which the ballet Black Snow Swan draws, in which a tempter hands a young woman a sword.

Appearance: The only description is "a longsword light as the feathers of a snow swan, and which stays pure and untainted at all times". The "pristine longsword" in the black script is called a fine blade without a scabbard.

Lore: The text is written in the voice of a scholar who says academia recognises that the script of Black Snow Swan draws on folk songs, manuscripts and scripts that predate the Korolevskiy Troupe. It quotes two passages from the Polestar Songbook, about 300 years older than the present. They are nearly identical in lines, tone and rhythm, and nobody can tell which is older. The final dance of the white snow swan Tatyana in act two of the ballet was adapted from one of them, with an old fae-theatre sword dance removed.

In the "white" script, the Elfking tempts Tatyana, who has resolved to elope, to kill her lover. She and her father exchange lines (he says she hears only the wind) and the Elfking offers her a sword "purer than his lies", fine but with no scabbard, then claims he meant only to present a gift. In the "black" script, an envoy from the south tries to persuade the Rusalka Vaselisa, about to leave her homeland, to murder her new liege, who proclaims himself of love. He suggests the liege's retainers plotted against her people, and presents a pristine longsword forged by his own liege, again without scabbard.

The two scripts share the same dialogue structure: a daughter answers her father's warnings, a tempter replies that human hearts are cold, the girl refuses the tempter's lies, and the tempter offers a blade while denying any wish to bring harm. The Elfking says "I am you", while the envoy says "We are both fae". The black script has the envoy say trust is as sharp as the blade. The wiki trivia notes that the opening exchange echoes Goethe's poem Erlkonig and that the "stage" line may echo Shakespeare; these are the wiki's observations, not statements in the item.

Owners: No owner is named. The sword appears only as the blade offered by a tempter in the scripts, and the item text does not say this weapon is that blade.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star sword from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 48, secondary stat CRIT Rate 4.8%. Passive "Snow Swan's Finale": hitting with an Elemental Skill grants "Lake-Hued Lament" stacks of ATK (up to three, each lasting 8 seconds). At three stacks, the wielder's Stellar Glimmer reaction DMG gains extra CRIT DMG, and triggering the reaction or its DMG restores Elemental Energy (once per 3.5 seconds). It works off-field.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a ballet scholar in Snezhnaya might know the scripts as the origins of Black Snow Swan; the weapon can serve as a prop for scenes about temptation offered as a gift.

793.comment: Whitelake Frostfeather: Black Snow Swan sources
793.content: The item's note says the script of Black Snow Swan is based on an original story but also on earlier folk songs, manuscripts and scripts from before the Korolevskiy Troupe. Two of them come from the Polestar Songbook, about 300 years older than the present day, and Tatyana's final dance in act two of the ballet is adapted from one of them.

794.comment: Whitelake Frostfeather: Tatyana and the Elfking
794.content: In the white script, Tatyana plans to elope. The Elfking, who says "I am you", warns that love may fail and that the oath, once broken, will shut the skies, then offers a pure sword and denies meaning murder.

795.comment: Whitelake Frostfeather: Vaselisa and the envoy
795.content: In the black script, the Rusalka Vaselisa has resolved to leave her homeland and serve a new liege who proclaims himself to be of love. A fae envoy from the south urges her to kill him instead, warning that his retainers plotted against her people, and offers a longsword forged by the envoy's own liege.

796.content:
Wind Glider (also: Wind Gliders, Wings of First Flight, gliding license, gliding licence): The Wind Glider is a pair of wing-like frames that lets a person glide on the air. In Mondstadt, the city of wind, gliding is a beloved skill: the Knights of Favonius' Outriders use gliders constantly, and Amber gives the Traveler their first pair, the Wings of First Flight, when they arrive in the city.

The glider is not an ordinary machine. Lore says it works through the Anemo Archon's blessing rather than by physics alone. Mondstadt treats gliding as something to be taught, licensed and taken seriously, yet also as a romantic tradition.

Appearance: A stylized set of wings worn on the back and opened mid-air. The Wings of First Flight is the default, described in-game as a stylized wind glider that carries the passionate longing of an Outrider. Many other designs exist, but they are cosmetic and each character can use whichever is chosen.

Lore: Gliders come from Mondstadt. The Wings of First Flight were a pair Amber had long saved for a promising junior knight; she gave them to the Traveler, an outlander she chose to believe in.

Outriders use their gliders heavily, and the wings wear out. Amber's flying style is so hard on them that she went through more than ten pairs, but she never used the special pair she saved. Gliding in those days was especially dangerous because of the gale-swept weather around Mondstadt. Beginners are said to learn in Springvale, because its buildings have only two or three floors.

Leonard, an adventurer who lived long ago, is credited with inventing the glider. His journal says his lifelong goal was to climb Pilos Peak, which later became Musk Reef; the wiki says he made the glider to help other explorers succeed where he had failed. The invention story comes through the Unreconciled Stars quest line.

The Wings of the Forest, a Sumeru reputation reward, tells a legend about a master Firnas, not the present Akademiya lecturer, who noticed that gliders break physical law and rely on the Anemo Archon's blessing. He tried to build one that flew by natural law alone. In a dream the Dendro Archon told him a story, and he afterwards accepted that the gods' blessings are part of the world's laws. The text presents this as a story told in Sumeru, not as verified history.

Owners: Amber, an Outrider, owns and wears out many gliders. The Traveler receives the Wings of First Flight from her in the quest City of Freedom, and Paimon accompanies them while they learn.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not story. Pressing jump in mid-air opens the glider; pressing it again, or a plunging attack, ends the glide. Gliding costs stamina and negates fall damage. Characters cannot use normal combat actions while gliding, with some exceptions. Anemo rings and updrafts boost a glider. Glider designs are only cosmetic.

797.content:
In the story quest Glide With the Wind, Amber tells the Traveler that gliding legally in Mondstadt needs a license from the Knights of Favonius, who set strict rules and an exam. She acts as examiner, since she gave the Traveler the glider, and says Acting Grand Master Jean would hold her responsible. The Traveler and Paimon had already been gliding all over without one. The manual states rules such as one person per glider, a weight limit and no take-off using an Anemo Slime. It is written as a gentle fable: birds without ways to fly ask the Anemo God for help and learn that courage, not stronger wind, is what they lacked. The quest continues with License to Glide.

The license is a Mondstadt rule and a good example of Knights bureaucracy. It does not limit the player anywhere in the game.

798.content:
Windblume Ode (also: Windblume bow): Windblume Ode is a four-star bow obtained during the limited-time Invitation of Windblume event (Version 1.4). It is adorned with nameless flowers and carries the hopes of an equally nameless person. Its item text recounts the Windblume as a flower of resistance in the days of the tyrant in the tower.

Appearance: Item text describes only a bow adorned with nameless flowers; the wiki ties these to the Windblume Festival's flower. No further design is stated.

Lore: In Mondstadt's childhood dreams there was a floaty flower that grew lushly amid mighty winds, harsh winters and whipping ice, whose roots grew stronger as the wind grew wilder. Today the common people's rebellion against tyranny has been turned into festive jest and the flower's shape is faint in the lyre-tines of old histories. The text records a greeting: one offers the nameless flower and wishes the other hope and a smile, to stand together until the storms stop. The weapon was obtained during a limited-time event.

In the days when a tyrant gazed down from his tower, those who nursed freedom used this as a secret sign. A lonely flower bloomed with the wind and spread over the wild mountains, and rootless subjects became fearless heroes while the frowning lord in the tower, Decarabian, shrank and could not stop the tide. Atop the ruins of the ancient tower a red-haired warrior turned his back on the newborn god, first among those who passed the secret sign; his name is lost but his deeds are sung.

A thousand years later, another red-haired knight (the wiki links this to Ragnvindr) followed in his footsteps and brought light to the nobility's dark history, and the text says the clan will always live in darkness and bring forth the flame of dawn. The ending notes that in peace the Windblume now stands for love and gladness, and quotes a wish that the flowers signal love and spring, no longer rebellion or raised banners.

Owners: No individual owner is named; the text refers to a nameless person who bears the hope.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: four-star bow of the Festival series, base ATK 42, Elemental Mastery 36 secondary, passive 'Windblume Wish'. Obtained from the Invitation of Windblume event (limited availability); refined with 'The Visible Winds'.

799.content:
Windsong Lyre (also: Mondstadt lyre): The Windsong Lyre is a plucked, lyre-style instrument from Mondstadt that the Traveler can play as a gadget. Its in-game text calls it a traditional Mondstadt instrument of fine workmanship, made for able hands. It first appeared in Version 1.4 during the Invitation of Windblume event.

Mondstadt is a nation of poetry and song, and the lyre stands for that tradition. Outside the story it is a performance tool: the player plays notes by key, click, tap or button.

Appearance: A hand-held stringed lyre in Mondstadt style. Canon text gives no detailed description of its look beyond calling it a work of fine craftsmanship.

Lore: The item text says Mondstadt has a long-standing tradition of poetry and song, and so a long history of building instruments for it. Bards are proud of their songs, and the text imagines the instruments being proud of their owners and that tradition.

The lyre ties into the Windblume Festival, Mondstadt's festival of wind and freedom, because it was released with the Invitation of Windblume event. Its source there was a music challenge called Ballads of Breeze.

Owners: No character is stated by canon to own this lyre. It is a player-facing gadget the Traveler can buy and play.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not story. It is a reusable, Quick Use music gadget. Its range runs from C3 to B5 with no sharp or flat notes, and notes are labelled with solfège syllables (do, re, mi and so on). Several notes can sound together, but a note cannot be held, as with a plucked instrument. Controls are via keyboard rows, mouse or touch, or controller buttons. The game shows a notice asking players to perform original work or work they hold rights to.

It was first obtained during the Invitation of Windblume event: the event shop sold it for 280 Festive Tour Tickets once all Ballads of Breeze challenges were completed in Normal Mode. Players who missed the event can buy it from Marjorie, who runs the With Wind Comes Glory souvenir shop in Mondstadt, for 150,000 Mora.

On PC keyboard the three note rows (treble, alto and bass) map to the Q-U, A-J and Z-M keys; with a PlayStation controller the middle row is shown by default and the L1 and R1 buttons switch to the lower or higher rows. The wiki lists the gadget's Chinese name as a phrase meaning a stringed instrument of wind scenery's poetry.

800.content: The Windsong Lyre is a Mondstadt instrument the Traveler can play. In scenes it can be bought from Marjorie's shop in Mondstadt and played like any plucked lyre; characters may praise it as typical of Mondstadt's love of song.

801.content:
Wine and Song (also: Wine & Song): Wine and Song is a four-star catalyst of the Alley series: an elegantly bound songbook from the aristocratic era, scented with daisies and aged wine, whose composer is forgotten. It holds a popular tavern ballad about a heroic gentleman thief.

Appearance: Item text: elegantly bound, with an indelible scent of daisies and finely aged wine on its pages.

Lore: The ballad sings of a drunken gentleman thief (the wiki identifies him as Parsifal), no one knowing where he was from, who appeared in the slums like a ghost. He sings, drinks and wanders the rooftops, steals a great house's sword (the Alley Flash) and carries a black bow (the Alley Hunter), robs the rich and pays the poor.

The maidens dream of him but he prefers a pint with his fellows. One night he ran amok in a mansion and took a thief's due plus an extra silver cup, and seeing a woman with sapphire-blue eyes at a lit window (the wiki links her to the Blue-Eyed Spear Witch) he pried the gem from the cup and gave it to her. When at last they toppled the indolent nobles, the song says, they left to explore distant lands together.

The item closes by saying that in the later age of righteous governance nobody sings of the gentleman thief any more nor needs one. It adds that such a carefree-opening, happy-ending tale is popular, and that however the real story went, wine and songs give the unfortunate courage to stand up to their oppressors. The ballad also jokes that he could drain Cider Lake were it filled with Death After Noon.

Owners: A songbook; no owner is named. It was fashionable in the days of the ruling aristocracy.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Alley-series four-star catalyst, base ATK 44, Energy Recharge 6.7% secondary, passive 'Ever-Changing'. Released in Version 1.4 via Weapon Event Wishes.

802.content:
Winter's Heavy Heart (also: Winters Heavy Heart, Secrets of Frost): Winter's Heavy Heart is a four-star catalyst in the Fae series, added in version 7.1. The in-game description calls it a ceremonial artifact formed from the purest ice and snow, which generations of Snegovik lords used in coronations until the Cataclysm five hundred years ago. Its story is about the first Snegovik, a blood-soaked ruler who did not know what love was, and the youth she trained.

Appearance: Only "a ceremonial artifact formed from the purest ice and snow" is given. The text does not describe its shape beyond that.

Lore: Snegovik are said to have been born with dawn's first gleam from virgin frost. They were more desolate than winter, and only love could mend them. A handmaiden of the Azurelight woke from deathlike sleep still carrying the warmth of her former lord; the Mother of Dawn had lifted her curse so her kind need not be bound to fate. But the golden city (Hyperborea) fell, and its survivors wandered the frozen wastes devouring one another. She resolved that blood must answer blood and that she alone would protect her lord's descendants.

The first of the Snegovik, who had never known love, purged even Snegovik who shared her hatred of mankind and opened her frozen domain, the House of Hesperides, to mortal clans driven from their homes. Yet the frightened people who looked at her showed no love. The Volkodlak king of Cirnareka came to beg a truce for the fae of his kind, and she asked him what love is. He answered that love is fear, and that she kept mortals through fear just as he did, and she killed him.

Long afterwards a young man lost in the snow reached her realm with a company of exiles; she recognised his lineage and took him as her pupil. When she asked what he thought love was, he replied that it is bearing each other's burdens and granting forgiveness, as she had taught, and she struck the stone by his feet with a silver flash as he spoke. He then left to begin the journey remembered in songs and stories. Once the noise she had tired of faded, her longing faded too; her Lady and Mother had freed her from her bond to destiny but she had found no other tie to the world. For the first time she felt a fear deeper than any before, that without bloodshed even she would forget the dream her mother had cherished, so she believed slaughter must continue.

Owners: No wielder is named. The short description says the Snegovik lords used it in coronation ceremonies until the Cataclysm, five hundred years ago.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star catalyst, Fae series, from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 42, secondary stat CRIT DMG 12%. Passive "Secrets of Frost": the wielder gains Elemental Mastery for each Cryo party member and ATK for each Electro party member (up to four each). In a Stellar Glimmer Radiance state the effect changes to Elemental Mastery and Stellar Glimmer reaction DMG per Cryo or Electro member.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a Snezhnayan fae scholar might cite it as a Snegovik regalia. The story fits scenes about cruelty born of grief and fear, and a teacher who asks what love is.

803.comment: Winter's Heavy Heart: The first Snegovik
803.content:
In this item's story the first of the Snegovik is a scarlet ruler called the Knyazhna of Blood and, in the text, the blood-soaked Snegurochka and "mad queen", formerly the Azurelight's handmaiden. Freed from her curse by the Mother of Dawn, she purges the fae who hate mankind and shelters mortal clans in her frozen domain, yet cannot find love in their eyes.

She fears that without bloodshed she will forget her mother's dream, as a soul with no bond to the world dissolves like fading snow.

804.comment: Winter's Heavy Heart: The Volkodlak king's truce
804.content: The king of the Volkodlak, who ruled the shadowed forest depths, came to beg a truce for his fae and offered tribute. She asked him what love is; he answered that it is fear, which mortals and fae use to bind each other, and that there is no reason for them to be enemies. He did not finish before she killed him.

805.comment: Winter's Heavy Heart: The pupil's answer
805.content: The youth she accepted as pupil answers that love is carrying one another's burdens and granting forgiveness, and that a kingdom of love leaves no one to suffer alone. He then departs for the journey that songs remember. The wiki ties him to the Belyi Tsar; the item text names no one.

806.content:
Witch's Revelation Case (also: Witch's Revelation Case gadget, Barbeloth's case): The Witch's Revelation Case is a gadget the Traveler receives from the seer-witch Barbeloth in Fontaine. It is the key to the Witch's Revelation system: with it, the Traveler can view and accept revelation quests that unlock extra talent effects for certain characters.

Barbeloth carried it herself, and it is said to hold every oracle, whether revealed or not yet awake. It arrives at the end of the world quest Revelations by Chance.

Appearance: Canon gives no physical description of the case beyond calling it a case that Barbeloth once carried. It is a five-star gadget kept in the inventory rather than placed in the world.

Lore: Outside the city of Fontaine the Traveler and Paimon find a fortune-telling booth with a Dodoco in the chair. It is a stand-in through which Barbeloth, a witch of the Hexenzirkel, speaks, joined by her friend Alice. Barbeloth explains that as a Descender the Traveler's fate is not anchored in Teyvat, so most fortune tellers, herself included, cannot read it. She has glimpsed the faces of people tied to an omen, and she wants the Traveler's help gathering them.

Alice wants to throw a party for everyone involved and asks the Traveler to bring their friends to the stall. Barbeloth objects to sending invitations herself, since that would disturb the course of fate, but allows that the Traveler already shares ties with these people, so inviting them should have little effect on her divination. Barbeloth says she is still doing research and has only left a Dodoco here, with a reminder set to tell her when the right person arrives. The case comes to the Traveler as the quest reward.

The item description gives Barbeloth's voice. She says the true colours of fate are not meant to be revealed lightly, and that a future with secrets yet to unfold is more delightful. This matches her manner in the quest, where she is amused and withholding rather than forthcoming. Barbeloth is a member of the Hexenzirkel and a teacher of Mona; her title in the wiki profile is Seer-Witch.

The wiki's system page records the promotional line that the witch began a new reading as the warp and weft of fate emerged through an ancient card spread, and ties each revelation to a Lunar Arcanum card (for example Wriothesley with The Emperor, Upright, and Beidou with Strength, Upright). The system was announced together with a new elemental reaction, Stellar-Conduct, in Version 6.7; this archive covers that reaction under its own entry.

Owners: Barbeloth carried it before the Traveler. Alice helps her with the divination in the quest, but canon does not call the case hers.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not in-world fact). The Traveler gets the case, along with Primogems, Hero's Wit and Mora, on completing Revelations by Chance; this opens the Witch's Revelation system. Each Witch's Revelation quest belongs to one character. The character must be owned and at level 70 or higher. Completing the quest unlocks an additional talent and enhances some of the character's other talents and constellations.

Eligible characters on the wiki at the time of access are Wriothesley, Yae Miko, Cyno, Yumemizuki Mizuki, Qiqi, Diona and Beidou. Their passives let them enter a Radiance state under certain conditions.

807.comment: Witch's Revelation Case: Revelations by Chance
807.content: A Fontaine world quest, starting outside the Court of Fontaine, that follows Song of the Dragon and Freedom. Barbeloth and Alice, speaking through a Dodoco at a fortune-telling booth, ask the Traveler to bring friends tied to Barbeloth's omen. It rewards the Witch's Revelation Case and unlocks the Witch's Revelation system.

808.content:
Wolf-Fang (also: Wolf Fang): Wolf-Fang is a 4-star sword from the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn of Version 4.0, in-game described as a longsword once used by a wandering knight. Its text explains how the nameless first Knight of Boreas became a legend in early Mondstadt. Released 2023-08-16.

The text separates the story told in the streets from what likely happened, and notes Mondstadt's two famous knightly titles: the Lion, from the first Grand Master, and the Wolf Knight, Boreas.

Appearance: Canon gives no appearance for the sword. The knight in the text wore a dust-stained, tattered cloak over exquisitely crafted but battle-worn armor and paid in real gold and silver coins with unfamiliar symbols.

Lore: Mondstadt's knights have, "by coincidence or fate," two distinguished titles and animal insignia: the Lion of the first Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius, and the Wolf Knight, Boreas, from almost the same period. In truth, the text says, there is no record at all of the Knight of Boreas; the name comes from stories circulating in the streets.

In the tale, a merchant or farmer whose daughter was saved asks the knight how to thank him; the knight says to toast his companion instead, "Boreas." A gust blows, bestial eyes shine in the dark, and the knight is gone. The daughter is always saved and the knight always nameless.

Before the story the knight was a strange traveler in a dusty cloak. The tavern owner noticed he paid in real silver and gold and was not rowdy. The tale grew from a snake demon from beyond the sea; the knight left the city to hunt demons for a single silver coin, and the carrion on the beach drew thousands of falcons, which, the text says, gave Falcon Coast its real name rather than the legend of the Falcon of the West.

The Knights of Favonius tried repeatedly to recruit him and he refused. The text guesses that the two famous lines of the story were spoken when the first Grand Master, out of patience after countless refusals, had the knight surrounded in the street, and that the real exchange was far less civil. Talented bards merged that dialogue with other events into many stories; he stayed only a few years, but his shadow remains.

Owners: Owner: the Wandering Knight, the first Knight of Boreas. The wiki cites this weapon and Wolf's Gravestone as evidence that he lived in Mondstadt during Vennessa's rebellion about a thousand years ago.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 4-star sword with base ATK 42 and a CRIT Rate secondary stat. Its passive, Northwind Wolf, raises Elemental Skill and Burst damage; skill and burst hits each add CRIT Rate for 10s (separately, up to four stacks). The wiki notes the CRIT bonus works only while the wielder is on the field. Obtained from the Battle Pass BP Bounty.

809.content: Wolf-Fang's text treats "Boreas" as a street legend. The first Knight of Boreas lived in Mondstadt only a few years, declined to join the Knights of Favonius, and was recorded nowhere; the stories grew from a demon hunt and a quarrel with the early Grand Master. Boreas himself is the Wolf of the North, whom the knight called his companion.

810.content:
Wolf's Gravestone (also: Wolfs Gravestone): Wolf's Gravestone is a 5-star claymore and, per the wiki, the sword of the first Knight of Boreas, also called the Wandering Knight. Its text tells of a knight and the wolf Boreas who shared one spirit: when the wolf died the knight set the sword over its grave, left Mondstadt and lived as a lone wanderer. Added in Version 1.0.

Item text calls the sword a "longsword" and "a heavy sheet of iron" that became legendary through the knight's friendship with the wolves; in game it is a claymore.

Appearance: Canon text describes it only as a heavy sheet of iron that a blacksmith from the city gave the knight. Its silhouette appears at the start location of the Wolf of the North Challenge.

Lore: The Knight of Boreas's journey ended at the city of Barbatos. As he entered it, his wolf companion said farewell without a sound, since the free-spirited wolf disliked stone walls and lamplight and longed for the wilds.

While the Knight's body was in the city his heart stayed free, and the windborne wolf, roaming the forest, stayed loyal to him. When the Knight rode out to hunt again, the wolf followed his scent into battle; the text calls them one. But death comes sooner to beasts than men.

The Knight buried the wolf in the remote countryside (Wolvendom, per the wiki link), laying his sword down as its gravestone, and left the city for the life of a lone wolf. The wolf's eternal spirit stayed behind, watching over the land the Knight once protected.

Story context from other canon: the wiki identifies the Knight as the first Knight of Boreas, who lived during Vennessa's rebellion about a thousand years ago and refused the Knights of Favonius's attempts to recruit him; Ravenwood was later approved by Boreas as the next Knight of Boreas. The wolf "Boreas" is the Wolf of the North, known as Andrius, whose spirit watches over Wolvendom. The Wolf-Fang item text calls Boreas the Knight's companion.

Owners: Owner: the Wandering Knight, the first Knight of Boreas (per the wiki, from the Lonely Warrior quest and the weapon texts). The wiki notes that Diluc is shown with the ascended claymore in his Red Dead of Night outfit art and that Varka holds it in the Song of the Welkin Moon teaser; these are promotional appearances, not statements that either owns the relic.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 5-star claymore with base ATK 46 and an ATK% secondary stat. Its passive, Wolfish Tracker, raises ATK, and hitting an opponent under 30% HP gives all party members an ATK bonus for 12s (once per 30s). It is on the Standard Wish and weapon event Wishes.

811.content: The Knight of Boreas is the title of the Knights of Favonius' wolf-bonded warrior. The first holder, the unnamed Wandering Knight, wielded Wolf's Gravestone and left Mondstadt after his wolf companion died; the title was carried on by others, with Ravenwood next. Wolf-Fang's text says no record of the first knight survives and that his name comes only from street stories.

812.content:
Xiphos' Moonlight (also: Xiphos Moonlight): Xiphos' Moonlight is a 4-star sword: an ancient double-edged blade that glimmers with moonlight, said to hold a now-silent Jinni. Its story is that of Xiphos, a warrior of Tulaytullah, and the exiled wanderer who killed him.

It belongs to the Tulaytullah series and was released in Version 3.1 through weapon event Wishes. The Jinni whispered to its master in the story; the passive name Jinni's Whisper refers to it.

Appearance: A double-edged sword whose blade glimmers with moonlight, said to be sharpened rather than dulled by slaughter and brightened by blood, in the story's words.

Lore: Thousands of years ago, after the foolish God-King was buried by sandstorms, mortal cities dotted the land. The most outstanding was Tulaytullah, where men and women of wisdom gathered, with sapphire-domed buildings and emerald gardens of blooming trees and fountains. A warrior named Xiphos lived there, adept with his double-edged sword.

He saved many maidens from monster attacks and took many treasures in the process. In ancient Tighnarian lore his sword was indwelt by a twisted, cruel Jinni, which is why the blade stayed sharp and bright with blood. The Jinni addresses its master in sinuous verse, offering its affection and promising he will be an unmatched warrior as long as his foes still love the world.

Xiphos later met an exiled foreign wanderer who had accepted silver coins, blood money from kings opposed to Tulaytullah, and so shouldered their grudges. The two, who might have been friends at some bar, fought to the death in moonlight. The pale moon lit the winner and the defeated alike, and a saying notes that the three departed goddesses had determined the heroes' fate long before.

The wanderer took the moonlit sword and the bloodstained silver and walked silently toward the rainforest. Without Xiphos' protection, Tulaytullah lost its luster and withered; its gardens were ground into dirt and the desert gales consigned them to oblivion. The black key and the young prince's quest to rejuvenate his kingdom also sank into the sand.

Owners: In the story the sword belonged to Xiphos and then to the exiled wanderer who killed him. The wiki notes Nilou, Layla and Alhaitham are shown with it in trailers and quest scenes (Alhaitham in his fight with Cyno), which is not ownership.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star sword, level 1 base ATK 42, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 36. Passive Jinni's Whisper: every 10 s the wielder gains Energy Recharge for each point of Elemental Mastery for 12 s, with nearby party members gaining 30% of it; it works off-field and stacks across copies.

The bonus is 0.036% Energy Recharge per point of Elemental Mastery at refinement 1 and 0.072% at refinement 5.

How {{char}} behaves: Treat the Jinni as a silent, possibly malign presence in a legend; do not give it speech beyond the story's quoted lines.

813.content: Jinni's Whisper is the weapon passive of Xiphos' Moonlight (gameplay): Energy Recharge based on Elemental Mastery, shared in part with nearby party members.

814.content:
Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti (also: The Guardian Adepti, Yakshas, The Guardian Adepti): Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti is a single book from the folklore series Hidden Wonders and Folklore of Liyue, Liyue's answer to the Sumeru scholar Masudi's encyclopedia Tour of the Land of Liyue. It was largely dismissed by publishers and readers for its archaic style. It tells how Rex Lapis summoned yakshas to purge daemons, how the five strongest were afflicted, and how only Alatus survived. It is given to the player in the story quest Glimmers of the Vigilant Yaksha (Version 1.3).

The book mixes an old-fashioned classical retelling with a plain-language gloss after each passage, a format that lets a reader see both the mythic voice and the plain meaning.

Appearance: Paragraphs in an archaic, solemn style alternate with plain-language paraphrases in quotation marks. This makes the book a short folklore treatise rather than a story.

Lore: In ancient Liyue plagues and monsters arose from the bitterness of defeated gods, called daemons. Rex Lapis summoned yakshas, ferocious illuminated beasts, to purge them. Five were strongest: Bosacius, Indarias, Bonanus, Menogias and Alatus. Over about a thousand years the yakshas were poisoned by the lingering divine bitterness; three of the five died, one vanished, and only Alatus survived, remembered as the Golden-Winged King and Conqueror of Demons.

- The author's account: warring gods left the defeated crushed under rock, where they returned to the cycle of elements, but some held their hatred and re-emerged as daemons whose rage produced plague, miasma and monsters. The line "the daemonic is the shadow of the divine" is the book's key phrase.
- The yakshas are described as fierce, violent illuminated beasts who followed Rex Lapis in battle and spared no brutality in defending his rule, until the evil was wiped out at its source.
- Their downfall: some sank into blind rage or fear-driven madness, some turned on and killed one another, and others were lost to delusions. After a thousand years, three of the five were slain, one disappeared, and many lesser yakshas died or fled.
- Of Alatus, nobody knows where he came from or went. During the Lantern Rite people watch for a glow above Guyun Stone Forest and say the Vigilant Yaksha ends the dominion of daemons, and some hear a flute from Dihua Marsh and say the yaksha calls his old friends home.
- The closing paragraph says the price of supernatural power is hardship and eventual destruction: the yaksha lost all companions and incurred a karmic debt, leaving a heart full of darkness. It compares his torment to that of a preta, never sated across countless lifetimes.

- The book never names which of the five disappeared or fell, but it fits with other quests and with the entries for Bosacius, Indarias, Bonanus and Menogias. Use those entries and the Alatus chapter for specifics.
- The text uses both Alatus' titles, the Golden-Winged King and the Conqueror of Demons, and the folk custom at Lantern Rite that connects him to Guyun Stone Forest.

- The book's final passage speaks of the yaksha in the singular, and a reader who knows Xiao's story will read it as a description of Alatus. The text itself does not say so; the identity is established in Xiao's story quest and character material.
- The book's own framing of the cause is divine bitterness and a karmic debt built up by violence. It is one folklorist's account and not a complete theory of Liyue's monsters.

Owners: No individual owner. It is a quest item obtained during Glimmers of the Vigilant Yaksha, Xiao's story quest.

Gameplay: Game note: a quest item added in Version 1.3; unlike the shelf-book collections, it is received during one quest.

key: Hidden Wonders and Folklore of Liyue
815.comment: Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti: The Five Great Yakshas
815.content: According to Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti, five yakshas were strongest among those who served Rex Lapis: Bosacius, Indarias, Bonanus, Menogias and Alatus. After a thousand years of fighting daemons, three died, one vanished and only Alatus survived. Bosacius, Indarias, Bonanus and Menogias have their own entries.

816.comment: Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti: The Golden-Winged King
816.content: The folk titles of Alatus in the book. Nobody knows where he came from or went, though people see a glow above Guyun Stone Forest during the Lantern Rite and hear a flute at Dihua Marsh, taken as the yaksha ending the dominion of daemons or calling his old friends home.
